'Bring me game and make tasty food for me. I will eat it and bless you in the presence of the LORD before I die.'
Now, my son, listen to me and do what I tell you.
Go to the flock and bring me two good young goats. I will make tasty food from them for your father, the way he loves it.
Then take it to your father so he can eat it and bless you before he dies."
Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Look, my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am a smooth man.
What if my father feels me? He would think I am tricking him, and I would bring a curse on myself instead of a blessing."
His mother said to him, "Let the curse fall on me, my son. Just listen to me. Go and get the goats for me."
So Jacob went and got the goats and brought them to his mother. She made tasty food, just the way his father liked it.
Rebekah took the best clothes of her older son Esau, which she had in the house, and put them on her younger son Jacob.
She put the goatskins on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck.
Then she put the tasty food and the bread she had made into Jacob's hands.
Jacob went to his father and said, "My father." Isaac asked, "Who are you, my son?"
Jacob said to his father, "I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done what you told me. Please get up, sit down, and eat some of my game so you can bless me."
Isaac said to his son, "How did you find it so quickly, my son?" Jacob said, "Because the LORD your God made it happen for me."
Isaac said to Jacob, "Please come close so I can feel you, my son, and know whether you really are my son Esau or not."
Jacob went close to his father Isaac, and Isaac felt him. Isaac said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are Esau's hands."
Isaac did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like his brother Esau's hands, so he blessed him.
Isaac asked, "Are you really my son Esau?" Jacob said, "I am."
Isaac said, "Bring it close to me, and I will eat some of my son's game so I can bless you." Jacob brought it close, and Isaac ate. Jacob also brought him wine, and he drank.
His father Isaac said to him, "Come close now and kiss me, my son."
So Jacob came close and kissed him. Isaac smelled the smell of his clothes and blessed him. He said, "Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.
May God give you the dew of heaven and the richness of the earth, along with plenty of grain and new wine.
May peoples serve you and nations bow down to you. Be master over your brothers, and may your mother's sons bow down to you. Cursed be those who curse you, and blessed be those who bless you."
As soon as Isaac finished blessing Jacob, Jacob had barely left his father Isaac's presence when his brother Esau came in from his hunting.
Esau had also made tasty food and brought it to his father. He said, "Father, please get up and eat some of your son's game so you can bless me."
His father Isaac asked him, "Who are you?" Esau said, "I am your son, your firstborn, Esau."
Isaac trembled violently and said, "Who was it, then, that hunted game and brought it to me? I ate all of it before you came, and I blessed him. Yes, he will be blessed."
When Esau heard his father's words, he cried out with a loud and very bitter cry. He said to his father, "Bless me too, my father!"
Isaac said, "Your brother came and tricked me, and he took your blessing."
Esau said, "Isn't he rightly named Jacob? He has cheated me twice now. He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing." Then he asked, "Haven't you saved a blessing for me?"
Isaac answered Esau, "I have made him your master, and I have given him all his brothers as servants. I have supported him with grain and new wine. What can I do for you now, my son?"
Esau said to his father, "Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, my father!" Then Esau wept loudly.
His father Isaac answered him, "Your home will be away from the rich soil of the earth and away from the dew of heaven above.
You will live by your sword, and you will serve your brother. But when you grow restless, you will throw off his yoke from your neck."
Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing his father had given him. Esau said to himself, "The days of mourning for my father will soon come, and then I will kill my brother Jacob."
Someone told Rebekah what her older son Esau had said. So she sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, "Your brother Esau is comforting himself by planning to kill you.
Now, my son, listen to me. Run away to my brother Laban in Haran.
Stay with him for a little while, until your brother's anger calms down.
When his anger has eased and he forgets what you did to him, I will send for you and bring you back. Why should I lose both of you in one day?"
Rebekah said to Isaac, "I am tired of living because of these Hittite women. If Jacob marries a Hittite woman like them, one of the women of this land, what good is life to me?"
Isaac called Jacob and blessed him. He said, "Do not marry a Canaanite woman.
Go to Paddan Aram, to the house of your mother's father Bethuel. Take a wife there from the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother."
May God Almighty bless you, make you fruitful, and multiply you, so you will become a group of nations.
May He give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and your children after you, so you may own the land where you now live as a foreigner, the land God gave to Abraham."
Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Paddan Aram, to Laban son of Bethuel the Aramean, the brother of Rebekah, Jacob and Esau's mother.
Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Paddan Aram to take a wife from there. When Isaac blessed Jacob, he also told him, "Do not marry a Canaanite woman."
Jacob listened to his father and mother and went to Paddan Aram.
Esau saw that Canaanite women did not please his father Isaac.
So Esau went to Ishmael and married Mahalath, the sister of Nebaioth and daughter of Abraham's son Ishmael, in addition to his other wives.
Jacob left Beersheba and traveled toward Haran.
He came to a certain place and stayed there for the night because the sun had set. He took one of the stones from that place, put it under his head, and lay down there.
He had a dream. In it, a ladder stood on the earth, and its top reached heaven. God's angels were going up and down on it.
The LORD stood above it and said, "I am the LORD, the God of your father Abraham and the God of Isaac. I will give you and your descendants the land you are lying on.
Your descendants will be like the dust of the earth. You will spread out to the west, east, north, and south. All the families of the earth will be blessed through you and your descendants.
I am with you. I will watch over you wherever you go. I will bring you back to this land. I will not leave you until I have done what I promised you."
Jacob woke up from his sleep and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it."
He was afraid and said, "How awesome this place is! This is none other than the house of God. This is the gate of heaven."
Early in the morning Jacob took the stone he had put under his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on top of it.
He named that place Bethel, though the city was first called Luz.
Jacob made a vow. He said, "If God will be with me and watch over me on this journey I am taking, and if He gives me food to eat and clothes to wear,
and if I return safely to my father's house, then the LORD will be my God.
This stone I have set up as a pillar will be God's house, and of everything You give me, I will give You a tenth."
Jacob set out again and traveled to the land of the people of the east.
He looked and saw a well in the field. Three flocks of sheep were lying beside it, because the flocks drank from that well. The stone on the mouth of the well was large.
When all the flocks gathered there, the shepherds rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well, watered the sheep, and put the stone back in its place.
Jacob said to them, "My brothers, where are you from?"
He asked, "Do you know Laban, Nahor's son?"

He said, "Look, the day is still long. It is not time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and go feed them." They answered, "We are from Haran." They said, "We know him." They said, "He is well. Look, his daughter Rachel is coming with the sheep."
They said, "We cannot until all the flocks are gathered and they roll the stone away from the mouth of the well. Then we will water the sheep."
While he was still speaking with them, Rachel came with her father's sheep, because she watched her father's sheep.
When Jacob saw Rachel, his uncle Laban's daughter, and Laban's sheep, Jacob went over, rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well, and watered Laban's sheep.
Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.
Jacob told Rachel that he was her father's relative and Rebekah's son. She ran and told her father.
When Laban heard the news about his nephew Jacob, he ran to meet him. He hugged him and kissed him and brought him to his house. Jacob told Laban everything.
Laban said to him, "Surely you are family." Jacob stayed with him a month.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "Should you work for me for nothing just because you are my relative? Tell me what your wages should be."
Laban had two daughters. The older was Leah, and the younger was Rachel.
Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.
Jacob loved Rachel, so he said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."
Laban said, "It is better that I give her to you than to another man. Stay with me."
So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed like only a few days to him because he loved her.
Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife. My time is up, and I want to be with her as my wife."
Laban gathered all the people of that place and made a feast.
In the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he spent the night with her.
Laban gave his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her servant.
In the morning, Jacob saw that it was Leah. He said to Laban, "What have you done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why have you tricked me?"
Laban said, "That is not how we do it in our place. We do not give the younger daughter before the firstborn."
Laban said, "Finish this week, and we will give you this one too, if you will serve me another seven years."
Jacob did so. He finished the week, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her servant.
Jacob also spent the night with Rachel. He loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served Laban another seven years.
The LORD saw that Leah was unloved, so He made it possible for her to have children, but Rachel could not have children.
Leah became pregnant and had a son. She named him Reuben, because she said, "The LORD has seen my suffering. Surely now my husband will love me."
She became pregnant again and had a son. She said, "The LORD heard that I was unloved, so He has given me this son too." She named him Simeon.
She became pregnant again and had a son. She said, "Now at last my husband will be joined to me, because I have borne him three sons." So she named him Levi.
She became pregnant again and had a son. She said, "This time I will praise the LORD." So she named him Judah. Then she stopped having children.
When Rachel saw that she was not having any children for Jacob, she became jealous of her sister. She said to Jacob, "Give me children, or I will die!"
Jacob became angry with Rachel and said, "Am I in God's place? He is the one who kept you from having children."
Rachel said, "Here is my servant Bilhah. Sleep with her. Then she can have children for me, and I can build a family through her."
So she gave him her servant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah became pregnant and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, "God has judged in my favor. He has heard my voice and given me a son." So she named him Dan.
Rachel's servant Bilhah became pregnant again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, "I have struggled hard with my sister, and I have won." So she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped having children, she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah, Leah's servant, bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, "What good fortune!" So she named him Gad.
Leah's servant Zilpah bore Jacob a second son.
Leah said, "I am so happy! Women will call me happy." So she named him Asher.
During the wheat harvest, Reuben went out and found mandrakes in the field. He brought them to his mother Leah. Rachel said to Leah, "Please give me some of your son's mandrakes."
Leah said, "Isn't it enough that you took my husband? Now you want my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel said, "Then he may sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes."
When Jacob came in from the field that evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must come to me tonight, because I have hired you with my son's mandrakes." So he slept with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she became pregnant and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has rewarded me for giving my servant to my husband." So she named him Issachar.
Leah became pregnant again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, "God has given me a good gift. Now my husband will stay with me, because I have borne him six sons." So she named him Zebulun.
Later she gave birth to a daughter and named her Dinah.
Then God remembered Rachel. He listened to her and opened her womb.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She said, "God has taken away my disgrace."
She named him Joseph and said, "May the LORD add another son to me."
After Rachel gave birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, "Send me on my way so I can go back to my own country.
Give me my wives and children, for whom I have served you, and I will go. You know how hard I have worked for you."
Laban said to him, "If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay. I have learned by divination that the LORD has blessed me because of you."
He added, "Name your wages, and I will pay them."
Jacob replied, "You know how I have served you and how your livestock has thrived under my care.
Indeed, you had little before I came, but now it has grown into a large amount, and the LORD has blessed you wherever I went. But now, when may I also provide for my own household?"
"What shall I give you?" Laban asked. Jacob answered, "You do not need to give me anything. If you will do this one thing for me, I will go back to feeding and watching your flocks."
"Let me go through all your flocks today and remove every speckled or spotted sheep, every dark-colored lamb, and every spotted or speckled goat. These will be my wages."
"In the future, my honesty will speak for me: Whenever you come to check on my wages, any goat that is not speckled or spotted, or any lamb that is not dark-colored, will be considered stolen."
"Good," said Laban. "Let it be as you have said."

That same day Laban removed the streaked and spotted male goats and all the speckled and spotted female goats—every one with white on it—and every dark-colored lamb, and he placed them under the care of his sons.
Then he put a three-day journey between himself and Jacob, while Jacob continued to tend the rest of Laban's flocks.
Jacob, however, took fresh-cut branches of poplar, almond, and plane trees, and peeled the bark, exposing the white inner wood of the branches.
Then he set the peeled branches in the watering troughs in front of the flocks when they came to drink. And since they mated when they came to drink,
the flocks bred in front of the branches and gave birth to young that were streaked, speckled, and spotted.
Then Jacob separated the lambs and made the flocks face the streaked and dark-colored animals in Laban's flocks. He kept his own flocks separate and did not put them with Laban's animals.
Whenever the stronger animals were in heat, Jacob would place the branches in the troughs in front of them, so they would breed near the branches.
But when the animals were weaker, he did not place the branches. So the weaker animals went to Laban, and the stronger ones went to Jacob.
Thus Jacob became very wealthy. He owned large flocks, female servants and male servants, camels, and donkeys.
Jacob heard what Laban's sons were saying: "Jacob has taken everything that belonged to our father, and he has gotten all this wealth from what was our father's."
Jacob also saw that Laban was not as friendly toward him as he had been before.
Then the LORD said to Jacob, "Return to the land of your fathers and to your relatives, and I will be with you."
So Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah and called them to the field where his flock was.
He said to them, "I can see that your father is not as friendly toward me as he was before, but the God of my father has been with me.
You know that I have served your father with all my strength.
Yet your father has cheated me and changed my wages ten times, but God did not let him harm me.
If he said, 'The spotted ones will be your wages,' then all the flock had spotted young. If he said, 'The speckled ones will be your wages,' then all the flock had speckled young.
So God has taken your father's livestock and given them to me. "
At the time the flock were mating, I looked up and saw in a dream that the male goats mating with the flock were striped, speckled, and spotted.
The angel of God said to me in the dream, 'Jacob,' and I said, 'Here I am.'
He said, 'Look up and see that all the male goats mating are striped, speckled, and spotted, for I have seen everything Laban has been doing to you.'
'I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar and where you made a vow to Me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land where you were born.'"
Rachel and Leah answered him, "Is there still any share or inheritance for us in our father's house?
Does he not count us as foreigners? He sold us, and he has used up the money he got for us.
Surely all the wealth God took from our father belongs to us and our children. So do whatever God has told you."
Then Jacob got up and put his sons and wives on camels.
He drove off all his livestock and all his property that he had gained, including the livestock he had acquired in Paddan Aram, to go to the land of Canaan to his father Isaac.
When Laban had gone to shear his sheep, Rachel stole her father's household gods.
Jacob also tricked Laban the Aramean by not telling him that he was running away.
So he fled with everything he had. He set out, crossed the Euphrates River, and headed toward the hill country of Gilead.
On the third day Laban was told that Jacob had fled.
He took his relatives with him and chased Jacob for seven days, catching up with him in the hill country of Gilead.
But God came to Laban the Aramean in a dream at night and said to him, "Be careful not to say anything to Jacob, either good or bad."
Laban caught up with Jacob. Jacob had set up his tent in the hill country, and Laban and his relatives camped in the hill country of Gilead.
Then Laban said to Jacob, "What have you done? You have tricked me and carried off my daughters like captives taken in war.
Why did you run away in secret and trick me? Why didn't you tell me, so I could have sent you off with joy and singing, with tambourines and harps?
You didn't even let me kiss my grandchildren and daughters goodbye. You have acted foolishly. "
I have the power to hurt you, but the God of your father spoke to me last night and said, 'Be careful not to speak to Jacob either good or bad.'
Now you have gone because you longed so much for your father's house. But why did you steal my gods?"
Jacob answered Laban, "I was afraid, because I thought you might take your daughters from me by force.
But if you find your gods, the one who has them will not live. In front of our relatives, point out anything of mine that is yours and take it." Jacob did not know that Rachel had stolen them.
So Laban went into Jacob's tent, Leah's tent, and the tent of the two female servants, but he did not find anything. He came out of Leah's tent and went into Rachel's tent.
Rachel had taken the household gods and put them in the camel's saddle, and she was sitting on them. Laban searched the whole tent but did not find them.
She said to her father, "My lord, don't be angry that I cannot stand up in front of you, because I am having my period." So he searched, but he did not find the household gods.
Then Jacob became angry and argued with Laban. Jacob said to Laban, "What is my crime? What is my sin, that you have chased after me so hotly?
You have searched through all my belongings. What have you found from all your household goods? Put it here in front of my relatives and yours, so they can decide between the two of us." "
These twenty years I have been with you. Your sheep and goats have not miscarried, and I have not eaten the rams of your flocks.
I did not bring you animals killed by wild animals. I took the loss myself. You demanded payment from me for anything stolen by day or by night.
I suffered in the heat by day and the cold by night, and sleep left my eyes. "
These twenty years I have been in your house. I served you fourteen years for your two daughters and six years for your flock, and you changed my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham, and the Fear of Isaac, had not been on my side, you would have sent me away empty-handed. But God has seen my hardship and the work of my hands, and He rebuked you last night."

Laban answered Jacob, "The daughters are my daughters, the children are my children, the flocks are my flocks, and everything you see is mine. But what can I do today about these daughters of mine or about the children they have had?
Come now, let us make an agreement, you and I, and let it be a witness between you and me."
So Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
Jacob said to his relatives, "Gather stones." So they gathered stones and made a heap, and they ate there by the heap.
Laban called it Jegar Sahadutha, but Jacob called it Galeed.
Laban said, "This heap is a witness between you and me today." Therefore he named it Galeed.
Laban also called it Mizpah, because he said, "May the LORD watch between you and me when we are away from each other.
If you mistreat my daughters or take other wives besides my daughters, even though no one else is with us, see, God is a witness between you and me."
Laban said to Jacob, "Look at this heap and this pillar that I have set up between you and me.
This heap and this pillar are witnesses that I will not cross over to your side of them to harm you, and you will not cross over to my side of them to harm me."
"May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge between us." So Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Then Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat bread. They ate and spent the night on the mountain.
Early in the morning Laban got up, kissed his sons and daughters, and blessed them. Then Laban left and went back home.
Jacob went on his way, and God's angels met him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, "This is God's camp." So he called that place Mahanaim.
Jacob sent messengers ahead to his brother Esau in the land of Seir, the country of Edom.
He told them, "Say to my lord Esau, 'I, your servant Jacob, have been staying with Laban until now.
I have oxen, donkeys, sheep, and male and female servants. I am sending this message to find favor with you.'"
The messengers came back to Jacob and said, "We went to your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you with four hundred men."
Jacob was very afraid and upset. He divided the people who were with him into two groups, along with the flocks, herds, and camels.
He said, "If Esau comes to one group and attacks it, the other group may escape."
Then Jacob said, "O God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, O the LORD, who said to me, 'Go back to your country and your relatives, and I will make things go well for you,'
I am not worthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. I crossed this Jordan with only my staff, and now I have become two camps.
Please save me from my brother, from Esau. I am afraid he will come and attack me, along with the mothers and their children.
But You have said, 'I will surely make things go well for you and make your descendants like the sand of the sea, too many to count.'"
That night Jacob stayed there. From what he had with him, he took a gift for his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty female camels with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty female donkeys and ten male donkeys.
He put them into the hands of his servants, each herd by itself. He told his servants, "Go ahead of me and keep some space between each herd."
He told the first servant, "When my brother Esau meets you and asks, 'Who do you belong to? Where are you going? And whose are these animals in front of you?'
say, 'They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift sent to my lord Esau. And he is coming behind us.'"
He also told the second, third, and all the others who followed the herds, "Say the same thing to Esau when you meet him.
Say, 'your servant Jacob is coming behind us.'" He thought, "I will calm his anger with the gift that goes ahead of me. After that, I will see his face. Maybe he will accept me."
So the gift went ahead of him, while he stayed that night in the camp.
During the night Jacob got up. He took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them and sent them across the stream, and he sent over everything he had.
Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until daybreak.
When the man saw that he could not overpower Jacob, he touched the socket of Jacob's hip. So Jacob's hip was put out of joint as he wrestled with him.
Then the man said, "Let me go, for the dawn is breaking." But Jacob said, "I will not let You go unless You bless me."
The man asked him, "What is your name?" "Jacob," he answered.
Then the man said, "your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men and have overcome."
Jacob said, "Please tell me Your name." But he replied, "Why do you ask my name?" Then he blessed him there.
So Jacob called the place Peniel, saying, "I have seen God face to face, and my life was spared."
The sun rose as he passed Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip.
That is why the people of Israel do not eat the tendon of the hip socket to this day, because the man touched the socket of Jacob's hip near the tendon.
Jacob looked up and saw Esau coming toward him with four hundred men. He divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two female servants.
He put the female servants and their children first, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph last.
Then Jacob went ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times as he came near his brother.
But Esau ran to meet him. He hugged Jacob, threw his arms around his neck, kissed him, and they both cried.
Esau looked up and saw the women and children. He asked, "Who are these with you?" Jacob answered, "They are the children God has graciously given your servant."
The female servants and their children came forward and bowed down.
Then Leah and her children came forward and bowed down. After them, Joseph and Rachel came forward and bowed down.
Esau asked, "What do you mean by all this group I met?" Jacob replied, "I sent it so I would find favor in my lord's eyes."
Esau said, "I already have plenty, my brother. Keep what you have."
Jacob said, "No, please. If I have found favor in your eyes, then accept this gift from my hand. I have seen your face, and it was like seeing the face of God, and you were pleased with me."
Jacob said, "Please take the blessing I brought you, because God has been gracious to me, and I have everything I need." Jacob urged him until Esau took it.
Esau said, "Let us travel on together. I will go ahead of you."
Jacob said, "My lord knows the children are weak, and the flocks and herds have young with them. If they are driven hard for one day, all the animals will die."
Jacob said, "Please let my lord go ahead of your servant. I will travel slowly, at the pace of the animals ahead of me and at the pace of the children, until I reach my lord at Seir."
Esau said, "Then let me leave some of my men with you." Jacob replied, "Why do that? Just let me find favor in my lord's eyes."
So that day Esau started back to Seir.
Jacob traveled to Succoth. He built a house for himself and made shelters for his animals. That is why the place was called Succoth.
When Jacob came from Paddan Aram, he arrived safely at the city of Shechem in the land of Canaan. He camped near the city.
He bought the piece of land where he had pitched his tent from the sons of Hamor, Shechem's father, for one hundred pieces of silver.
There he set up an altar and named it "God, the God of Israel."
Dinah was Leah’s daughter, whom she had borne to Jacob. Dinah went out to see the young women of the land.
Shechem, son of Hamor the Hivite and ruler of that area, saw her. He took her, lay with her, and forced her.
But he felt deeply attached to Dinah, Jacob’s daughter. He loved the young woman and spoke kindly to her.
Shechem said to his father Hamor, “Get this young woman for me as a wife.”
Jacob heard that Shechem had defiled his daughter Dinah. His sons were out in the fields with the livestock, so Jacob said nothing until they came home.
Hamor, Shechem’s father, went to Jacob to talk with him.

Jacob’s sons came in from the fields when they heard what happened. They were deeply hurt and very angry, because Shechem had done a shameful thing in Israel by sleeping with Jacob’s daughter. That should never be done.
Hamor spoke with them and said, “My son Shechem longs for your daughter. Please give her to him as a wife.
Marry into our families. Give your daughters to us, and take our daughters for yourselves.
You can live with us. The land is open before you. Live here, trade here, and buy property here.
Shechem said to Dinah’s father and brothers, “Let me find favor in your eyes. I’ll give whatever you ask.
Set the bride price and gift as high as you want; I’ll pay it. Just give me the young woman as a wife.”
Jacob’s sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, because Shechem had defiled Dinah their sister.
They said to them, “We can’t do this. We can’t give our sister to a man who isn’t circumcised, because that would bring shame on us.
We will agree only if you become like us by having every male among you circumcised.
Then we’ll give our daughters to you, and we’ll take your daughters for ourselves. We’ll live with you and become one people.
But if you won’t listen to us and be circumcised, then we’ll take our daughter and leave.”
Hamor and Shechem, son of Hamor, were pleased with their words.
The young man didn’t delay doing this, because he delighted in Jacob’s daughter. He was the most honored man in his father’s house.
Hamor and Shechem went to the gate of their city and spoke to the men there. They said, “
These men are peaceful toward us. Let them live in the land and trade in it. The land is wide enough for them. We can take their daughters as wives and give them our daughters.
But they will agree to live with us and become one people only on this condition: every male among us must be circumcised, just as they are.
Won’t their livestock, property, and all their animals become ours? So let’s agree with them, and they’ll live with us.”
All the men who went out through the city gate listened to Hamor and Shechem. Every male was circumcised.
On the third day, when the men were still sore, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, took their swords. They came into the city boldly and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and Shechem with the sword, took Dinah from Shechem’s house, and left.
Jacob’s other sons came upon the dead bodies and plundered the city because their sister had been defiled.
They took the flocks, herds, donkeys, and everything else in the city and in the fields.
They carried off all the wealth, wives, and children, and plundered everything in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have brought trouble on me by making me hated among the people of this land, the Canaanites and Perizzites. I have only a few men. They may gather against me and attack me, and then I and my household will be destroyed.”
They said, “Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?”
God said to Jacob, "Get up, go up to Bethel, and live there. Make an altar there to the God who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau."
Jacob said to his household and to everyone with him, "Put away the foreign gods among you, make yourselves clean, and change your clothes.
Let's get up and go up to Bethel. I will make an altar there to the God who answered me on the day I was in trouble and stayed with me on the road I traveled."
So they gave Jacob all the foreign gods they had and the earrings in their ears. Jacob buried them under the oak near Shechem.
They traveled on, and God put fear into the cities around them, so no one chased Jacob's sons.
Jacob and all the people with him came to Luz, which is Bethel, in the land of Canaan.
There he built an altar and named the place El Bethel, because God had shown Himself to him there when he fled from his brother Esau.
Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died. She was buried under the oak below Bethel, and Jacob named it Allon Bacuth.
When Jacob came back from Paddan-aram, God appeared to him again and blessed him.
God said to him, "Your name is Jacob. You will not be called Jacob anymore. Your name will be Israel." Then He called him Israel.
God also said, "I am God Almighty. Be fruitful and multiply. A nation and a group of nations will come from you, and kings will come from your descendants.
The land I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you, and I will give it to your descendants after you."
God went up from him in the place where He had spoken to him.
Jacob set up a stone pillar there. He poured a drink offering and oil on it.
Jacob named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
They left Bethel. While they were still a little way from Ephrath, Rachel began to give birth, and she had a hard labor.
When the labor was hardest, the midwife said to her, "Do not be afraid, for this is another son for you."
As Rachel was dying, she named her son Ben-oni, but his father named him Benjamin.
Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrath, that is, Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. It marks Rachel's tomb to this day.
Israel moved on and set up his tent beyond Migdal Eder.
While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went in and slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine. Israel heard about it. Jacob now had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
The sons of Bilhah, Rachel's servant: Dan and Naphtali.
The sons of Zilpah, Leah's servant: Gad and Asher. These were the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Paddan-aram.
Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, near Kiriath Arba (that is, Hebron), where Abraham and Isaac had lived.
Isaac took his last breath and died. He was old and had lived a full life. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
These are the descendants of Esau, who is also called Edom.
Esau married women from Canaan: Adah, daughter of Elon the Hittite; Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite;
and Basemath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth.
Adah had Eliphaz for Esau, and Basemath had Reuel.
Oholibamah had Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These sons of Esau were born to him in Canaan.

Esau took his wives, sons, daughters, and all the people in his house. He also took his livestock, all his animals, and everything he had gained in Canaan. Then he moved to a land away from his brother Jacob.
Their belongings were too many for them to stay together. The land where they lived could not hold both of them because of their livestock.
So Esau, who is also called Edom, settled in the hill country of Seir.
This is the family history of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in the hill country of Seir.
These are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, son of Esau’s wife Adah, and Reuel, son of Esau’s wife Basemath.
The sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
Timna was a concubine of Esau’s son Eliphaz, and she gave birth to Amalek for him. These are the sons of Esau’s wife Adah.
The sons of Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Esau’s wife Basemath.
The sons of Esau’s wife Oholibamah, daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon, were Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.
These are the chiefs among Esau’s sons: the chiefs of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Kenaz,
Korah, Gatam, and Amalek. These are the chiefs of Eliphaz in Edom, and they are the sons of Adah.
The chiefs of Esau’s son Reuel were Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the chiefs of Reuel in Edom, and they are the sons of Esau’s wife Basemath.
The chiefs of Esau’s wife Oholibamah were Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the chiefs of Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
These are the sons of Esau, that is, Edom, and these are their chiefs.
These are the sons of Seir the Horite, who lived in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, the sons of Seir in Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Timna was Lotan’s sister.
The sons of Shobal were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam.
The sons of Zibeon were Aiah and Anah. This is the Anah who found hot springs in the wilderness while he was grazing his father Zibeon’s donkeys.
The sons of Anah were Dishon and Oholibamah, daughter of Anah.
The sons of Dishon were Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan.
The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, by their chiefs, in the land of Seir.
These are the kings who ruled in Edom before any king ruled over the Israelites:
Bela son of Beor ruled in Edom. His city was called Dinhabah.
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah from Bozrah ruled in his place.
When Jobab died, Husham from the land of the Temanites ruled in his place.
When Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad ruled in his place. He had defeated Midian in the field of Moab. His city was called Avith.
When Hadad died, Samlah from Masrekah ruled in his place.
When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth on the River ruled in his place.
When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor ruled in his place.
When Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, Hadar ruled in his place. His city was called Pau. His wife’s name was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, daughter of Mezahab.
These are the names of Esau’s chiefs by their families and places, by their names: Timna, Alvah, Jetheth,
Magdiel, and Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom by the places where they lived in the land they owned. Esau was the father of the Edomites.
Jacob lived in the land where his father had stayed, the land of Canaan.

This is the story of Jacob's family. Joseph was seventeen years old. He tended the flocks with his brothers, the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, his father's wives. He brought their father a bad report about them.
Israel loved Joseph more than all his other sons, because Joseph was the son of his old age. He made Joseph a richly decorated robe.
When his brothers saw that their father loved Joseph more than any of them, they hated him and could not speak kindly to him.
Joseph had a dream and told his brothers about it, and they hated him even more.
He said to them, "Listen to this dream I had.
We were tying up bundles of grain in the field. Suddenly my bundle stood up straight, and your bundles gathered around and bowed down to it."
His brothers said, "Do you really think you will be king over us? Will you rule over us?" So they hated him even more because of his dreams and what he said.
Then Joseph had another dream and told it to his brothers. He said, "Listen, I had another dream. The sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me."
He also told his father and brothers. His father scolded him, "What is this dream you had? Will your mother and I and your brothers actually come and bow to the ground before you?"
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept the matter in mind.
His brothers had gone to graze their father's flocks near Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, "Aren't your brothers tending sheep at Shechem? Come, I am going to send you to them." "Here I am," Joseph replied.
Israel said, "Go and see if your brothers and the flocks are well. Then bring me word." So Israel sent him from the Valley of Hebron, and Joseph arrived at Shechem.
A man found Joseph wandering in the field and asked, "What are you looking for?"
Joseph said, "I am looking for my brothers. Can you tell me where they are grazing their flocks?"
The man said, "They have moved on from here. I heard them say they were going to Dothan." So Joseph went after his brothers and found them at Dothan.
When they saw him from a distance, before he reached them, they plotted to kill him.
They said to one another, "Here comes that dreamer! Come on, let's kill him and throw him into one of the pits.
We'll say a wild animal ate him. Then we'll see what becomes of his dreams."
When Reuben heard this, he tried to save Joseph. He said, "Let's not kill him. Don't shed blood. Throw him into this pit in the wilderness, but don't lay a hand on him."
Reuben said this to rescue Joseph and take him back to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his robe, the ornate robe he was wearing.
They took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.
Then they sat down to eat. Looking up, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were carrying spices, balm, and myrrh, and they were on their way to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, "What do we gain by killing our brother and hiding his blood?
Come, let's sell him to the Ishmaelites. Let's not hurt him ourselves, because he is our brother, our own flesh and blood." His brothers agreed.
When some Midianite traders passed by, they pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites for twenty shekels of silver. The Ishmaelites took Joseph to Egypt.
When Reuben returned to the pit and saw that Joseph was not there, he tore his clothes.
He went back to his brothers and said, "The boy is gone! What am I going to do?"
Then they took Joseph's robe, slaughtered a goat, and dipped the robe in the blood.
They sent the ornate robe to their father and said, "We found this. Look at it. Is this your son's robe or not?"
Jacob recognized it and said, "It is my son's robe! A wild animal has surely torn him apart. Joseph has been torn to pieces."
Jacob tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourned for his son for many days.
All his sons and daughters came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, "No, I will go down to the grave mourning for my son." So Jacob wept for him.
Meanwhile, the Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an official of Pharaoh and captain of the guard.
At that time, Judah left his brothers and went down to stay with a man named Hirah from Adullam.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He married her and slept with her.
She became pregnant and gave birth to a son, and he named him Er.
She conceived again and gave birth to a son and named him Onan.
She gave birth to another son and named him Shelah. She had him at Kezib.
Judah got a wife for Er, his firstborn. Her name was Tamar.
But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the LORD's eyes. So the LORD put him to death.
Then Judah said to Onan, "Sleep with your brother's wife and do your duty as a brother-in-law to her. Raise up children for your brother."
But Onan knew the child would not be his. So whenever he slept with his brother's wife, he spilled his seed on the ground so he would not father children for his brother.
What he did was wicked in the LORD's eyes, so the LORD put him to death too.

Judah said to his daughter-in-law Tamar, "Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up." He thought, "He might die too, like his brothers." So Tamar went to live in her father's house.
After a long time, Judah's wife, the daughter of Shua, died. When Judah had finished mourning, he went up to Timnah with his friend Hirah the Adullamite to see the men who were shearing his sheep.
Someone told Tamar, "Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep."

She took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil, and sat at the entrance to Enaim, which is on the road to Timnah. She did this because she saw that Shelah had grown up, but she had not been given to him as a wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute because she had covered her face.
He turned to her by the road and said, "Come now, let me sleep with you." He did not know she was his daughter-in-law. She asked, "What will you give me to sleep with you?"
"I'll send you a young goat from my flock," he said. "Will you give me something as a pledge until you send it?" she asked.
He said, "What pledge should I give you?" "Your seal and its cord, and the staff in your hand," she answered. So he gave them to her and slept with her, and she became pregnant by him.
After she left, she took off her veil and put on her widow's clothes again.
Meanwhile Judah sent the young goat by his friend the Adullamite to get his pledge back from the woman, but he did not find her.
He asked the men where she was and said, "Where is the shrine prostitute who was beside the road at Enaim?" "There hasn't been any shrine prostitute here," they said.
So he went back to Judah and said, "I didn't find her. Besides, the men who live there said, 'There hasn't been any shrine prostitute here.'"
Then Judah said, "Let her keep them, or people will make fun of us. After all, I did send her this goat, but you couldn't find her."
About three months later Judah was told, "Your daughter-in-law Tamar is guilty of prostitution, and as a result she is now pregnant." Judah said, "Bring her out and have her burned to death!"
As she was being brought out, she sent a message to her father-in-law. "I am pregnant by the man who owns these," she said. "Please look at these and see whose seal and cord and staff these are."
Judah recognized them and said, "She is more in the right than I am, since I wouldn't give her to my son Shelah." And he did not sleep with her again.
When the time came for her to give birth, there were twin boys in her womb.
As she was giving birth, one of them put out his hand; so the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it on his wrist and said, "This one came out first."
But when he drew his hand back, his brother came out, and she said, "So this is how you have broken out!" And he was named Perez.
Then his brother, who had the scarlet thread on his wrist, came out. And he was named Zerah.
Now Joseph had been taken down to Egypt. Potiphar, an Egyptian officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had taken him there.
The LORD was with Joseph, so he prospered, and he stayed in the house of his Egyptian master.
His master saw that the LORD was with him and that the LORD made everything he did succeed.
So Joseph found favor in his eyes and served him. He put Joseph in charge of his household and gave him authority over all that he owned.

From the time he put Joseph in charge of his house and all he had, the LORD blessed the Egyptian's house because of Joseph. The LORD's blessing was on all the Egyptian had, both in the house and in the field.
So he left all he owned in Joseph's care. He didn't know what he had except the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.
After these things, his master's wife looked at Joseph with desire and said, "Lie with me."
But he refused. He said to his master's wife, "Look, my master doesn't know what is in the house with me. He has put everything he owns in my hands.
No one in this house is greater than I am, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How could I do this great wickedness and sin against God?"
She spoke to Joseph day after day, but he wouldn't listen to her to lie beside her or be with her.
One day, he went into the house to do his work, and none of the household servants were there.
She grabbed him by his garment and said, "Lie with me." But he left his garment in her hand and ran out of the house.
When she saw that he had left his garment in her hand and run outside,
she called to the men of her household and said, "Look! He brought us a Hebrew man to make fun of us. He came in to lie with me, and I cried out loudly.
When he heard me raise my voice and cry out, he left his garment beside me and ran outside."
She kept his garment beside her until his master came home.
Then she spoke to him, saying, "The Hebrew servant you brought us came in to me to make fun of me.
But when I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garment beside me and ran outside."
When his master heard the words his wife spoke to him, saying, "This is what your servant did to me," his anger burned.
Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were bound. He stayed there in prison.
But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him kindness. He gave him favor in the eyes of the prison warden.
The prison warden put all the prisoners under Joseph's charge. Whatever needed to be done there, Joseph was in charge of doing it.
The prison warden didn't worry about anything under Joseph's hand, because the LORD was with him, and the LORD made whatever he did succeed.
After these things, Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker wronged their master, the king of Egypt.
Pharaoh was angry with his two officers, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
He put them in prison in the house of the captain of the guard, in the same prison where Joseph was held.
The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of them, and Joseph served them. They stayed in prison for a while.
Both of them, the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were confined in the prison, had a dream the same night. Each man had his own dream, and each dream had its own meaning.
When Joseph came to them in the morning, he saw that they were upset.
He asked Pharaoh's officers who were with him in custody in his master's house, "Why do your faces look so sad today?"
They said, "We have had a dream, and there is no one to interpret it." Joseph said, "Don't interpretations come from God? Please tell them to me."
Then the chief cupbearer told his dream to Joseph: "In my dream there was a vine before me.
"On the vine were three branches. As soon as it budded, its blossoms came out, and its clusters ripened into grapes.
"Pharaoh's cup was in my hand. I took the grapes and pressed them into Pharaoh's cup, and I placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand."
Joseph said, "This is its meaning: The three branches are three days.
Within three days Pharaoh will restore you to favor and give you back your position. You will put Pharaoh's cup in his hand, as you used to do when you were his cupbearer.
"But when it goes well with you, please remember me and show me kindness. Mention me to Pharaoh, and get me out of this house.
For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and here also I have done nothing to deserve being thrown into this prison."
When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was good, he said to Joseph, "I also had a dream. There were three baskets of bread on my head.
"In the top basket were all kinds of baked goods for Pharaoh, and the birds were eating them out of the basket on my head."
Joseph answered, "This is its meaning: The three baskets are three days.
"Within three days Pharaoh will have you put to death and hang you on a tree. The birds will eat your flesh."
On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he made a feast for all his servants. He brought the chief cupbearer and the chief baker before his servants.
He restored the chief cupbearer to his position, and he placed the cup in Pharaoh's hand.
But he hanged the chief baker, just as Joseph had interpreted to them.
Yet the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph; he forgot him.
After two full years, Pharaoh dreamed that he was standing by the Nile.
Seven cows, sleek and fat, came up out of the Nile and grazed among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows, ugly and thin, came up from the Nile and stood beside the cows on the riverbank.
The ugly, thin cows ate the seven sleek, fat cows. Then Pharaoh woke up.
He fell asleep again and had a second dream. Seven heads of grain, healthy and good, were growing on a single stalk.
After them, seven other heads of grain, thin and scorched by the east wind, sprouted up.
The thin heads of grain swallowed the seven healthy, full heads. Then Pharaoh woke up. It had been a dream.
In the morning his spirit was troubled, so he sent for all the magicians and wise men of Egypt. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could interpret them for him.
Then the chief cupbearer said to Pharaoh, "Today I remember my faults.
Pharaoh was once angry with his servants, and he imprisoned me and the chief baker in the house of the captain of the guard.
Each of us had a dream the same night, and each dream had its own meaning.
A young Hebrew was there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him our dreams, and he interpreted them for us, giving each man the interpretation of his dream.
Things happened exactly as he said: I was restored to my position, and the other man was hanged."
So Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they quickly brought him from the dungeon. When he had shaved and changed his clothes, he came in before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I had a dream, and no one can interpret it. But I have heard it said about you that when you hear a dream you can interpret it."
"I cannot do it," Joseph replied to Pharaoh, "but God will give Pharaoh the answer he needs."
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "In my dream I was standing on the bank of the Nile,
when out of the river came up seven cows, fat and sleek, and they grazed among the reeds.
After them, seven other cows came up—scrawny, very ugly and thin. I had never seen such ugly cows in all the land of Egypt.
The thin, ugly cows ate up the seven fat cows that came up first.
But when they had eaten them, no one could tell that they had done so, because they looked just as ugly as before. Then I woke up.
"In my dream I also saw seven heads of grain, full and good, growing on a single stalk.
After them, seven other heads of grain sprouted—withered, thin and scorched by the east wind.
The thin heads of grain swallowed the seven good heads. I told this to the magicians, but none of them could explain it to me."
Then Joseph said to Pharaoh, "The dreams of Pharaoh are one and the same. God has revealed to Pharaoh what He is about to do.
The seven good cows are seven years, and the seven good heads of grain are seven years; it is one dream.
The seven lean, ugly cows that came up afterward are seven years, and so are the seven worthless heads of grain scorched by the east wind. They are seven years of famine.
It is just as I told Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what He is about to do.
"Seven years of great abundance are coming throughout the land of Egypt,
but seven years of famine will follow them. Then all the abundance in Egypt will be forgotten, and the famine will ruin the land.
The abundance will not be remembered in the land because of the famine that follows it, for it will be very severe.
The reason the dream was given to Pharaoh in two forms is that the matter has been firmly decided by God, and God will do it soon."
"Now then, let Pharaoh look for a smart and wise man and put him in charge of the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh appoint officials over the land to take a fifth of the harvest of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.
"They should collect all the food of these good years that are coming and store up the grain under the authority of Pharaoh, to be kept in the cities for food.
This food should be held in reserve for the country, to be used during the seven years of famine, so that the country may not be destroyed by the famine."
The plan seemed good to Pharaoh and to all his officials.
So Pharaoh asked his officials, "Can we find anyone like this man, one in whom is the spirit of God?"
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Since God has made all this known to you, there is no one so smart and wise as you.
You will be in charge of my palace, and all my people are to submit to your orders. Only with respect to the throne will I be greater than you.
I hereby put you in charge of the whole land of Egypt."
Then Pharaoh took his signet ring from his finger and put it on Joseph's finger. He dressed him in robes of fine linen and put a gold chain around his neck.
He had Joseph ride in a chariot as his second-in-command, and men shouted before him, "Make way!" He put him in charge of the whole land of Egypt.
Then Pharaoh said to Joseph, "I am Pharaoh, but without your word no one will lift a hand or foot in all Egypt."
Pharaoh gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-Paneah and gave him Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, to be his wife. And Joseph went throughout the land of Egypt.
Joseph was thirty years old when he entered the service of Pharaoh king of Egypt. And Joseph went out from Pharaoh's presence and traveled throughout Egypt.
During the seven years of abundance the land produced plentifully.
Joseph collected all the food produced in those seven years in the land of Egypt and stored it in the cities. In each city he put the food grown in the fields around it.
Joseph stored up huge amounts of grain, like the sand of the sea, until he stopped keeping records because there was so much.
Before the years of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph by Asenath daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh and said, "It is because God has made me forget all my trouble and all my father's household."
The second son he named Ephraim and said, "It is because God has made me fruitful in the land of my suffering."
The seven years of abundance in Egypt came to an end,
and the seven years of famine began, just as Joseph had said. There was famine in all the other lands, but in the whole land of Egypt there was bread.
When all Egypt began to feel the hunger, the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. Then Pharaoh told all the Egyptians, "Go to Joseph and do what he tells you."
When the famine had spread over the whole country, Joseph opened the storehouses and sold grain to the Egyptians, for the famine was severe throughout Egypt.
And all the world came to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph, because the famine was severe everywhere.
When Jacob saw that there was grain in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why are you just staring at each other?
I heard there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy some for us, so we can live and not die."
So ten of Joseph's brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph's brother, with them, because he said, "Something bad might happen to him."
The sons of Israel came with the others who were buying grain, because the famine was also in Canaan.
Now Joseph was the ruler of the land, and he sold grain to everyone. When Joseph's brothers arrived, they bowed down to him with their faces to the ground.
Joseph saw his brothers and recognized them, but he acted like a stranger and spoke harshly to them. "Where do you come from?" he asked. They answered, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food."
Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered the dreams he had had about them and said, "You are spies! You came to find weak spots in our land."
"No, my lord," they said. "Your servants came to buy food.
We are all sons of one man. We are honest men; your servants are not spies."
"No," he said. "You came to find weak spots in our land."
They said, "Your servants are twelve brothers, sons of one man in Canaan. The youngest is with our father today, and one is gone."
Joseph said to them, "It is just as I said: you are spies."
Joseph said, "By this you will be tested: by the life of Pharaoh, you will not leave here unless your youngest brother comes here.
Send one of you to get your brother, while the rest are kept in custody, so your words may be tested and we can see if you are telling the truth. If not, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies."
He put them all in custody for three days.
On the third day, Joseph said to them, "Do this and live, for I fear God.
If you are honest men, let one brother be kept in prison while you go and take grain to feed your families.
But bring your youngest brother to me, so your words can be proven true and you will not die." And they did so.
Then they said to one another, "Truly we are guilty because of our brother. We saw his trouble when he begged us, but we would not listen. That is why this trouble has come on us."
Reuben answered, "Didn't I tell you, 'Do not sin against the boy'? But you would not listen. Now we must answer for his blood."
They did not know Joseph understood them, because an interpreter was between them.
He turned away from them and wept. Then he came back and spoke to them. He took Simeon from them and tied him up in front of them.
Joseph gave orders to fill their bags with grain, to return each man's silver to his sack, and to give them food for the journey. They did as he said.
They loaded the grain on their donkeys and left.
At the place where they stopped for the night, one of them opened his sack to feed his donkey and saw his silver at the top of the sack.
He said to his brothers, "My silver has been returned! Here it is in my sack!" They panicked and trembled. They said to one another, "What has God done to us?"
When they reached their father Jacob in Canaan, they told him everything that had happened. They said,
"The man who rules the land spoke harshly to us and treated us like spies.
We said to him, 'We are honest men; we are not spies.
We are twelve brothers, sons of one father. One is gone, and the youngest is with our father in Canaan.'
Then the man who rules the land said, 'By this I will know you are honest: leave one brother with me, take grain for the hunger in your homes, and go.
Bring your youngest brother to me, and then I will know you are not spies but honest men. I will give your brother back to you, and you can trade in the land.'"
As they emptied their sacks, each man found his bundle of silver in his sack. When they and their father saw the silver, they were afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, "You have taken my children from me. Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and now you want to take Benjamin. Everything is against me."
Reuben said to his father, "You can kill my two sons if I do not bring Benjamin back to you. Put him in my care, and I will bring him back to you."

Jacob said, "My son will not go down with you, for his brother is dead and he is the only one left. If something bad happens to him on the journey you are taking, you will send me to my grave in grief."
Now the famine was severe in the land.
When they had eaten all the grain they brought from Egypt, their father said, "Go back and buy us a little more food."
But Judah said to him, "The man warned us firmly, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'
If you send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food for you.
But if you do not send him, we will not go down, because the man said to us, 'You will not see my face unless your brother is with you.'"
Israel said, "Why did you treat me so badly by telling the man you had another brother?"

They said, "The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family. He asked, 'Is your father still alive? Do you have another brother?' We answered him as best we could. How could we know he would say, 'Bring your brother down'?"
Judah said to his father Israel, "Send the boy with me, and we will go at once so that we may live and not die—both we and you and our little ones.
I will be responsible for him. You can hold me accountable. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, then I will be guilty before you all my life.
If we had not delayed, we could have gone and come back twice by now."

Their father Israel said to them, "If it must be, then do this: Take some of the best products of the land in your bags and carry a gift down to the man—a little balm and honey, gum, myrrh, pistachios, and almonds.
Take double the money with you. Carry back the money that was returned in the mouths of your sacks. Maybe it was a mistake.
Take your brother too, and go back to the man at once.
May God Almighty grant you mercy before the man, so that he will let your other brother and Benjamin go with you. As for me, if I am bereaved, I am bereaved."
So the men took the gift, double money, and Benjamin. They hurried down to Egypt and stood before Joseph.
When Joseph saw Benjamin with them, he said to the steward of his house, "Take these men to my house. Slaughter an animal and prepare it, because these men will eat with me at noon."
The man did as Joseph said and brought the men to Joseph's house.

The men were afraid because they were brought to Joseph's house. They said, "We are being brought here because of the money that was returned in our sacks the first time. He wants to attack us, overpower us, and make us slaves, along with our donkeys."
They went up to the steward at the door of the house and spoke to him.
"Please, my lord," they said, "we came down the first time to buy food.
When we reached the lodging place and opened our sacks, each man's money was in the mouth of his sack—the exact amount. So we brought it back with us.
We have also brought more money to buy food. We do not know who put our money in our sacks."
The steward said, "Peace to you. Do not be afraid. Your God and the God of your father has put treasure in your sacks. I received your money." Then he brought Simeon out to them.
The steward took the men into Joseph's house. He gave them water, and they washed their feet. He gave fodder to their donkeys.
They prepared the gift for Joseph's arrival at noon, because they had heard they would eat there.
When Joseph came home, they brought him the gift from their hands and bowed to the ground before him.
He asked about their well-being and said, "Is your old father well, the one you told me about? Is he still alive?"
They said, "Your servant our father is well; he is still alive." Then they bowed down and paid homage.
Joseph looked up and saw his brother Benjamin, his mother's son. He said, "Is this your youngest brother you told me about? God be gracious to you, my son."
Joseph hurried out because he was deeply moved over his brother. He looked for a place to weep and went into his room and wept there.
He washed his face and came out. He controlled himself and said, "Serve the food."
They served him by himself, them by themselves, and the Egyptians who ate with him by themselves, because Egyptians could not eat with Hebrews. It was disgusting to Egyptians.
They sat before him in order of age, from oldest to youngest, and the men stared at one another in wonder.
He sent portions to them from his table, but Benjamin's portion was five times as much as any of theirs. They drank and were merry with him.
Joseph told the man who ran his house, "Fill the men's sacks with as much food as they can carry. Put each man's silver in the mouth of his sack.
Put my silver cup in the mouth of the youngest brother's sack, along with the silver for his grain." The servant did exactly what Joseph said.
At dawn, the men were sent away with their donkeys.
They had not gone far from the city when Joseph said to his house manager, "Get up and chase the men. When you catch them, say to them, 'Why have you paid back good with evil?
Isn't this the cup my master drinks from and uses to tell the future? You have done wrong.'"
The manager caught up with them and said these words to them.
They said to him, "Why does my lord say such things? Your servants would never do anything like that!
Look, we brought back the silver we found in our sacks from Canaan. How could we steal silver or gold from your lord's house?
If any of your servants is found with it, he will die, and the rest of us will become my lord's slaves."
He said, "Very well, as you say. The one who has it will be my slave, but the rest of you are innocent."
Each man quickly lowered his sack to the ground and opened it.
The steward searched, beginning with the oldest and ending with the youngest. The cup was found in Benjamin's sack.
They tore their clothes. Each man loaded his donkey, and they went back to the city.
Judah and his brothers came to Joseph's house. He was still there, and they fell to the ground before him.
Joseph said to them, "What is this you have done? Don't you know that a man like me can find things out?"
Judah said, "What can we say to my lord? What can we speak? How can we prove we are innocent? God has found out our guilt. Here we are, my lord's slaves, both we and the one who had the cup."
Joseph said, "Far be it from me to do that! The man who had the cup will be my slave. The rest of you go up in peace to your father."
Then Judah went up to him and said, "Please, my lord, let your servant speak a word in my lord's ears. Do not let your anger burn against your servant, for you are like Pharaoh.
My lord asked his servants, 'Do you have a father or a brother?'
"We said to my lord, 'We have an old father, and a young brother born in his old age. His brother is dead, and he is the only son left of his mother. His father loves him.'
You said to your servants, 'Bring him down to me so I can see him.'
We said to my lord, 'The boy cannot leave his father. If he leaves, his father will die.'
But you said to your servants, 'Unless your youngest brother comes with you, you will not see my face again.'
"When we went back to your servant my father, we told him what my lord said.
Our father said, 'Go back and buy us a little food.'
We said, 'We cannot go down unless our youngest brother is with us. We cannot see the man's face unless our youngest brother is with us.'
Your servant our father said to us, 'You know that my wife had two sons for me.
One left me, and I said, "He must have been torn apart," and I have not seen him since.
If you take this one from me too, and harm comes to him, you will send me to my grave in sorrow.'
"Now if I go back to your servant my father without the boy, and his life is bound up with the boy's life,
he will die when he sees the boy is gone. Your servants will send him to his grave in sorrow.
Your servant promised my father, 'If I do not bring him back to you, I will bear the blame before my father all my life.'
Now let your servant stay here as my lord's slave instead of the boy. Let the boy go back with his brothers.
How can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? I cannot bear to see the trouble that would come to my father."

Joseph could not hold back his feelings in front of everyone who was standing near him. He called out, "Send everyone out of the room!" So no one else stayed with Joseph when he told his brothers who he was.
He cried so loudly that the Egyptians heard him, and Pharaoh's household heard him too.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am Joseph! Is my father still alive?" His brothers could not answer him because they were so shocked at seeing him.
Then Joseph said to his brothers, "Please come closer to me." They came closer, and he said, "I am Joseph, your brother, the one you sold into Egypt.
"Now do not be sad, and do not be angry with yourselves, because you sold me here. God sent me ahead of you to save lives.
There has been a famine in the land for two years now, and there are five more years when there will be no plowing or harvest.
God sent me ahead of you to keep a small group of your family alive in the land and to save you by a great rescue.
So it was not you who sent me here, but God. He has made me a father to Pharaoh, lord of all his house, and ruler over all the land of Egypt.
"Hurry and go up to my father. Tell him, 'This is what your son Joseph says: "God has made me lord of all Egypt. Come down to me. Do not wait."'
You will live in the land of Goshen, and you will be near me. You, your children, and your grandchildren, along with your flocks, your herds, and everything you own, will be close to me.
I will take care of you there, because there are still five more years of famine. Otherwise, you, your household, and everything you own could become poor.
Look, your own eyes see, and my brother Benjamin's eyes see, that I am the one speaking to you.
Tell my father about all my honor in Egypt and about everything you have seen. Then hurry and bring my father down here."
Joseph fell on his brother Benjamin's neck and cried, and Benjamin cried on his neck.
He kissed all his brothers and cried over them. After that, his brothers talked with him.
The news was heard in Pharaoh's house: "Joseph's brothers have come." Pharaoh and his servants were pleased.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Tell your brothers, 'Do this: load your animals and go to the land of Canaan.
Bring your father and your families and come to me. I will give you the best land in Egypt, and you will eat the best food in the land.'
You are also to tell them, 'Take wagons from Egypt for your children and your wives, and bring your father and come.
Do not worry about your belongings, because the best of all Egypt will be yours.'"
The sons of Israel did so. Joseph gave them wagons, as Pharaoh had commanded, and he gave them food for the journey.
He gave each of them a change of clothes, but to Benjamin he gave three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothes.
He sent his father ten donkeys loaded with the best things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread, and food for his father on the journey.
He sent his brothers away, and they left. He said to them, "Do not argue on the way."
They went up from Egypt and came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan.
They told him, "Joseph is still alive! In fact, he is the ruler of all the land of Egypt." Jacob was stunned, because he did not believe them.
But when they told him everything Joseph had said to them, and when he saw the wagons Joseph had sent to carry him, Jacob's spirit revived.
Israel said, "That is enough. My son Joseph is still alive. I will go and see him before I die."
Israel set out with everything he owned and came to Beersheba. There he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.
That night God spoke to Israel in a vision and said, "Jacob, Jacob!" Jacob answered, "Here I am."
God said, "I am God, the God of your father. Do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, because I will make you into a great nation there.
I will go down to Egypt with you, and I will bring you back again. Joseph will be with you when you die."
Jacob got up from Beersheba. The sons of Israel carried their father Jacob, along with their little children and wives, in the carts Pharaoh had sent.
They took their livestock and everything they had gained in Canaan. Jacob and all his family went with him to Egypt.
He brought with him his sons and grandsons, his daughters and granddaughters—in fact, all his descendants.
These are the names of Israel's sons and their families who came to Egypt. Reuben was Jacob's oldest son.
Reuben's sons were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi.
Simeon's sons were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite woman.
Levi's sons were Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Judah's sons were Er, Onan, Shelah, Perez, and Zerah. Er and Onan died in Canaan. Perez's sons were Hezron and Hamul.
Issachar's sons were Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron.
Zebulun's sons were Sered, Elon, and Jahleel.
These were the sons Leah had for Jacob in Paddan Aram, along with his daughter Dinah. In all, her sons and daughter were 33 people.
Gad's sons were Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi, and Areli.
Asher's sons were Imnah, Ishvah, Ishvi, and Beriah, and their sister was Serah. Beriah's sons were Heber and Malchiel.
These were the children of Zilpah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah. She had 16 children for Jacob.
The sons of Jacob's wife Rachel were Joseph and Benjamin.
In Egypt, Joseph had two sons by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. Their names were Manasseh and Ephraim.
Benjamin's sons were Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Gera, Naaman, Ehi, Rosh, Muppim, Huppim, and Ard.
In all, Rachel's children and grandchildren who were counted were 14 people.
Naphtali's sons were Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem.
These were the children born to Jacob by Bilhah, whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel. In all, they were 7 people.
All those who came to Egypt with Jacob—his own descendants, not counting his sons' wives—were 66 people.
Joseph had two sons born in Egypt. So all the people in Jacob's household who came to Egypt were 70.
Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph to show the way to Goshen. So they came to the land of Goshen.
Joseph got his chariot ready and went to Goshen to meet his father Israel. He saw him, hugged him, and wept for a long time.
Israel said to Joseph, "Now I can die, because I have seen your face and know that you are alive."
Joseph said to his brothers and his father, "I will go up and tell Pharaoh, 'My brothers and my father's household, who were in Canaan, have come to me.
The men are shepherds. They take care of animals and have brought their sheep, cattle, and everything they own.'
When Pharaoh calls you and asks, 'What is your work?'
say, 'Your servants have been keepers of livestock from our youth until now, both we and our fathers.' Then you may live in Goshen, because every shepherd is detestable to the Egyptians."
Joseph went to Pharaoh and said, "My father and my brothers have come from Canaan with their sheep, cattle, and everything they own. They are now in Goshen."
He took five of his brothers and presented them to Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked them, "What is your work?" His brothers answered, "Your servants are shepherds, just as our fathers were."
They also said to Pharaoh, "We have come to live here for a while because there is no pasture for your servants' flocks. The famine is very severe in Canaan. Please let your servants live in Goshen."
Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Your father and your brothers have come to you.
The land of Egypt is before you. Settle your father and your brothers in the best land. Let them live in Goshen. If you know any capable men among them, put them in charge of my livestock."
Joseph brought his father Jacob and presented him to Pharaoh, and Jacob blessed Pharaoh.
Pharaoh asked Jacob, "How old are you?"
Jacob said to Pharaoh, "I have lived as a foreigner for one hundred thirty years. My years have been few and hard, and I have not lived as long as my fathers did."
Jacob blessed Pharaoh and left his presence.
Joseph settled his father and brothers in Egypt and gave them property in the best land, in the land of Rameses, as Pharaoh had ordered.
He also provided food for his father, his brothers, and all his father's household, according to the number of their children.
