There was no food in all the land, because the famine was very severe. Egypt and Canaan were worn out by the famine.
Joseph collected all the money in Egypt and Canaan that people paid for grain, and he brought it to Pharaoh's palace.
When the money in Egypt and Canaan was gone, all the Egyptians came to Joseph and said, "Give us food! Why should we die in front of you? Our money is gone."
Joseph said, "Bring your livestock, and I will give you food in exchange for it, since your money is gone."
So they brought their livestock to Joseph, and he gave them food in exchange for horses, flocks, herds, and donkeys. He supported them with food that year in exchange for all their livestock.

When that year ended, they came to him the next year and said, "We will not hide from our master that our money is gone and our livestock belongs to our master. Nothing is left for our master except our bodies and our land."

"Why should we die before your eyes, both we and our land? Buy us and our land for food, and we and our land will be Pharaoh's servants. Give us seed so we may live and not die, and so the land will not become empty."
So Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh, because every Egyptian sold his field when the famine became severe. The land became Pharaoh's.
He moved the people to the cities from one end of Egypt to the other.
He did not buy the priests' land, because the priests received a set allowance from Pharaoh and lived on it. That is why they did not sell their land.
Joseph said to the people, "Now that I have bought you and your land for Pharaoh, here is seed for you. Sow the land.
At harvest, give one-fifth to Pharaoh. The other four-fifths will be yours for seed for the fields, for food, for your households, and for your children."
They said, "You have saved our lives. Let us find favor in your eyes, and we will be Pharaoh's servants."
So Joseph made it a law over Egypt that lasts to this day: Pharaoh gets one-fifth. Only the priests' land did not belong to Pharaoh.
Israel settled in Egypt, in Goshen. They acquired property there, were very fruitful, and multiplied greatly.
Jacob lived in Egypt seventeen years, so he lived one hundred forty-seven years in all.

When the time came for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said, "If I have found favor with you, put your hand under my thigh and promise to deal kindly and truly with me: Do not bury me in Egypt.
When I die, carry me out of Egypt and bury me where my fathers are buried." Joseph said, "I will do as you say."
"Swear to me," Jacob said. So Joseph swore to him, and Israel bowed at the head of his bed.
After these things, Joseph was told, “Your father is sick.” So he took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, along with him.
When Jacob was told, “Your son Joseph has come to you,” Israel gathered his strength and sat up in bed.
Jacob said to Joseph, “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan and blessed me.
He said to me, ‘I will make you fruitful and multiply you. I will make you into a large group of peoples, and I will give this land to your descendants after you as a lasting possession.’”
“And now your two sons, who were born to you in Egypt before I came to you here, are mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.
But any children you have after them will be yours. They will be counted under their brothers’ names when the land is divided.

As for me, when I was coming back from Paddan, Rachel sadly died on the way in the land of Canaan, still some distance from Ephrath. I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem).”
When Israel saw Joseph’s sons, he asked, “Who are these?”
Joseph said to his father, “They are the sons God has given me here.” Then Jacob said, “Please bring them to me so I can bless them.”
Israel’s eyes were weak from old age, so he could not see well. Joseph brought his sons to him, and Israel kissed them and hugged them.
Israel said to Joseph, “I never thought I would see your face again, but God has let me see your children too.”
Then Joseph took them from Israel’s knees and bowed down with his face to the ground.
Joseph took both boys—Ephraim in his right hand, toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand, toward Israel’s right hand—and brought them close to him.

But Israel reached out his right hand and put it on Ephraim’s head, even though Ephraim was the younger. He crossed his hands and put his left hand on Manasseh’s head, even though Manasseh was the firstborn.
Then he blessed Joseph and said, “May the God my fathers Abraham and Isaac followed, the God who has been my shepherd all my life until today,
the Angel who has saved me from all harm—may He bless these boys. May they be called by my name and by the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a great number on the earth.”
When Joseph saw that his father had put his right hand on Ephraim’s head, he was upset. He took his father’s hand to move it from Ephraim’s head to Manasseh’s head.
Joseph said to his father, “No, my father. This one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on his head.”

But his father refused and said, “I know, my son, I know. He will also become a people, and he will also be great. But his younger brother will be greater than he is, and his descendants will become many nations.”
So he blessed them that day, saying, “Israel will bless its children by saying, ‘May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh.’” In this way he put Ephraim before Manasseh.
Then Israel said to Joseph, “Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers.
And to you I give one more share than your brothers: the ridge of Shechem, which I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow.”
Jacob called his sons and said, "Gather together, and I will tell you what will happen to you in the days to come.
Assemble and listen, sons of Jacob. Listen to Israel, your father."
"Reuben, you are my firstborn. You are my strength and the first sign of my power. You were to have the highest honor and the greatest strength.
But you are as unstable as water. You will not lead, because you went up to your father's bed and dishonored it."
"Simeon and Levi are brothers. Their swords are weapons of violence.
I will not join their secret plans. I will not take part in their meetings. In their anger they killed a man. They crippled an ox for no good reason.
Their anger is cursed because it is fierce. Their fury is cursed because it is cruel. I will scatter them among Jacob's people. I will spread them throughout Israel."
"Judah, your brothers will praise you. Your hand will be on your enemies' necks. Your father's sons will bow down to you.
Judah is a young lion. My son, you have gone up from the kill. He crouches and lies down like a lion. Like a lioness, who would dare to wake him?"
"The scepter will not leave Judah. The ruler's staff will stay with him. It will last until Shiloh comes. Then the nations will obey him.
He ties his donkey to a grapevine. He ties his young donkey to the best vine. He washes his clothes in wine. He washes his robe in grape juice.
His eyes are darker than wine. His teeth are whiter than milk."
"Zebulun will live by the sea. He will be a harbor for ships. His border will reach toward Sidon.
Issachar is a strong donkey, lying down between the sheep pens.
He saw that rest was good and that the land was pleasant. So he bent his shoulder to the load. He became a servant who had to work for others."
"Dan will judge his people. He will be one of the tribes of Israel.
Dan will be a snake by the road. He will be a viper by the path. He bites the horse's heels, and the rider falls backward.
I wait for Your salvation, O the LORD."
"Gad will be attacked by raiders, but he will strike back at them.
Asher's food will be rich. He will provide food fit for a king.
Naphtali is a deer set free. He speaks beautiful words."
"Joseph is a fruitful vine. He is a fruitful vine by a spring. His branches climb over a wall.
Archers attacked him. They shot at him and hated him.
But his bow stayed strong. His arms stayed quick. This strength came from the Mighty One of Jacob. It came from the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel."
"May the God of your father help you. May the Almighty bless you with blessings from heaven above, from the deep below, and from the breasts and womb.
Your father's blessings are greater than the blessings of my ancestors. They reach to the highest hills. They rest on Joseph's head. They rest on the prince among his brothers."
"Benjamin is a hungry wolf. In the morning he eats the prey. In the evening he divides the spoil."
All these are the twelve tribes of Israel. This is what their father said to them. He blessed each one with the blessing meant for him.
Then he commanded them, "I am about to die and join my ancestors. Bury me with my fathers in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite,
the cave in the field of Machpelah, near Mamre in Canaan. Abraham bought the field from Ephron the Hittite to use as a burial place.
Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried there. Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried there. I buried Leah there.
The field and the cave in it were bought from the Hittites."
When Jacob finished commanding his sons, he pulled his feet into the bed. He breathed his last and joined his ancestors.
Joseph fell on his father's face, wept over him, and kissed him.
Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father Israel, and the physicians embalmed him.
The embalming took forty days, for that is the full time for embalming. The Egyptians mourned him for seventy days.
When the days of mourning had passed, Joseph spoke to Pharaoh's household and said, "If I have found favor in your eyes, please tell Pharaoh,
'My father made me swear, "Look, I am about to die. Bury me in the grave I dug for myself in the land of Canaan." Now let me go up and bury my father, and I will return.'"
Pharaoh said, "Go up and bury your father, just as he made you swear."
So Joseph went up to bury his father. All of Pharaoh's servants went with him, along with the elders of his household and all the elders of Egypt.
Joseph's whole household, his brothers, and his father's household went too. Only their children, flocks, and herds stayed in Goshen.
Chariots and horsemen also went up with him. It was a very large group.
They came to the threshing floor of Atad, beyond the Jordan, and mourned there with a very great and heavy lament. Joseph mourned for his father seven days.
When the Canaanites who lived there saw the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad, they said, "This is a heavy mourning for the Egyptians." So that place was named Abel-mizraim, beyond the Jordan.
Jacob's sons did for him exactly as he had commanded.
They carried him to Canaan and buried him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field near Mamre. Abraham had bought that field from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place.
After burying his father, Joseph returned to Egypt with his brothers and everyone who had gone with him.
When Joseph's brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, "What if Joseph holds a grudge against us and pays us back for all the wrong we did to him?"
So they sent a message to Joseph, saying, "Your father gave this command before he died:
'Please forgive your brothers' wrongdoing and sin, because they treated you badly. Now please forgive the wrongdoing of the servants of your father's God.'" When Joseph heard this, he wept.
Then his brothers came, fell down before him, and said, "We are your servants."
Joseph said to them, "Don't be afraid. Am I in the place of God?"
"You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good, to keep many people alive, as He is doing today."
"So don't be afraid. I will provide for you and your children." He comforted them and spoke kindly to them.
Joseph stayed in Egypt with his father's household. He lived 110 years.
Joseph saw Ephraim's children to the third generation, and the children of Machir, Manasseh's son, were born while Joseph was still alive.
Joseph said to his brothers, "I am about to die, but God will surely come to help you. He will bring you out of this land and take you to the land He promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."
Then Joseph made the sons of Israel swear an oath, saying, "God will surely come to help you, and you must carry my bones up from here."
Joseph died at 110 years old. They embalmed him and placed him in a coffin in Egypt.
These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob. Each man came with his family:
Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher.
Jacob’s whole family numbered seventy people. Joseph was already in Egypt.
Joseph and all his brothers and that whole generation died.
But the Israelites were fruitful and increased greatly. They multiplied and grew very strong, so the land was filled with them.
Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, began to rule in Egypt.
He said to his people, “Look, the Israelites have become too numerous and too strong for us.
Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more. If war comes, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country.”
So they put taskmasters over them to oppress them with forced labor. They built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh.
But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and spread. So the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites.
They made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar and with all kinds of work in the fields. In all their hard labor, the Egyptians worked them ruthlessly.
Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other Puah:
“When you help the Hebrew women give birth, look at the child. If it is a boy, kill him; but if it is a girl, let her live.”
But the midwives feared God and did not do what the king of Egypt had told them to do. They let the boys live.
So the king of Egypt called for the midwives and asked them, “Why have you done this? Why have you let the boys live?”
The midwives answered Pharaoh, “Hebrew women are not like Egyptian women. They are strong and give birth before the midwives arrive.”
So God was kind to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous.
And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own.
Then Pharaoh gave this order to all his people: “Every Hebrew boy who is born must be thrown into the Nile, but every girl may live.”
A man from the family of Levi married a woman from the family of Levi.
She became pregnant and had a son. She saw that he was a good baby, and she hid him for three months.
When she could not hide him any longer, she got a basket made of reeds. She coated it with tar and pitch, put the baby in it, and placed it among the reeds along the bank of the Nile.
His sister stood far away to see what would happen to him.
Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe in the Nile, and her young women walked along the riverbank. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant girl to bring it.
She opened it and saw the baby. He was crying, and she felt sorry for him. "This is one of the Hebrew babies," she said.
Then his sister asked Pharaoh's daughter, "Shall I go and get one of the Hebrew women to nurse the baby for you?"
"Yes, go," she answered. So the girl went and got the baby's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter said to her, "Take this baby and nurse him for me, and I will pay you." So the woman took the baby and nursed him.
When the child grew older, she took him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, "I drew him out of the water."
Later, when Moses had grown up, he went out to where his own people were and watched them at their hard work. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people.
He looked around, and when he saw no one, he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
The next day he went out and saw two Hebrews fighting. He asked the one who was in the wrong, "Why are you hitting your fellow Hebrew?"
The man said, "Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you thinking of killing me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid and thought, "What I did must have become known."
When Pharaoh heard about this, he tried to kill Moses, but Moses fled from Pharaoh and went to live in Midian. He sat down by a well.
Now a priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father's flock.
Some shepherds came and drove them away, but Moses got up and helped them. He watered their flock.
When the girls returned to Reuel, their father, he asked, "Why have you returned so early today?"
They answered, "An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds. He even drew water for us and watered the flock."
He asked his daughters, "Where is he? Why did you leave him? Invite him to have something to eat."
Moses agreed to stay with the man, who gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage.
She gave birth to a son, and Moses named him Gershom, saying, "I have become a foreigner in a foreign land."
During that long time, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned in their slavery and cried out. Their cry for help because of their slavery went up to God.
God heard their groaning and remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
So God looked on the Israelites and was concerned about them.
Now Moses was taking care of the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock to the far side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire from the middle of a bush. Moses looked and saw that the bush was on fire but was not burning up.
Moses said, "I will go over and see this amazing sight. Why isn't the bush burning up?"
When the LORD saw that he had gone over to look, God called to him from inside the bush, "Moses! Moses!" And Moses said, "Here I am."
"Do not come closer," He said. "Take off your sandals, because the place where you are standing is holy ground."
"I am the God of your father," He said. "I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Then Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God.
The LORD said, "I have seen how My people are suffering in Egypt. I have heard their cry because of their slave drivers. I know how much they are hurting.

So I have come down to save them from the Egyptians and to bring them up to a good and wide land—a land flowing with milk and honey. It is the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.
Now the cry of the Israelites has reached Me, and I have seen how the Egyptians are crushing them.
So now, go. I am sending you to Pharaoh to bring My people, the Israelites, out of Egypt."
But Moses said to God, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out of Egypt?"
God said, "I will be with you. This will be the sign for you that I have sent you: After you bring the people out of Egypt, you will worship God on this mountain."
Moses said to God, "Suppose I go to the Israelites and tell them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask, 'What is His name?' What should I tell them?"
God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." Then He said, "Tell the Israelites, 'I AM has sent me to you.'

God also said to Moses, "Tell the Israelites, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—has sent me to you. This is My name forever, and this is how I am to be remembered for all generations.'"

"Go and gather the elders of Israel. Tell them, 'The LORD, the God of your fathers—the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—has appeared to me and said, "I have watched over you and have seen what is being done to you in Egypt.
I have also said I will bring you up out of the suffering in Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—a land flowing with milk and honey."

And they will listen to your voice, and you and the elders of Israel shall go to the king of Egypt and say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has met with us. Now please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God.'
But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go, not even by a strong hand.
So I will stretch out My hand and strike Egypt with all the wonders that I will do in it; after that he will let you go.
I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians, and when you go, you shall not go empty.

Instead, every woman shall ask her neighbor and any woman who lives in her house for silver and gold jewelry and clothing. You shall put them on your sons and daughters. In this way you will plunder the Egyptians."
Moses answered, "What if they do not believe me or listen to me? They may say the LORD never appeared to you."
The LORD asked him, "What is that in your hand?" Moses said, "A staff."
The LORD said, "Throw it on the ground." Moses threw it on the ground, and it became a snake. Moses ran from it.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Reach out your hand and grab it by the tail." Moses reached out his hand and took hold of it, and it became a staff again in his hand.
The LORD said, "This will help them believe that I am the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and that I have appeared to you."
The LORD also said, "Put your hand inside your cloak." Moses put his hand inside his cloak. When he took it out, his hand was covered with a skin disease and was white like snow.
The LORD said, "Put your hand back inside your cloak." Moses put it back, and when he took it out again, it was healthy like the rest of his body.
The LORD said, "If they do not believe you or listen to the first sign, they may believe the second sign.
If they still do not believe these two signs or listen to you, take some water from the Nile and pour it on the dry ground. The water you take from the river will turn to blood on the ground."

Moses said to the LORD, "Please, Lord, I am not a good speaker. I have never been good with words, not yesterday, not the day before, and not since You began speaking to Your servant. I speak slowly and with difficulty."
The LORD said to him, "Who made man's mouth? Who makes a person unable to speak or deaf, or able to see or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?"
"Now go. I will help you speak, and I will teach you what to say."
But Moses said, "Please, Lord, send someone else."
Then the LORD became angry with Moses and said, "What about your brother Aaron the Levite? I know he speaks well. He is already on his way to meet you, and he will be glad to see you.
You will speak to him and tell him what to say. I will help both of you speak, and I will teach you what to do.
He will speak to the people for you. He will be your spokesman, and you will be like God to him.
Take this staff in your hand so you can do the signs with it."
Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said, "Let me go back to my own people in Egypt and see if they are still alive." Jethro said, "Go safely."
The LORD said to Moses in Midian, "Go back to Egypt, because all the men who wanted to kill you are dead."
So Moses took his wife and sons, put them on a donkey, and started back to Egypt. He took the staff of God in his hand.

The LORD said to Moses, "When you return to Egypt, be sure to do all the wonders I have given you the power to do in front of Pharaoh. But I will make his heart stubborn, and he will not let the people go.
Then say to Pharaoh, 'This is what the LORD says: Israel is My firstborn son.
I told you to let My son go so he could worship Me. But you refused to let him go, so I will kill your firstborn son.'"
At a place where they stayed for the night on the way, the LORD met Moses and was about to kill him.
Zipporah took a flint knife, cut off her son's foreskin, touched Moses' feet with it, and said, "You are a bloody husband to me."
So the LORD let him go. At that time she said, "A bloody husband because of circumcision."
The LORD said to Aaron, "Go into the desert to meet Moses." Aaron went and met him at the mountain of God, and kissed him.
Moses told Aaron everything the LORD had sent him to say and all the signs He had commanded him to do.
Then Moses and Aaron gathered all the elders of the people of Israel.
Aaron spoke all the words the LORD had spoken to Moses, and he did the signs in front of the people.
The people believed. When they heard that the LORD had cared for them and had seen their suffering, they bowed down and worshiped.
Afterward Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Let My people go, so that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness.’”
But Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and I will not let Israel go.”

Then they said, “The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, or He may strike us with plague or sword.”
But the king of Egypt said to them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you distracting the people from their work? Get back to your labor!”
Pharaoh also said, “Look, the people of the land are now numerous, and you are stopping them from their labor.”
That same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters and foremen of the people:
“You are no longer to supply the people with straw for making bricks. They must go and gather their own straw.
But require of them the same quota of bricks as before; do not reduce it. For they are lazy. That is why they are crying out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’
Make the work harder for the men so they will be occupied and not pay attention to lies.”
Then the taskmasters and foremen of the people went out and said to them, “This is what Pharaoh says: ‘I am no longer giving you straw.
Go and get your own straw wherever you can find it, but your workload will not be reduced.’”
So the people scattered throughout the land of Egypt to gather stubble for straw.
The taskmasters kept pressing them, saying, “Fulfill your quota each day, just as you did when straw was provided.”
Then the Israelite foremen, whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had set over the people, were beaten and asked, “Why have you not fulfilled your quota of bricks yesterday or today, as you did before?”
So the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why are you treating your servants this way?
No straw is given to your servants, yet we are told, ‘Make bricks!’ Look, your servants are being beaten, but the fault is with your own people.”
Pharaoh replied, “You are slackers! Slackers! That is why you are saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.’
Now get to work. You will be given no straw, but you must still deliver the full quota of bricks.”
The Israelite foremen realized they were in trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily quota of bricks.”
When they left Pharaoh, they met Moses and Aaron, who were waiting to meet them.
“May the LORD look upon you and judge you,” they said, “for you have made us a stench to Pharaoh and his officials, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us!”
So Moses returned to the LORD and asked, “Lord, why have You brought trouble on this people? Why did You ever send me?
Ever since I went to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has brought trouble on this people, and You have not rescued Your people at all.”
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Now you will see what I will do to Pharaoh. Because of My great power, he will let them go, and because of My great power, he will force them out of his land.”
God spoke to Moses and said, “I am the LORD.
I appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but they did not know Me by My name, the LORD.
I also made My promise to them to give them the land of Canaan, the land where they lived as foreigners.
I have also heard the Israelites groaning because the Egyptians force them to work as slaves, and I have remembered My promise.

Therefore tell the Israelites, ‘I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under Egypt’s heavy burdens. I will rescue you from being their slaves. I will set you free with great power and mighty judgments.
I will take you as My own people, and I will be your God. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who brought you out from under Egypt’s heavy burdens.
I will bring you into the land I promised to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as your own land. I am the LORD.’”
Moses told this to the Israelites, but they did not listen to him. They were discouraged and worn out from hard labor.
Then the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
“Go and tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the Israelites go out of his land.”
But Moses said to the LORD, “If the Israelites will not listen to me, how will Pharaoh listen to me? I am not a good speaker.”
Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron. He commanded them concerning the Israelites and Pharaoh king of Egypt to bring the Israelites out of Egypt.
These are the leaders of their family groups: The sons of Reuben, Israel’s oldest son, were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These are the clans of Reuben.
The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul, the son of a Canaanite woman. These are the clans of Simeon.
These are the names of Levi’s sons by their family lines: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years.
The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei, by their clans.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. These are the clans of the Levites by their family lines.
Amram married his aunt Jochebed, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. Amram lived 137 years.
The sons of Izhar were Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri.
The sons of Uzziel were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri.
Aaron married Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
The sons of Korah were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These are the clans of the Korahites.
Aaron’s son Eleazar married one of Putiel’s daughters, and she bore him Phinehas. These are the leaders of the Levite families by their family groups.
It was this Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said, “Bring the Israelites out of Egypt by their groups.”
They were the ones who spoke to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to bring the Israelites out of Egypt. This was Moses and Aaron.
On the day the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,
the LORD spoke to Moses and said, “I am the LORD. Tell Pharaoh king of Egypt everything I say to you.”
But Moses said to the LORD, “I am not a good speaker. How will Pharaoh listen to me?”
The LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will be your prophet.
You must speak everything I command you, and your brother Aaron must tell Pharaoh to let the Israelites leave his country.
But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and I will multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt.
"Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will lay My hand on Egypt, and with mighty judgments I will bring out My people, the Israelites, from the land of Egypt.
And the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I stretch out My hand against Egypt and bring the Israelites out from among them."
So Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded them.
Moses was eighty years old and Aaron was eighty-three when they spoke to Pharaoh.
Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron,
"When Pharaoh says to you, 'Show us a miracle,' you must tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh, and it will become a snake.'"
So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did as the LORD had commanded. Aaron threw his staff down in front of Pharaoh and his officials, and it became a snake.
Then Pharaoh also called for the wise men and sorcerers, and the Egyptian magicians did the same thing by their magic.
Each one threw down his staff, and they became snakes. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.
Yet Pharaoh's heart became hard, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is stubborn; he refuses to let the people go.
Go to Pharaoh in the morning. You will see him going out to the water. Stand on the bank of the Nile to meet him. Take in your hand the staff that was turned into a snake.
Say to him, 'The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has sent me to you to say, "Let My people go, so that they may worship Me in the wilderness." But until now you have not listened.'
This is what the LORD says: 'By this you will know that I am the LORD: I am going to strike the water of the Nile with the staff in My hand, and it will turn to blood.'
The fish in the Nile will die, the river will stink, and the Egyptians will be unable to drink its water."

Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt—over their rivers, canals, ponds, and all their pools of water—so that they may become blood. There will be blood throughout the land of Egypt, even in wooden buckets and stone jars.'"
Moses and Aaron did just as the LORD had commanded. In front of Pharaoh and his officials, Aaron raised the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned to blood.
The fish in the Nile died, and the river smelled so bad that the Egyptians could not drink its water. There was blood throughout the land of Egypt.
But the Egyptian magicians did the same thing by their magic, and Pharaoh's heart became hard. He would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take this to heart either.
All the Egyptians dug around the Nile for water to drink, because they could not drink the water of the river.
Seven days passed after the LORD struck the Nile.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.
If you refuse to let them go, I will plague all your country with frogs.
The Nile will teem with frogs. They will come up into your palace, into your bedroom and onto your bed, into the houses of your officials and your people, and into your ovens and kneading bowls.
The frogs will come up on you, your people, and all your officials.'"
And the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, canals, and ponds, and make the frogs come up onto the land of Egypt.'"
So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land.
But the magicians did the same thing by their magic, and they also brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Pray to the LORD to take the frogs away from me and my people, and I will let your people go to sacrifice to the LORD."

Moses said to Pharaoh, "I'll let you choose when I should pray for you, your officials, and your people, so that the frogs will be taken away from you and your houses. They will stay only in the Nile."
"Tomorrow," Pharaoh said. Moses replied, "It will be as you say, so that you may know that there is no one like the LORD our God.
The frogs will leave you and your houses and your officials and your people; they will stay only in the Nile."
Then Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh's presence, and Moses cried out to the LORD about the frogs He had brought on Pharaoh.
And the LORD did as Moses asked, and the frogs died in the houses, courtyards, and fields.
They were piled into countless heaps, and the land stank.
But when Pharaoh saw that there was relief, he hardened his heart and would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Tell Aaron, 'Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that it becomes gnats throughout the land of Egypt.'"
So Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and gnats came upon people and animals. All the dust of the earth became gnats throughout the land of Egypt.
The magicians tried to produce gnats by their magic, but they could not. And the gnats were on people and animals.
The magicians said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

Then the LORD said to Moses, "Rise early in the morning and present yourself before Pharaoh as he goes out to the water. Tell him, 'This is what the LORD says: Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.

If you do not let My people go, I will send swarms of flies on you, your officials, your people, and your houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be full of swarms, and even the ground they stand on.
But on that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where My people live, so that no swarms of flies will be there. Then you will know that I am the LORD in the middle of the earth.
I will put a difference between My people and your people. Tomorrow this sign will happen.'"
And the LORD did so. Thick swarms of flies poured into Pharaoh's palace and the houses of his officials, and throughout Egypt the land was ruined by the swarms.
Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said, "Go, sacrifice to your God within the land."

But Moses said, "It would not be right to do that, because the sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God would be disgusting to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice something the Egyptians hate right in front of them, won't they stone us?
We must go a three days' journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the LORD our God, as He commands us."
Pharaoh said, "I will let you go to sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness, but you must not go very far. Pray for me."

Moses answered, "As soon as I leave you, I will pray to the LORD, and tomorrow the swarms will leave Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. But Pharaoh must not trick anyone again by refusing to let the people go to sacrifice to the LORD."
So Moses left Pharaoh's presence and prayed to the LORD.
And the LORD did as Moses asked and removed the swarms from Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. Not one fly was left.
But this time Pharaoh hardened his heart too, and he did not let the people go.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh and tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let My people go so they can serve Me.
But if you refuse to let them go and still keep them,
then the hand of the LORD will bring a terrible disease on your livestock in the fields—on the horses, donkeys, camels, cattle, and sheep.
The LORD will make a difference between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt, so none of the animals that belong to the Israelites will die.
The LORD set a time and said, 'Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land.'
The next day the LORD did it. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal from the Israelites' livestock died.
Pharaoh sent men to check, and not one animal from the Israelites' livestock was dead. But Pharaoh's heart was hard, and he would not let the people go.
Then the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, "Take handfuls of soot from a furnace, and let Moses throw it toward the sky in front of Pharaoh.
It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and it will turn into boils that break out into sores on people and animals all over Egypt."
So they took soot from the furnace and stood in front of Pharaoh. Moses threw it up toward the sky, and it became boils that broke out into sores on people and animals.
The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, because the boils were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians.
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Get up early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh. Tell him, 'This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: Let My people go so they can serve Me.
This time I will send all My plagues on you personally, on your officials, and on your people, so you will know there is no one like Me in all the earth.
By now I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with disease, and you would have been wiped off the earth.
But I have let you live for this reason: to show you My power and to make My name known in all the earth.
You are still setting yourself up against My people and will not let them go.
So tomorrow at this time I will send a very heavy hailstorm. There has never been a storm like it in Egypt since the day it was founded.
Now send word and bring your livestock and everything you have in the fields into shelter. Every person and animal left in the fields will die when the hail comes down on them.'"
Some of Pharaoh's officials who feared the LORD's word hurried their servants and livestock into the houses.
But those who did not take the LORD's word seriously left their servants and livestock in the fields.
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so hail will fall on all the land of Egypt—on people, animals, and every plant in the fields throughout Egypt."
Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and the LORD sent thunder and hail, with lightning running across the ground. The LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt.
The hail was very heavy, with lightning flashing in it. There had never been a storm like it in Egypt since it became a nation.
The hail struck everything in the fields throughout Egypt—people, animals, every plant, and every tree in the fields.
Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, there was no hail.
Then Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, "This time I have sinned. The LORD is right, and my people and I are wrong.
Pray to the LORD, because there has been enough of God's thunder and hail. I will let you go, and you will not have to stay any longer."
Moses said to him, "As soon as I leave the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD. The thunder will stop, and there will be no more hail, so you may know that the earth belongs to the LORD.
But I know that you and your officials still do not fear the LORD God."
The flax and barley were ruined because the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom.
But the wheat and spelt were not ruined because they grow later.
Moses left Pharaoh and went out of the city. He spread out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder and hail stopped. Rain no longer poured down on the earth.
When Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail, and thunder had stopped, he sinned again. He and his officials hardened their hearts.
Pharaoh's heart was hard, and he did not let the Israelites go, just as the LORD had said through Moses.
Then the the LORD said to Moses, "Go to Pharaoh. I have made his heart and his servants' hearts hard, so I can show My signs among them.
You will tell your son and your grandson how I made Egypt look foolish and about the signs I put among them. Then you will know that I am the the LORD."
Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and said, "This is what the the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: 'How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me? Let My people go so they can serve Me.
If you refuse to let My people go, tomorrow I will bring locusts into your land.
They will cover the land so no one can see it. They will eat what the hail left, and they will eat every tree that grows for you in the field.

Your houses and your servants' houses and all the houses in Egypt will be full. Your fathers and grandfathers never saw anything like this from the day they lived here until now.'" Then he turned and left Pharaoh.
Pharaoh's servants said to him, "How long will this man keep causing trouble for us? Let the men go so they can serve the the LORD their God. Don't you know yet that Egypt is ruined?"
Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, and he said, "Go, serve the the LORD your God. But who is going?"
Moses said, "We will go with our young and old. We will go with our sons and daughters, our sheep and cattle, because we have a festival to the the LORD."
He said to them, "May the the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones! Look, you have evil in mind.
No, only the men may go and serve the the LORD, because that is what you asked for." Then he drove them out from his presence.
Then the the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over Egypt for the locusts. Let them come over Egypt and eat every plant in the land, all that the hail left."
Moses stretched out his staff over Egypt. The the LORD brought an east wind over the land all that day and night. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts.
The locusts came over all Egypt and settled everywhere in Egypt. There had never been such a heavy locust plague before, and there never will be again.

They covered the whole land, and the land became dark. They ate every plant and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left. No green thing was left on the trees or in the fields anywhere in Egypt.
Pharaoh hurried to call Moses and Aaron. He said, "I have sinned against the the LORD your God and against you.
Now please forgive my sin once more. Plead with the the LORD your God to take this deadly plague away from me."
Moses left Pharaoh and pleaded with the the LORD.
The the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind. It carried the locusts away and drove them into the Red Sea. Not one locust was left anywhere in Egypt.
But the the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the Israelites go.
Then the the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand toward the sky so darkness will come over Egypt, darkness so thick it can be felt."
Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky. Thick darkness covered all Egypt for three days.
People could not see each other, and no one got up from where he was for three days. But all the Israelites had light where they lived.
Pharaoh called Moses and said, "Go, serve the the LORD. Only leave your flocks and herds behind. Your little ones may go with you."
Moses said, "You must also give us animals for sacrifices and burnt offerings, so we can offer them to the the LORD our God.

Our livestock must go with us. Not one hoof will be left behind, because we need some of them to serve the the LORD our God. We do not know what we will need to serve the the LORD until we get there."
But the the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let them go.
Pharaoh said to him, "Get away from me! Be careful never to see my face again, because on the day you see my face, you will die."
Moses said, "You are right. I will never see your face again."
The LORD said to Moses, “I will bring one more plague on Pharaoh and on Egypt. After that, he will let you go from here. When he lets you go, he will drive you out completely.”
“Tell the people that every man should ask his neighbor, and every woman should ask her neighbor, for silver and gold items.”
The LORD gave the people favor with the Egyptians. Also, Moses was highly respected in Egypt by Pharaoh’s officials and by the people.
Moses said, “This is what the LORD says: ‘About midnight I will go out among the Egyptians.
Every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh’s oldest son on his throne to the oldest son of the slave woman at the mill, and all the firstborn animals.
There will be a great cry throughout Egypt, worse than ever before and never to be repeated.
But among the Israelites, not even a dog will bark at people or animals. Then you will know that the LORD makes a difference between Egypt and Israel.’
All these officials of your will come down to me and bow before me and say, ‘Get out—you and all the people who follow you!’ After that, I will leave.” Moses left Pharaoh, burning with anger.
But the LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not listen to you, so My miracles will be multiplied in Egypt.”
Moses and Aaron did all these miracles before Pharaoh, but the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the Israelites leave his land.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt,
“This month is to be the first month of the year for you.
Tell the whole community of Israel that on the tenth day of this month, each man must take a lamb for his family—one lamb for each household.
If a household is too small for a whole lamb, he and his nearest neighbor may share one, counting the people by how much each one can eat.
The lamb must be a year-old male without defect. You may take it from the sheep or the goats.
Keep it until the fourteenth day of the month. Then the whole community of Israel must kill their lambs at twilight.
Take some of the blood and put it on the two doorposts and the top of the doorframe of the houses where you eat the lamb.
“That night you must eat the meat roasted over fire, along with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
Do not eat it raw or boiled in water. Roast it over fire, with its head, legs, and inner parts.
Do not leave any of it until morning. Burn whatever is left in the morning.
This is how you must eat it: with your belt fastened, your sandals on your feet, and your staff in your hand. Eat it quickly. It is the LORD’s Passover.
On that night I will pass through Egypt and strike every firstborn—both people and animals. I will bring judgment on all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD.
The blood will be a sign for you on the houses where you are. When I see the blood, I will pass over you. No deadly plague will touch you when I strike Egypt.
“This day will be a memorial for you. You must celebrate it as a feast to the LORD. It is a law for you and your descendants forever.

For seven days you must eat unleavened bread. On the first day, remove all yeast from your houses. Anyone who eats anything with yeast from the first day through the seventh day must be cut off from Israel.
On the first day you must hold a holy meeting, and on the seventh day you must hold another holy meeting. No work may be done on those days, except preparing food for everyone.
Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, because on this very day I brought your armies out of Egypt. Keep this day as a law for all your generations forever.
In the first month, from the evening of the fourteenth day until the evening of the twenty-first day, you must eat unleavened bread.
For seven days no yeast may be found in your houses. Anyone who eats anything made with yeast, whether a foreigner or a native of the land, must be cut off from the community of Israel.
Eat nothing made with yeast. In all your homes, eat unleavened bread.”
Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them, “Draw out and take lambs for your families, and slaughter the Passover lamb.
Take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood in the basin, and put some of the blood on the top of the doorframe and on both doorposts. None of you may go outside the door of his house until morning.

For the LORD will pass through to strike Egypt. When He sees the blood on the top of the doorframe and on both doorposts, the LORD will pass over that door. He will not let the destroyer enter your houses to strike you.
You must keep this command as a law for you and your sons forever.
“When you enter the land that the LORD will give you, just as He promised, you must keep this service.
When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’
you must say, ‘It is the Passover sacrifice to the LORD. He passed over the houses of the Israelites in Egypt when He struck Egypt and spared our houses.’” The people bowed down and worshiped.
The Israelites did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.
At midnight the LORD struck every firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh on his throne to the firstborn of the prisoner in the dungeon, and all the firstborn of the livestock.
Pharaoh and all his officials and all the Egyptians got up during the night. There was a loud cry in Egypt, because there was no house without someone dead.
During the night Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, “Get up and leave my people, both you and the Israelites. Go and worship the LORD, as you have said.
Take your flocks and herds, as you said, and go. Bless me too.”
The Egyptians urged the people to leave the country quickly, because they said, “We will all die!”
So the people took their dough before it was leavened, with their kneading bowls wrapped in their clothes on their shoulders.
The Israelites did what Moses had said and asked the Egyptians for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing.
The LORD had given the people favor in the eyes of the Egyptians, so they gave them what they asked for. In this way they plundered Egypt.
The Israelites traveled from Rameses to Succoth. There were about six hundred thousand men on foot, not counting children.
A mixed crowd also went up with them, along with very large flocks and herds.
They baked the dough they had brought from Egypt into unleavened cakes, because it had not risen. They had been driven out of Egypt and could not wait, and they had not prepared any other food.
The Israelites had lived in Egypt for four hundred thirty years.
At the end of four hundred thirty years, on that very day, all the LORD’s armies left Egypt.
It was a night of watching for the LORD, to bring them out of Egypt. This same night is a night of watching for the LORD for all the Israelites throughout their generations.
The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the rule for the Passover: no foreigner may eat it.
Any slave you have bought may eat it after you circumcise him.
A temporary resident or hired worker may not eat it.
It must be eaten in one house. You must not take any of the meat outside the house, and you must not break any of its bones.
“The whole community of Israel must keep this.

If a foreigner living among you wants to celebrate the LORD’s Passover, all his males must be circumcised. Then he may take part and be like a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person may eat it.
The same law applies to the native and to the foreigner living among you.”
All the Israelites did just as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.
On that very day the LORD brought the Israelites out of Egypt by their armies.
Then the LORD said to Moses,
"Set apart for Me every firstborn male. The first offspring of every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast."
So Moses said to the people, "Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. For the LORD brought you out of it by His great power. No leavened bread may be eaten.
Today, in the month of Abib, you are going out.

And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites, which He swore to your fathers to give you, a rich and fertile land, you shall observe this ceremony in this month.
For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD.
Unleavened bread shall be eaten throughout the seven days, and no leavened bread shall be seen among you, nor shall yeast be seen anywhere within your borders.
And on that day you are to explain to your son, 'It is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.'
"It shall be a sign for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead, so that the LORD's law may be in your mouth. For the LORD brought you out of Egypt with His great power.
Therefore you shall keep this rule at its set time year after year.
And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, as He swore to you and your fathers, and gives it to you,
you are to present to the LORD the first offspring of every womb. All the firstborn males of your livestock belong to the LORD.
You must redeem every firstborn donkey with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you must redeem.
In the future, when your son asks you, 'What does this mean?' you are to tell him, 'With great power the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

And when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both of man and beast. Therefore I sacrifice to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons.'
So it shall be a sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead that with great power the LORD brought us out of Egypt."

When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them along the road through the land of the Philistines, though it was shorter. For God said, "If the people face war, they might change their minds and return to Egypt."
So God led the people around by the way of the wilderness toward the Red Sea. And the Israelites left Egypt ready for battle.
Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear an oath, saying, "God will surely take care of you, and you must carry my bones up with you from this place."
They set out from Succoth and camped at Etham on the edge of the wilderness.
And the LORD went before them in a pillar of cloud to guide them on their way by day, and in a pillar of fire to give them light by night, so that they could travel by day or night.
Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night left its place before the people.
Then the LORD spoke to Moses. He said,
"Tell the Israelites to turn back and camp before Pi Hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. Camp by the sea, directly across from Baal Zephon.
Pharaoh will think the Israelites are wandering around the land in confusion. He will say, 'The desert has trapped them.'
I will make Pharaoh stubborn, so he will chase them. Then I will gain glory through Pharaoh and his whole army. The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD." So the Israelites did this.
When the king of Egypt heard that the people had fled, Pharaoh and his officials changed their minds. They said, "What have we done? We let Israel go, and now they won't serve us."
So he ordered his chariot ready and took his army with him.
He took six hundred of his best chariots and all the other chariots of Egypt, with officers over each of them.
The LORD made Pharaoh stubborn, and he chased the Israelites as they marched out with confidence.
The Egyptians chased them with all Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and horsemen. They caught up with the Israelites while they camped by the sea near Pi Hahiroth, across from Baal Zephon.
As Pharaoh came closer, the Israelites looked up and saw the Egyptians coming after them. They were very afraid and cried out to the LORD.
They said to Moses, "Were there no graves in Egypt? Is that why you brought us to the desert to die? What have you done to us by bringing us out of Egypt?
Didn't we tell you in Egypt, 'Leave us alone so we can serve the Egyptians'? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the desert!"
Moses said to the people, "Do not be afraid. Stand firm, and you will see the rescue the LORD will give you today. The Egyptians you see today, you will never see again.
The LORD will fight for you; you only need to be still."
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Why are you crying out to Me? Tell the Israelites to move on.
Raise your staff and stretch out your hand over the sea. Divide the water so the Israelites can walk through the sea on dry ground.
I will make the Egyptians stubborn so they will follow them. Then I will gain glory through Pharaoh, his whole army, his chariots, and his horsemen.
The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I gain glory through Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen."
The angel of God had been leading Israel's camp. He moved and went behind them. The pillar of cloud also moved from in front and stood behind them.
It came between the Egyptian army and the Israelite army. All night the cloud was dark on one side and bright on the other. Neither army came near the other all night.
Then Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. All night the LORD pushed the sea back with a strong east wind and made it dry land. The waters split apart.
The Israelites walked through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.
The Egyptians chased them into the sea—all Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and horsemen.
In the early morning, the LORD looked down from the pillar of fire and cloud at the Egyptian army and threw them into confusion.
He made their chariot wheels stick so they had trouble driving. The Egyptians said, "The LORD is fighting for them against Egypt!"
Then the LORD said to Moses, "Stretch out your hand over the sea. The waters will come back over the Egyptians, their chariots, and their horsemen."
So Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. At daybreak the sea returned to its normal place. The Egyptians were running toward it, and the LORD swept them into the sea.
The waters came back and covered the chariots and horsemen—the whole army of Pharaoh that had followed the Israelites into the sea. Not one of them survived.
But the Israelites had walked through the sea on dry ground, with a wall of water on their right and on their left.
That day the LORD saved Israel from the Egyptians. Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the shore.
When the Israelites saw the great power the LORD had used against the Egyptians, the people feared the LORD. They trusted in the LORD and in Moses, His servant.
Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the the LORD: "I will sing to the the LORD, for He is great and glorious. The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea.
The LORD is my strength and my song; He has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will praise Him, my father's God, and I will lift Him up.
The LORD is a warrior; the LORD is His name.
Pharaoh's chariots and his army He has thrown into the sea; his best officers sank in the Red Sea.
The deep waters covered them; they sank to the bottom like a stone.
Your right hand, LORD, is strong and glorious. Your right hand, LORD, smashed the enemy.
In the greatness of Your majesty You threw down those who stood against You. You sent out Your burning anger; it burned them up like dry grass.
By the power of Your breath the waters piled up. The rushing water stood like a wall; the deep waters became solid in the heart of the sea."
The enemy said, "I will chase them, I will catch them, I will take their treasures. I will get all I want. I will pull out my sword; my hand will destroy them." "
But You blew with Your breath, and the sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who among the gods is like You, LORD? Who is like You—glorious in holiness, awesome in glory, doing wonders?
You stretched out Your right hand, and the earth swallowed them.
In Your faithful love You lead the people You rescued. In Your strength You guide them to Your holy place.
The nations will hear and tremble; terror will grip the people of Philistia.
The leaders of Edom will be afraid; the strong men of Moab will shake with fear; the people of Canaan will melt away.
Fear and dread will fall on them. By the power of Your arm they will be still as stone until Your people pass by, LORD, until the people You bought pass by.
You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain You promised them. LORD, You made that place for Your home; it is the holy place, LORD, that Your hands built.
The LORD will rule forever and ever."
When Pharaoh's horses, chariots, and riders went into the sea, the LORD brought the sea water back over them. But the Israelites walked on dry ground through the sea.
Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand. All the women followed her, with tambourines and dancing.
Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for He is great and glorious. The horse and its rider He has thrown into the sea."
Then Moses led Israel away from the Red Sea into the Desert of Shur. They traveled three days in the desert and found no water.
When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water because it was bitter. That is why the place is called Marah.
The people complained to Moses and asked, "What are we going to drink?"
Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD showed him a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water became sweet. There the LORD gave them a rule and a law, and there He tested them.

He said, "If you listen carefully to the voice of the the LORD your God and do what is right in His eyes, if you pay attention to His commands and keep all His rules, I will not bring on you any of the diseases I brought on Egypt, for I am the LORD, who heals you."
Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs and seventy palm trees. They camped there by the water.
On the fifteenth day of the second month after the Israelites left Egypt, the whole community of Israelites traveled from Elim and came to the Desert of Sin, between Elim and Sinai.
There in the desert, the whole community of Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron.

“If only we had died by the the LORD’s hand in Egypt! There we sat by pots of meat and ate all the bread we wanted, but you have brought us into this desert to starve this whole group to death!” the Israelites said to them.

Then the the LORD said to Moses, “I am going to rain down bread from heaven for you. Each day the people must go out and gather enough for that day. In this way I will test them to see if they will follow My instructions.
On the sixth day, they must prepare what they bring in, and it will be twice as much as they gather on the other days.”
So Moses and Aaron said to all the Israelites, “This evening you will know that it was the the LORD who brought you out of Egypt.
In the morning you will see the the LORD’s glory, because He has heard your grumbling against Him. Who are we, that you should grumble against us?

The the LORD will give you meat to eat this evening and bread to satisfy you in the morning, because the the LORD has heard your grumbling against Him. Who are we? Your grumbling is not against us but against the the LORD.”
Then Moses said to Aaron, “Tell the whole community of Israelites to come before the the LORD, for He has heard their grumbling.”
As Aaron spoke to the whole community of Israelites, they looked toward the desert, and there in a cloud the the LORD’s glory appeared.
Then the the LORD said to Moses,
“I have heard the grumbling of the Israelites. Tell them, ‘At twilight you will eat meat, and in the morning you will be filled with bread. Then you will know that I am the the LORD your God.’”
That evening quail came and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp.
When the dew was gone, thin flakes like frost lay on the desert floor.
When the Israelites saw it, they asked one another, “What is it?” For they did not know what it was. So Moses told them, “It is the bread the the LORD has given you to eat.”
Moses said, “This is what the the LORD has commanded: ‘Each of you is to gather as much as he needs. You may take an omer for each person in your tent.’”
So the Israelites did this. Some gathered much, and some gathered little.
When they measured it by the omer, the one who gathered much did not have too much, and the one who gathered little did not have too little. Each gathered as much as he needed.
Then Moses said to them, “No one may keep any of it until morning.”
But they did not listen to Moses; some people kept part of it until morning, and it became full of maggots and began to smell. So Moses was angry with them.
Every morning each person gathered as much as he needed, and when the sun grew hot, it melted away.
On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much food—two omers for each person—and all the leaders of the community came and reported this to Moses.

He told them, “This is what the the LORD has said: ‘Tomorrow is a day of complete rest, a holy Sabbath to the the LORD. Bake what you want to bake, and boil what you want to boil. Then set aside whatever is left and keep it until morning.’”
So they set it aside until morning, as Moses had commanded, and it did not stink or have maggots.
“Eat it today,” Moses said, “for today is a Sabbath to the the LORD. Today you will not find any of it in the field.
For six days you may gather it, but on the seventh day, the Sabbath, there will be none.”
Yet on the seventh day some of the people went out to gather, but they did not find any.
Then the the LORD said to Moses, “How long will you refuse to keep My commandments and instructions?

Understand that the the LORD has given you the Sabbath; that is why on the sixth day He gives you bread for two days. On the seventh day, everyone is to stay where he is; no one is to leave his place.”
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The people of Israel called the bread manna. It was white like coriander seed and tasted like wafers made with honey.

Then Moses said, “This is what the the LORD has commanded: ‘Keep an omer of manna for the generations to come, so that they may see the bread I gave you to eat in the desert when I brought you out of Egypt.’”
And Moses said to Aaron, “Take a jar and put an omer of manna in it. Then place it before the the LORD to be kept for the generations to come.”
So Aaron placed it before the Testimony, as the the LORD had commanded Moses.
The Israelites ate manna for forty years, until they came to a land where they settled. They ate manna until they came to the border of Canaan.
An omer is a tenth of an ephah.
All the Israelites traveled from the Desert of Sin, moving from place to place as the LORD had commanded. They camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.
So the people argued with Moses. They said, “Give us water to drink.” Moses replied, “Why are you arguing with me? Why are you testing the LORD?”
The people were thirsty there, and they complained against Moses. They said, “Why did you bring us up out of Egypt? Was it to kill us, our children, and our livestock with thirst?”
Moses cried out to the LORD, “What should I do with these people? They are almost ready to stone me.”
The LORD said to Moses, “Go on ahead of the people. Take some of the elders of Israel with you, and take in your hand the staff you used to strike the Nile. Then go.
I will stand there before you on the rock at Horeb. Strike the rock, and water will come out of it for the people to drink.” So Moses did this in the sight of the elders of Israel.
He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled and tested the LORD by saying, “Is the LORD among us or not?”
The Amalekites came and attacked the Israelites at Rephidim.
Moses said to Joshua, “Choose some men for us and go out to fight the Amalekites. Tomorrow I will stand on top of the hill with God’s staff in my hand.”
So Joshua did what Moses told him and fought the Amalekites. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
As long as Moses held up his hand, the Israelites were winning. But when he lowered his hand, the Amalekites were winning.
Moses’ hands became tired. So they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on each side. His hands stayed steady until sunset.
So Joshua defeated the Amalekites and their army with the sword.
Then the LORD said to Moses, “Write this down in a book as a reminder, and tell it to Joshua: I will completely wipe out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.”
Moses built an altar and named it “The LORD is my banner.”
He said, “Because the LORD has sworn that the LORD will be at war against the Amalekites from generation to generation.”
Now Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, heard about everything God had done for Moses and for His people Israel. He heard how the the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.
After Moses had sent his wife Zipporah away, his father-in-law Jethro took her back.
He also brought her two sons. One son was named Gershom, because Moses had said, “I have been a stranger in a foreign land.”
The other son was named Eliezer, because Moses had said, “My father’s God was my helper. He saved me from Pharaoh’s sword.”
Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came to Moses in the wilderness where he was camped at the mountain of God. He brought Moses’ wife and sons with him.
Jethro sent a message to Moses: “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am coming to you, along with your wife and her two sons.”
Moses went out to meet his father-in-law. He bowed down and kissed him. They greeted each other and went into the tent.

Moses told his father-in-law everything the the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians for Israel’s sake. He also told him about all the hardships they had faced on the way, and how the the LORD had saved them.
Jethro was glad about all the good things the the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the Egyptians’ power.
Jethro said, “Praise the the LORD, who rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of Pharaoh, and who rescued the people from under the Egyptians’ power.
Now I know that the the LORD is greater than all other gods, because He showed His power when they acted proudly against His people.”
Then Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. Aaron and all the elders of Israel came to eat a meal with Moses’ father-in-law in God’s presence.
The next day Moses sat down to judge the people, and they stood around him from morning until evening.

When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that Moses was doing for the people, he said, “What is this you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand around you from morning until evening?”
Moses answered his father-in-law, “The people come to me to seek God’s will.
Whenever they have a dispute, they come to me. I judge between them, and I teach them God’s rules and His instructions.”
Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “What you are doing is not good.
You and the people with you will surely wear yourselves out, because this work is too heavy for you. You cannot do it alone.
“Now listen to me. I will give you advice, and God will be with you. You must be the people’s representative before God and bring their concerns to Him.
Teach them the rules and laws, and show them the way they should live and the work they should do.
But choose capable men from all the people—men who fear God, are trustworthy, and hate dishonest gain. Put them in charge of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.

Let them judge the people at all times. They will bring every difficult case to you, but they will decide the smaller cases themselves. That will make your load lighter, and they will share it with you.
If you do this, and God so commands you, then you will be able to stand, and all these people will go to their place in peace.”
Moses listened to his father-in-law and did everything he said.
So Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them leaders over the people—leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens.
They judged the people at all times. They brought the hard cases to Moses, but they handled the smaller cases themselves.
Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own country.
In the third month after the Israelites left Egypt, they came to the Desert of Sinai.
They traveled from Rephidim and camped in the Sinai Desert, right in front of the mountain.
Moses went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain and said, "Tell the family of Jacob and announce to the Israelites:
"You have seen what I did to Egypt. I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself.
Now if you truly listen to My voice and keep My covenant, you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations, because all the earth is Mine.
You will be for Me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. These are the words you are to speak to the Israelites."
Moses came back and called for the elders of the people. He set before them all the words the LORD had commanded him.
All the people answered together, "We will do everything the LORD has spoken." Then Moses brought the people's words back to the LORD.

The LORD said to Moses, "I am going to come to you in a thick cloud, so the people may hear when I speak with you, and so they may always believe in you." Then Moses told the LORD what the people had said.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go to the people and consecrate them today and tomorrow. Have them wash their clothes.
Be ready by the third day, because on that day the LORD will come down on Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people."
"Put boundaries around the people all around. Tell them, 'Be careful not to go up the mountain or touch its edge. Whoever touches the mountain must be put to death.
No hand may touch it. Whether person or animal, it must be stoned or shot with arrows. No one who touches it will live. When the trumpet sounds a long blast, they may go up the mountain.'"
Moses went down the mountain to the people and consecrated them, and they washed their clothes.
He said to the people, "Be ready in three days. Do not go near a woman."
On the third day, when morning came, there was thunder and lightning. A thick cloud covered the mountain, and a very loud trumpet sounded. All the people in the camp trembled.
Moses brought the people out of the camp to meet God, and they stood at the foot of the mountain.
Mount Sinai was completely covered with smoke because the LORD had come down on it in fire. Its smoke rose like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain shook violently.
The sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder. Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice.
The LORD came down on the top of Mount Sinai and called Moses to the top. Moses went up.
The LORD said to Moses, "Go down and warn the people so they do not break through to see the LORD, or many of them will die.
Even the priests who come near the LORD must consecrate themselves, or the LORD will break out against them."
Moses said to the LORD, "The people cannot come up Mount Sinai, because you warned us and said, 'Set boundaries around the mountain and consecrate it.'"
The LORD said to him, "Go down, then come back up with Aaron. But the priests and the people must not break through to come up to the LORD, or He will break out against them."
So Moses went down to the people and told them.
Then God spoke all these words:
I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the place where you were slaves.
You must not have any other gods besides Me.
You must not make for yourself a carved idol, or any likeness of anything in heaven above, on the earth below, or in the water under the earth.

You must not bow down to them or serve them, because I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God. I punish children for the sins of their parents up to the third and fourth generation of those who hate Me.
But I show faithful love to thousands of those who love Me and keep My commands.
You must not misuse the name of the LORD your God, because the LORD will not leave unpunished anyone who misuses His name.
Remember the Sabbath day and keep it holy.
You may work six days and do all your tasks.

But the seventh day is a Sabbath for the LORD your God. On that day you must not do any work—not you, your son, your daughter, your male or female servant, your animals, or the foreigner living inside your gates.
For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and everything in them. Then He rested on the seventh day. So the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.
Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live a long time in the land the LORD your God is giving you.
You must not give false testimony against your neighbor.
You must not covet your neighbor's house. You must not covet your neighbor's wife, or his male or female servant, his ox, his donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.
