Then Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the pass of Heres.
Gideon captured a young man from Succoth and questioned him. The young man wrote down for him the names of Succoth's leaders and elders—seventy-seven men.

Then Gideon went to the men of Succoth and said, "Here are Zebah and Zalmunna. You taunted me about them and said, 'Are Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand? Why should we give bread to your tired men?'"
He took the elders of the city, along with thorns and briers from the desert, and used them to punish the men of Succoth.
He also tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of that city.
Gideon asked Zebah and Zalmunna, "Where are the men you killed at Tabor?" "They were like you," they said. "Each one looked like a son of a king."
Gideon said, "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As the LORD lives, if you had spared them, I would not kill you."
Then he said to Jether, his oldest son, "Get up and kill them." But the young man did not draw his sword, because he was afraid. He was still young.

Zebah and Zalmunna said, "Get up and kill us yourself, because a man's strength matches his courage." So Gideon got up and killed Zebah and Zalmunna. He took the crescent ornaments from their camels' necks.
The men of Israel said to Gideon, "Rule over us—you, your son, and your grandson—because you saved us from Midian."
Gideon said, "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. The LORD will rule over you."
Gideon also said, "Let me ask you for one thing: each of you give me an earring from the things you took in battle." (The Midianites had worn gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites.)
They said, "We will gladly give them." So they spread out a cloth, and each man threw his earring onto it.

The gold earrings Gideon asked for weighed about seventeen hundred shekels. That was besides the crescents, the pendants, the purple clothes worn by the Midianite kings, and the chains on the camels' necks.
Gideon made the gold into a sacred vest and put it in his city, Ophrah. All Israel was unfaithful to God by worshiping it there, and it became a trap for Gideon and his family.
Midian was brought low before Israel and did not raise its head again. The land had peace for forty years during Gideon's life.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went home and lived there.
Gideon had seventy sons of his own, because he had many wives.
His concubine in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon son of Joash died at a good old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites turned again and were unfaithful to God by worshiping the Baals. They made Baal-berith their god.
The Israelites did not remember the LORD their God, who had saved them from all their enemies around them.
They also did not show kindness to the family of Jerubbaal—that is, Gideon—for all the good he had done for Israel.
Abimelech son of Jerubbaal went to his mother's brothers in Shechem. He spoke to them and to all his mother's family, saying,

"Please speak to all the leaders of Shechem: 'Which is better for you—that seventy men, all sons of Jerubbaal, rule over you, or that one man rule over you? Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.'"
His mother's brothers spoke all these words to the leaders of Shechem. Their hearts turned toward Abimelech, for they said, "He is our brother."
They gave him seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith. Abimelech used it to hire worthless and reckless men, and they followed him.
He went to his father's house in Ophrah and killed his brothers, the seventy sons of Jerubbaal, on one stone. But Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, was left alive, because he hid.
Then all the leaders of Shechem and all Beth Millo gathered. They went to the great tree at the pillar in Shechem and made Abimelech king.
When Jotham heard about it, he went and stood on top of Mount Gerizim. He raised his voice and called out, "Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, so that God may listen to you. "
The trees once went to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree, 'Reign over us.'
The olive tree answered, 'Should I stop giving my oil, which honors God and people, just to wave over the trees?'
Then the trees said to the fig tree, 'Come, you reign over us.' "
But the fig tree answered, 'Should I stop my sweetness and good fruit just to wave over the trees?'
Then the trees said to the vine, 'Come, you reign over us.'
But the vine answered, 'Should I stop my new wine, which cheers God and people, just to wave over the trees?'
So all the trees said to the thornbush, 'Come, you reign over us.'
The thornbush said to the trees, 'If you are truly anointing me king over you, come and take shelter in my shade. But if not, let fire come out of the thornbush and burn up the cedars of Lebanon.' "
Now then, if you have acted faithfully and honestly in making Abimelech king, and if you have been good to Jerubbaal and his family, and if you have treated him as he deserved—
for my father fought for you. He risked his life and saved you from Midian.

But today you have risen against my father's house. You killed his seventy sons on one stone, and you made Abimelech, the son of his female servant, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your brother.
If you have truly acted faithfully and honestly toward Jerubbaal and his family today, then be happy with Abimelech, and let him be happy with you.
But if not, may fire come from Abimelech and burn up the leaders of Shechem and Beth Millo, and may fire come from the leaders of Shechem and Beth Millo and burn up Abimelech."
Jotham ran away and fled. He went to Beer and lived there because of his brother Abimelech.
Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years.
Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem. The leaders of Shechem turned against Abimelech.

This happened to punish the violence done to the seventy sons of Jerubbaal. Their blood was placed on Abimelech, their brother, who killed them, and on the leaders of Shechem, who helped him kill his brothers.
The leaders of Shechem set ambushes on the hilltops. They robbed everyone who passed by. When Abimelech was told about it, ...
Gaal son of Ebed came with his brothers and moved into Shechem. The leaders of Shechem trusted him.
They went out to the fields, picked grapes, and trampled them. They held a festival and went into the temple of their god. They ate and drank, and they cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed said, "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, with Zebul as his officer? Serve the men of Hamor, Shechem's father. Why should we serve Abimelech?
If only this people were in my hand! Then I would remove Abimelech." Then he said to Abimelech, "Muster your army and come out."
Zebul, the city ruler, heard Gaal's words, and he became very angry.
He sent messengers to Abimelech in secret, saying, "Gaal son of Ebed and his brothers have come to Shechem. They are stirring up the city against you.
Now then, come at night with the people who are with you, and lie in wait in the field.
In the morning, when the sun rises, get up early and attack the city. When Gaal and the people with him come out against you, do to him whatever your hand finds to do."
Abimelech and all the people with him got up at night. They lay in wait against Shechem in four groups.
Gaal son of Ebed went out and stood at the entrance of the city gate. Abimelech and the people with him got up from their hiding places.
Gaal saw the people and said to Zebul, "Look, people are coming down from the mountains!" Zebul said, "You are seeing the shadows of the mountains as if they were men."
Gaal spoke again and said, "Look, people are coming down from the center of the land, and one group is coming by way of the Diviners' Oak."
Zebul said to him, "Where is your mouth now? You said, 'Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?' Are not these the people you despised? Go out now and fight them."
Gaal went out in front of the leaders of Shechem and fought Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and Gaal fled. Many fell wounded all the way to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech stayed at Arumah, and Zebul drove Gaal and his brothers out of Shechem.
The next day the people went out to the field, and Abimelech was told.
He took the people, divided them into three groups, and lay in wait in the field. When he saw the people coming out of the city, he attacked them.
Abimelech and his groups rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the city gate. The other two groups rushed on everyone in the field and struck them down.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city, killed the people in it, tore it down, and sowed it with salt.
When all the leaders of the tower of Shechem heard this, they went into the stronghold of the temple of El-berith.
Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the tower of Shechem had gathered there.

Abimelech and all the people with him went up Mount Zalmon. He took an ax, cut a branch from a tree, lifted it onto his shoulder, and said to the people with him, "Hurry and do what you have seen me do."
So each man cut a branch and followed Abimelech. They piled the branches against the stronghold and set it on fire. All the people of the tower of Shechem died—about a thousand men and women.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez. He camped against it and captured it.
There was a strong tower in the middle of the city. All the men and women and city leaders fled there. They shut themselves in and went up to the roof of the tower.
Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it. He approached the entrance to burn it with fire.
But a woman threw an upper millstone down on Abimelech's head and crushed his skull.
He quickly called his armor-bearer and said, "Draw your sword and kill me, so people won't say, 'A woman killed him.'" His young man thrust him through, and he died.
When the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, each of them went home.
So God paid back Abimelech for the evil he had done to his father by killing his seventy brothers.
God also paid back all the evil of the men of Shechem on their own heads. The curse of Jotham son of Jerubbaal came on them.
After Abimelech died, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man from Issachar, rose up to save Israel. He lived in Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim.
He judged Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir.
After him, Jair the Gileadite rose up and judged Israel for twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys. They also had thirty towns in the land of Gilead, and those towns are still called Havvoth Jair today.
Jair died and was buried in Kamon.

The Israelites again did evil in the sight of the the LORD. They served the Baals and the Ashtoreths, along with the gods of Aram, Sidon, Moab, the Ammonites, and the Philistines. They left the the LORD and stopped serving Him.
So the the LORD's anger burned against Israel. He sold them into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites.
That year they crushed and oppressed the Israelites for eighteen years. This affected all the Israelites who lived east of the Jordan in the land of the Amorites, which is in Gilead.
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight Judah, Benjamin, and the people of Ephraim. Israel was in great trouble.
The Israelites cried out to the the LORD, saying, "We have sinned against You. We have left our God and served the Baals."
The LORD said to the Israelites, "Did I not save you from the Egyptians, the Amorites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines?
The Sidonians, the Amalekites, and the Maonites oppressed you, and you cried out to Me. I saved you from their power.
But you left Me and served other gods. So I will not save you again.
Go and cry out to the gods you chose. Let them save you in your time of trouble."
The Israelites said to the the LORD, "We have sinned. Do to us whatever seems good to You, but please save us today."
They got rid of the foreign gods among them and served the the LORD. He could no longer bear Israel's suffering.
The Ammonites were called together and camped in Gilead. The Israelites gathered and camped at Mizpah.
The leaders of Gilead said to one another, "Who is the man who will start the fight against the Ammonites? He will be the leader of everyone who lives in Gilead."
Jephthah the Gileadite was a mighty warrior. He was the son of a prostitute, and Gilead was his father.
Gilead's wife also had sons. When they grew up, they drove Jephthah away. They said, "You will not share in our father's inheritance, because you are the son of another woman."
So Jephthah ran away from his brothers and lived in the land of Tob. Worthless men gathered around him and went out with him.
After some time, the Ammonites fought against Israel.
When the Ammonites attacked Israel, the elders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah back from Tob.
They said to him, "Come and be our commander, so we can fight the Ammonites."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "Didn't you hate me and drive me out of my father's house? Why do you come to me now, when you are in trouble?"
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "That is why we are coming back to you now. Go with us and fight the Ammonites, and you will be head over all who live in Gilead."
Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, "If you bring me back to fight the Ammonites and the LORD gives them into my hand, I will be your head."
The elders of Gilead said to Jephthah, "The LORD is witness between us. We will do just as you say."
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead. The people made him head and commander over them. Then Jephthah spoke all his words before the LORD at Mizpah.
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites. They said, "What do you have against me, that you come to fight in my land?"
The king of the Ammonites answered Jephthah's messengers, "When Israel came up from Egypt, they took my land from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. Now give it back peacefully."
Jephthah sent messengers again to the king of the Ammonites.
He said, "This is what Jephthah says: Israel did not take the land of Moab or the land of the Ammonites.
When Israel came up from Egypt, they traveled through the wilderness to the Red Sea and came to Kadesh.

Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, asking to pass through his land, but the king of Edom would not listen. Israel also sent messengers to the king of Moab, but he refused. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

Then they went through the wilderness and around the land of Edom and Moab. They came from the east to the land of Moab and camped beyond the Arnon. They did not enter Moab's border, because the Arnon was Moab's border.
"Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, asking to pass through his land to their place.
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his border. He gathered all his people, camped at Jahaz, and fought against Israel.
But the LORD, the God of Israel, gave Sihon and all his people into Israel's hand. Israel struck them down and took all the land of the Amorites, where those people lived.
Israel took all the territory of the Amorites from the Arnon to the Jabbok and from the wilderness to the Jordan.
"Now the LORD, the God of Israel, has driven out the Amorites before His people Israel. Should you take their land?
You may keep whatever your god Chemosh gives you. But we will keep everything the LORD our God has given us by driving them out before us.
Are you better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever argue with Israel or fight against them?
Israel has lived in Heshbon and its villages, Aroer and its villages, and all the cities along the Arnon for three hundred years. Why didn't you take them back during that time?
I have not sinned against you, but you are doing me wrong by fighting me. May the LORD, the Judge, judge today between the Israelites and the Ammonites."
But the king of the Ammonites did not listen to Jephthah's message.
Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jephthah. He passed through Gilead and Manasseh, passed through Mizpah of Gilead, and from Mizpah he crossed over to the Ammonites.
Jephthah made a vow to the LORD. He said, "If you will give the Ammonites into my hand,
then whatever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return safely from the Ammonites will belong to the LORD, and I will offer it as a burnt offering."
So Jephthah crossed over to fight the Ammonites, and the LORD gave them into his hand.
He struck them down from Aroer to Minnith, capturing twenty cities, as far as Abel-keramim. It was a very great defeat, and the Ammonites were defeated by the Israelites.
When Jephthah came to his home at Mizpah, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. She was his only child; he had no son or daughter besides her.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, "Oh, my daughter! You have brought me great trouble. You are the one who has troubled me, because I made a promise to the LORD and I cannot take it back."
She said to him, "My father, you made a promise to the LORD. Do to me what you said, because the LORD has taken vengeance for you on your enemies, the Ammonites."
She said to her father, "Let me have this one thing: leave me alone for two months, so I can go up and down the mountains and cry because I will never marry. I and my friends will go."
He said, "Go," and sent her away for two months. She and her friends went up on the mountains and mourned because she would never marry.
After two months she returned to her father, and he did to her what he had promised. She had never been with a man.
This became a custom in Israel: every year the young women of Israel spend four days remembering the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite.
The men of Ephraim got together and went north. They said to Jephthah, "Why did you go to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We’ll burn your house down with you in it!"
Jephthah answered them, "My people and I were in a big fight with the Ammonites. I called you, but you didn't rescue me from them."
"When I saw that you wouldn't save me, I risked my life and went to fight the Ammonites. The LORD handed them over to me. So why are you coming to fight me now?"
Then Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought Ephraim. The men of Gilead struck them down because the Ephraimites had said, "You Gileadites are runaways living among Ephraim and Manasseh."
The men of Gilead captured the Jordan crossings to stop the Ephraimites. Whenever an escaped Ephraimite said, "Let me cross," the men of Gilead asked, "Are you an Ephraimite?" If he said, "No,"
they told him, "Say 'Shibboleth.'" He said, "Sibboleth," because he couldn't say it right. Then they grabbed him and killed him at the Jordan crossing. 42,000 Ephraimites died at that time.
Jephthah led Israel for six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in a city in Gilead.
After him, Ibzan from Bethlehem led Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He married his daughters to men outside his family, and he brought in thirty young women from outside for his sons to marry. He led Israel for seven years.
Then Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem.
After him, Elon from Zebulun led Israel for ten years.
Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried in Aijalon in Zebulun.
After him, Abdon son of Hillel from Pirathon led Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, and they rode on seventy donkeys. He led Israel for eight years.
Then Abdon son of Hillel from Pirathon died and was buried in Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
Again the Israelites did evil in the eyes of the the LORD, and the the LORD handed them over to the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, from the family of Dan, named Manoah. His wife could not have children.
The angel of the the LORD appeared to the woman and said to her, “You are barren and have no children, but you will become pregnant and give birth to a son.
Now be careful. Do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean.
For you are pregnant and will give birth to a son. No razor will touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from birth. He will begin to save Israel from the Philistines.”
The woman went in and told her husband, “A man of God came to me. He looked like an angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask where he came from, and he did not tell me his name.

He said to me, ‘You will become pregnant and give birth to a son. Now do not drink wine or strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean, because the boy will be a Nazirite to God from birth until the day he dies.’”
Manoah prayed to the the LORD and said, “O Lord, please let the man of God You sent come to us again and teach us what to do for the boy who will be born.”
God listened to Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman while she was sitting in the field. Her husband Manoah was not with her.
The woman hurried and told her husband, “The man who came to me the other day has appeared to me again today.”
Manoah got up and followed his wife. When he came to the man, he asked, “Are you the man who spoke to my wife?” “I am,” he said.
Then Manoah asked, “When your words come true, what should the boy’s way of life be, and what should he do?”
The angel of the the LORD said to Manoah, “Your wife must be careful to do everything I told her.
She must not eat anything from the grapevine. She must not drink wine or strong drink, and she must not eat anything unclean. She must obey everything I commanded her.”
Manoah said to the angel of the the LORD, “Please let us keep you here so we can prepare a young goat for you.”

The angel of the the LORD said to Manoah, “Even if you keep me, I will not eat your food. But if you prepare a burnt offering, offer it to the the LORD.” Manoah did not know that he was the angel of the the LORD.
Manoah asked the angel of the the LORD, “What is your name, so we can honor you when your words come true?”
“Why do you ask my name?” said the angel of the the LORD. “It is too wonderful to explain.”
Manoah took a young goat and a grain offering and offered them on the rock to the the LORD. The angel did an amazing thing while Manoah and his wife watched.
As the flame went up from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the the LORD went up in the flame. Manoah and his wife saw it, and they fell facedown on the ground.
The angel of the the LORD did not appear to Manoah and his wife again. Then Manoah knew he was the angel of the the LORD.
Manoah said to his wife, “We will surely die, because we have seen God!”

She said to him, “If the the LORD had wanted to kill us, He would not have accepted our burnt offering and grain offering. He would not have shown us all these things, and He would not have told us this now.”
The woman gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The boy grew, and the the LORD blessed him.
The Spirit of the the LORD began to move him in the camp of Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
Samson went down to Timnah and saw a Philistine woman there.
He went back and told his father and mother, “I have seen a Philistine woman in Timnah. Get her for me as a wife.”

His parents said, “Isn’t there a woman among the daughters of your brothers or among all our people? Do you have to go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?” But Samson said to his father, “Get her for me, because she is the one I want.”
His parents did not know this was from the LORD, because He was looking for a chance to act against the Philistines. At that time the Philistines ruled over Israel.
Samson went down to Timnah with his father and mother. They came to the vineyards near Timnah, and suddenly a young lion roared at him.
The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on him, and he tore the lion apart as easily as tearing a young goat. He had nothing in his hand. He did not tell his father or mother what he had done.
Then he went down and talked to the woman, and she pleased him.
Some time later, Samson went back to marry her. On the way he turned aside to look at the lion’s carcass. He found a swarm of bees and honey inside it.
He scraped the honey into his hands and ate it as he walked. He gave some to his father and mother, and they ate it. He did not tell them the honey came from the lion’s carcass.
Samson’s father went down to the woman, and Samson gave a feast there, as young men used to do.
When they saw him, they brought thirty companions to be with him.
Samson said to them, “Let me tell you a riddle. If you can solve it during the seven days of the feast and find the answer, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.
But if you can’t explain it to me, you must give me thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes.” They said, “Tell us your riddle; we want to hear it.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came something to eat; out of the strong came something sweet.” For three days they could not solve the riddle.
On the seventh day they said to Samson’s wife, “Get your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father’s house with fire. Did you invite us here to rob us?”

Samson’s wife wept in front of him and said, “You only hate me; you don’t love me. You gave a riddle to my people and didn’t explain it to me.” He said, “I haven’t even explained it to my father and mother. Should I explain it to you?”
She wept in front of him all seven days of the feast. On the seventh day he told her the answer because she kept pressing him. Then she told the riddle to her people.

Before sunset on the seventh day, the men of the city said to him, “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” Samson replied, “If you hadn’t used my wife, you wouldn’t have solved my riddle.”

The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully on him. He went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty of their men. He took their clothes and gave them to the men who had explained the riddle. His anger burned, and he went up to his father’s house.
Samson’s wife was given to his companion, who had been his friend.
After a few days, during the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife and brought a young goat with him. He said, "I'm going in to my wife in her room." But her father wouldn't let him go in.
Her father said, "I really thought you hated her, so I gave her to your companion. Isn't her younger sister better than she is? Please take her instead."
Samson told them, "This time I won't be blamed for the harm I do to the Philistines."
Then Samson went out and caught three hundred foxes. He took torches, tied the foxes together tail to tail, and put one torch between each pair of tails.
He set fire to the torches and released the foxes into the Philistines' standing grain. The fire burned everything from the stacked grain to the standing grain, and even the olive vineyards.

The Philistines asked who had done this. They were told that Samson, the son-in-law of the man from Timnah, had done it because his father-in-law had given Samson's wife to his companion. So the Philistines went up and burned her and her father to death.
Samson said to them, "If you do that, I won't stop until I've taken revenge on you."
He struck them down with a great slaughter and then went down to live in a cave in the rock of Etam.
The Philistines went up and camped in Judah, spreading out near Lehi.
The men of Judah asked, "Why have you come against us?" They answered, "We came to tie up Samson and treat him the way he treated us."

Three thousand men of Judah went down to the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Don't you know the Philistines rule over us? What have you done to us?" He said to them, "I only did to them what they did to me."
They said to him, "We've come down to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines." Samson said, "Swear to me that you won't kill me yourselves."
They said, "No, we'll only tie you up and hand you over to them. We won't kill you." So they tied him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.
When he reached Lehi, the Philistines shouted as they met him. Then the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him. The ropes on his arms became like burned flax, and his bonds fell off his hands.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out and took it, and struck down a thousand men with it.
Samson said, "With a donkey's jawbone I've piled them in heaps. With a donkey's jawbone I've killed a thousand men."
When he finished speaking, he threw the jawbone away and named that place Ramath Lehi.
Samson was very thirsty, so he called to the LORD and said, "You have given this great victory through Your servant. Now must I die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?"
Then God split open the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. Samson drank, his strength returned, and he revived. So he named the place En Hakkore, and it is still in Lehi today.
Samson judged Israel for twenty years during the time of the Philistines.
Samson went to Gaza. There he saw a prostitute and spent the night with her.
The people of Gaza were told, “Samson has come here!” They surrounded the city and hid to ambush him all night at the gate. They stayed quiet all night, saying, “We will kill him at dawn.”

Samson lay there until midnight. Then he got up at midnight, took hold of the doors of the city gate and the two posts, pulled them out along with the bar, put them on his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the hill facing Hebron.
After that, he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek. Her name was Delilah.

The Philistine rulers came to her and said, “Trick him. Find out what makes his strength so great and how we can overpower him. Then we can tie him up and hurt him. Each of us will give you 1,100 pieces of silver.”
Delilah said to Samson, “Tell me, please, what makes your strength so great and how you can be tied up and hurt.”
Samson said, “If they tie me with seven fresh bowstrings that have not dried, I will become weak and be like any other man.”
Then the Philistine rulers brought her seven fresh bowstrings that had not dried, and she tied him up with them.
Men were hiding in the room. She said, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He snapped the bowstrings like a thread snaps in a flame. So no one found out the secret of his strength.
Delilah said to Samson, “You have tricked me and lied to me. Now tell me the truth: how can you be tied up?”
He said, “If they tie me tightly with new ropes that have never been used, I will become weak and be like any other man.”
So Delilah took new ropes and tied him up with them. Then she said, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” Men were hiding in the room. He snapped the ropes off his arms like a thread.
Delilah said to Samson, “You have tricked me and lied to me. Tell me now how you can be tied up.” He said, “If you weave the seven braids of my hair into the fabric on the loom...”
She fastened it with a pin and called out, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He woke up and pulled out the pin and the fabric.
Then she said to him, “How can you say you love me when your heart isn't with me? You have tricked me three times now and haven't told me what makes your strength so great.”
She kept nagging him every day with her words until he was worn out and felt he could die.

So he told her his whole heart. He said, “No razor has ever touched my head, because I have been set apart to God since I was in my mother's womb. If my hair is cut, my strength will leave me, and I will become weak and be like any other man.”

When Delilah saw that he had told her his whole heart, she sent for the Philistine rulers and said, “Come back this time, because he has told me his whole heart.” So the Philistine rulers came, bringing the money with them.
She got him to sleep on her knees. Then she called a man and had him shave off the seven braids of Samson's head. She began to weaken him, and his strength left him.
She said, “Samson, the Philistines are here!” He woke up and said, “I will go out like before and shake myself free.” But he did not know that the LORD had left him.
The Philistines seized him, gouged out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza. They bound him with bronze shackles, and he ground grain in the prison.
But his hair began to grow back after it had been shaved.
The Philistine rulers gathered to offer a great sacrifice to their god Dagon and to celebrate. They said, “Our god has handed Samson, our enemy, over to us.”
When the people saw him, they praised their god, saying, “Our god has handed over to us our enemy, the one who ruined our land and killed so many of us.”
When they were in a good mood, they said, “Call Samson so he can entertain us.” So they called Samson from the prison, and he performed for them. Then they stood him between the pillars.
Samson said to the young man holding his hand, “Let me feel the pillars that hold up the building, so I can lean on them.”
The building was full of men and women. All the Philistine rulers were there, and about three thousand men and women were on the roof watching Samson perform.
Then Samson called to the LORD and said, “O Lord the LORD, please remember me. Give me strength just this once, O God, so I may get revenge on the Philistines for my two eyes.”
Samson grabbed the two middle pillars that held up the building and leaned against them, one with his right hand and one with his left.

Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines.” Then he pushed with all his strength, and the building fell on the rulers and all the people in it. So he killed more people when he died than he had killed during his life.
Then his brothers and his father's whole family went down, brought him back, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. He had judged Israel for twenty years.
Now there was a man from the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.

He said to his mother, “The 1,100 pieces of silver that were taken from you—you put a curse on them and said where I could hear, ‘The silver is with me; I took it.’” His mother said, “May the LORD bless my son.”
He gave the silver back to his mother. His mother said, “I dedicated this silver to the LORD from my own hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image. Now I give it back to you.”
So he returned the silver to his mother. She took 200 pieces of silver and gave them to a silversmith, who made them into a carved image and a metal image. They were kept in Micah’s house.
Micah had a house of gods. He made an ephod and household idols, and he put one of his sons in charge of them. That son became his priest.
In those days Israel had no king, and everyone did what seemed right to him.
There was a young man from Bethlehem in Judah. He was a Levite, and he was living there among the clan of Judah.
He left that city, Bethlehem in Judah, to find a place to stay wherever he could. He traveled until he reached Micah’s house in the hill country of Ephraim.
Micah asked him, “Where do you come from?” He answered, “I am a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and I am going to find a place to stay wherever I can.”
Micah said, “Stay with me and be my father and priest. I will give you ten pieces of silver a year, a set of clothes, and your food.” So the Levite stayed.
The Levite agreed to live with the man, and the young man became like one of Micah’s sons.
Micah put the Levite in charge of his shrine, and he became Micah’s priest. He lived in Micah’s house.
Then Micah said, “Now I know that the LORD will be good to me, because I have a Levite as my priest.”
In those days there was no king in Israel. The tribe of Dan was looking for land to settle in, because they had not yet received their share of land among the tribes of Israel.

So the Danites sent five strong men from their clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to scout the land and explore it. They said to them, "Go and explore the land." The men came to the hill country of Ephraim, to Micah's house, and stayed there.
While they were at Micah's house, they recognized the young Levite's voice. They turned aside and asked him, "Who brought you here? What are you doing here? What do you have here?"
He told them, "Micah has done all of this for me. He hired me, and I am his priest."
They said to him, "Please ask God if our trip will succeed."
The priest answered, "Go in peace. The LORD is watching over your journey."

Then the five men left and came to Laish. They saw that the people there lived safely, like the Sidonians—quiet and secure. The land had everything they needed, and there was no ruler to oppress them. They were far from the Sidonians and had no dealings with anyone.
When they returned to their brothers at Zorah and Eshtaol, their brothers asked, "How did it go?"
They said, "Come on, let's go up and attack them. We have seen the land, and it is very good. Don't hold back! Don't be slow to go and take the land.
When you get there, you will find a peaceful people and a spacious land, because God has given it into your hands. It is a place where nothing is lacking."
So six hundred Danites set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, armed for battle.
They went up and camped at Kiriath Jearim in Judah. That is why the place west of Kiriath Jearim is called Mahaneh Dan to this day.
From there they passed through the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah's house.

Then the five men who had scouted Laish said to their brothers, "Did you know that in these houses there are an ephod, household idols, a carved image, and a cast idol? Now think about what you should do."
They turned aside and went to the house of the young Levite at Micah's house and greeted him.
The six hundred Danites stood at the entrance of the gate, armed for battle.
The five men who had scouted the land went in and took the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast idol, while the priest stood at the gate with the six hundred armed men.
When these men entered Micah's house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household idols, and the cast idol, the priest asked them, "What are you doing?"
They said to him, "Be quiet. Come with us and be a father and priest to us. Is it better for you to be priest to one man's house, or to be priest to a tribe and family in Israel?"
The priest was glad. He took the ephod, the household idols, and the carved image, and went among the people.
They put the children, the livestock, and their belongings in front of them and turned to leave.
When they had gone a good distance from Micah's house, the men who lived in the houses near Micah gathered and chased the Danites.
They called out to the Danites, who turned around and said to Micah, "What is wrong with you? Why have you gathered these men?"
He said, "You took the gods I made, and my priest, and went away. What do I have left? How can you ask me, 'What is wrong with you?'"
The Danites said to him, "Do not let your voice be heard among us, or angry men will attack you, and you and your household will lose your lives."
So the Danites went on their way, and Micah went back to his house, because he saw that they were stronger than he was.
The Danites took what Micah had made, and his priest, and went to Laish, to a peaceful and secure people. They attacked them with the sword and burned the city.
No one came to rescue them, because the city was far from Sidon, and they had no dealings with anyone. It was in the valley that belongs to Beth Rehob. The Danites rebuilt the city and lived there.
They named the city Dan, after their ancestor Dan, who was born to Israel. The city had been called Laish before.
The Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Manasseh, and his sons were priests for the tribe of Dan until the land was taken into captivity.
They kept Micah's carved image the whole time the house of God was at Shiloh.
In those days Israel had no king. A Levite who lived in the far side of the hill country of Ephraim took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.
His concubine was unfaithful to him. She left him and went to her father's house in Bethlehem in Judah, where she stayed for four months.

Her husband got up and went after her to speak kindly to her and bring her back. His servant and two donkeys went with him. Her father welcomed him into the house, and when the young woman's father saw him, he was glad to meet him.
Her father insisted that he stay, so he stayed with him three days. They ate and drank and spent the nights there.
On the fourth day they got up early in the morning, and he got ready to leave. The young woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Eat something to give you strength, and then you can go."
So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. The young woman's father said, "Please stay another night and enjoy yourself."
The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law urged him, so he stayed there that night.
On the fifth day he got up early to leave. The young woman's father said, "Please eat something to strengthen you. Wait until the day is almost over." So the two of them ate.

When the man got up to leave with his concubine and servant, his father-in-law, the young woman's father, said to him, "Look, the day is almost over. Please stay tonight. The day is almost gone. Stay here and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can get up early and go on your way."
But the man would not stay the night. He got up and left. He came to Jebus, that is, Jerusalem, with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine.
When they were near Jebus, the day was very late. The servant said to his master, "Come, let's turn aside to this Jebusite city and spend the night there."
His master said to him, "No, we won't go into a foreign city whose people are not Israelites. We'll go on to Gibeah."
He said to his servant, "Come, let's go to one of these places and spend the night in Gibeah or Ramah."
So they went on. The sun went down as they came near Gibeah in Benjamin.
They turned aside there to spend the night in Gibeah. He went in and sat down in the city square, but no one invited them into a house to spend the night.
That evening an old man came in from his work in the fields. He was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah. The people of that place were Benjamites.
He looked up and saw the traveler in the city square. The old man asked, "Where are you going, and where do you come from?"

He answered, "We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to the far side of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there. I went to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am going to the house of the the LORD. But no one has taken me into his home.
We have straw and feed for our donkeys, and bread and wine for me, your servant, the young woman, and the servant who is with me. We don't need anything."
The old man said, "Peace be with you. Let me take care of all your needs. Just don't spend the night in the square."
So he brought him into his house and fed the donkeys. They washed their feet and ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, some wicked men of the city surrounded the house and beat on the door. They shouted to the old man, the owner of the house, "Bring out the man who came to your house so we can have sex with him."
The owner of the house went out to them and said, "No, my brothers, don't do this evil thing. This man has come into my house. Don't do such a disgraceful thing.
Look, here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. I will bring them out. You can have your way with them and do what you want with them. But don't do this disgraceful thing to this man."
But the men would not listen to him. So he took his concubine and brought her out to them. They raped her and abused her all night until morning. At dawn they let her go.
At dawn the woman came back and fell at the door of the man's house where her master was, and lay there until daylight.
In the morning her master got up, opened the doors of the house, and went out to continue his journey. There was his concubine, fallen at the doorway of the house, with her hands on the threshold.
He said to her, "Get up; let's go." But she did not answer. Then he put her on his donkey and went home.
When he reached home, he took a knife, grabbed his concubine, and cut her into twelve pieces, limb by limb. Then he sent the pieces throughout all Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has ever happened or been seen since the day the Israelites came up out of Egypt until now. Think about it, take advice, and speak."
All the Israelites, from Dan to Beersheba and through the land of Gilead, came together as one man before the LORD at Mizpah.
The leaders of all the people and all the tribes of Israel stood in God's assembly. There were 400,000 foot soldiers who carried swords.
The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone up to Mizpah. The Israelites said, "Tell us how this terrible thing happened."
The Levite, the husband of the woman who was killed, answered, "I and my concubine came to Gibeah in Benjamin to spend the night.
The men of Gibeah rose up against me. They surrounded the house at night and meant to kill me. They abused my concubine, and she died.
I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent the pieces through all the land that belongs to Israel. They did a shameful and terrible thing in Israel.
Look, all you Israelites, give your advice and counsel here."
All the people rose as one man and said, "None of us will go to his tent. No one will turn back to his house.
But this is what we will do to Gibeah: We will go up against it by lot.

We will take ten men out of every hundred from all the tribes of Israel, and a hundred out of every thousand, and a thousand out of every ten thousand. They will get food for the people. Then, when they come to Gibeah in Benjamin, they can punish the men for the terrible thing they did in Israel."
So all the men of Israel gathered against the city as one man.
The tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin. They said, "What is this wicked thing that has happened among you?
Now hand over the wicked men in Gibeah. We will put them to death and remove this evil from Israel." But the Benjaminites would not listen to their brothers, the Israelites.
Instead, the Benjaminites gathered from their cities to Gibeah to go out and fight the Israelites.
That day the Benjaminites mustered 26,000 swordsmen from their cities, plus 700 chosen men from Gibeah.
Among all these soldiers were 700 left-handed men. Each one could sling a stone and hit a target as small as a hair without missing.
The Israelites, not counting Benjamin, mustered 400,000 swordsmen, all trained for war.
The Israelites went up to Bethel and asked God, "Who should go up first to fight against the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Judah first."
The Israelites got up in the morning and camped near Gibeah.
They went out to fight the Benjaminites and lined up for battle at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and killed 22,000 Israelite soldiers that day.
The Israelites encouraged each other and took the same positions they had on the first day.
They went up and wept before the LORD until evening. They asked, "Should we go up again to fight our brothers, the Benjaminites?" The LORD said, "Go up against them."
So the Israelites advanced against the Benjaminites on the second day.
The Benjaminites came out from Gibeah to meet them on the second day and killed 18,000 more Israelite soldiers, all of them swordsmen.
Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up to Bethel. They wept and sat before the LORD. They fasted until evening and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to the LORD.
The Israelites asked the LORD a question. In those days the ark of God's covenant was there.

Phinehas son of Eleazar, son of Aaron, was serving before it. He asked, "Should we go up once more to fight our brothers the Benjaminites, or should we stop?" The LORD said, "Go, for tomorrow I will hand them over to you."
Israel set men in hiding around Gibeah.
On the third day the Israelites went up against the Benjaminites. They lined up against Gibeah, just as they had done before.

The Benjaminites came out to meet them and were drawn away from the city. They began to strike down Israelites as before, killing about thirty men on the roads. One road goes up to Bethel, and the other goes through the fields to Gibeah.
The Benjaminites said, "They are running from us, just like before." But the Israelites said, "Let's pull back and draw them away from the city to the roads."
All the Israelites moved from their places and lined up at Baal Tamar. Israel's men in hiding rushed out from their place west of Gibeah.
Then 10,000 chosen men from all Israel advanced against Gibeah. The battle was fierce, and the Benjaminites did not know that disaster was close to them.
The LORD defeated the Benjaminites before Israel. The Israelites killed 25,100 Benjaminites that day, all swordsmen.
Then the Benjaminites saw that they were beaten. The Israelites gave ground to the Benjaminites because they trusted the men in hiding near Gibeah.
The men in hiding rushed in and spread out. They struck the whole city with the sword.
The Israelites and the men in hiding had agreed on a signal: a great cloud of smoke would rise from the city.
Then the Israelites turned in the battle. The Benjaminites had begun to strike down about thirty Israelites. They thought, "Surely they are defeated before us, just like before."
But the smoke signal began to rise from the city. The Benjaminites looked back and saw the whole city going up in smoke to the sky.
Then the Israelites turned back, and the Benjaminites were terrified because they saw that disaster had come on them.
So they fled from Israel toward the wilderness, but the battle caught up with them. The Israelites from the cities destroyed them in their midst.
They surrounded the Benjaminites, chased them, and trampled them down without rest as far as a place east of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand Benjaminites fell, all brave warriors.
They turned and fled toward the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. The Israelites killed 5,000 of them on the roads. They pursued them to Gidom and struck down 2,000 more.
So 25,000 Benjaminites fell that day, all swordsmen and brave warriors.
But 600 men turned and fled to the wilderness to the rock of Rimmon. They stayed there four months.
The Israelites went back to the Benjaminites and put to the sword everyone they found in the cities, including people and animals. They also set all the cities on fire.
The men of Israel had sworn at Mizpah, "None of us will give his daughter to a Benjamite as a wife."
The people went to Bethel and sat there before God until evening. They cried out and wept bitterly.
They said, "Why, the LORD God of Israel, has this happened in Israel? Why is one tribe missing today?"
The next day the people got up early and built an altar there. They offered burnt offerings and peace offerings.

Then the Israelites asked, "Who among all the tribes of Israel did not come up to the the LORD's gathering?" They had sworn a serious oath: anyone who did not come up to the the LORD at Mizpah would be put to death.
The Israelites felt sorry for their brother Benjamin. They said, "Today one tribe has been cut off from Israel."
They asked, "What can we do to get wives for the men who are left? We swore by the the LORD that we would not give them our daughters."
They asked, "Which tribe of Israel did not come up to the the LORD at Mizpah?" Then they found that no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp for the gathering.
When they counted the people, not one person from Jabesh-gilead was there.
The community sent 12,000 brave soldiers and told them, "Go and kill the people of Jabesh-gilead with your swords, even the women and children."
"Here is what you must do: destroy every male and every woman who has been with a man."
They found four hundred young women in Jabesh-gilead who had never been with a man. They brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan.
The whole community sent messengers to the Benjamites at the Rock of Rimmon and offered them peace.
Benjamin came back then, and the Israelites gave them the women they had spared from Jabesh-gilead. But there were not enough women for all of them.
The people felt sorry for Benjamin, because the the LORD had broken one of Israel's tribes.
The elders of the community asked, "What can we do to find wives for the men who are left? The women of Benjamin have been wiped out.
The men of Benjamin who are left must keep their family line, so one tribe will not disappear from Israel.
But we cannot give them our daughters, because the Israelites swore, 'Anyone who gives a wife to a Benjamite is cursed.'"
They said, "There is a yearly festival to the the LORD in Shiloh. It is north of Bethel, east of the road that goes from Bethel to Shechem, and south of Lebonah."
They told the Benjamites, "Go and hide in the vineyards."
"Watch, and when the young women of Shiloh come out to dance, rush out of the vineyards. Each man can grab a wife from the Shiloh women and take her back to Benjamin."

"If their fathers or brothers come to complain, we will say, 'Please be kind to them. We did not take a wife for each man during the war, and you did not give them wives either, so you will not be at fault.'"
The Benjamites did that. They took as many wives as they needed from the dancers, carried them off, went back to their land, rebuilt their cities, and lived there.
Then the Israelites left and went back to their own tribes and families, each to his own land.
In those days Israel had no king, and everyone did what seemed right to him.
In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land. A man from Bethlehem in Judah went to live in the land of Moab for a while. He went with his wife and his two sons.
The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and his two sons were named Mahlon and Chilion. They were Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They went to Moab and stayed there.
But Naomi's husband, Elimelech, died, and she was left with her two sons.
Elimelech's sons married Moabite women. One was named Orpah, and the other was named Ruth. They lived there about ten years.
Then both Mahlon and Chilion died, and Naomi was left without her husband and her two sons.
She heard in Moab that the LORD had taken care of His people and given them food. So she and her daughters-in-law got ready to leave Moab and go back to Judah.
She left the place where she had been living, along with her two daughters-in-law, and they started down the road back to Judah.
Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you, to your mother's home. May the LORD be kind to you, just as you were kind to your husbands who died and to me.
May the LORD give you a peaceful home with a new husband." Then she kissed them, and they cried loudly.
They said to her, "No, we'll go back with you to your people."
Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters. Why would you come with me? Do I still have sons who could become your husbands?
Turn back, my daughters; go your own way. I'm too old to have a husband. Even if I thought I still had hope—even if I got married tonight and had sons—
would you wait for them to grow up? Would you stay single for them? No, my daughters. My life is much more bitter than yours, because the LORD has turned against me."
They cried loudly again. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye, but Ruth held on to her.
Naomi said, "Look, your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and her gods. Go back with her."
Ruth said, "Don't ask me to leave you or to stop following you. Where you go, I'll go. Where you stay, I'll stay. Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God.
Where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. May the LORD punish me severely if anything but death separates us."
When Naomi saw that Ruth was determined to go with her, she stopped arguing.
So the two of them walked on until they reached Bethlehem. When they arrived, the whole town was excited about them. The women asked, "Is this Naomi?"
She said to them, "Don't call me Naomi. Call me Mara, because the Almighty has made my life very bitter.
I left here full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi when the LORD has spoken against me and the Almighty has brought disaster on me?"
So Naomi came back from Moab with her daughter-in-law Ruth, who was from Moab. They arrived in Bethlehem just as the barley harvest was starting.
Now Naomi had a relative on her husband's side. He was a wealthy and respected man from the family of Elimelek, and his name was Boaz.
Ruth the Moabite said to Naomi, "Let me go to the fields and pick up leftover grain behind anyone who is kind to me." Naomi said, "Go ahead, my daughter."
So Ruth went out, entered a field, and began to glean behind the harvesters. It happened that the field belonged to Boaz, who was from the family of Elimelek.
Just then Boaz arrived from Bethlehem and said to the harvesters, "The LORD be with you!" They answered, "The LORD bless you!"
Boaz asked the man in charge of the harvesters, "Whose young woman is this?"
The overseer replied, "She is the Moabite who came back with Naomi from the country of Moab."

The overseer added, "She asked, 'Please let me glean and gather among the sheaves after the harvesters.' She came into the field and has been on her feet from morning until now, except for a short rest in the shelter."
So Boaz said to Ruth, "Listen to me, my daughter. Do not go to glean in another field, and do not leave this one. Stay here with my young women.
Watch the field where the men are harvesting, and follow along after my young women. I have told the men not to touch you. When you are thirsty, go and drink from the jars the men have filled."
At this, she bowed down with her face to the ground and said, "Why have I found favor in your eyes, that you notice me, a foreigner?"

Boaz replied, "I have been told all about what you have done for your mother-in-law since your husband died. You left your father and mother and your homeland and came to live with a people you did not know before.
May the LORD repay you for what you have done. May you be richly rewarded by the LORD, the God of Israel, under His wings you have come to take refuge."
"May I continue to find favor in your eyes, my lord," she said. "You have put me at ease by speaking kindly to your servant, though I do not have the standing of one of your servants."

At mealtime Boaz said to her, "Come over here. Have some bread and dip it in the vinegar." When she sat down with the harvesters, he offered her some roasted grain. She ate all she wanted and had some left over.
As she got up to glean, Boaz gave orders to his men, "Let her gather among the sheaves, and do not embarrass her.
Even pull out some stalks for her from the bundles and leave them for her to pick up, and do not rebuke her."
So Ruth gleaned in the field until evening. Then she threshed the barley she had gathered, and it amounted to about an ephah.
She carried it back to town, and her mother-in-law saw how much she had gathered. Ruth also brought out and gave her what she had left over after she had eaten enough.

Her mother-in-law asked her, "Where did you glean today? Where did you work? Blessed be the man who took notice of you!" Then Ruth told her mother-in-law about the one at whose place she had been working. "The name of the man I worked with today is Boaz," she said.

"The LORD bless him!" Naomi said to her daughter-in-law. "He has not stopped showing his kindness to the living and the dead." She added, "That man is our close relative; he is one of our guardian-redeemers."
Then Ruth the Moabite said, "He even said to me, 'Stay with my workers until they finish harvesting all my grain.'"
Naomi said to Ruth, her daughter-in-law, "It will be good for you, my daughter, to go with his young women, so that you will not be bothered in another field."
So Ruth stayed close to the young women of Boaz to glean until the barley and wheat harvests were finished. And she lived with her mother-in-law.
Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, said to her, "My daughter, shouldn't I find a safe home for you, so things go well for you?
Now Boaz, whose young women you worked with, is he not our relative? Look, tonight he is winnowing barley at the threshing floor.
So wash up, put on perfume, and put on your best clothes. Then go down to the threshing floor, but don't let the man know you are there until he has finished eating and drinking.
When he lies down, notice the place where he lies. Then go and uncover his feet and lie down there. He will tell you what you should do."
Ruth said, "I will do everything you say."
So she went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had told her to do.
Boaz ate and drank, and he felt happy. Then he went to lie down at the far end of the grain pile. Ruth came quietly, uncovered his feet, and lay down.
In the middle of the night, the man woke up and turned over. He was startled to find a woman lying at his feet.
"Who are you?" he asked. "I am Ruth, your servant," she replied. "Please make me your wife, because you are our family redeemer."
"May you be blessed by the LORD, my daughter," he said. "You have shown even greater kindness now than before, because you didn't chase after young men, whether poor or rich.
"And now, my daughter, don't be afraid. I will do for you everything you ask, because everyone in town knows you are a woman of noble character.
"It is true that I am a redeemer, but there is another redeemer who is closer to our family than I am.
"Stay here tonight. In the morning, if he wants to redeem you, good—let him do it. But if he is not willing, then, as the LORD lives, I will redeem you myself. Now lie down until morning."
So she lay at his feet until morning. She got up before anyone could recognize another person. He said, "Let it not be known that the woman came to the threshing floor."
He said, "Bring the shawl you are wearing and hold it out." So she held it, and he measured out six measures of barley and put it on her. Then she went into the city.
When she came to her mother-in-law, Naomi asked, "How did it go, my daughter?" Then Ruth told her everything the man had done for her.
Ruth said, "He gave me these six measures of barley, for he said, 'You must not go back empty-handed to your mother-in-law.'"
Naomi said, "Wait here, my daughter, until you learn how this turns out. The man won't rest until he settles the matter today."
Boaz went up to the town gate and sat down. The other family redeemer, the one Boaz had talked about, came by. Boaz said, "Come over here, friend, and sit down." So the man came over and sat down.
Boaz took ten of the town leaders and said, "Sit here." They sat down.
Then Boaz said to the redeemer, "Naomi, who came back from Moab, is selling the field that belonged to our relative Elimelech.

"I wanted to tell you about it. Buy it here in front of the people sitting here and in front of the leaders of my people. If you want to redeem it, redeem it. If you do not, tell me, so I will know. You are the only one who can redeem it before me, and I come next." The other man said, "I will redeem it."
Then Boaz said, "On the day you buy the field from Naomi, you also take Ruth the Moabite, the wife of the dead man, as your wife. You do this to keep the dead man's name alive on his land."
The other redeemer said, "I cannot redeem it for myself. If I did, I might ruin my own family's land. You take my right to redeem it, because I cannot redeem it."
In Israel, people used to settle a land buy-back or a trade this way. To make it official, one man took off his sandal and gave it to the other man. Everyone knew this proved the deal.
So the other redeemer said to Boaz, "Buy it for yourself." Then he took off his sandal.
Then Boaz said to the leaders and all the people, "You are witnesses today that I have bought from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, Chilion, and Mahlon.

I have also bought Ruth the Moabite, Mahlon's wife, to be my wife. I do this to keep the dead man's name alive on his land, so his name will not disappear from his family or from his hometown. You are witnesses today."

All the people at the gate and the leaders said, "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman coming into your house like Rachel and Leah, who together built the family of Israel. May you prosper in Ephrathah and be famous in Bethlehem.
May your family be like the family of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah, because of the children the LORD will give you through this young woman."
So Boaz took Ruth, and she became his wife. He slept with her, and the LORD gave her a child. She had a son.
Then the women said to Naomi, "Praise the LORD! He did not leave you today without a family redeemer. May his name be famous in Israel.
He will give you new life and take care of you in your old age. Your daughter-in-law, who loves you and is better to you than seven sons, has given birth to him."
Naomi took the child, held him close, and cared for him.
The women living nearby said, "Naomi has a son!" They named him Obed. He became the father of Jesse, and Jesse became the father of David.
This is the family line of Perez: Perez was the father of Hezron.
Hezron was the father of Ram. Ram was the father of Amminadab.
Amminadab was the father of Nahshon. Nahshon was the father of Salmon.
Salmon was the father of Boaz. Boaz was the father of Obed.
Obed was the father of Jesse. Jesse was the father of David.
There was a man named Elkanah from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim. He was the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite.
He had two wives. One was named Hannah, and the other was named Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none.
Every year Elkanah went up from his town to worship and sacrifice to the LORD of Hosts at Shiloh. Eli's two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests of the LORD there.
On the day Elkanah sacrificed, he gave portions to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters.
But to Hannah he gave a double portion, because he loved her, even though the LORD had closed her womb.
Because the LORD had closed her womb, her rival kept bothering her and made her angry.
This happened year after year. Whenever Hannah went up to the LORD's house, Peninnah provoked her, so Hannah cried and would not eat.
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Hannah, why are you crying? Why won't you eat? Why is your heart sad? Am I not worth more to you than ten sons?"
After they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh, Hannah got up. Now Eli the priest was sitting on his seat by the doorpost of the LORD's temple.
She was crushed in spirit, and she prayed to the LORD and wept bitterly.

She made a vow, saying, "the the LORD of Hosts, if You will look on the trouble of Your servant and remember me, and not forget Your servant, but give Your servant a son, then I will give him to the LORD for all the days of his life, and no razor will touch his head."
As she kept praying before the LORD, Eli watched her mouth.
Hannah was praying in her heart. Only her lips moved, and her voice was not heard. So Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli said to her, "How long will you stay drunk? Get rid of your wine."
Hannah answered, "No, my lord. I am a woman with a troubled spirit. I have not drunk wine or strong drink. I have poured out my soul before the LORD.
Do not think of your servant as a worthless woman. I have been speaking from my great sorrow and grief."
Eli answered, "Go in peace. May the God of Israel grant your petition that you asked of Him."
She said, "May your servant find favor in your eyes." Then the woman went on her way and ate, and her face was no longer sad.
Early the next morning they worshiped before the LORD and returned home to Ramah. Elkanah was intimate with his wife Hannah, and the LORD remembered her.
In time Hannah became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel, saying, "Because I asked him of the LORD."
The next year Elkanah and his whole household went up to offer the yearly sacrifice to the LORD and to keep his vow.
But Hannah did not go up. She told her husband, "I will not go until the boy is weaned. Then I will take him to appear before the LORD, and he will stay there forever."
Her husband Elkanah said to her, "Do what you think is best. Stay until you have weaned him. May the LORD keep His word." So the woman stayed home and nursed her son until she weaned him.

After she had weaned him, she took him up with her, along with a three-year-old bull, an ephah of flour, and a skin of wine, and brought him to the house of the LORD at Shiloh. The boy was still young.
They slaughtered the bull and brought the boy to Eli.
She said, "As surely as you live, my lord, I am the woman who stood here beside you praying to the LORD.
I prayed for this boy, and the LORD has given me what I asked of Him.
So now I give him to the LORD. For as long as he lives, he is given to the LORD." And he worshiped the LORD there.
Hannah prayed, “My heart rejoices in the LORD; The LORD has made me strong. My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies, because I rejoice in Your salvation.
There is no one holy like the LORD; there is no one besides You. There is no Rock like our God.
Stop speaking so proudly; do not let arrogance come from your mouths. The LORD is a God who knows, and He weighs what people do.
The bows of the warriors are broken, but those who stumbled are armed with strength.
Those who were full now hire themselves out for bread, but those who were hungry are hungry no more. The woman who could not have children now has seven, but the woman with many sons wastes away.” “
The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings people down to the grave and raises them up.
The LORD makes people poor and makes them rich; He brings them low and lifts them up.

He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap; He seats them with princes and gives them a seat of honor. The foundations of the earth belong to the LORD, and He has set the world on them.
He guards the feet of His faithful servants, but the wicked are silenced in the darkness. No one wins by strength alone.

Those who fight against the LORD will be broken. The Most High thunders from heaven; the LORD will judge the ends of the earth. He will give strength to His king and raise up the power of His Anointed.”
Then Elkanah went home to Ramah, but the boy stayed to serve the LORD under Eli the priest.
Eli's sons were worthless men who did not know the LORD.
This was the priests' custom with the people: Whenever anyone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant would come with a three-pronged fork in his hand while the meat was boiling.
He would stick it into the pot, kettle, cauldron, or pan, and the priest would take whatever the fork brought up. They did this to all the Israelites who came to Shiloh.
Even before the fat was burned, the priest's servant would come and say to the man who was sacrificing, "Give the priest meat to roast. He will not take boiled meat from you, only raw meat."
If the man said that the fat should be burned first and then the priest could take whatever he wanted, the servant would answer, "No, give it now. If not, I will take it by force."
So the young men's sin was very great before the LORD, because they treated the LORD's offering with contempt.
Samuel served the LORD as a boy. He wore a linen ephod.
Each year his mother made him a little robe and brought it when she went with her husband to offer the yearly sacrifice.
Eli would bless Elkanah and his wife and say, "May the LORD give you children by this woman in place of the one she gave to the LORD." Then they would go home.
The LORD visited Hannah, and she conceived and bore three sons and two daughters. The boy Samuel grew up with the LORD.
Eli was very old. He heard everything his sons were doing to all Israel, and that they were sleeping with the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting.
So he said to them, "Why do you do these things? I hear from all the people about your evil deeds.
No, my sons; the report I hear is not good. You are making the LORD's people sin.

If one person sins against another, God may mediate for them. But if a person sins against the LORD, who can pray for them?" Yet they would not listen to their father, because the LORD wanted to put them to death.
The boy Samuel kept growing. He was in favor with the LORD and with people.
A man of God came to Eli and said, "This is what the LORD says: 'When your ancestors were in Egypt under Pharaoh, did I not reveal Myself to your father's family?

I chose them out of all the tribes of Israel to be My priests, to go up to My altar, to burn incense, and to wear an ephod before Me. I also gave your father's family all the food offerings from the Israelites.
Why do you scorn My sacrifice and offering that I commanded for My dwelling? Why do you honor your sons more than Me by fattening yourselves with the best of every offering from My people Israel?'"

"Therefore the LORD, the God of Israel, declares: 'I promised that your family and your father's family would serve Me forever.' But now the LORD declares: 'Far be it from Me! Those who honor Me I will honor, but those who despise Me will be treated with contempt.'
The time is coming when I will take away your strength and your father's family's strength, so that no one in your family will live to old age.
You will see trouble in My dwelling. Israel will prosper, but no one in your family will live to old age."
"Any of your descendants who are not cut off from My altar will bring sorrow and grief to you, and all the rest of your family will die young.
This will be a sign to you: Both of your sons, Hophni and Phinehas, will die on the same day.
I will raise up for Myself a faithful priest who will do what is in My heart and mind. I will build a lasting house for him, and he will walk before My Anointed One always.
Then everyone left in your family will come and bow down to him for a piece of silver and a loaf of bread, saying, 'Please give me a priest's job so I can have something to eat.'"
Now the boy Samuel was serving the LORD before Eli. In those days the word of the LORD was rare, and visions were not common.
One day Eli, whose eyes were so weak he could not see, was lying down in his place.
The lamp of God had not yet gone out, and Samuel was lying down in the LORD's temple, where the ark of God was.
Then the LORD called Samuel. He answered, "Here I am."
Samuel ran to Eli and said, "Here I am, because you called me." But Eli said, "I did not call you. Go back and lie down." So Samuel went back and lay down.
The LORD called Samuel again. Samuel got up and went to Eli. He said, "Here I am, because you called me." But Eli said, "My son, I did not call you. Go back and lie down."
Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, and the word of the LORD had not yet been shown to him.
The LORD called Samuel a third time. Samuel got up, went to Eli, and said, "Here I am, because you called me." Then Eli understood that the LORD was calling the boy.
So Eli said to Samuel, "Go lie down. If He calls you, say, 'Speak, the LORD, for Your servant is listening.'" So Samuel went and lay down in his place.
Then the LORD came and stood there. He called as before, "Samuel! Samuel!" Samuel answered, "Speak, for your servant is listening."

The LORD said to Samuel, "Look, I am about to do something in Israel that will make both ears of everyone who hears it tingle. "On that day I will carry out against Eli everything I spoke about his family, from beginning to end. "I have told him that I will judge his family forever because of the sin he knew about. His sons cursed God, and he did not stop them. "Therefore I swore to Eli's family that their sin will never be forgiven by sacrifice or offering."
Samuel lay down until morning. Then he opened the doors of the LORD's house. Samuel was afraid to tell Eli about the vision.
Eli called Samuel and said, "My son." Samuel answered, "Here I am."
Eli asked, "What did He say to you? Please do not hide it from me. May God do to you and even more if you hide from me one word of all that He said to you."
Samuel told him everything and hid nothing. Then Eli said, "He is the LORD. Let Him do what seems good to Him."
Samuel grew up, and the LORD was with him. He did not let any of Samuel's words fail.
All Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, knew that Samuel was a trusted prophet of the LORD.
The LORD kept appearing at Shiloh, because He revealed Himself to Samuel there by His word.
Samuel’s message came to all Israel. Israel went out to fight the Philistines and camped at Ebenezer, while the Philistines camped at Aphek.
The Philistines lined up to fight Israel, and as the battle spread, Israel was defeated. The Philistines killed about four thousand Israelite soldiers in the field.

When the troops came back to camp, the elders of Israel asked, “Why has the LORD let us be defeated today by the Philistines? Let us bring the ark of the covenant of the LORD from Shiloh so that He may go with us and save us from our enemies.”

So the people sent men to Shiloh, and they brought back the ark of the covenant of the LORD of Hosts, who sits between the cherubim. Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were there with the ark of God.
When the ark of the covenant of the LORD came into the camp, all Israel gave such a loud shout that the ground shook.
The Philistines heard the shout and asked, “What is this loud shouting in the Hebrew camp?” When they learned that the ark of the LORD had come into the camp, they were afraid.
They said, “A god has come into the camp!” They also said, “Woe to us! Nothing like this has happened before.
Woe to us! Who will save us from these mighty gods? These are the gods who struck the Egyptians with every kind of plague in the wilderness.
Be strong and act like men, Philistines, or you will become slaves to the Hebrews, as they were to you. Be men and fight!”
So the Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated. Every man fled to his tent. The slaughter was very great—thirty thousand Israelite foot soldiers fell.
The ark of God was captured, and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, died.
That same day a man from Benjamin ran from the battle line all the way to Shiloh. His clothes were torn, and dust was on his head.
When he arrived, Eli was sitting on a chair beside the road, watching, because his heart trembled for the ark of God. The man went into the city to report, and the whole city cried out.
Eli heard the outcry and asked, “What is this noise?” So the man hurried in and told Eli.
Eli was ninety-eight years old, and his eyes were so weak that he could not see.
The man said to Eli, “I am the one who came from the battle. I fled from the battle today.” “What happened, my son?” Eli asked.
The messenger answered, “Israel has fled before the Philistines, and many people have been killed. Your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, are dead, and the ark of God has been captured.”
As soon as he mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward off his chair beside the gate. His neck was broken, and he died, for he was an old, heavy man. He had judged Israel for forty years.

Now Eli’s daughter-in-law, the wife of Phinehas, was pregnant and about to give birth. When she heard that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she knelt down and gave birth, because her labor pains came on.
