As she was dying, the women beside her said, “Do not be afraid, for you have given birth to a son!” But she did not answer or pay attention.
She named the boy Ichabod, saying, “The glory has departed from Israel,” because the ark of God had been captured and because of her father-in-law and her husband.
“The glory has departed from Israel,” she said, “for the ark of God has been captured.”
The Philistines took the ark of God and brought it from Ebenezer to Ashdod.
They took the ark of God and brought it into the temple of Dagon and set it beside Dagon.
When the people of Ashdod got up early the next morning, there was Dagon, fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the the LORD. So they took Dagon and put him back in his place.

But when they got up early the next morning, Dagon had fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the the LORD. The head of Dagon and both his hands were cut off and were lying on the threshold. Only the body of Dagon was left.
That is why, to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter Dagon's temple in Ashdod do not step on the threshold.
The hand of the the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its nearby towns. He brought ruin on them and struck them with tumors.
When the men of Ashdod saw what was happening, they said, "The ark of the God of Israel must not stay with us, because His hand is heavy on us and on our god Dagon."

So they sent for all the Philistine rulers and asked, "What should we do with the ark of the God of Israel?" The Philistine rulers answered, "Let the ark of the God of Israel be moved to Gath." So they moved the ark of the God of Israel.
But after they moved it, the hand of the the LORD was against the city, causing great panic. He struck the people of the city, young and old, with an outbreak of tumors.
So they sent the ark of God to Ekron. But when the ark of God arrived in Ekron, the people of Ekron cried out, "They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us to kill us and our people!"

They sent for all the Philistine rulers and said, "Send away the ark of the God of Israel. Let it go back to its own place, so it will not kill us and our people." For deadly panic had spread through the whole city, and God's hand was very heavy there.
The men who did not die were struck with tumors, and the cry of the city went up to heaven.
The ark of the LORD stayed in the land of the Philistines for seven months.
The Philistines called their priests and fortune-tellers and asked, "What should we do with the ark of the LORD? Tell us how to send it back to its place."

They answered, "If you send back the ark of the God of Israel, do not send it empty. You must return a guilt offering with it. Then you will be healed, and you will know why His hand has not left you."

"What guilt offering should we send to Him?" they asked. "Five gold tumors and five gold mice," they answered. "Send one for each Philistine ruler, because the same plague came on all of you and your rulers.
Make gold models of your tumors and of your mice that are ruining the land. Give honor to the God of Israel. Maybe He will stop being so hard on you, your gods, and your land."
"Why are you hardening your hearts, like Pharaoh and the Egyptians did? When the LORD punished them, didn't they send the people away?"
"Now get a new cart and two cows that have never been yoked. Hitch the cows to the cart, and take their calves away from them and keep them at home."
"Put the ark of the LORD on the cart. Put the gold objects you are sending back as a guilt offering in a box beside it. Then send it on its way."

"Watch what happens. If it goes up the road to Beth Shemesh, then the LORD has brought this terrible trouble on us. But if it does not, then we will know His hand did not touch us, and it just happened by chance."
The men did just that. They took two milk cows, hitched them to the cart, and kept the calves at home.
They put the ark of the LORD on the cart, along with the box containing the gold mice and the models of their tumors.

The cows went straight down the road toward Beth Shemesh, staying on the main road. They mooed as they walked and did not turn right or left. The Philistine rulers followed them to the border of Beth Shemesh.
The people of Beth Shemesh were harvesting wheat in the valley. They looked up and saw the ark, and they were glad to see it.
The cart came to the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh and stopped by a large stone. The people split the wood of the cart and offered the cows as a burnt offering to the LORD.

The Levites took down the ark of the LORD and the box with the gold objects, and they placed them on the large stone. That day the men of Beth Shemesh offered burnt offerings and sacrificed to the LORD.
The five Philistine rulers saw all this and went back to Ekron that same day.
These are the gold tumors the Philistines sent back as a guilt offering to the LORD: one for Ashdod, one for Gaza, one for Ashkelon, one for Gath, and one for Ekron.

The gold mice matched the number of Philistine cities belonging to the five rulers, from fortified cities to small villages. The large stone of Abel, where they set the ark of the LORD, still stands in the field of Joshua of Beth Shemesh.

But the LORD struck some of the men of Beth Shemesh because they looked into the ark of the LORD. He struck down seventy men, and the people mourned because the LORD had struck them with a terrible plague.
The men of Beth Shemesh said, "Who can stand before this Holy God? Who will take the ark away from us?"
So they sent messengers to the people of Kiriath Jearim and said, "The Philistines have returned the ark of the LORD. Come down and take it up to you."
Then the men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the the LORD. They brought it into the house of Abinadab on the hill and set apart his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the the LORD.
From that day the ark stayed in Kiriath-jearim for a long time—twenty years in all. All the people of Israel longed for the the LORD.

Then Samuel said to all the people of Israel, "If you are coming back to the the LORD with all your heart, then get rid of the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths among you. Prepare your hearts for the the LORD, and serve Him alone. Then He will save you from the Philistines."
So the Israelites put away the Baals and Ashtoreths and served the the LORD alone.
Then Samuel said, "Gather all Israel at Mizpah, and I will pray to the the LORD for you."

When they had gathered at Mizpah, they drew water and poured it out before the the LORD. That day they fasted and confessed, "We have sinned against the the LORD." And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah.
When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, their rulers came up to attack Israel. The Israelites heard about it and were afraid of the Philistines.
The Israelites said to Samuel, "Do not stop crying out to the the LORD our God for us, so that He may save us from the Philistines."
Then Samuel took a young lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the the LORD. He cried out to the the LORD for Israel, and the the LORD answered him.

While Samuel was offering the burnt offering, the Philistines came near to fight against Israel. But that day the the LORD thundered with a loud thunder against the Philistines and threw them into confusion, so they were beaten before Israel.
Then the men of Israel went out from Mizpah and chased the Philistines. They struck them down all the way to a place below Beth-car.
Afterward, Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, saying, "The The LORD has helped us this far."
So the Philistines were subdued and did not come into Israel's territory again. The hand of the the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel.

The cities from Ekron to Gath that the Philistines had taken from Israel were returned to Israel. Israel also took back their territory from the Philistines. And there was peace between Israel and the Amorites.
Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life.
Year after year he traveled around to Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, judging Israel in all those places.
Then he would return to Ramah, because his home was there, and there he judged Israel too. He built an altar to the the LORD there.
When Samuel was old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel.
The first son was named Joel, and the second was named Abijah. They served as judges in Beersheba.
But his sons did not follow his ways. They turned aside after money, took bribes, and twisted justice.
So all the elders of Israel gathered and came to Samuel at Ramah.
They said to him, "You are old, and your sons do not follow your ways. Now appoint a king for us to judge us, like all the other nations."
But when they said, "Give us a king to judge us," Samuel was displeased, and he prayed to the the LORD.
The the LORD said to Samuel, "Listen to the people in everything they say to you. They have not rejected you; they have rejected Me as their King.
They are doing the same thing they have done since the day I brought them out of Egypt. They have left Me and served other gods, and now they are doing it to you.
So listen to them. But you must warn them strongly and tell them how the king who rules over them will treat them."
Samuel told all the words of the the LORD to the people who asked him for a king.
He said, "This is how the king who rules over you will treat you: He will take your sons and put them in his chariots and cavalry. They will run in front of his chariots.
He will choose commanders of thousands and commanders of fifties. He will make some plow his fields and reap his harvest. Others will make his weapons and equipment for his chariots.
He will take your daughters to make perfume, cook, and bake.
He will take your best fields, vineyards, and olive groves and give them to his servants.
He will take a tenth of your grain and vineyards and give it to his officials and servants.
He will take your male and female servants, your best young men, and your donkeys, and put them to work for him.
He will take a tenth of your flocks, and you will become his servants.
On that day you will cry out because of the king you chose, but the the LORD will not answer you."
But the people refused to listen to Samuel. "No!" they said. "We want a king over us.
Then we will be like all the other nations, with a king to judge us and to go out before us and fight our battles."
Samuel heard all the people's words and repeated them to the LORD.
The the LORD said to Samuel, "Listen to their voice. Appoint a king for them." Then Samuel told the men of Israel, "Each of you go back to his own town."
There was a man from Benjamin named Kish. He was the son of Abiel, the son of Zeror, the son of Becorath, the son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, and he was a brave and strong man.
He had a son named Saul, young and good-looking. No one among the Israelites was better looking than he was. From his shoulders up, he was taller than anyone else.
Now the donkeys of Saul’s father, Kish, were lost. So Kish said to his son Saul, “Take one of the servants with you and go look for the donkeys.”

So Saul passed through the hill country of Ephraim and through the land of Shalishah, but they did not find them. Then they passed through the land of Shaalim, but the donkeys were not there. Then he passed through the land of Benjamin, but they still did not find them.
When they came to the land of Zuph, Saul said to his servant, “Come, let us return, or my father will stop worrying about the donkeys and start worrying about us.”
But the servant answered, “Look, there is a man of God in this city. He is respected, and everything he says comes true. Let us go there now. Maybe he can tell us which way to go.”
Then Saul said to his servant, “If we go, what can we bring the man? The bread in our bags is gone, and we have no gift to bring to the man of God. What do we have?”
The servant answered Saul again, “Look, I have a quarter shekel of silver. I will give it to the man of God, and he will tell us our way.”
In Israel in those days, when a man went to ask God something, he would say, “Come, let us go to the seer,” because a prophet was then called a seer.
Saul said, “Good idea; come, let us go.” So they went to the city where the man of God was.
As they were going up the hill to the city, they met some young women coming out to draw water. They asked them, “Is the seer here?”
“Yes,” they answered, “he is just ahead of you. Hurry now, for today he has come to the city because the people have a sacrifice on the high place.

As soon as you enter the city, you will find him before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people will not eat until he comes, because he must bless the sacrifice. After that, those who are invited will eat. Go up now; today you will find him.”
So they went up to the city. As they were entering it, there was Samuel coming out to meet them on his way to the high place.
Now the the LORD had told Samuel one day before Saul came,

“Tomorrow at this time I will send you a man from the land of Benjamin, and you shall anoint him ruler over My people Israel. He will save My people from the Philistines, for I have looked at My people, because their cry has reached Me.”
When Samuel saw Saul, the the LORD said to him, “Here is the man I told you about. He will rule over My people.”
Then Saul came up to Samuel at the gate and said, “Please tell me where the seer’s house is.”
Samuel replied, “I am the seer. Go up ahead of me to the high place, for today you shall eat with me. In the morning I will send you on your way, and I will tell you all that is on your heart.
As for the donkeys you lost three days ago, do not worry about them, for they have been found. And who does all that Israel wants belong to, if not to you and your father’s house?”
Saul answered, “Am I not a Benjamite from the smallest tribe of Israel, and is not my clan the least of all the clans of Benjamin? Why then have you spoken to me like this?”
Then Samuel took Saul and his servant and brought them into the hall. He gave them a place at the head of the guests. There were about thirty men.
Samuel said to the cook, “Bring the portion I gave you, the one I told you to set aside.”

So the cook brought the leg with what was on it and set it before Saul. Then Samuel said, “Here is what was kept for you. Eat, for it was saved for you for this special time, when I said, ‘I have invited the people.’” So Saul ate with Samuel that day.
After they came down from the high place into the city, Samuel spoke with Saul on the roof.
They got up early, and at dawn Samuel called to Saul on the roof, “Get up, so I can send you on your way.” So Saul got up, and both he and Samuel went outside.
As they were going down to the edge of the city, Samuel said to Saul, “Tell your servant to go on ahead of us, but you stay here a while, so that I may tell you the word of God.”
Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul's head, kissed him, and said, "Has not the LORD anointed you leader over His inheritance?

When you leave me today, you will meet two men near Rachel's tomb in Zelzah in the territory of Benjamin. They will say to you, 'The donkeys you went to look for have been found. And now your father has stopped worrying about them and is worried about you. He is asking, "What should I do about my son?"'

Then you will go on from there until you reach the great tree at Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and another a skin of wine.
They will greet you and offer you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from them."

"After that you will go to Gibeah of God, where there is a Philistine outpost. As you approach the town, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place. Lyres, tambourines, flutes, and harps will be playing in front of them, and they will be prophesying.
The Spirit of the LORD will come powerfully on you, and you will prophesy with them. You will be changed into a different person.
Once these signs have happened, do whatever you can, for God is with you.
Go down ahead of me to Gilgal. I will surely come down to you to sacrifice burnt offerings and peace offerings, but you must wait seven days until I come to you and tell you what you are to do."
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul's heart, and all those signs were fulfilled that day.
When they arrived at Gibeah, a group of prophets met him, and the Spirit of God came powerfully on him, and he prophesied among them.
When all those who had known him before saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked each other, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?"
A man who lived there answered, "And who is their father?" So it became a saying, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
After Saul stopped prophesying, he went up to the high place.
Saul's uncle asked him and his servant, "Where have you been?" Saul replied, "We were looking for the donkeys. But when we saw they were not there, we went to Samuel."
Saul's uncle said, "Tell me what Samuel said to you."
Saul replied, "He assured us that the donkeys had been found." But he did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship.
Samuel called the people together to the LORD at Mizpah.
He said to the Israelites, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I saved you from the Egyptians and from all the kingdoms that oppressed you.'
But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and hardships. You said to Him, 'No, set a king over us.' Now then, stand before the LORD by your tribes and clans."
So Samuel brought all the tribes of Israel near, and the tribe of Benjamin was chosen.
Then he brought the tribe of Benjamin near by its clans, and the clan of the Matrites was chosen. Finally Saul son of Kish was chosen. But when they looked for him, he could not be found.
So they asked the the LORD again, "Has the man come here yet?" And the the LORD said, "Yes, he has hidden himself among the supplies."
They ran and brought him out, and as he stood among the people he was a head taller than any of the others.
Samuel said to all the people, "Do you see the man the the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people." And all the people shouted, "Long live the king!"
Then Samuel explained to the people the rules of the kingdom. He wrote them in a book and placed it before the the LORD. Then he sent all the people away, each to his own home.
Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, and some brave men went with him, men whose hearts God had touched.
But some worthless men said, "How can this man save us?" They despised him and brought him no gifts. But Saul kept silent.
Nahash the Ammonite marched against Jabesh-gilead and set up camp there. All the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Make an agreement with us, and we will serve you.”
But Nahash the Ammonite answered, “I will make an agreement with you on one condition: I will cut out the right eye of each of you, and I will bring shame on all Israel.”
The elders of Jabesh said to him, “Give us seven days so we can send messengers through all Israel. If no one comes to rescue us, we will give ourselves up to you.”
When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and told the people these words, all the people cried loudly.
Just then Saul was coming in from the field with his oxen. Saul asked, “What is wrong with the people? Why are they weeping?” They told him what the men of Jabesh had said.
When Saul heard these words, the Spirit of God came powerfully upon him, and he became very angry.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them by messengers through all Israel. He said, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not follow Saul and Samuel.” Then the fear of the LORD fell on the people, and all of them came out together.
When Saul counted them at Bezek, there were 300,000 men of Israel and 30,000 men of Judah.

They said to the messengers who had come, “Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead, ‘Rescue will come to you tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.’” So the messengers went and told the men of Jabesh, and they rejoiced.
Then the men of Jabesh said to the Ammonites, “Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you can do to us whatever you want.”

The next day Saul divided the people into three groups. During the early morning they entered the Ammonite camp and killed them until the heat of the day. Those who were left scattered, so that no two of them were left together.
Then the people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not rule over us? Bring those men, and we will kill them.”
But Saul said, “No one will be killed today, because today the LORD has rescued Israel.”
Then Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.”
So all the people went to Gilgal. There they made Saul king before the LORD. They offered peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.
Then Samuel said to all Israel, "I have listened to everything you said to me, and I have placed a king over you.
Now here is the king walking ahead of you. I am old and gray, and my sons are here with you. I have walked before you since I was young until today.

Here I am. Testify against me before the LORD and before His anointed: Whose ox have I taken? Whose donkey have I taken? Whom have I cheated or oppressed? From whom have I accepted a bribe to look the other way? Tell me, and I will make it right."
"You have not cheated us or oppressed us," they replied, "and you have not taken anything from anyone."
Samuel said, "The LORD is a witness against you, and His anointed is a witness today, that you have not found anything in my hand." They answered, "He is a witness."
Then Samuel said to the people, "The LORD is the One who appointed Moses and Aaron and brought your fathers out of Egypt.
Now stand here, and I will present my case against you before the LORD, reminding you of all the right things the LORD has done for you and your fathers.
When Jacob went to Egypt, your fathers cried out to the LORD. He sent Moses and Aaron, who brought your fathers out of Egypt and settled them here."
"But they forgot the LORD their God, so He handed them over to Sisera, commander of Hazor's army, to the Philistines, and to the king of Moab, and their enemies fought against them.
Then they cried out to the LORD and said, 'We have sinned because we left the LORD and served the Baals and Ashtoreths. Now save us from our enemies, and we will serve You.'
So the LORD sent Jerubbaal, Barak, Jephthah, and Samuel, and He rescued you from your enemies on every side, so you could live in safety.
But when you saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, was coming against you, you said to me, 'No, we want a king to rule over us'—even though the LORD your God was your king."
"Now here is the king you chose, the one you asked for. The LORD has placed a king over you.
If you fear the LORD, serve Him, and obey His voice, and if you do not rebel against the LORD's command, then you and the king who rules over you will follow the LORD your God.
But if you do not obey the LORD's voice and rebel against Him, then the LORD's hand will be against you, just as it was against your fathers."
"Now stand still and see this great thing the LORD is about to do before your eyes.

Isn't today the wheat harvest? I will call on the LORD, and He will send thunder and rain. Then you will know and see how great the wrong is that you have done in the LORD's sight by asking for a king."
So Samuel called on the LORD, and that same day the LORD sent thunder and rain. All the people were very afraid of the LORD and Samuel.
Then all the people said to Samuel, "Pray to the LORD your God for us, your servants, so we will not die. We have added to all our sins the wrong of asking for a king."
"Do not be afraid," Samuel replied. "You have done all this wrong, but do not turn away from following the LORD. Serve the LORD with all your heart.
Do not turn aside after worthless things that cannot help or save you, because they are worthless."
"For the sake of His great name, the LORD will not abandon His people, because it pleased the LORD to make you His people.
I would never sin against the LORD by stopping my prayers for you. I will also teach you the good and right way.
Only fear the LORD and serve Him faithfully with all your heart. Think about the great things He has done for you.
But if you keep doing wrong, both you and your king will be swept away."
Saul was one year old when he became king, and he reigned over Israel for two years.

Saul chose three thousand men from Israel. Two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and one thousand were with Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the troops home.
Then Jonathan attacked the Philistine outpost at Geba, and the Philistines heard about it. So Saul blew a trumpet throughout the land and said, "Let the Hebrews hear!"
All Israel heard the news: "Saul has attacked a Philistine outpost, and now Israel has become a stench to the Philistines." Then the people were called together to join Saul at Gilgal.

The Philistines gathered to fight Israel. They had thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and so many foot soldiers that they were like sand on the seashore. They went up and camped at Michmash, east of Beth-aven.
When the Israelites saw that they were in trouble, because their army was hard pressed, they hid in caves, in thickets, among rocks, and in cellars and cisterns.
Some Hebrews even crossed the Jordan to the land of Gad and Gilead. But Saul stayed at Gilgal, and all the troops with him were trembling with fear.
Saul waited seven days for the time Samuel had set, but Samuel did not come to Gilgal, and the troops began to scatter.
So Saul said, "Bring me the burnt offering and the peace offerings." Then he offered the burnt offering.
Just as he finished offering it, Samuel arrived. Saul went out to meet him and greet him.
Samuel said, "What have you done?" Saul answered, "I saw that the troops were leaving me, and that you did not come at the set time, and that the Philistines were gathering at Michmash.
So I thought, 'Now the Philistines will come down against me at Gilgal, and I have not sought the favor of the LORD.' So I felt forced to offer the burnt offering."
Samuel said, "You have acted foolishly. You have not kept the command that the LORD your God gave you. If you had, the LORD would have made your kingdom over Israel last forever.
But now your kingdom will not last. The LORD has found a man after His own heart and appointed him ruler over His people, because you have not kept the LORD's command."
Then Samuel left and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah in Benjamin. Saul counted the troops who were with him. There were about six hundred men.
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the troops with them were staying in Geba of Benjamin, while the Philistines camped at Michmash.
Raiders went out from the Philistine camp in three groups. One group headed toward Ophrah in the land of Shual,
another toward Beth-horon, and the third toward the border that overlooks the Valley of Zeboim and the wilderness.
There was no blacksmith in all Israel, because the Philistines had said, "The Hebrews must not make swords or spears."
So all Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen their plowshares, hoes, axes, and sickles.
The price was two-thirds of a shekel for sharpening plowshares and hoes, and one-third of a shekel for forks, axes, and for fixing an oxgoad.
So on the day of battle, no sword or spear was found in the hand of anyone with Saul or Jonathan. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.
A Philistine garrison went out to the pass at Michmash.
One day Jonathan son of Saul said to his young armor-bearer, "Come, let us cross over to the Philistine outpost on the other side." But he did not tell his father.
Saul was sitting under a pomegranate tree in Migron near Gibeah with about six hundred men.
Ahijah son of Ahitub, Ichabod's brother, son of Phinehas, son of Eli, priest of the the LORD at Shiloh, was wearing an ephod. The people did not know Jonathan had left.
Between the passes Jonathan planned to cross to the Philistine outpost, there was a cliff on one side and a cliff on the other. One was called Bozez and the other Seneh.
One cliff stood to the north toward Michmash, and the other to the south toward Geba.

Jonathan said to his young armor-bearer, "Come, let us cross over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men. Perhaps the the LORD will work for us, because nothing can stop the the LORD from saving, whether by many or by few."
His armor-bearer said, "Do all that is in your heart. Go ahead; I am with you all the way."
Jonathan said, "Look, we will cross over to those men and show ourselves to them.
If they say to us, 'Wait until we come to you,' then we will stand where we are and not go up to them.
But if they say, 'Come up to us,' then we will go up, for that will be our sign that the the LORD has given them into our hands."
So the two of them showed themselves to the Philistine outpost, and the Philistines said, "Look, Hebrews are coming out of the holes where they were hiding."

The men of the outpost said to Jonathan and his armor-bearer, "Come up to us, and we will show you something." Jonathan said to his armor-bearer, "Follow me, for the the LORD has given them into the hand of Israel."
Jonathan climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer behind him. The Philistines fell before Jonathan, and his armor-bearer killed them as he followed.
In that first attack, Jonathan and his armor-bearer killed about twenty men in an area about half an acre.
Then terror struck the whole camp, both in the field and among all the people. The outpost and the raiders also trembled. The ground shook; it was a great panic from God.
Saul's watchmen at Gibeah in Benjamin saw the Philistine army melting away, running here and there.
Saul said to the people with him, "Count and see who has left us." They counted, and Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing.
Saul said to Ahijah, "Bring the ark of God here." For at that time the ark of God was with the Israelites.
While Saul was speaking to the priest, the turmoil in the Philistine camp kept growing. So Saul said to the priest, "Stop; don't ask God anything more now."
Then Saul and all his men shouted and went into battle. They found the Philistines in total confusion, with everyone's sword against his neighbor.
The Hebrews who had gone over to the Philistines before now joined the Israelites with Saul and Jonathan.
When all the Israelites hiding in the hill country of Ephraim heard that the Philistines were running away, they also chased them in battle.
So the the LORD saved Israel that day, and the battle moved past Beth-aven.

Now the men of Israel were worn out that day, because Saul had made the people take an oath: "Cursed is the man who eats food before evening, before I have taken revenge on my enemies." So no one ate.
The whole army entered the forest, and there was honey on the ground.
When the army entered the forest, they saw honey dripping, but no one put his hand to his mouth, because they feared the oath.

But Jonathan had not heard his father make the people swear. He stretched out the tip of his staff that was in his hand, dipped it into the honeycomb, and put his hand to his mouth. His eyes brightened.
Then one of the men told him, "Your father made the army swear a strict oath: 'Cursed is the man who eats food today.'" The people were exhausted.
Jonathan said, "My father has brought trouble on the land. See how my eyes have brightened because I tasted a little of this honey.
How much better it would have been if the people had eaten freely today from the plunder they found. Then the slaughter of the Philistines would have been even greater."
That day they struck down the Philistines from Michmash to Aijalon, and the people were very tired.
The people rushed on the plunder and took sheep, cattle, and calves. They slaughtered them on the ground and ate the meat with the blood.
They told Saul, "Look, the people are sinning against the the LORD by eating meat with the blood." Saul said, "You have broken faith. Roll a large stone over to me today."

Saul said, "Scatter among the people and tell them, 'Each of you bring your ox or your sheep here and slaughter it in this place and eat. Do not sin against the the LORD by eating meat with the blood.'" So that night everyone brought his ox and slaughtered it there.
Saul built an altar to the the LORD. It was the first altar he built to the the LORD.

Saul said, "Let us go down after the Philistines by night and plunder them until dawn. Let us not leave one of them." They said, "Do whatever seems good to you." But the priest said, "Let us draw near to God here."
Saul asked God, "Shall I go down after the Philistines? Will You give them into Israel's hand?" But God did not answer him that day.
Saul said, "Come here, all you leaders of the people, and find out what sin has been committed today.
As surely as the the LORD lives, who saves Israel, even if it is my son Jonathan, he shall surely die." But no one answered him.
Then he said to all Israel, "You stand on one side, and I and my son Jonathan will stand on the other." The people said to Saul, "Do what seems good to you."
Saul prayed to the the LORD, the God of Israel, "Give a clear answer." Jonathan and Saul were chosen, and the people were cleared.
Saul said, "Cast lots between me and my son Jonathan." Jonathan was chosen.
Saul said to Jonathan, "Tell me what you have done." Jonathan told him, "I only tasted a little honey with the tip of the staff in my hand. Here I am; I am ready to die."
Saul said, "May God punish me severely if you are not put to death, Jonathan."

But the people said to Saul, "Should Jonathan die, he who has brought this great victory in Israel? No, that must not happen! As surely as the the LORD lives, not one hair of his head will fall to the ground, for he has worked with God today." So the people rescued Jonathan, and he did not die.
Then Saul stopped pursuing the Philistines, and the Philistines went to their own place.

After Saul had secured his kingdom over Israel, he fought against all his enemies on every side: Moab, the Ammonites, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. Wherever he turned, he defeated them.
He fought bravely and defeated the Amalekites, saving Israel from those who had plundered them.
Saul's sons were Jonathan, Ishvi, and Malchishua. His older daughter was named Merab, and his younger daughter was named Michal.
Saul's wife was Ahinoam daughter of Ahimaaz. The commander of his army was Abner son of Ner, Saul's uncle.
Kish was the father of Saul, and Ner was the father of Abner and the son of Abiel.
There was hard fighting against the Philistines all the days of Saul. Whenever Saul saw a mighty man or any brave man, he took him into his service.
Samuel said to Saul, “The LORD sent me to anoint you king over His people Israel. So now listen to the words of the LORD.”
“This is what the LORD of Hosts says: I will punish Amalek for what they did to Israel when they ambushed them on the way up from Egypt.”
“Go now and attack Amalek. Destroy everything they have. Do not spare them. Kill men and women, children and infants, oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.”
So Saul called the people together and counted them at Telaim: 200,000 foot soldiers and 10,000 men from Judah.
Saul came to the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley.

Saul said to the Kenites, “Leave now. Get away from the Amalekites, or I will destroy you with them. You showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up from Egypt.” So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.
Saul struck down the Amalekites from Havilah to Shur, which is east of Egypt.
He captured Agag, king of Amalek, alive, but he killed all the other people with the sword.

Saul and the people spared Agag and the best sheep, cattle, fat calves, and lambs—everything that looked good. They did not want to destroy those things completely. But they destroyed everything that was weak or worthless.
Then the word of the LORD came to Samuel:
“I am sorry I made Saul king, because he has turned away from following Me and has not obeyed My commands.” Samuel was angry and cried out to the LORD all night.
Early in the morning Samuel got up to meet Saul. Someone told him, “Saul has gone to Carmel. Look, he has set up a monument for himself. Now he has turned and gone down to Gilgal.”
Samuel came to Saul, and Saul said, “The LORD bless you! I have obeyed the LORD’s command.”
Samuel said, “Then why do I hear sheep bleating and cattle lowing?”
Saul said, “The people brought them from the Amalekites. They spared the best sheep and cattle to sacrifice to the LORD your God. But we destroyed the rest.”
Samuel said to Saul, “Wait, and I will tell you what the LORD said to me last night.” “Tell me,” Saul said.
Samuel said, “Even though you think you are unimportant, you are the leader of Israel's tribes. The LORD anointed you king over Israel.
The LORD sent you on a mission and said, ‘Go and completely destroy the sinful Amalekites. Fight them until they are wiped out.’
Why then did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush to take the plunder and do evil in the LORD’s sight?”
Saul said to Samuel, “I did obey the LORD. I went on the mission the LORD gave me. I brought back Agag king of Amalek, and I destroyed the Amalekites.
But the people took some of the plunder—sheep and cattle, the best of the things meant to be destroyed—to sacrifice to the LORD your God at Gilgal.”
Samuel said, “Does the LORD delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices as much as in obeying the LORD? To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen is better than the fat of rams.
For rebellion is like the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is like worshiping false gods. Because you rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.”
Saul said to Samuel, “I have sinned. I disobeyed the LORD’s command and your words, because I was afraid of the people and listened to them.
Now please forgive my sin and come back with me, so I may worship the LORD.”
Samuel said to Saul, “I will not go back with you, because you have rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected you as king over Israel.”
As Samuel turned to leave, Saul grabbed the corner of his robe, and it tore.
Samuel said to him, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.
The Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man that He should change His mind.”
Saul said, “I have sinned. But please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel. Come back with me, so I may bow down to the LORD your God.”
So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.
Then Samuel said, “Bring Agag king of Amalek to me.” Agag came to him cheerfully, for Agag thought, “Surely the threat of death is over.”
Samuel said, “As your sword made women childless, so your mother will be childless among women.” Then Samuel cut Agag to pieces before the LORD in Gilgal.
Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah of Saul.
Samuel did not see Saul again until the day Saul died. But Samuel mourned for Saul. And the LORD regretted that He had made Saul king over Israel.

The LORD said to Samuel, “How long will you mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, because I have chosen one of his sons to be king for Me.”
Samuel said, “How can I go? If Saul hears about it, he will kill me.” The LORD said, “Take a young cow with you and say, ‘I have come to sacrifice to the the LORD.’
Invite Jesse to the sacrifice, and I will show you what to do. You are to anoint for Me the one I tell you about.”
Samuel did what the the LORD said and went to Bethlehem. The elders of the town met him, trembling, and asked, “Are you here peacefully?”
He said, “Peacefully. I have come to sacrifice to the the LORD. Make yourselves ready and come with me to the sacrifice.” Then he set Jesse and his sons apart and invited them to the sacrifice.
When they arrived, Samuel saw Eliab and said, “Surely the the LORD’s chosen one stands before Him.”
But the the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not judge by his looks or height, because I have rejected him. People look at what can be seen, but the the LORD looks at the heart.”
Then Jesse called Abinadab and had him walk in front of Samuel. But Samuel said, “The The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse then had Shammah walk by. Samuel said, “The The LORD has not chosen this one either.”
Jesse had seven of his sons walk in front of Samuel, but Samuel said to Jesse, “The The LORD has not chosen any of these.”
Samuel asked Jesse, “Are these all your sons?” Jesse answered, “There is still the youngest. He is out tending the sheep.” Samuel said, “Send for him. We will not sit down to eat until he gets here.”
So Jesse sent for him and brought him in. He was reddish, with beautiful eyes and a handsome appearance. The The LORD said, “Get up and anoint him, for this is the one.”
So Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed David among his brothers. The Spirit of the the LORD came powerfully on David from that day on. Then Samuel went back to Ramah.
Now the Spirit of the the LORD had left Saul, and an evil spirit from the the LORD tormented him.
Saul’s servants said to him, “Look, an evil spirit from God is troubling you.”
“Let our lord tell his servants who are with you to look for a man who can play the harp well. When the evil spirit from God comes on you, he can play, and you will feel better.”
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a man who plays well, and bring him to me.”
One of the servants answered, “I have seen a son of Jesse of Bethlehem who plays skillfully. He is a brave and mighty warrior, good with words, and handsome. The The LORD is with him.”
So Saul sent messengers to Jesse and said, “Send me your son David, who is with the sheep.”
Jesse took a donkey loaded with bread, a skin of wine, and a young goat, and sent them to Saul with his son David.
David came to Saul and entered his service. Saul loved him very much, and David became his armor-bearer.
Saul sent a message to Jesse: “Let David stay with me, because he has found favor with me.”
Whenever the evil spirit from God came on Saul, David would take his harp and play. Then Saul would feel relieved and better, and the evil spirit would leave him.
The Philistines gathered their armies for war. They camped at Socoh in Judah, between Socoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim.
Saul and the men of Israel gathered too. They camped in the Valley of Elah and lined up for battle against the Philistines.
The Philistines stood on one hill, and Israel stood on another hill, with the valley between them.
A champion came out of the Philistine camp. His name was Goliath, from Gath. He was about nine feet, nine inches tall.
He wore a bronze helmet and a bronze coat of armor that weighed about 125 pounds.
He had bronze armor on his legs and a bronze spear between his shoulders.
The shaft of his spear was like a weaver's beam, and its iron point weighed about 15 pounds. A man carrying his shield walked in front of him.
Goliath stood and shouted to Israel's battle lines, "Why do you come out to fight? Am I not a Philistine, and aren't you Saul's servants? Choose a man and let him come down to me.
If he can fight me and kill me, we will be your servants. But if I beat him and kill him, you will be our servants and serve us.
I challenge Israel's army today. Give me a man, and we will fight one on one."
When Saul and all Israel heard this, they were very afraid.
David was the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse had eight sons. By then Jesse was an old man.
His three oldest sons—Eliab, Abinadab, and Shammah—had gone with Saul to war.
David was the youngest. The three oldest followed Saul.
David went back and forth from Saul to tend his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
For forty days the Philistine came out every morning and evening and took his stand.
Jesse said to his son David, "Take this basket of roasted grain and these ten loaves of bread to your brothers in the camp.
Take these ten cheeses to the commander of their thousand. See how your brothers are doing, and bring back a report."
Saul and all the men of Israel were in the Valley of Elah, fighting the Philistines.
David got up early, left the sheep with a keeper, and went as Jesse had told him. He reached the camp just as the army was marching out to fight. They were shouting the war cry.
Israel and the Philistines lined up against each other.
David left his supplies with the supply keeper, ran to the battle line, and greeted his brothers.
While he was talking with them, Goliath, the Philistine champion from Gath, stepped out from the Philistine lines and shouted the same challenge. David heard it.
All the Israelites ran from him and were very afraid.

They said, "Have you seen this man? He keeps coming up to challenge Israel. The king will give great riches to the man who kills him. He will also give him his daughter and make his family free from taxes in Israel."

David asked the men standing near him, "What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away this shame from Israel? Who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy the armies of the living God?"
The people answered him the same way: "This is what will be done for the man who kills him."

When Eliab, David's oldest brother, heard him talking to the men, he got angry. He said, "Why did you come down here? Who is watching those few sheep in the desert? I know how proud and wicked your heart is. You came down just to watch the battle."
David said, "What have I done now? Can't I even ask a question?"
He turned away from Eliab to another man and asked the same thing. The people gave him the same answer.
When Saul heard what David said, he sent for him.
David said to Saul, "Don't let anyone lose heart because of this Philistine. Your servant will go and fight him."
Saul said, "You can't go fight this Philistine. You are only a boy, and he has been a warrior since he was young."
David said to Saul, "Your servant has been keeping his father's sheep. When a lion or a bear came and carried off a sheep from the flock,
I went after it, struck it, and saved the sheep from its mouth. When it turned on me, I grabbed it by its jaw and struck and killed it.
Your servant has killed both the lion and the bear. This uncircumcised Philistine will be like one of them, because he has insulted the armies of the living God."
David added, "The LORD who saved me from the paw of the lion and the bear will save me from this Philistine." Saul said, "Go, and may the LORD be with you."
Saul put his own clothes on David. He put a bronze helmet on his head and dressed him in armor.
David strapped Saul's sword over the armor, but he could not walk because he was not used to them. David said to Saul, "I can't go in these, because I'm not used to them." So he took them off.
He took his staff in his hand and picked five smooth stones from the stream. He put them in his shepherd's bag. With his sling in his hand, he approached the Philistine.
The Philistine came closer and closer to David, with his shield bearer in front of him.
When he looked and saw David, he despised him because he was only a boy, ruddy and handsome.
The Philistine said to David, "Am I a dog, that you come at me with sticks?" Then he cursed David by his gods.
"Come here," the Philistine said, "and I'll give your flesh to the birds and the wild animals."
David said to him, "You come to me with sword, spear, and javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel's armies, whom you have insulted.

Today the LORD will hand you over to me. I will strike you down and cut off your head. I will give the dead bodies of the Philistines to the birds and the wild animals. Then all the earth will know that there is a God in Israel.
Everyone here will know that the LORD does not save with sword or spear. The battle belongs to the LORD, and He will hand all of you over to us."
As the Philistine moved closer to attack, David ran quickly toward him.
David reached into his bag, took out a stone, and slung it. It hit the Philistine on the forehead. The stone sank into his forehead, and he fell facedown on the ground.
So David won over the Philistine with a sling and a stone. He struck him down and killed him, even though David had no sword.
David ran and stood over the Philistine. He took the Philistine's sword, drew it, and killed him by cutting off his head. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they ran away.

The men of Israel and Judah shouted and chased the Philistines all the way to the entrance of Gath and to the gates of Ekron. The Philistines fell dead along the road to Shaaraim, all the way to Gath and Ekron.
When the Israelites came back from chasing them, they plundered the Philistine camp.
David took the Philistine's head and brought it to Jerusalem. He put the Philistine's weapons in his own tent.
When Saul saw David going out to meet the Philistine, he asked Abner, the commander of the army, "Whose son is this young man, Abner?" Abner answered, "As surely as you live, O king, I don't know."
The king said, "Find out whose son this young man is."
When David came back after killing the Philistine, Abner brought him to Saul. David was still holding the Philistine's head.
Saul asked him, "Whose son are you, young man?" David answered, "I am the son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem."
After David finished speaking to Saul, Jonathan and David became close friends. Jonathan loved David as much as he loved himself.
That day Saul kept David with him and did not let him go back to his father's house.
Jonathan made a special agreement with David because he loved him as much as himself.
Jonathan took off the robe he was wearing and gave it to David, along with his armor, sword, bow, and belt.
David went out wherever Saul sent him and did well. Saul put him in charge of the soldiers. This pleased all the people and Saul's officers.
When they came back, as David returned from killing the Philistine, women came out from all the cities of Israel to meet King Saul. They sang and danced with joy, playing tambourines and lyres.
The women sang as they played, "Saul has killed thousands, but David has killed tens of thousands."
Saul became very angry, and this song upset him. He said, "They gave David tens of thousands, but they gave me only thousands. What is left for him but the kingdom?"
From that day on, Saul watched David with suspicion.
The next day an evil spirit from God came powerfully on Saul. He raved inside the house while David played the harp, as he did each day. Saul held a spear in his hand.
Saul threw the spear and said, "I will pin David to the wall." But David dodged it twice.
Saul was afraid of David because the LORD was with David but had left Saul.
Saul moved David away from him and made him commander of a thousand. David went out and came in before the people.
David was successful in everything he did, and the LORD was with him.
When Saul saw how successful David was, he was afraid of him.
All Israel and Judah loved David because he led them.

Saul said to David, "Here is my older daughter Merab. I will give her to you as your wife. Only be brave for me and fight the LORD's battles." Saul thought, "I won't harm him myself. Let the Philistines do it."
David said to Saul, "Who am I, and what is my family in Israel, that I should become the king's son-in-law?"
When the time came to give Merab to David, she was given instead to Adriel the Meholathite.
Michal, Saul's daughter, loved David. When people told Saul, he was pleased.
Saul said, "I will give her to him so she becomes a trap for him, and the Philistines will turn against him." Saul said to David a second time, "Today you will become my son-in-law."
Saul ordered his servants, "Speak to David privately and say, 'The king is pleased with you, and all his servants love you. Now become the king's son-in-law.'"
The servants told David these words. David said, "Do you think it is easy to become the king's son-in-law? I am a poor man and not very important."
The servants reported to Saul what David had said.
Saul said, "Tell David, 'The king does not want a bride price. He wants one hundred Philistine foreskins to get revenge on his enemies.'" Saul planned to make David fall by the Philistines' hands.
The servants told David, and he was pleased to become the king's son-in-law. Before the time was up,

David and his men went out and killed two hundred Philistines. He brought their foreskins and gave the full number to the king so he could become the king's son-in-law. Then Saul gave him his daughter Michal as his wife.
Saul saw and knew that the LORD was with David. Michal loved David.
Saul became even more afraid of David. Saul was David's enemy from then on.
Whenever Philistine leaders came out to fight, David had more success than all of Saul's servants. So his name became very respected.
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants to kill David. But Jonathan was very fond of David.
Jonathan told David, "My father Saul is trying to kill you. Be careful in the morning. Stay in a safe place and hide.
I will go out and stand beside my father in the field where you are. I will speak to him about you. Then I will see what he says and tell you."
Jonathan spoke well of David to his father Saul. He said, "King, do not sin against your servant David. He has not sinned against you, and what he has done has helped you very much.
He risked his life when he struck the Philistine. The LORD brought a great victory for all Israel. You saw it and were glad. Why would you sin by killing an innocent man for no reason?"
Saul listened to Jonathan and swore, "As surely as the LORD lives, David will not be put to death."
Jonathan called David and told him everything. Then he brought David to Saul, and David was with him as before.
Later, war broke out again. David went out and fought the Philistines. He hit them with a heavy defeat, and they ran away from him.
But an evil spirit from the LORD came upon Saul while he sat in his house with his spear in his hand. David was playing music for him.
Saul tried to pin David to the wall with the spear, but David slipped away. The spear struck the wall, and David ran and escaped that night.
Saul sent messengers to David's house to watch him and kill him in the morning. Michal, David's wife, warned him, "If you do not save yourself tonight, tomorrow you will be killed."
Michal let David down through a window. He left and ran away, and he got away safely.
Michal took a household idol and put it in the bed. She put goat's hair at its head and covered it with clothes.
When Saul sent messengers to take David, Michal said, "He is sick."
Saul sent the messengers back to see David. He told them, "Bring him to me in the bed so I can kill him."
The messengers went in and found the idol in the bed, with goat's hair at its head.
Saul said to Michal, "Why did you trick me like this? Why did you let my enemy go?" Michal answered, "He said to me, 'Let me go. Why should I kill you?'"
David ran away and escaped. He went to Samuel at Ramah and told him all that Saul had done to him. Then David and Samuel went and stayed in Naioth.
Someone told Saul, "David is in Naioth in Ramah."
Saul sent messengers to capture David. But when they saw a group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing over them, the Spirit of God came upon the messengers, and they also prophesied.
When Saul heard this, he sent another group of messengers, and they also prophesied. Then he sent a third group, and they prophesied too.
Finally, Saul went to Ramah himself. He came to the large well at Secu and asked, "Where are Samuel and David?" Someone answered, "They are in Naioth in Ramah."
Saul went to Naioth in Ramah. The Spirit of God came upon him too, and he walked along prophesying until he reached Naioth.
He took off his clothes and prophesied before Samuel. He lay naked all that day and all that night. That is why people say, "Is Saul also among the prophets?"
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came to Jonathan. He said, "What have I done? What is my guilt? What sin have I committed against your father that he wants to kill me?"
Jonathan said to him, "Never! You will not die. Look, my father does nothing, big or small, without telling me. Why would my father hide this from me? It is not so."

David swore again and said, "Your father knows very well that I have found favor in your eyes. He has said, 'Do not let Jonathan know this, or he will be upset.' But as surely as the the LORD lives, and as your soul lives, I am only one step away from death."
Jonathan said to David, "Whatever you say, I will do for you."
David said to Jonathan, "Look, tomorrow is the new moon, and I am supposed to sit and eat with the king. But you can send me away, and I will hide in the field until the third evening.
If your father misses me at all, then say, 'David begged me to let him run to Bethlehem, his hometown, because the whole family has a yearly sacrifice there.'
If he says, 'That is fine,' then your servant is safe. But if he is angry, then know that he has decided to harm me.
So show kindness to your servant, because you have brought your servant into a covenant with the the LORD. But if I am guilty, kill me yourself. Why should you bring me to your father?"
Jonathan said, "Never! If I find out that my father has decided to harm you, I will certainly tell you."
David said to Jonathan, "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?"
Jonathan said to David, "Come, let us go out into the field." So they both went out into the field.

Jonathan said to David, "By the the LORD, the God of Israel, when I have checked on my father by this time tomorrow—or the third day—and if things are good for David, I will send word to you and let you know.
But if my father wants to harm you, may the the LORD punish me severely if I do not tell you and send you away so you can go in peace. May the the LORD be with you, as He has been with my father.
If I am still alive, show me the the LORD's kindness so I will not die.
And do not cut off your kindness from my family forever—not even when the the LORD has cut off every one of David's enemies from the earth."
So Jonathan made a covenant with David's family, saying, "May the the LORD hold David's enemies accountable."
Jonathan also made David swear again because of his love for him, for he loved him as he loved his own life.
Jonathan said to him, "Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed, because your seat will be empty.
On the third day, go down quickly to the place where you hid before, and stay by the stone Ezel.
I will shoot three arrows to the side, as if I were shooting at a target.

Then I will send the boy, saying, 'Go, find the arrows.' If I say to the boy, 'Look, the arrows are on this side of you; pick them up,' then come, for as the the LORD lives, it is safe for you, and there is no danger.
But if I say to the young man, 'Look, the arrows are beyond you,' go your way, for the the LORD has sent you away.
As for the matter we have spoken about, the the LORD is between you and me forever."
So David hid in the field. When the new moon came, the king sat down to eat.
The king sat in his usual place by the wall. Jonathan sat across from him, and Abner sat beside Saul, but David's place was empty.
Saul said nothing that day, for he thought, "Something has happened to him; he must not be clean."
But on the second day, the day after the new moon, David's place was still empty. Saul said to his son Jonathan, "Why hasn't the son of Jesse come to the meal, either yesterday or today?"
Jonathan answered Saul, "David begged me to let him go to Bethlehem.

He said he needed to go because their family had a sacrifice in the city and his brother had told him to come. He also asked that, if he had found favor in my eyes, he be allowed to get away and see his brothers. That is why he has not come to the king's table."
Saul's anger burned against Jonathan. He said to him, "You son of a stubborn rebel! Do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame and to the shame of your mother?
As long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, neither you nor your kingdom will be secure. Now send for him and bring him to me, for he must die."
Jonathan answered his father Saul, "Why should he be put to death? What has he done?"
But Saul threw his spear at him to kill him. Then Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David.
Jonathan got up from the table in fierce anger. He did not eat any food on the second day of the new moon, because he was upset about David and because his father had shamed him.
In the morning Jonathan went out into the field for the meeting with David, and a small boy was with him.
He said to his boy, "Run and find the arrows I shoot." As the boy ran, Jonathan shot an arrow beyond him.
When the boy came to the place where Jonathan's arrow had landed, Jonathan called after him, "Isn't the arrow beyond you?"
Jonathan called again, "Hurry! Go fast! Do not stop!" Jonathan's boy picked up the arrows and brought them to his master.
The boy did not know what was going on, but Jonathan and David knew.
Jonathan gave his weapons to his boy and said, "Go, carry them into the city."
As soon as the boy had gone, David rose from the south side of the stone and fell facedown to the ground. He bowed three times. Then the two men kissed and wept together, David weeping more.

Jonathan said to David, "Go in peace. We have both sworn by the name of the the LORD that the the LORD will be between me and you and between my descendants and your descendants forever." Then David got up and left, and Jonathan went back into the city.
David went to Nob to see Ahimelech the priest. Ahimelech trembled when he met David. He asked, "Why are you alone? No one is with you."
David answered, "The king sent me on a secret mission. He told me, 'No one is to know anything about this mission or what I commanded you. I have told the young men to meet me at a certain place.'"
"Now, what do you have on hand? Give me five loaves of bread, or whatever you can find."
The priest answered, "I have no ordinary bread here. But there is holy bread if the young men have kept themselves from women."
David answered, "Women have been kept away from us, as usual when I travel. The young men's bodies are holy even on ordinary trips. How much more so today!"
So the priest gave him the holy bread. No other bread was there except the bread of the Presence, which had been removed from before the LORD to be replaced by hot bread on the day it was taken away.
That day one of Saul's servants was held back before the LORD. His name was Doeg the Edomite, the chief of Saul's herdsmen.
David asked Ahimelech, "Do you have a spear or sword here? I did not bring my sword or other weapons, because the king's business was urgent."

The priest said, "The sword of Goliath the Philistine, whom you killed in the Valley of Elah, is here. It is wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod. If you want it, take it. There is no other sword here." David said, "There is none like it. Give it to me."
That same day David got up and fled from Saul. He went to Achish, king of Gath.
Achish's servants said to him, "Isn't this David, the king of the land? Didn't the women sing about him in their dances, 'Saul has killed his thousands, and David his ten thousands'?"
David was deeply troubled by these words and was very afraid of Achish, king of Gath.
So he changed his behavior before them. He acted like a madman in their hands. He scratched on the doors of the gate and let saliva run down his beard.
Achish said to his servants, "Look, you can see the man is insane. Why did you bring him to me?
Do I not have enough madmen already? Why did you bring this man to act insane in front of me? Is he going to come into my house?"
David left that place and escaped to the cave of Adullam. When his brothers and all his father's household heard about it, they went down to him there.
All the men who were in trouble, all the men who owed money, and all the men who were bitter and unhappy gathered to him. He became their leader, and about four hundred men were with him.
David left there and went to Mizpah in Moab. He said to the king of Moab, "Please let my father and mother stay with you until I know what God will do for me."
He left them in the care of the king of Moab, and they stayed with him the whole time David was in the stronghold.
The prophet Gad told David, "Do not stay in the stronghold. Go into the land of Judah." So David left and went to the forest of Hereth.
Saul heard that David and his men had been found. Saul was sitting under the tamarisk tree in Ramah, holding his spear, with all his servants standing around him.
Saul said to the servants standing around him, "Listen, men of Benjamin! Will Jesse's son give all of you fields and vineyards? Will he make all of you commanders of thousands and hundreds?

For all of you have plotted against me. No one tells me when my son makes an agreement with Jesse's son. None of you is concerned about me or tells me that my son has stirred up my servant to ambush me, as he is doing today."
Doeg the Edomite, who was standing with Saul's servants, said, "I saw Jesse's son go to Ahimelech son of Ahitub at Nob.
He asked the the LORD for him, gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine."
Then the king sent for Ahimelech the priest, son of Ahitub, and all his father's family—the priests at Nob—and they all came to the king.
Saul said, "Listen now, son of Ahitub." He answered, "Here I am, my lord."
Saul said to him, "Why have you and Jesse's son plotted against me by giving him bread and a sword and asking God for him, so he could turn against me and ambush me, as he is doing today?"
Ahimelech answered the king, "Who among all your servants is as faithful as David? He is the king's son-in-law, captain of your bodyguard, and honored in your house.
Have I only now started asking God for him? I would never do that! Do not let the king accuse me or any of my father's household, for your servant knew nothing about this, either small or great."
The king said, "You will surely die, Ahimelech—you and all your father's household."

The king said to the guards standing around him, "Go and kill the priests of the the LORD, because they have taken David's side. They knew he was running away and did not tell me." But the king's servants refused to harm the priests of the the LORD.
Then the king said to Doeg, "You go and strike down the priests!" So Doeg the Edomite went and struck down the priests. That day he killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod.
He also put the town of Nob, the priests' town, to the sword, killing men and women, children and babies, and even oxen, donkeys, and sheep.
But one son of Ahimelech son of Ahitub escaped and fled to David. His name was Abiathar.
Abiathar told David that Saul had killed the priests of the the LORD.
David said to Abiathar, "I knew that day, when Doeg the Edomite was there, that he would tell Saul. I am responsible for the death of all your father's household.
Stay with me. Do not be afraid, for the one who is trying to kill me is trying to kill you too. You will be safe with me."
People told David, "The Philistines are fighting against Keilah and stealing grain from the threshing floors."
David asked the LORD, "Should I go and attack these Philistines?" The LORD said, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."
David's men said to him, "We are afraid here in Judah. How much more if we go to Keilah to fight the Philistine armies!"
David asked the LORD again. The LORD answered him, "Go down to Keilah, because I am handing the Philistines over to you."
David and his men went to Keilah and fought the Philistines. They struck them with a great blow, drove off their livestock, and saved the people of Keilah.
When Abiathar son of Ahimelech fled to David at Keilah, he came with an ephod in his hand.
Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah. Saul said, "God has handed him over to me, because he has trapped himself in a town with gates and bars."
Saul called all the people to war, to go down to Keilah and besiege David and his men.
David learned that Saul was plotting harm against him. He said to Abiathar the priest, "Bring the ephod here."
David said, "The LORD God of Israel, Your servant has heard that Saul is trying to come to Keilah to destroy the city because of me.
"Will the men of Keilah hand me over to him? Will Saul come down, as Your servant has heard? The LORD God of Israel, please tell Your servant." The LORD said, "He will come down."
David asked, "Will the men of Keilah hand me and my men over to Saul?" The LORD said, "They will."
David and his men, about six hundred, got up and left Keilah. They went wherever they could. When Saul heard that David had escaped from Keilah, he stopped pursuing him.
David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and in the hill country of the wilderness of Ziph. Saul looked for him every day, but God did not hand David over to him.
David saw that Saul had come out to seek his life. David was in the wilderness of Ziph at Horesh.
Jonathan, Saul's son, came to David at Horesh and encouraged him to trust in God.
He said to David, "Don't be afraid. My father Saul won't find you. You will be king over Israel, and I will be second to you. Even my father Saul knows that."
The two of them made a covenant before the LORD. David stayed at Horesh, and Jonathan went home.
The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Isn't David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh, on the hill of Hachilah south of Jeshimon?
Now, O king, come down whenever you want. Our part is to hand him over to you."
Saul said, "May the LORD bless you, for you have had pity on me.
Go and make sure of it. Learn and watch where he usually goes and who has seen him there, because I am told he is very crafty.

Look around and learn about all the hiding places where he hides. Then come back to me with sure information, and I will go with you. If he is in the land, I will search him out among all the clans of Judah."
They got up and went to Ziph ahead of Saul. David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the Arabah south of Jeshimon.
Saul and his men went to look for David. When David was told, he went down to the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. Saul heard about it and chased David into the wilderness of Maon.

Saul was on one side of the mountain, and David and his men were on the other side. David was hurrying to get away from Saul, while Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them.
Then a messenger came to Saul and said, "Hurry! The Philistines have raided the land."
So Saul turned back from chasing David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place is called the Rock of Escape.
David went up from there and stayed in the strongholds of En Gedi.
After Saul came back from fighting the Philistines, someone told him, "David is in the Desert of En Gedi."
So Saul took three thousand of Israel's best young men and went to look for David and his men near the rocks where the wild goats live.
He came to the sheep pens along the road. There was a cave there, and Saul went in to use the bathroom. David and his men were sitting far back in the cave.

David's men said to him, "This is the day the LORD spoke about when He said to you, 'I will give your enemy into your hands, and you can do to him whatever seems good to you.'" Then David got up quietly and cut off the corner of Saul's robe.
Afterward, David felt guilty because he had cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
He said to his men, "The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my master, the LORD's anointed, or lift my hand against him, because he is the LORD's anointed."
With these words David stopped his men and did not let them rise up against Saul. Then Saul got up from the cave and went on his way.
After that, David got up and went out of the cave. He called after Saul, "My lord the king!" When Saul looked back, David bowed low with his face to the ground.
David said to Saul, "Why do you listen to people who say, 'David is trying to hurt you'?

"This day your own eyes have seen how the LORD gave you into my hand in the cave. Some told me to kill you, but I spared you. I said, 'I will not lift my hand against my lord, because he is the LORD's anointed.'

"Look, my father, look at this piece of your robe in my hand! I cut off the corner of your robe, but I did not kill you. See that there is no wrong or rebellion in my hands. I have not sinned against you, though you are hunting me to take my life.
"May the LORD judge between you and me. May the LORD pay you back for what you have done to me, but my hand will not touch you.
"As the old saying goes, 'Evil comes from evil people,' so my hand will not touch you.
"Who am I that the king of Israel is chasing me? I'm no more than a dead dog or a flea.
"May the LORD be the judge and decide between us. May He look into my case and defend it. May He save me from your hand."
When David finished saying this, Saul asked, "Is that your voice, David my son?" Then Saul cried out loud.
"You are more righteous than I am. You have done good to me, but I have done evil to you.
"Today you have shown how well you treated me. When the LORD gave me into your hand, you did not kill me.
"When a man finds his enemy, does he let him go unharmed? May the LORD reward you with good for what you have done to me today.
"Now I know for sure that you will be king and that the kingdom of Israel will be established by you.
"Now swear to me by the LORD that you will not wipe out my family after me or destroy my name from my father's house."
David swore to Saul. Then Saul went home, but David and his men went up to the stronghold.
Samuel died. All the people of Israel gathered, mourned for him, and buried him at his home in Ramah. Then David got up and went down to the Desert of Paran.
A man in Maon had property in Carmel. He was very rich, with three thousand sheep and one thousand goats. He was shearing his sheep in Carmel.
The man’s name was Nabal, and his wife’s name was Abigail. She was wise and beautiful, but he was harsh and mean in the way he acted. He was a Calebite.
While David was in the wilderness, he heard that Nabal was shearing his sheep.
So David sent ten young men and said, “Go up to Nabal at Carmel and greet him in my name.
Say to him, ‘Peace to you, to your house, and to all you have.’
I have heard that you have shearers. Your shepherds were with us. We did not insult them, and nothing of theirs was missing the whole time they were in Carmel.

Ask your servants, and they will tell you. So let these young men find favor with you, because we have come on a feast day. Please give whatever you have on hand to your servants and to your son David.”
David’s young men went and said all this to Nabal in David’s name. Then they waited.
Nabal answered David’s servants, “Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse? There are many servants today who are running away from their masters.
Why should I take my bread, my water, and the meat I have cooked for my shearers and give it to men I do not even know where they come from?”
David’s young men turned and went back. They told him everything Nabal had said.
David said to his men, “Each of you, strap on your sword.” So David strapped on his sword, and about four hundred men went with him. Two hundred men stayed with the supplies.
One of the young men told Abigail, Nabal’s wife, “David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet our master, but he insulted them.
These men were very good to us. They did not mistreat us, and we did not miss anything the whole time we were with them in the fields.
They were like a wall around us, both day and night, the whole time we were with them tending the sheep.
Now think about what you should do, because trouble is coming to our master and to his whole household. He is such a worthless man that no one can talk to him.”

Abigail hurried and took two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five sheep that were already prepared, five measures of roasted grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of pressed figs. She loaded them on donkeys.
She said to her servants, “Go on ahead of me. I will follow you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
As she rode her donkey down the mountain path, David and his men were coming down toward her, and she met them.
David had said, “I guarded everything this man owned in the wilderness for nothing. Not one thing of his was missing. But he has paid me back evil for good.
May God punish David’s enemies, and even more, if by morning I leave alive even one man of all who belong to him.”
When Abigail saw David, she hurried and got off her donkey. She fell facedown on the ground and bowed before David.
She fell at his feet and said, “My lord, let the blame be on me. Please let your servant speak to you and listen to my words.
My lord, please do not pay attention to this worthless man Nabal. He is just like his name—Nabal means ‘fool,’ and that is what he is. But I, your servant, did not see the young men you sent.

Now, my lord, as surely as the the LORD lives and you live, the the LORD has kept you from bloodshed and from avenging yourself with your own hand. May your enemies and everyone who wants to harm my lord be like Nabal.
Now let this gift your servant has brought to my lord be given to the young men who follow my lord.” “

Please forgive your servant’s wrong. For the the LORD will surely make my lord’s family strong and lasting, because my lord fights the the LORD’s battles. May no evil be found in you as long as you live.
Even if someone rises up to chase you and take your life, your life will be kept safe by the the LORD your God. But He will throw away the lives of your enemies, like a stone thrown from a sling.
When the the LORD has done for my lord everything He promised, and has made you leader over Israel,
you will not have this grief or this guilty conscience from shedding blood without cause or from taking your own revenge. When the the LORD has been good to my lord, remember your servant.”
David said to Abigail, “Praise the the LORD, the God of Israel, who sent you to meet me today.
Blessed be your good sense, and blessed be you, for keeping me today from bloodshed and from avenging myself.
As surely as the the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, who kept me from harming you, if you had not hurried to meet me, not one man of Nabal’s would have been left alive by morning.”
Then David accepted what she brought and said to her, “Go home in peace. I have listened to you, and I have granted your request.”
Abigail went to Nabal. He was in his house, holding a feast fit for a king. He was in good spirits and very drunk. She did not tell him anything until morning.
In the morning, when the wine had worn off, she told him everything. His heart failed, and he became like a stone.
About ten days later, the the LORD struck Nabal, and he died.
