When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, “Praise the the LORD! He has defended my cause against Nabal’s insult and has kept His servant from doing wrong. The the LORD has brought Nabal’s evil back on his own head.” Then David sent messengers to ask Abigail to become his wife.
David’s servants went to Abigail at Carmel and said, “David has sent us to you to take you as his wife.”
She got up, bowed facedown to the ground, and said, “Here is your servant, ready to wash the feet of my lord’s servants.”
Abigail hurried and got up. She rode on a donkey, with five of her young women walking behind her. She went with David’s messengers and became his wife.
David had also married Ahinoam from Jezreel. So both of them were his wives.
But Saul had given his daughter Michal, David’s wife, to Palti son of Laish, who was from Gallim.
The Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah and said, "Isn't David hiding on the hill of Hakilah, facing Jeshimon?"
So Saul got up and took three thousand chosen men of Israel with him. He went down to the wilderness of Ziph to look for David.
Saul camped beside the road on the hill of Hakilah, facing Jeshimon. David stayed in the wilderness. When he saw that Saul had come after him there,
David sent out spies and learned for sure that Saul had come.
David got up and went to the place where Saul had camped. He saw where Saul and Abner son of Ner, the army commander, were lying. Saul was lying in the camp, and the people were camped around him.
David said to Ahimelech the Hittite and to Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, "Who will go down with me to Saul in the camp?" Abishai said, "I will go down with you."
So David and Abishai went to the people by night. There was Saul, sleeping in the camp. His spear was stuck in the ground at his head. Abner and the people were sleeping around him.
Abishai said to David, "Today God has given your enemy into your hand. Now let me pin him to the ground with one spear thrust. I won't need a second."
But David said to Abishai, "Don't destroy him. Who can hurt the the LORD's anointed and not be guilty?"
David also said, "As the the LORD lives, the the LORD will strike him down, or his day will come and he will die, or he will go into battle and be swept away."
"The The LORD forbid that I should hurt the the LORD's anointed. Now take the spear by his head and the water jar, and let's go."

So David took the spear and the water jar from beside Saul's head, and they left. No one saw them or knew about it, and no one woke up, because they were all asleep. A deep sleep from the the LORD had fallen on them.
David crossed over to the other side and stood on top of the hill far away, with a large space between them.
David called out to the people and to Abner son of Ner, "Won't you answer, Abner?" Abner answered, "Who are you who is calling to the king?"
David said to Abner, "Aren't you a man? Who is like you in Israel? Why didn't you guard your lord the king? Someone came in to destroy the king, your lord.

What you did was not good. As the the LORD lives, you deserve death because you did not guard your lord, the the LORD's anointed. Now look where the king's spear and water jar are, the ones that were by his head."
Saul recognized David's voice and said, "Is that your voice, my son David?" David said, "It is my voice, my lord king."
David said, "Why does my lord chase his servant? What have I done? What wrong is in my hand?

Now please, my lord king, listen to your servant's words. If the the LORD has stirred you up against me, may He accept an offering. But if people have done it, may they be cursed before the the LORD. They have driven me out today from sharing in the the LORD's land, as if telling me to worship other gods.
Don't let my blood fall to the ground far from the the LORD's presence. The king of Israel has come out to look for one tiny flea, like hunting a bird in the hills."
Saul said, "I have sinned. Return, my son David. I will not harm you again, because my life was precious in your eyes today. I have acted foolishly and made a great mistake."
David answered, "Here is the king's spear. Let one of the young men come over and get it.
The The LORD will repay each man for his right living and faithfulness. The the LORD handed you over to me today, but I would not hurt the the LORD's anointed.
Just as your life was precious in my eyes today, so may my life be precious in the the LORD's eyes, and may He save me from all trouble."
Saul said to David, "Blessed are you, my son David! You will do great things and surely win." Then David went on his way, and Saul went back to his place.

David said to himself, "One day Saul will kill me. The only good thing for me is to escape to the land of the Philistines. Then Saul will give up looking for me anywhere in Israel, and I will be safe from him."
So David and the six hundred men with him crossed over to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
David and his men stayed in Gath with Achish. Each man brought his family. David had his two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, who had been Nabal's wife from Carmel.
When Saul heard that David had fled to Gath, he stopped looking for him.
David said to Achish, "If I have found favor in your eyes, give me a place in one of the country towns so I can live there. Why should your servant live in the royal city with you?"
So Achish gave him Ziklag that day, and Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah ever since.
David lived in the land of the Philistines for a year and four months.
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites, and the Amalekites. These people had lived in the land from ancient times, from Shur all the way to Egypt.
David attacked the land and did not leave anyone alive, man or woman. He took sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing. Then he returned to Achish.
Achish asked, "Where did you raid today?" David answered, "Against the Negev of Judah, the Negev of the Jerahmeelites, and the Negev of the Kenites."

David did not leave anyone alive to bring to Gath, because he thought, "They might tell on us and say, 'This is what David did, and this is how he acts,' as long as he lives in the land of the Philistines."
Achish believed David and said, "He has made himself hated by his people Israel, so he will be my servant forever."
In those days the Philistines gathered their forces to fight against Israel. Achish said to David, "You need to know that you and your men will march out with me in the army."
David said to Achish, "Then you will know what your servant will do." Achish said to David, "Then I will make you my bodyguard for life."
Now Samuel was dead. All Israel had mourned for him and buried him in Ramah, in his own town. Saul had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land.
The Philistines gathered and camped at Shunem. Saul gathered all Israel, and they camped at Gilboa.
When Saul saw the Philistine camp, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
Saul asked the LORD for help, but the LORD did not answer him, not by dreams, not by the Urim, and not by prophets.
Saul said to his servants, "Find me a woman who is a medium, so I can go to her and ask her about this." His servants said to him, "There is a woman who is a medium at Endor."
So Saul disguised himself and put on other clothes. He went with two men, and they came to the woman at night. He said, "Please call up a spirit for me, and bring up for me the one I name."
The woman said to him, "You know what Saul has done. He has cut off the mediums and spiritists from the land. Why are you trying to trap me and get me killed?"
Saul swore to her by the LORD, "As the LORD lives, no punishment will come to you for this."
Then the woman said, "Whom shall I bring up for you?" He said, "Bring up Samuel for me."
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out loudly. She said to Saul, "Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!"
The king said to her, "Do not be afraid. What do you see?" The woman said to Saul, "I see a god coming up out of the earth."
He said, "What does he look like?" She said, "An old man is coming up, and he is wearing a robe." Then Saul knew it was Samuel. He bowed with his face to the ground.

Samuel said to Saul, "Why have you disturbed me by bringing me up?" Saul said, "I am in great trouble. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, neither by prophets nor by dreams. So I have called you to tell me what I should do."
Samuel said, "Why do you ask me, since the LORD has turned from you and become your enemy?"
The LORD has done to you what He said through me. He has torn the kingdom from your hand and given it to your neighbor David.
Because you did not obey the LORD and did not carry out His fierce anger against Amalek, the LORD has done this to you today.
The LORD will also give Israel and you into the hand of the Philistines. Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me. The LORD will also give the army of Israel into the hand of the Philistines.
Then Saul quickly fell full length on the ground. He was very afraid because of Samuel's words. He had no strength, because he had not eaten food all day and all night.
The woman came to Saul and saw that he was very upset. She said, "Look, your servant has listened to your voice. I put my life in my hands and obeyed what you said to me."
"Now please listen to your servant. Let me set a piece of bread before you, and eat, so you will have strength when you go on your way."
But he refused and said, "I will not eat." His servants and the woman urged him, and he listened to their voice. Then he got up from the ground and sat on the bed.
The woman had a fattened calf in the house. She hurried and slaughtered it. She took flour, kneaded it, and baked unleavened bread.
She set it before Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they got up and went away that night.
The Philistines brought all their armies together at Aphek, while Israel camped by the spring in Jezreel.
The Philistine leaders marched out by hundreds and thousands, and David and his men marched at the rear with Achish.

The Philistine leaders asked, "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Achish answered, "Isn't this David, servant of Saul, king of Israel? He has been with me for days or even years, and I have found nothing wrong with him since the day he came to me."

But the Philistine leaders were angry with Achish and said, "Send the man back to the place you put him. He must not fight with us, or he might turn against us during the battle. What better way could he win back his master's favor than by bringing him our heads?
Isn't this the David people sang about in their dances: 'Saul has killed his thousands, and David his tens of thousands'?"

So Achish called David and said, "As surely as the the LORD lives, you have been honest and good in my eyes. I would be glad for you to go out and come in with me in the army, because I have found no wrong in you since you came to me. But the leaders are not pleased with you.
So go back now and leave in peace, so you won't displease the Philistine leaders."
David said, "What have I done? What fault have you found in me since I have been with you, that I can't go and fight the enemies of my lord the king?"
Achish answered, "I know you are as good as an angel of God in my eyes. But the Philistine leaders have said, 'He must not go into battle with us.'
So get up early in the morning, you and your men who came with you. Go back to the place I gave you. Leave at dawn, as soon as it is light."
So David and his men got up early and went back to Philistine territory, while the Philistines went up to Jezreel.
On the third day, David and his men reached Ziklag. The Amalekites had attacked the Negev and Ziklag, and they had burned Ziklag to the ground.
They took the women captive, from the youngest to the oldest, but they did not kill anyone. They took them away and went on their way.
When David and his men came to the city, they found it burned down. Their wives, sons, and daughters had been taken captive.
David and the people with him cried out loud and wept until they had no strength left to cry.
David's two wives, Ahinoam from Jezreel and Abigail, Nabal's widow from Carmel, had been taken captive.
David was in great trouble because the men were bitter and talked about stoning him. Each man was upset about his own sons and daughters. But David found strength in the LORD his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, the son of Ahimelech, "Bring me the ephod." Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David asked the LORD, "Should I chase this raiding party? Will I catch them?" The LORD answered, "Chase them. You will catch them, and you will rescue the captives."
David and his six hundred men set out and came to the Besor Valley. The men who were left behind stayed there.
Two hundred men were too tired to cross the valley, so they stayed behind. David and four hundred men went on after the enemy.
They found an Egyptian in a field. They brought him to David and gave him water to drink. They also gave him food, and he ate.
They gave him a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins. After he ate, he felt stronger. He had not eaten or drunk anything for three days and three nights.
David asked him, "Who do you belong to? Where are you from?" He said, "I am a young Egyptian. I serve an Amalekite. My master left me behind three days ago because I got sick.
We raided the Negev of the Cherethites and the land that belongs to Judah. We also raided the Negev of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag."
David asked him, "Can you lead me down to that raiding party?" He said, "Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or hand me over to my master. Then I will lead you down to them."

He led David down, and there they were, spread out over the land. They were eating, drinking, and celebrating because of the large amount of plunder they had taken from the Philistines and from Judah.
David attacked them from dusk until the next evening. No one escaped except four hundred young men who rode away on camels.
David got back everything the Amalekites had taken. He also rescued his two wives.
Nothing was missing, from the smallest to the greatest, sons, daughters, and all the plunder. David brought everything back.
He took all the flocks and herds and drove them ahead of the other animals. The men said, "This is David's plunder."
David came to the two hundred men who had been too tired to follow him. They had stayed at the Besor Valley. They came out to meet David and the people with him. David greeted them.

But some of the worthless and wicked men who had gone with David said, "They did not go with us, so we should not give them any of the plunder we recovered. Each man can take his wife and children and go."
David said, "No, my brothers. You must not do that with what the LORD has given us. He protected us and gave the raiding party into our hands.
Who will listen to you in this? The share of the man who goes into battle will be the same as the share of the man who stays with the supplies. They will share alike."
From that day on, David made this a rule and law for Israel, and it is still followed today.
When David came to Ziklag, he sent some of the plunder to the elders of Judah. They were his friends. He said, "Here is a gift for you from the plunder taken from the LORD's enemies."
He sent gifts to those in Bethel, Ramoth in the Negev, Jattir,
Racal, the cities of the Jerahmeelites, the cities of the Kenites,
and Hebron. He also sent gifts to all the other places where David and his men had traveled.
The Philistines fought against Israel. The Israelite men ran away from them, and many fell dead on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines chased Saul and his sons. They killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchishua, who were Saul's sons.
The fighting grew fierce around Saul. Archers found him and shot him, and he was badly wounded.

Saul said to the man carrying his armor, "Draw your sword and run me through with it. Otherwise these uncircumcised men will come and run me through and mistreat me." But the armor-bearer was afraid to do it. So Saul took his own sword and fell on it.
When the armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he fell on his sword too and died with him.
So Saul, his three sons, his armor-bearer, and all his men died together that day.

When the Israelites across the valley and beyond the Jordan saw that their army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they left their towns and ran away. Then the Philistines moved in and lived there.
The next day, the Philistines came to strip the dead. They found Saul and his three sons lying on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head, took his armor, and sent messengers all over Philistia to announce the news to their idols' temples and to the people.
They put his armor in the temple of Ashtoreth and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan.
When the people of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
all the brave men got up and traveled all night. They took Saul's body and his sons' bodies down from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there.
Then they took the bones and buried them under a tamarisk tree in Jabesh. They fasted seven days.
After Saul died, David returned from defeating the Amalekites and stayed in Ziklag for two days.
On the third day, a man came from Saul's camp. His clothes were torn, and dirt was on his head. When he reached David, he fell to the ground and bowed down.
David asked him, "Where do you come from?" He answered, "I have escaped from the camp of Israel."
David said, "What happened? Tell me." He replied, "The people ran from the battle. Many fell and died. Saul and his son Jonathan are dead too."
David asked the young man who brought the news, "How do you know Saul and his son Jonathan are dead?"
The young man said, "I happened to be on Mount Gilboa. Saul was leaning on his spear. The chariots and horsemen were close behind him.
He turned and saw me, and he called to me. I answered, 'Here I am.'
He asked, 'Who are you?' I answered, 'I am an Amalekite.'
He said, 'Stand beside me and kill me. I am in great pain, but I am still alive.'
So I stood beside him and killed him. I knew he could not live after he fell. I took the crown from his head and the bracelet from his arm, and I brought them to my lord."
David grabbed his clothes and tore them. All the men with him did the same.
They mourned, wept, and fasted until evening for Saul, for his son Jonathan, for the people of the LORD, and for the nation of Israel. They had fallen by the sword.
David asked the young man who brought the news, "Where are you from?" He answered, "I am the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite."
David said to him, "Why were you not afraid to raise your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?"
Then David called one of his young men and said, "Go and strike him down." The man struck the Amalekite, and he died.
David said to him, "You are to blame for your own death. Your own mouth spoke against you when you said, 'I killed the LORD's anointed.'"
David sang this song of sadness for Saul and his son Jonathan.
He said it should be taught to the people of Judah. It is written in the Book of Jashar. He said: "
Israel's glory has fallen on your heights. How the mighty have fallen! "
Do not tell it in Gath. Do not announce it in the streets of Ashkelon. The daughters of the Philistines might rejoice. The daughters of the uncircumcised might celebrate. "
You mountains of Gilboa, may no dew or rain fall on you. May your fields give no harvest. For there the shield of the mighty was disgraced. It was Saul's shield, left uncared for. "
Jonathan's bow did not turn back from the blood of the fallen. Saul's sword did not return empty. "
Saul and Jonathan were loved and lovely in life. In death they were not parted. They were faster than eagles and stronger than lions. "
You daughters of Israel, weep for Saul. He clothed you in rich scarlet. He put gold ornaments on your clothes. "
How the mighty have fallen in the middle of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights. "
I am deeply troubled for you, my brother Jonathan. You were very kind to me. Your love for me was more wonderful than the love of women. "
How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!"
After this, David asked the the LORD, "Should I go up to one of the towns of Judah? Where should I go?" The The LORD said, "Go up to Hebron."
So David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
David also brought the men who were with him, each with his family, and they settled in the towns around Hebron.
Then the men of Judah came and anointed David king over the house of Judah. They told David, "The men of Jabesh-gilead buried Saul."
David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead. He said, "May the LORD bless you, because you showed this kindness to Saul your lord by burying him.
"Now may the LORD show you kindness and faithfulness. I will also show you good because you did this.
"Now let your hands be strong and be valiant men, because Saul your lord is dead. Also, the house of Judah has anointed me king over them."
Meanwhile, Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Saul's son Ish-bosheth and brought him across to Mahanaim.
He made him king over Gilead, the Ashurites, Jezreel, Ephraim, Benjamin, and all Israel.
Ish-bosheth son of Saul was forty years old when he became king over Israel, and he ruled for two years. The house of Judah, however, followed David.
David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah for seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul left Mahanaim for Gibeon.
Joab son of Zeruiah and David's servants went out and met them at the pool of Gibeon. They sat down, one group on one side of the pool and the other group on the other side.
Abner said to Joab, "Let the young men get up and compete before us." Joab said, "Let them get up."
So they got up and were counted off: twelve for Benjamin and Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve from David's servants.
Each man grabbed his opponent by the head and thrust his sword into his side. They fell together. So that place was called Helkath-hazzurim, which is at Gibeon.
The battle was very fierce that day. Abner and the men of Israel were defeated by David's servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Asahel was as fast on his feet as a wild gazelle.
Asahel chased Abner and did not turn to the right or to the left.
Abner looked behind him and asked, "Are you Asahel?" "I am," he answered.
Abner said, "Turn aside to your right or left. Seize one of the young men and take his armor." But Asahel would not stop chasing him.
Abner said again, "Stop chasing me! Why should I strike you down? How could I face your brother Joab?"

But Asahel refused to turn aside. Abner struck him in the stomach with the back end of his spear. The spear came out behind him, and he fell and died there. Everyone who came to the place where Asahel had fallen and died stopped.
Joab and Abishai pursued Abner. The sun was going down when they reached the hill of Ammah, near Giah, on the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjamites rallied behind Abner. They formed one group and stood on top of a hill.
Abner called to Joab, "Must the sword devour forever? Don't you know it will be bitter in the end? How long before you tell the people to stop chasing their brothers?"
Joab answered, "As surely as God lives, if you had not spoken, the men would not have stopped until morning from chasing their brothers."
So Joab blew the trumpet. All the people stopped. They no longer pursued Israel, and they did not fight anymore.
Abner and his men marched through the Arabah all night. They crossed the Jordan and went through all of Bithron, and they came to Mahanaim.
Joab returned from pursuing Abner and gathered all the people. Nineteen of David's servants were missing, besides Asahel.
But David's servants had struck down three hundred sixty Benjamites who were with Abner.
They took Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Joab and his men marched all night and reached Hebron at daybreak.
The war between Saul’s house and David’s house lasted a long time. David kept growing stronger, while Saul’s house kept growing weaker.
David had sons born to him in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel.
His second son was Chileab, by Abigail, Nabal’s widow from Carmel. His third was Absalom, son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur.
His fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith. His fifth was Shephatiah, son of Abital.
His sixth was Ithream, by Eglah, David’s wife. These sons were born to David in Hebron.
While the war between Saul’s house and David’s house continued, Abner was strengthening Saul’s house.
Saul had a concubine named Rizpah, daughter of Aiah. Ish-bosheth said to Abner, “Why did you go in to my father’s concubine?”

Abner was very angry at Ish-bosheth’s words and said, “Am I some worthless dog from Judah? I have shown kindness to the house of your father Saul, to his brothers and friends, and I have not handed you over to David. Yet today you charge me with a wrong about this woman!
May God deal with Abner, be it ever so severely, if I do not do for David what the LORD has sworn to him:
to move the kingdom from Saul’s house and set up David’s throne over Israel and Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner a word, because he was afraid of him.
Abner sent messengers to David on his behalf, saying, “Whose land is this? Make your covenant with me, and I will help you bring all Israel to you.”
David said, “Good! I will make a covenant with you. But I ask one thing of you: Do not come to see me unless you bring Michal, Saul’s daughter, with you.”
David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth son of Saul, saying, “Give me my wife Michal. I paid for her with a hundred Philistine foreskins.”
So Ish-bosheth sent and took her from her husband Paltiel son of Laish.
Her husband Paltiel followed her, weeping, all the way to Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, “Go back!” and he went back.
Abner spoke with the elders of Israel and said, “For some time now you have wanted David to be king over you.
Now do it! For the LORD has said about David, ‘By My servant David I will save My people Israel from the Philistines and from all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke to the people of Benjamin. Then he went to Hebron to tell David everything that Israel and all Benjamin thought was good.
Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, and David made a feast for Abner and his men.
Abner said to David, “Let me go and gather all Israel to my lord the king, so they can make a covenant with you, and you can rule over all your heart desires.” Then David sent Abner away in peace.
Just then Joab and David’s men came back from a raid, bringing much spoil with them. Abner was not with David in Hebron, because David had sent him away in peace.
When Joab and all his men arrived, he was told, “Abner son of Ner came to the king, and the king sent him away in peace.”
Joab went to the king and said, “What have you done? Abner came to you. Why did you send him away? Now he is gone.
You know Abner son of Ner. He came to deceive you and learn your movements and everything you are doing.”
Joab left David and sent messengers after Abner. They brought him back from the well at Sirah, but David did not know about it.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside at the gate to speak with him privately. There he stabbed Abner in the stomach, and Abner died for the blood of Asahel, Joab’s brother.
When David heard about it, he said, “I and my kingdom are forever innocent before the LORD in the matter of Abner son of Ner’s blood.

May the guilt fall on Joab’s head and on all his father’s house. May Joab’s house never be without someone who has a discharge, or a leper, or someone who leans on a staff, or someone who dies by the sword, or someone who has no bread.”
Joab and his brother Abishai killed Abner because he had killed their brother Asahel in the battle at Gibeon.
David said to Joab and all the people with him, “Tear your clothes, put on sackcloth, and mourn for Abner.” Then King David followed the coffin.
They buried Abner in Hebron. The king wept aloud at Abner’s tomb, and all the people wept.
The king sang a lament for Abner, saying, “Should Abner die like a fool dies?
Your hands were not bound, and your feet were not in chains. You fell as one falls before wicked men.” And all the people wept over him again.
All the people came to make David eat bread while it was still day, but David swore, “May God deal with me, be it ever so severely, if I taste bread or anything else before the sun goes down.”
All the people noticed, and it pleased them. Everything the king did pleased all the people.
So all Israel knew that day that the king had no part in killing Abner son of Ner.
The king said to his servants, “Do you not know that a prince and a great man has fallen today in Israel?
I am weak today, though I am the anointed king. These men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his wickedness.”
When Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, heard that Abner had died in Hebron, he lost his courage, and all Israel was alarmed.

Saul's son had two men who led raiding bands. One was named Baanah, and the other was Rechab. They were sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, from the tribe of Benjamin, because Beeroth was counted as part of Benjamin.
The people of Beeroth had run away to Gittaim and lived there as outsiders up to this day.

Jonathan, Saul's son, had a son who was lame in both feet. He was five years old when news came from Jezreel that Saul and Jonathan had died. His nurse picked him up and ran, but as she hurried away, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.
Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, went to Ish-bosheth's house at the hottest part of the day, around noon, while he was resting.
They came into the house as if to get wheat, and they stabbed him in the stomach. Then Rechab and his brother Baanah escaped.
They had come into the house while he lay on his bed in his bedroom. They struck him, killed him, cut off his head, and took it with them. They traveled all night through the Arabah.

They brought the head of Ish-bosheth to David in Hebron and said to the king, "Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who tried to take your life. Today the LORD has given my lord the king revenge against Saul and his family."
David answered Rechab and his brother Baanah, sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said, "As the LORD lives, who has saved my life from every trouble,
when someone told me, 'Saul is dead,' thinking he was bringing good news, I grabbed him and killed him at Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news.
So how much more should I deal with wicked men who killed a good man in his own house on his bed? Should I not now demand his blood from your hand and remove you from the earth?"
David commanded his young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung them by the pool in Hebron. They took the head of Ish-bosheth and buried it in Abner's tomb in Hebron.
Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and said, "We are your own flesh and blood.
Even while Saul was king over us, you were the one who led Israel out and brought them back. And the LORD said to you, 'You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over Israel.'"
So all the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and King David made a covenant with them there before the LORD. They anointed David king over Israel.
David was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years.
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

Now the king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites who lived in the land. The Jebusites said to David, "You will never get in here; even the blind and the lame can keep you out." They thought, "David cannot get in here."
Nevertheless, David captured the stronghold of Zion, that is, the City of David.

On that day David said, "Whoever attacks the Jebusites must climb up through the water shaft to reach the lame and blind who are David's enemies." That is why it is said, "The blind and the lame will not enter the house."
So David took up residence in the fortress and called it the City of David. He built it up all around, from the supporting terraces inward.
And David became greater and greater, because the LORD God of Hosts was with him.
Now Hiram king of Tyre sent messengers to David, along with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons, and they built a palace for David.
And David realized that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom for the sake of His people Israel.
After he had arrived from Hebron, David took more concubines and wives from Jerusalem, and more sons and daughters were born to him.
These are the names of the children born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,
When the Philistines heard that David had been anointed king over Israel, they all went up to seek him out. But David heard about it and went down to the stronghold.
Now the Philistines had come and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
So David inquired of the LORD, "Should I go up against the Philistines? Will You hand them over to me?" The LORD said to David, "Go, for I will surely hand the Philistines over to you."
So David went to Baal-perazim, where he defeated them. Then he said, "Like a flood of water, the LORD has burst through my enemies before me." So he named that place Baal-perazim.
There the Philistines abandoned their idols, and David and his men carried them off.
Once again the Philistines came up and spread out in the Valley of Rephaim.
So David inquired of the LORD again, and He said, "Do not go straight up; circle around behind them and attack them in front of the balsam trees.
As soon as you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, move quickly, because then the LORD has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines."
So David did as the LORD had commanded, and he struck down the Philistines from Gibeon to Gezer.
David gathered all the chosen men of Israel again, thirty thousand in all.
David and all the people with him left Baale Judah to bring up from there the ark of God. It is called by the Name, the name of the the LORD of Hosts, who is enthroned between the cherubim.
They set the ark of God on a new cart and brought it from the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill. Uzzah and Ahio, sons of Abinadab, were guiding the new cart.
The ark of God was on it, and Ahio was walking in front of it.
David and all Israel were celebrating with all their might before the the LORD, playing castanets, harps, lyres, tambourines, rattles, and cymbals.
When they came to the threshing floor of Nakon, Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God, because the oxen stumbled.
The LORD's anger burned against Uzzah because of his irreverent act; so God struck him down, and he died there beside the ark of God.
Then David was angry because the the LORD's wrath had broken out against Uzzah, and to this day that place is called Perez Uzzah.
David was afraid of the the LORD that day and said, "How can the ark of the the LORD ever come to me?"
He was not willing to take the ark of the the LORD to be with him in the City of David. Instead, he took it to the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite.
The ark of the the LORD remained in the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite for three months, and the the LORD blessed him and his entire household.

Now King David was told, "The The LORD has blessed the household of Obed-Edom and everything he has, because of the ark of God." So David went to bring up the ark of God from the house of Obed-Edom to the City of David with rejoicing.
When those who were carrying the ark of the the LORD had taken six steps, David sacrificed a bull and a fattened calf.
Wearing a linen ephod, David was dancing before the the LORD with all his might.
He and all Israel were bringing up the ark of the the LORD with shouts and the sound of trumpets.

As the ark of the the LORD was entering the City of David, Michal daughter of Saul watched from a window. When she saw King David leaping and dancing before the the LORD, she despised him in her heart.
They brought the ark of the the LORD and set it in its place inside the tent that David had pitched for it, and David sacrificed burnt offerings and peace offerings before the the LORD.
After he had finished sacrificing the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the the LORD of Hosts.
Then he gave a loaf of bread, a cake of dates, and a cake of raisins to each person in the whole crowd of Israelites, both men and women. And all the people went to their homes.

When David returned home to bless his household, Michal daughter of Saul came out to meet him and said, "How the king of Israel has honored himself today! He uncovered himself before the slave girls of his servants, like a vulgar man would!"

David said to Michal, "It was before the the LORD, who chose me rather than your father or anyone from his house when he appointed me ruler over the the LORD's people Israel—I will celebrate before the the LORD.
I will become even more undignified than this, and I will be humiliated in my own eyes. But by these slave girls you spoke of, I will be held in honor."
And Michal daughter of Saul had no children until the day of her death.
After the king was living in his house and the LORD had given him rest from all his enemies around him,
the king said to Nathan the prophet, "Look, I am living in a house of cedar, but the ark of God is staying in a tent."
Nathan said to the king, "Go and do everything in your heart, for the LORD is with you."
That night the word of the LORD came to Nathan.
"Go and tell My servant David, 'This is what the LORD says: Will you build Me a house to live in?
I have not lived in a house since the day I brought the Israelites up from Egypt until now. I have been moving around in a tent and a tabernacle.
Everywhere I went with all the Israelites, did I ever say a word to any tribe I commanded to shepherd My people Israel, asking, "Why have you not built Me a house of cedar?"'
"Now then, tell My servant David, 'This is what the LORD of Hosts says: I took you from the pasture, from following the sheep, to be ruler over My people Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went. I cut off all your enemies before you. I have made your name great, like the names of the greatest men on earth.
I will set a place for My people Israel and plant them. They will live in their own place and not be disturbed anymore. Wicked people will not trouble them as they did before.
This is also from the day I appointed judges over My people Israel. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The LORD has also told you that He will make a royal house for you.
When your days are over and you die and join your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, one who comes from your body. I will establish his kingdom.
He will build a house for My name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be a Father to him, and he will be a Son to Me. When he sins, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men.
My faithful love will not leave him, as I took it away from Saul, whom I removed from before you.
Your house and your kingdom will be sure forever before you. Your throne will be established forever.'
Nathan told David all these words and this vision.
Then King David went in and sat before the LORD. He said, "Who am I, Lord GOD, and what is my family, that You have brought me this far?
And yet this was a small thing in Your eyes, Lord GOD. You have also spoken about Your servant's family line for a long time to come. This is how You deal with people, Lord GOD.
What more can David say to You? You know Your servant, Lord GOD.
For Your word's sake and according to Your heart, You have done all this greatness and made it known to Your servant.
Therefore You are great, Lord GOD. There is no one like You, and there is no God besides You, according to all we have heard with our ears.

And who is like Your people Israel? It is one nation on earth that God went out to redeem for Himself, to make a name for Himself, and to do great and awesome things for Your land, before Your people whom You redeemed from Egypt, from the nations and their gods.
You established Your people Israel as Your own people forever, and You, the LORD, became their God.
"Now, the LORD God, let the word You spoke about Your servant and his house be established forever. Do as You have spoken.
Let Your name be great forever, so that people say, 'The the LORD of Hosts is God over Israel,' and let the house of Your servant David be established before You.
For You, the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, have revealed to Your servant, saying, 'I will build a house for you.' That is why Your servant found courage to pray this prayer to You.
Now, Lord GOD, You are God, and Your words are true. You have promised this good thing to Your servant.
Now be pleased to bless the house of Your servant, so it may be before You forever. For You, Lord GOD, have spoken, and with Your blessing the house of Your servant will be blessed forever."
After this, David defeated the Philistines and brought them under his rule. He took Metheg-ammah from them.

He also defeated Moab. He made the Moabites lie down on the ground and measured them with a rope. He measured two lines to be put to death and one full line to be kept alive. So the Moabites became David’s servants and brought him tribute.
David defeated Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when Hadadezer went to restore his power at the Euphrates River.
David captured 1,700 horsemen and 20,000 foot soldiers from him. He crippled all the chariot horses but left enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Arameans of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David killed 22,000 of them.
David placed military posts in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became his servants and brought tribute. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David took the gold shields carried by Hadadezer’s servants and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Betah and Berothai, cities of Hadadezer, King David took a large amount of bronze.
When Toi king of Hamath heard that David had defeated all of Hadadezer’s army,

he sent his son Joram to King David to greet him and bless him, because David had fought and defeated Hadadezer. Hadadezer had been at war with Toi. Joram brought articles of silver, gold, and bronze.
King David dedicated these to the the LORD, along with the silver and gold he had dedicated from all the nations he had subdued:
from Aram, Moab, the Ammonites, the Philistines, Amalek, and the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
David became famous when he returned and struck down 18,000 Edomites in the Valley of Salt.
He put military posts throughout Edom, and all Edom became David’s servants. The LORD gave David victory wherever he went.
David reigned over all Israel and did what was just and right for all his people.
Joab son of Zeruiah was over the army. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Zadok son of Ahitub and Ahimelech son of Abiathar were priests. Seraiah was the secretary.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites, and David’s sons were priests.
David asked, "Is there anyone still left of Saul's family? I want to show kindness to him because of Jonathan."
Saul's family had a servant named Ziba. They called him to David. The king said to him, "Are you Ziba?" Ziba said, "Yes, I am your servant."
The king said, "Is there no one left of Saul's family? I want to show God's kindness to him." Ziba said to the king, "Jonathan still has a son. Both his feet are lame."
The king said to him, "Where is he?" Ziba said to the king, "He is in Lo-debar, at the house of Machir son of Ammiel."
King David sent for him and brought him from Machir's house in Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the grandson of Saul, came to David. He bowed with his face to the ground. David said, "Mephibosheth!" Mephibosheth said, "Here I am, your servant."
David said to him, "Don't be afraid. I will show kindness to you because of your father Jonathan. I will give back all the land of your father Saul. You will always eat at my table."
Mephibosheth bowed and said, "What am I, your servant, that you should care about someone as worthless as me?"
The king called Ziba, Saul's servant, and said to him, "I have given your master's son everything that belonged to Saul and his family.

You, your sons, and your servants will farm the land for him. You will bring in the crops so your master's son will have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master's son, will always eat at my table." Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba said to the king, "Your servant will do everything my lord the king commands." The king said, "Mephibosheth will eat at my table like one of the king's sons."
Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica. Everyone living in Ziba's house was a servant to Mephibosheth.
Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table. He was lame in both feet.
After this, the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun became king in his place.

David said, "I will show kindness to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father showed kindness to me." So David sent his servants to comfort Hanun after his father's death. David's servants came to the land of the Ammonites.

The Ammonite leaders said to Hanun, their lord, "Do you think David is honoring your father by sending men to comfort you? Hasn't David sent his servants to you to look over the city, spy on it, and destroy it?"
So Hanun took David's servants, shaved off half their beards, cut their clothes in half at the buttocks, and sent them away.
When David heard about it, he sent men to meet them, because they were very ashamed. The king said, "Stay at Jericho until your beards grow, then come back."

When the Ammonites saw they had made David angry, they hired twenty thousand Aramean foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, one thousand men from the king of Maacah, and twelve thousand men from Tob.
When David heard about it, he sent Joab and all his best soldiers.
The Ammonites came out and lined up for battle at the city gate. The Arameans from Zobah and Rehob, along with the men from Tob and Maacah, stood by themselves in the field.
Joab saw that he was being attacked from the front and the back. He chose the best soldiers in Israel and lined them up against the Arameans.
He put the rest of the army under the command of his brother Abishai and lined them up against the Ammonites.
Joab said, "If the Arameans are too strong for me, you will help me. If the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will go help you.
Be strong. Let us be strong for our people and for the cities of our God. May the the LORD do what seems good to Him."
Joab and his men moved forward to fight the Arameans, and the Arameans ran away from him.
When the Ammonites saw the Arameans running, they also ran away from Abishai and went back into the city. Then Joab returned from the Ammonites and went to Jerusalem.
When the Arameans saw they had been beaten by Israel, they gathered together.
Hadadezer brought in Arameans from beyond the Euphrates River, and they came to Helam. Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, led them.
When David was told about it, he gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan River, and came to Helam. The Arameans lined up to face David and fought against him.
The Arameans ran away from Israel. David killed seven hundred chariot drivers and forty thousand horsemen. He also struck down Shobach, their army commander, and Shobach died there.
When all the kings who served Hadadezer saw they had been beaten by Israel, they made peace with Israel and served them. The Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites again.
In the spring, when kings go out to war, David sent Joab, his officers, and all Israel to fight the Ammonites. They attacked Rabbah, but David stayed in Jerusalem.
One evening David got up from his bed and walked on the roof of the king's palace. From the roof he saw a woman bathing. She was very beautiful.
David sent someone to find out who she was. The man said, "Isn't this Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam and wife of Uriah the Hittite?"
David sent messengers to get her. She came to him, and he slept with her. She had just finished her monthly purification, and then she went home.
The woman became pregnant. She sent word to David and said, "I am pregnant."
David sent a message to Joab: "Send me Uriah the Hittite." Joab sent Uriah to David.
Uriah came to David. David asked how Joab was, how the soldiers were, and how the war was going.
David said to Uriah, "Go to your house and wash your feet." As Uriah left the palace, the king sent a gift after him.
But Uriah slept at the entrance to the palace with all his master's servants. He did not go down to his house.
David was told, "Uriah did not go down to his house." David asked Uriah, "You have just come from a trip. Why didn't you go down to your house?"

Uriah said to David, "The ark and Israel and Judah are staying in tents. My master Joab and his servants are camping in the open field. Should I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife? As surely as you live, I will not do this."
David said to Uriah, "Stay here today. Tomorrow I will send you back." So Uriah stayed in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him to eat and drink with him and made him drunk. That evening Uriah went out to sleep on his bed with his master's servants, but he did not go down to his house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it with Uriah.
In the letter he wrote, "Put Uriah in the front line where the fighting is hardest. Then pull back from him so he will be struck down and die."
While Joab was attacking the city, he put Uriah in a place where he knew there were strong soldiers.
The men of the city came out and fought Joab. Some of David's men fell, and Uriah the Hittite died too.
Joab sent David a report of the whole battle.
He told the messenger, "When you have finished telling the king everything about the battle,
the king may get angry and ask, 'Why did you go so close to the city to fight? Didn't you know they would shoot from the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerub-Besheth? Didn't a woman throw a millstone on him from the wall, so he died at Thebez? Why did you go so close to the wall?' Then say, 'Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too.'"
The messenger went and told David everything Joab had sent him to say.
The messenger said to David, "The men overpowered us and came out against us in the open country, but we pushed them back to the entrance of the gate.
The archers shot at your servants from the wall, and some of the king's servants died. Your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead too."
David said to the messenger, "Say this to Joab: 'Do not let this upset you. The sword destroys one person as well as another. Keep fighting hard against the city and destroy it.' Encourage him."
Uriah's wife heard that her husband was dead. She mourned for him.
When her time of mourning was over, David sent for her and brought her to his house. She became his wife and bore him a son. But what David had done displeased the LORD.
The LORD sent Nathan to David. When he arrived, he said to him, "There were two men in one city. One was rich, and the other was poor.
The rich man had very many sheep and cattle.

But the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb that he had bought. He raised it, and it grew up with him and his children. It ate from his food, drank from his cup, and slept in his lap. It was like a daughter to him.

A traveler came to the rich man, but the rich man did not want to take from his own sheep or cattle to feed the guest. Instead, he took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for the man who had come to him."
David became very angry with the man and said to Nathan, "As surely as the LORD lives, the man who did this deserves to die!
He must pay back the lamb four times over, because he did this and showed no pity."
Nathan said to David, "You are the man! This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from Saul's hand.
I gave you your master's house and your master's wives. I gave you the people of Israel and Judah. If that had not been enough, I would have given you even more. "'

Why have you despised the word of the LORD by doing evil in His sight? You struck down Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife to be your wife. You killed him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now the sword will never leave your house, because you despised Me and took Uriah the Hittite's wife to be your wife.

This is what the LORD says: I am going to bring trouble on you from your own house. Before your eyes I will take your wives and give them to your neighbor. He will lie with your wives in the sunlight.
You did it in secret, but I will do this in front of all Israel and in the sunlight.'"
David said to Nathan, "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan said to David, "The LORD has taken away your sin; you will not die.
But because by this deed you have completely scorned the LORD, the son born to you will die."
Then Nathan went home. The LORD struck the child that Uriah's wife had borne to David, and the child became very sick.
David sought God on behalf of the child. He fasted, went in, and lay on the ground all night.
The elders of his house stood over him to help him up from the ground, but he would not get up, and he would not eat with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David's servants were afraid to tell him the child was dead, because they said, "While the child was alive, we spoke to him, but he would not listen to us. How can we tell him the child is dead? He might do something terrible."
David saw his servants whispering together, and he understood the child was dead. He asked his servants, "Is the child dead?" They said, "He is dead."

Then David got up from the ground, washed, anointed himself, changed his clothes, went into the house of the LORD, and worshiped. Then he came to his house and asked for food. They set food before him, and he ate.
His servants asked him, "What is this thing you have done? While the child was alive, you fasted and wept. But when the child died, you got up and ate."
He said, "While the child was alive, I fasted and wept, for I thought, 'Who knows? The LORD may be gracious to me, and the child may live.'
But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me."
David comforted his wife Bathsheba, went in to her, and lay with her. She gave birth to a son, and he named him Solomon. The LORD loved him.
He sent word through Nathan the prophet and named him Jedidiah because of the LORD.
Joab fought against Rabbah of the Ammonites and captured the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David and said, "I have fought against Rabbah and captured the water city.
Now gather the rest of the people, camp against the city, and capture it. Otherwise I will capture the city, and it will be named after me."
David gathered all the people, went to Rabbah, fought against it, and captured it.

He took the crown from the head of their king. Its weight was a talent of gold, and it had a precious stone. It was placed on David's head. He also brought out a great amount of plunder from the city.

He brought out the people who were in it and put them to work with saws, iron picks, and iron axes, and made them work at the brick kilns. David did the same to all the Ammonite cities. Then David and all the people returned to Jerusalem.
After this, Absalom son of David had a beautiful sister named Tamar, and Amnon, another son of David, loved her.
Amnon was so upset about his sister Tamar that he made himself sick. She was a virgin, and he felt he could not have her.
Amnon had a friend named Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah. Jonadab was a very clever man.
Jonadab asked him, "Why do you, the king's son, look so worn out every morning? Won't you tell me?" Amnon said to him, "I love Tamar, my brother Absalom's sister."

Jonadab said, "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be sick. When your father comes to see you, say, 'Please let my sister Tamar come and make me some bread. Let her make it where I can watch, and I'll eat it from her hand.'"
So Amnon lay down and pretended to be sick. When the king came to see him, Amnon said, "Please let my sister Tamar come and make two cakes for me where I can watch, and I'll eat them from her hand."
David sent word to Tamar at home: "Go to your brother Amnon's house and make food for him."
Tamar went to her brother Amnon's house. He was lying down. She took dough, kneaded it, made cakes in front of him, and baked them.
She took the pan and served them to him, but he refused to eat. Amnon said, "Send everyone out." So everyone left.
Amnon said to Tamar, "Bring the food into the bedroom and feed me from your hand." Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them to her brother Amnon in the bedroom.
As she brought them to him to eat, he grabbed her and said, "Come to bed with me, my sister."
She said, "No, my brother! Don't force me. That shouldn't be done in Israel. Don't do this foolish thing.
Where would I go with my shame? And you would be like one of the fools in Israel. Please, talk to the king. He won't refuse to give me to you."
But he wouldn't listen to her. He was stronger than she was, so he forced her and lay with her.
Then Amnon hated her with a very great hatred. The hatred he felt for her was greater than the love he had felt for her. Amnon said to her, "Get up and get out!"
She said to him, "No! Sending me away like this is a greater wrong than what you already did to me." But he wouldn't listen to her.
He called his servant who waited on him and said, "Get this woman out of here and lock the door behind her."
So the servant put her out and locked the door behind her. She was wearing a long robe with sleeves, because that was what the king's unmarried daughters wore.
Tamar put ashes on her head and tore the long robe she was wearing. She put her hand on her head and went away, crying as she walked.

Her brother Absalom said to her, "Has your brother Amnon been with you? Keep quiet for now, my sister. He is your brother. Don't take this to heart." So Tamar stayed in her brother Absalom's house, feeling crushed.
When King David heard about all this, he was very angry.
Absalom didn't speak to Amnon either good or bad, because Absalom hated Amnon for forcing his sister Tamar.
Two years later, Absalom had sheep shearers at Baal-hazor near Ephraim. Absalom invited all the king's sons.
Absalom came to the king and said, "Your servant has sheep shearers. Please let the king and his servants come with your servant."
The king said to Absalom, "No, my son. We shouldn't all go, or we'd be a burden to you." Absalom urged him, but David didn't want to go and blessed him.
Absalom said, "If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us." The king said, "Why should he go with you?"
Absalom kept pressing him, and David sent Amnon and all the king's sons with him.
Absalom ordered his servants, "Watch Amnon. When he's feeling good from the wine and I tell you, 'Strike Amnon,' then kill him. Don't be afraid. I'm the one giving the order. Be strong and brave."
Absalom's servants did to Amnon what Absalom had ordered. Then all the king's sons got up, each mounted his mule, and fled.
While they were on the way, a report reached David: "Absalom has struck down all the king's sons, and not one is left."
The king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay on the ground. All his servants stood by with their clothes torn.

Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, answered, "Don't let my lord the king think all the young men, the king's sons, are dead. Only Amnon is dead. Absalom has been planning this since the day Amnon forced his sister Tamar.
So now, my lord the king, don't take it to heart that all the king's sons are dead. Only Amnon is dead."
Meanwhile Absalom fled. The watchman looked up and saw many people coming along the road from the hillside behind him.
Jonadab said to the king, "Look, the king's sons are coming. It happened just as your servant said."
As soon as he finished speaking, the king's sons came in, weeping loudly. The king and all his servants also wept very bitterly.
Absalom fled and went to Talmai son of Ammihud, king of Geshur. David mourned for his son every day.
Absalom stayed in Geshur for three years.
King David longed to go to Absalom, because he had been comforted about Amnon's death.
Joab, the son of Zeruiah, knew that the king longed for Absalom.

So Joab sent to Tekoa and brought a wise woman from there. He said to her, “Please pretend to mourn. Put on mourning clothes. Do not anoint yourself with oil. Act like a woman who has mourned a dead person for a long time.
Go to the king and speak to him like this.” Then Joab told her what to say.
The woman from Tekoa went to the king. She fell on her face to the ground, bowed, and said, “Help me, O king!”
The king asked, “What is wrong?” She said, “I am a widow. My husband is dead.
Your servant had two sons. They fought in the field, and no one was there to stop them. One struck the other and killed him.

Now the whole family has risen against your servant. They say, ‘Hand over the one who struck his brother. We will put him to death for the life of his brother whom he killed. We will also destroy the heir.’ They want to snuff out the last hope I have left. Then my husband will not have a name or a descendant on the earth.”
The king said to the woman, “Go home, and I will give orders concerning you.”
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, “My lord the king, let the guilt be on me and on my father's family. The king and his throne are innocent.”
The king said, “If anyone says anything to you, bring him to me. He will not bother you again.”

She said, “Please let the king remember the LORD your God, so the avenger of blood will not destroy anymore, and they will not destroy my son.” He said, “As the LORD lives, not one hair of your son will fall to the ground.”
Then the woman said, “Please let your servant speak one more word to my lord the king.” He said, “Speak.”
The woman said, “Why then have you planned such a thing against God's people? By saying this, the king condemns himself, because he has not brought back his banished son.
We all must die. We are like water spilled on the ground that cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away life. Instead, He makes a way so a banished person can come back.
Now I have come to speak this word to my lord the king because the people made me afraid. Your servant thought, ‘I will speak to the king. Maybe the king will do what his servant asks.
The king will hear and deliver his servant from the hand of the man who would destroy me and my son together from the land God gave us.’
Then your servant said, ‘The word of my lord the king will give me rest. For my lord the king is like an angel of God in telling good from evil. May the LORD your God be with you.’”
The king answered the woman, “Please do not hide anything from me that I am about to ask you.” The woman said, “Let my lord the king speak.”

The king said, “Is Joab's hand in all this with you?” The woman answered, “As your soul lives, my lord the king, no one can turn aside from anything my lord the king says. Yes, your servant Joab commanded me. He put all these words in the mouth of your servant.
Your servant Joab did this to change how this matter would turn out. My lord is wise, like the wisdom of an angel of God, to know everything on earth.”
The king said to Joab, “All right, I have done this. Go bring back the young man Absalom.”

Joab fell with his face to the ground, bowed, and blessed the king. Joab said, “Today your servant knows he has found favor in your eyes, my lord the king, because the king has granted his servant's request.”
Joab got up and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “He may go to his own house, but he must not see my face.” So Absalom went to his own house and did not see the king's face.
In all Israel there was no one as handsome as Absalom. From the sole of his foot to the top of his head there was no blemish in him.
When he cut his hair—he cut it at the end of every year because it became heavy on him—the weight of his hair was two hundred shekels by the king's standard.
Three sons and one daughter were born to Absalom. His daughter's name was Tamar. She was a beautiful woman.
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without seeing the king's face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab to send him to the king, but Joab would not come. He sent a second time, but Joab still would not come.
So Absalom said to his servants, “Look, Joab's field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom's servants set the field on fire.
Joab got up and went to Absalom's house. He said, “Why did your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom said to Joab, “Look, I sent to you and said, ‘Come here, so I can send you to the king to ask, “Why did I come from Geshur? It would have been better for me to stay there.” Now let me see the king's face. If there is guilt in me, let him put me to death.’”
Joab went to the king and told him. The king called for Absalom, and he came. Absalom bowed with his face to the ground before the king. The king kissed Absalom.
After this, Absalom got a chariot and horses. He also had fifty men run ahead of him.

Absalom would get up early and stand beside the road to the city gate. Whenever someone had a case to bring to the king for judgment, Absalom would call to him and ask, "Which city are you from?" The man would answer, "I am your servant from one of the tribes of Israel."
Absalom would say to him, "Look, your case sounds good and fair. But the king has no one to hear you."
Absalom would also say, "If only someone would make me judge in the land! Then everyone who had a dispute or case could come to me, and I would give him justice."
Whenever anyone came near to bow to him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of the man, and kiss him.
Absalom did this for all the Israelites who came to the king for judgment. In this way, he won the loyalty of the people of Israel.
After forty years, Absalom said to the king, "Please let me go to Hebron to keep a promise I made to the LORD."
"For when I lived in Geshur in Aram, I promised, 'If the LORD brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship the LORD.'"
The king said to him, "Go in peace." So Absalom got up and went to Hebron.
Then Absalom sent secret messengers to all the tribes of Israel. They said, "As soon as you hear the trumpet, say, 'Absalom is king in Hebron!'"
Two hundred men from Jerusalem went with Absalom. They had been invited, and they went without knowing the plan.
While Absalom was offering sacrifices, he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's advisor, from his city of Giloh. The plot grew strong, and more and more people joined Absalom.
A messenger came to David and said, "The people of Israel have given their loyalty to Absalom."

Then David said to all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, "Come, let us run away! If we don't, we won't escape from Absalom. Hurry, or he will catch us, bring disaster on us, and kill the people of the city with swords."
The king's servants said to the king, "We are your servants. We will do whatever our lord the king chooses."
The king left, and his whole household went with him. But he left ten concubines to take care of the house.
The king left, and all the people followed him. They stopped at the last house.
All his servants passed by him, along with all the Cherethites, Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath. They passed in front of the king.
The king said to Ittai the Gittite, "Why are you going with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and an exile from your homeland."
"You came only yesterday. Should I make you wander with us today when I don't know where I'm going? Go back and take your brothers with you. May the LORD show you kindness and faithfulness."
Ittai answered the king, "As surely as the LORD lives, and as surely as my lord the king lives, I will go wherever my lord the king goes, whether it means life or death."
David said to Ittai, "Go ahead, then." So Ittai the Gittite marched on with all his men and all the little ones who were with him.
The whole land was crying loudly as all the people passed by. The king crossed the Kidron Valley, and all the people moved toward the wilderness road.
Zadok was there too, with all the Levites. They were carrying the ark of the covenant of God. They set down the ark of God, and Abiathar came up while all the people finished passing out of the city.
The king said to Zadok, "Take the ark of God back to the city. If I find favor in the LORD's eyes, He will bring me back and let me see it and His home again."
"But if He says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then here I am. Let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him."
The king said to Zadok the priest, "Are you not a seer? Go back to the city in peace, with your son Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar. You and Abiathar take your two sons with you."
"See, I will wait at the fords in the wilderness until word comes from you to tell me."
So Zadok and Abiathar took the ark of God back to Jerusalem and stayed there.
David went up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went. His head was covered, and he walked barefoot. All the people with him also covered their heads and went up, weeping as they climbed.
David had been told, "Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom." So David prayed to the LORD, "Please make Ahithophel's advice foolish."
When David reached the summit, where people used to worship God, Hushai the Arkite came to meet him. His robe was torn, and dust was on his head.
David said to him, "If you go with me, you will only be a burden to me."

"But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, 'I will be your servant, O king; I was your father's servant in the past, but now I am your servant,' then you can help me by working against Ahithophel's advice."
"Aren't Zadok and Abiathar the priests there with you? Tell them everything you hear from the king's house."
"Their two sons, Ahimaaz son of Zadok and Jonathan son of Abiathar, are there with them. Send me word through them about everything you hear."
So Hushai, David's friend, went into the city. Absalom was just entering Jerusalem.

David had gone just a little past the top of the hill when Ziba, Mephibosheth's servant, met him. Ziba had two donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, one hundred clusters of raisins, one hundred pieces of summer fruit, and a skin of wine.

The king asked Ziba, "What are these for?" Ziba answered, "The donkeys are for the king's family to ride. The bread and fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is for anyone who gets tired in the desert to drink."
The king asked, "Where is your master?" Ziba said to the king, "He is staying in Jerusalem." He added that his master had said, "Today the people of Israel will give me back my father's kingdom."
The king said to Ziba, "Everything that belonged to Mephibosheth is now yours." Ziba bowed and said, "I bow before you. May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king."
When David reached Bahurim, a man from Saul's family came out cursing. His name was Shimei son of Gera.
He threw stones at David and at all the king's servants, and at all the people and mighty men on David's right and left.
Shimei cursed him and shouted, "Get out! Get out, you murderer! You worthless man!

The LORD has paid you back for all the blood of Saul's family. You took his place as king, but the LORD has given the kingdom to your son Absalom. Now you are caught in your own evil, because you are a murderer."
Abishai son of Zeruiah said to the king, "Why should this worthless man curse my lord the king? Let me go over and cut off his head."
The king said, "What business is this of yours, sons of Zeruiah? If the LORD has told him to curse David, no one can ask why he is doing it."

David said to Abishai and all his servants, "Look, my own son is trying to kill me. How much more should I expect this man from Benjamin to curse me! Leave him alone and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to.
Perhaps the LORD will see my trouble and repay me with good for this cursing today."
So David and his men went on their way. Shimei walked along the hillside opposite him, cursing as he went, throwing stones and flinging dust.
The king and all the people with him arrived tired, and there he rested.
Absalom and all the men of Israel came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel was with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David's friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said, "Long live the king! Long live the king!"
Absalom said to Hushai, "Is this your loyalty to your friend? Why didn't you go with your friend?"
Hushai said to Absalom, "No! I will serve the one whom the LORD and all Israel have chosen, and I will stay with him.
Besides, whom should I serve? Should I not serve his son? Just as I served your father, I will serve you."
Absalom said to Ahithophel, "Give your advice. What should we do?"

Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Go in to your father's concubines, whom he left to watch the house. All Israel will hear that you have made yourself hated by your father, and everyone with you will feel stronger."
So they set up a tent for Absalom on the roof, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel.
In those days, Ahithophel's advice was like getting advice from God Himself. Both David and Absalom treated it that way.
Ahithophel said to Absalom, "Let me choose twelve thousand men. I will get up tonight and chase David.
I will attack him while he is tired and weak. I will terrify all the people with him so they run away, and then I will strike down only the king.
I will bring all the people back to you. The man you are after is the only one we need to kill. After that, everyone else can come home in peace."
This plan sounded good to Absalom and to all the elders of Israel.
But Absalom said, "Call Hushai the Arkite too. Let us hear what he has to say."
When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom said to him, "Ahithophel has given this advice. Should we follow his plan? If not, you speak."
Hushai said to Absalom, "The advice Ahithophel gave this time is not good.

You know your father and his men. They are brave and fierce. They are like a bear in the field whose cubs have been taken. Your father is a seasoned warrior, and he will not stay with the troops at night.
Right now he is probably hiding in a cave or some other place. If a few of your men fall at the start, people will hear and say, 'Absalom's followers have been defeated.'
Then even the bravest men, with hearts like a lion's, will lose their nerve, because all Israel knows your father is a mighty warrior and the men with him are brave.
So I advise that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan to Beersheba, as many as the sand by the sea. Then you yourself should go into battle.
We will come upon him wherever he is. We will fall on him like dew on the ground. Not one man will be left, not one of all the men with him.
If he retreats into a city, all Israel will bring ropes to that city. We will drag it into the valley until not even a small stone is left."

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, "The advice of Hushai the Arkite is better than the advice of Ahithophel." For the LORD had decided to ruin Ahithophel's good advice, so that He could bring disaster on Absalom.
Then Hushai told Zadok and Abiathar the priests, "Ahithophel advised Absalom and the elders of Israel like this, but I advised them like this."
"Now send quickly and tell David, 'Do not spend the night in the desert plains, but cross over at once, or the king and all his people may be wiped out.'"
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying at En Rogel. A female servant went and told them. They were to go and report to King David, since they could not be seen going into the city.
But a young man saw them and told Absalom. So the two hurried away and came to the house of a man in Bahurim. He had a well in his courtyard, and they climbed down into it.
The man's wife took a covering and spread it over the well's opening. Then she scattered grain over it, so no one would know.

When Absalom's servants came to the woman at the house, they asked, "Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?" The woman said, "They crossed the brook." The men searched but did not find them, so they returned to Jerusalem.
After they left, the two men came up out of the well and went to tell King David. They said to David, "Get up and cross the water quickly, because Ahithophel has advised this against you."
So David and all the people with him got up and crossed the Jordan. By dawn everyone had crossed; not one was left behind.
When Ahithophel saw that his advice was not followed, he saddled his donkey and went home to his town. He put his house in order and hanged himself. He died and was buried in his father's tomb.
David went to Mahanaim. Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel.
Absalom had made Amasa commander of the army in place of Joab. Amasa was the son of Ithra the Israelite. Ithra had married Abigail, daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother.
Israel and Absalom camped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah of the Ammonites, Machir son of Ammiel from Lo Debar, and Barzillai the Gileadite from Rogelim
brought beds, basins, pottery, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep, and cheese.
They brought these for David and his people to eat, because they said, "The people are hungry, tired, and thirsty in the desert."
David counted his soldiers and put commanders over groups of a thousand and a hundred.
He sent out a third of the army with Joab, a third with Abishai son of Zeruiah, Joab's brother, and a third with Ittai the Gittite. The king told the troops, "I will go out with you too."

But the people said, "You must not go. If we run away, they won't care about us. Even if half of us die, they won't care. But you are worth ten thousand of us. It's better for you to stay in the city and help us from there."
The king said, "I'll do what seems best to you." So the king stood by the gate while all the troops marched out by hundreds and by thousands.
The king ordered Joab, Abishai, and Ittai, "For my sake, be gentle with the young man Absalom." All the people heard the king give this order to his commanders about Absalom.
The army went into the field to fight Israel. The battle happened in the forest of Ephraim.
David's men defeated the people of Israel. That day, twenty thousand men died in a great defeat.
The fighting spread across the whole land. That day, the forest killed more people than the sword did.

Absalom ran into David's servants. He was riding a mule. The mule went under the thick branches of a big oak tree, and Absalom's head got stuck in the tree. He hung in the air while the mule kept going.
A man saw this and told Joab, "I just saw Absalom hanging in an oak tree!"
