Joab said, "What? You saw him? Why didn't you strike him to the ground? I would have given you ten pieces of silver and a belt."
The man answered, "Even if a thousand pieces of silver were put in my hand, I wouldn't hurt the king's son. We heard the king order you, Abishai, and Ittai, 'Protect the young man Absalom.'
If I had killed him—and the king finds out everything—you would have left me to answer for it."
Joab said, "I won't wait for you." He took three spears and drove them into Absalom's heart while Absalom was still alive in the oak tree.
Ten young men who carried Joab's weapons surrounded Absalom, struck him, and killed him.
Then Joab blew the trumpet, and the troops stopped chasing Israel because Joab held them back.
They took Absalom, threw him into a large pit in the forest, and piled a huge mound of stones over him. Then all the Israelites went home.

While he was alive, Absalom had set up a stone pillar for himself in the King's Valley. He said, "I have no son to keep my name alive." He named the pillar after himself, and people still call it Absalom's Monument today.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok said, "Let me run and tell the king the good news that the LORD has saved him from his enemies."
Joab said, "You are not the right man to bring news today. You can bring news another day, but not today, because the king's son is dead."
Then Joab said to a Cushite, "Go tell the king what you have seen." The Cushite bowed to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok kept asking, "No matter what happens, please let me run after the Cushite." Joab said, "Why do you want to run, my son? You won't get a reward."
"No matter what happens, I want to run," he said. So Joab said, "Run!" Then Ahimaaz ran across the plain and passed the Cushite.
David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof of the gate by the wall, looked out, and saw a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, "If he is alone, he must be bringing good news." As the man came closer,
the watchman saw another man running. So he called out to the gatekeeper, "Look! Another man is running alone!" "This one is also bringing good news," said the king.
The watchman said, "I can see that the first man runs like Ahimaaz son of Zadok." "He is a good man," said the king. "He must be bringing good news."

Then Ahimaaz called to the king, "All is well!" He bowed down with his face to the ground before the king and said, "Blessed be the LORD your God, who has handed over the men who raised their hands against my lord the king."
The king asked, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz said, "When Joab sent your servant, I saw a big uproar, but I don't know what it was."
The king said, "Step aside." So he stood to the side.
Just then the Cushite arrived and said, "May my lord the king hear good news! The LORD has given you justice today by saving you from all who rose up against you!"
The king asked the Cushite, "Is the young man Absalom safe?" The Cushite answered, "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you be like that young man!"

The king was deeply upset. He went up to the room above the gate and wept. As he walked, he cried, "Oh, my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! I wish I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son!"
Someone told Joab, "The king is crying and mourning for Absalom."
So the victory that day turned into sadness for all the people, because they heard the king was grieving for his son.
The people slipped into the city that day, like people who are ashamed when they run away from a battle.
The king covered his face and cried out loudly, "O my son Absalom! Absalom, my son, my son!"
Joab went into the king's house and said, "Today you have shamed the faces of all your servants who saved your life today, and the lives of your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your concubines.

You love those who hate you and hate those who love you. You have shown today that the commanders and servants mean nothing to you. Today I see that if Absalom were alive and all of us were dead, it would please you.

Now get up, go out, and speak kindly to your servants. I swear by the LORD that if you do not go out, not one man will stay with you tonight. That would be worse for you than all the trouble you have had since you were young."
Then the king got up and sat at the gate. The people were told, "The king is sitting at the gate." All the people came before the king, but Israel had fled, each man to his tent.
All the people in all the tribes of Israel were arguing, "The king saved us from our enemies and from the Philistines. Now he has fled from the land because of Absalom.
Absalom, whom we anointed over us, died in battle. So why are you silent about bringing the king back?"

King David sent word to Zadok and Abiathar the priests: "Speak to the elders of Judah and say, 'Why are you the last to bring the king back to his house? The word of all Israel has reached the king, asking for him to come home.
You are my brothers, my own flesh and bone. Why are you the last to bring the king back?'
And say to Amasa, 'Are you not my own flesh and bone? May God do to me, and more, if you are not commander of the army before me always in place of Joab.'"
He won the hearts of all the men of Judah as one man, so they sent to the king, "Return, you and all your servants."
So the king returned and came as far as the Jordan. Judah came to Gilgal to meet the king and help bring him across the Jordan.
Shimei son of Gera, a Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
A thousand men from Benjamin were with him, along with Ziba, the servant of Saul's house, his fifteen sons, and twenty servants. They rushed across the Jordan ahead of the king.
The ferry crossed to bring the king's household over and to do what seemed good to him. Shimei son of Gera fell before the king as he crossed the Jordan.
He said to the king, "My lord, do not count me guilty. Do not remember what your servant did wrong on the day my lord the king left Jerusalem. Do not take it to heart.
Your servant knows he sinned. Today I am the first of Joseph's house to come down to meet my lord the king."
Abishai son of Zeruiah answered, "Shouldn't Shimei be put to death for this? He cursed the LORD's anointed."
David said, "What do I have to do with you, sons of Zeruiah, that you are against me today? Should any man be put to death in Israel today? Don't I know today that I am king over Israel?"
The king said to Shimei, "You will not die." The king swore to him.
Mephibosheth, Saul's son, came down to meet the king. He had not cared for his feet, trimmed his beard, or washed his clothes from the day the king left until he returned safely.
When he came to Jerusalem to meet the king, the king said, "Why didn't you go with me, Mephibosheth?"
He answered, "My lord the king, my servant tricked me. I said, 'I will saddle my donkey and ride with the king,' because your servant is lame.
He slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is like an angel of God. Do what seems good to you.
All my father's family were only dead men before my lord the king, yet you set your servant among those who eat at your table. What right do I have to ask for more from the king?"
The king said, "Why say more? I have decided that you and Ziba will divide the field."
Mephibosheth said, "Let him take it all, since my lord the king has come home in peace."
Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim and crossed the Jordan with the king to send him on his way.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years old. He had provided for the king while he stayed at Mahanaim, because he was a very rich man.
The king said to Barzillai, "Cross with me, and I will take care of you with me in Jerusalem."
Barzillai said to the king, "How many days are left in my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?
I am eighty years old today. Can I tell good from bad? Can your servant taste what he eats or drinks? Can I still hear singers? Why should your servant be a burden to my lord the king?
Your servant will go a little way across the Jordan with the king. Why should the king repay me with such a reward?
Please let your servant go back and die in my own city, near my parents' tomb. But here is your servant Chimham. Let him cross with my lord the king, and do for him what seems good to you."
The king said, "Chimham will cross with me. I will do for him what seems good to you, and whatever you choose for me I will do for you."
All the people crossed the Jordan, and the king crossed too. He kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and Barzillai went back home.
The king went on to Gilgal, and Chimham went with him. All the people of Judah and half the people of Israel brought the king across.

Then all the men of Israel came to the king and said, "Why have our brothers, the men of Judah, stolen you away? They brought the king and his household across the Jordan, and all of David's men with him."
All the men of Judah answered the men of Israel, "Because the king is our close relative. Why are you angry about this? Have we eaten at the king's expense? Has he given us any gift?"

The men of Israel answered the men of Judah, "We have ten shares in the king, and we have more right to David than you. Why did you despise us? Weren't we the first to talk about bringing our king back?" But the words of the men of Judah were harsher than the words of the men of Israel.

A worthless man named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, happened to be there. He blew a trumpet and shouted, "We have no share in David, and no part in Jesse's son! Men of Israel, go home to your tents!"
So all the men of Israel turned away from David and followed Sheba son of Bichri. But the men of Judah stayed with their king, from the Jordan all the way to Jerusalem.

When David came to his house in Jerusalem, he took the ten concubines he had left to watch the house. He put them in a guarded room, took care of them, but did not sleep with them. They lived like widows until they died.
The king said to Amasa, "Call the men of Judah together for me in three days, and be here yourself."
Amasa went to call Judah, but he took longer than the time set for him.
David said to Abishai, "Sheba son of Bichri will hurt us more than Absalom did. Take your master's men and chase him. If he finds a fortified city, he may get away from us."
Joab's men, the Kerethites, the Pelethites, and all the mighty men went out. They left Jerusalem to chase Sheba son of Bichri.
When they reached the great stone at Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Joab was wearing his armor, with a sword strapped at his waist in its sheath. As he moved forward, the sword slipped out.
Joab said to Amasa, "Are you well, my brother?" Then Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab's hand. Joab stabbed him in the stomach, and Amasa's insides spilled onto the ground. He died without another blow. Then Joab and his brother Abishai chased Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's young men stood by Amasa and shouted, "Whoever is for Joab and whoever is for David, follow Joab!"
Amasa was rolling in his blood in the middle of the road. When the man saw that everyone stopped to look, he dragged Amasa off the road into a field and threw a cloth over him.
Once Amasa was moved from the road, everyone passed by and followed Joab to chase Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel Beth Maacah. All the Berites joined him and followed him in.
Joab's men came and surrounded him in Abel Beth Maacah. They built a siege ramp against the city wall, and the whole army with Joab was tearing down the wall.
A wise woman called out from the city, "Listen! Listen! Please tell Joab to come here so I can speak with him."
Joab came near, and the woman asked, "Are you Joab?" He said, "I am." She said, "Listen to your servant." He said, "I am listening."
She said, "Long ago people said to ask for advice at Abel, and that settled things."
"I am one of the peaceful, faithful people of Israel. You are trying to destroy a city that is like a mother in Israel. Why would you destroy the inheritance of the the LORD?"
Joab answered, "Far be it from me! Far be it from me to swallow up or destroy!"

"That is not what I want. A man named Sheba son of Bichri, from the hill country of Ephraim, has rebelled against King David. Hand him over alone, and I will leave the city." The woman said to Joab, "His head will be thrown to you over the wall."

The woman went to all the people with her wise plan. They cut off the head of Sheba son of Bichri and threw it to Joab. He blew the trumpet, and the men left the city and went home. Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was over all the army of Israel. Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Kerethites and Pelethites.
Adoram was in charge of forced labor. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Sheva was the secretary. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Ira the Jairite was David's priest.
During David's reign, a famine lasted three years in a row. David asked the LORD for help. The LORD said, "It is because of the blood Saul and his family spilled. He killed the Gibeonites."

So the king called the Gibeonites and spoke to them. The Gibeonites were not Israelites; they were a small group left from the Amorites. The Israelites had promised not to harm them, but Saul had tried to wipe them out because he was eager to help Israel and Judah.
David asked the Gibeonites, "What should I do for you? How can I make this right so you will bless the LORD's land?"
The Gibeonites said, "We do not want silver or gold from Saul or his family. We also do not want any Israelite put to death." David said, "Tell me what you want, and I will do it."
They answered the king, "The man who destroyed us and tried to wipe us out of Israel's land..."
"Let seven of his male descendants be handed over to us. We will hang them before the LORD at Gibeah, Saul's hometown, the place the LORD chose." The king said, "I will give them to you."
The king spared Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, Saul's son, because of the promise David and Jonathan had made before the LORD.

But the king took Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons Rizpah daughter of Aiah had borne to Saul. He also took the five sons of Michal, Saul's daughter, whom she had borne to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.
He gave them to the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on a hill before the LORD. All seven died together. They were put to death early in the harvest, when the barley harvest began.

Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it on a rock for herself. She stayed there from the start of the harvest until rain fell from the sky. She kept the birds of the air from landing on the bodies during the day, and she kept the wild animals away at night.
David was told what Rizpah, Saul's concubine, had done.

So David went and took the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the men of Jabesh Gilead. They had stolen them from the public square in Beth Shan, where the Philistines had hung them on the day they killed Saul at Gilboa.
David brought up the bones of Saul and Jonathan. They also gathered the bones of those who had been hanged.
They buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan in Zela, in Benjamin's land, in the tomb of Saul's father Kish. After they did everything the king commanded, God answered prayer for the land.
Later, war broke out again between the Philistines and Israel. David and his men went down to fight. David became very tired.
Ishbi-Benob, one of the descendants of Rapha, had a bronze spear that weighed three hundred shekels. He carried a new sword and planned to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah came to help David. He struck the Philistine and killed him. Then David's men made a promise to him: "Never again will you go out with us to battle, so that Israel will not lose its leader."
After this, another battle took place with the Philistines at Gob. Sibbecai the Hushathite killed Saph, who was also one of Rapha's descendants.
In another battle with the Philistines at Gob, Elhanan son of Jaare the weaver killed Goliath the Gittite. Goliath's spear shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam.
There was still another battle at Gath. A huge man was there with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all. He also came from Rapha's family.
When he made fun of Israel, Jonathan, son of David's brother Shimea, killed him.
These four men were Rapha's descendants in Gath. They died at the hands of David and his men.
David spoke the words of this song to the LORD when the LORD saved him from all his enemies and from Saul.
"The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer.
My God is my rock, where I take refuge. He is my shield and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge. My Savior, You save me from violence.
I call on the LORD, who is worthy of praise, and I am saved from my enemies.
"The waves of death surrounded me, and the floods of wickedness terrified me.
The cords of the grave wrapped around me; the snares of death confronted me.
In my distress I called to the LORD; I cried out to my God. From His temple He heard my voice, and my cry reached His ears.
"Then the earth shook and trembled; the foundations of the heavens quaked, because He was angry.
Smoke rose from His nostrils, and consuming fire came from His mouth; burning coals blazed from it.
He parted the heavens and came down, with thick darkness under His feet.
He rode on a cherub and flew; He was seen on the wings of the wind.
He made darkness His covering, surrounding Him with rain clouds and thick clouds of the skies.
From the brightness before Him, coals of fire blazed.
The LORD thundered from heaven, and the Most High raised His voice.
He shot arrows and scattered them; lightning routed them.
The channels of the sea appeared, and the foundations of the world were exposed at the rebuke of the LORD, at the blast of breath from His nostrils.
"He reached down from on high and took hold of me; He drew me out of deep waters.
He rescued me from my powerful enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me.
They confronted me in my day of disaster, but the LORD was my support.
He brought me out into open space; He rescued me because He delighted in me.
"The LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness; He has repaid me according to the cleanness of my hands.
For I have kept the ways of the LORD and have not wickedly turned from my God.
For all His ordinances are before me, and I have not turned away from His statutes.
I have been blameless before Him and have kept myself from my sin.
So the LORD has rewarded me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness in His sight.
"To the faithful You show Yourself faithful; to the blameless You show Yourself blameless.
To the pure You show Yourself pure, but to the crooked You show Yourself shrewd.
You save an afflicted people, but Your eyes are on the haughty to bring them down.
For You are my lamp, O the LORD, and the LORD lights up my darkness.
With Your help I can run through a troop; with my God I can leap over a wall.
As for God, His way is perfect; the word of the LORD is flawless. He is a shield to all who take refuge in Him.
"For who is God besides the LORD? And who is the Rock except our God?
God is my strong fortress, and He makes my way blameless.
He makes my feet like the feet of a deer and sets me on the heights.
He trains my hands for battle, so my arms can bend a bronze bow.
You have given me the shield of Your salvation, and Your gentleness has made me great.
You widen the path beneath me, so my feet do not slip.
"I pursued my enemies and destroyed them; I did not turn back until they were consumed.
I crushed them and pierced them so they could not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
You armed me with strength for battle; You made my foes bow before me.
You made my enemies turn their backs to me, and I destroyed those who hated me.
They looked, but there was no one to save them—to the LORD, but He did not answer them.
I ground them as fine as dust of the earth; I crushed and trampled them like mud in the streets.
You have delivered me from the attacks of my people; You have preserved me as head of nations. A people I did not know serves me.
Foreigners submit to me; as soon as they hear, they obey me.
Foreigners fade away and come trembling from their strongholds.
The LORD lives! Blessed be my Rock! May God, the Rock of my salvation, be exalted!
He is the God who avenges me and brings peoples under my rule.
He delivers me from my enemies. You lift me up above my foes; You rescue me from violent men.
Therefore I will praise You among the nations, O the LORD, and I will sing praises to Your name.
He gives great victories to His king and shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever."
These are David's last words. David son of Jesse speaks. God raised him up. The God of Jacob anointed him. He was Israel's sweet singer.
The Spirit of the LORD spoke through him. God's word was on his tongue.
The God of Israel spoke. The Rock of Israel told him that a ruler over people must be fair and rule with respect for God.
Such a ruler is like the light of morning when the sun rises on a clear morning. He is like the brightness after rain that makes grass grow from the ground.
My family is not perfect before God, but He made an everlasting covenant with me. It is complete and secure in every way. He will bring my salvation and every desire to fulfillment.
But worthless people are all like thorns thrown away, because no one can pick them up by hand.
Anyone who touches them must use iron and a spear shaft. They are burned up completely in the fire.
These are the names of David's mighty warriors: Josheb-Basshebeth, a Tahkemonite, was chief of the Three. He killed eight hundred men at one time with his spear.

Next was Eleazar son of Dodo the Ahohite. He was one of the three mighty men. He stood with David against the Philistines when they gathered for battle at Pas-dammim, while Israel's soldiers ran away.

But Eleazar stayed and fought the Philistines until his hand was so tired it stuck to his sword. The LORD gave a great victory that day. The soldiers came back to Eleazar, but only to take things from the dead.
Next was Shammah son of Agee the Hararite. The Philistines gathered at Lehi, where a field was full of lentils. The people ran away from the Philistines.
But Shammah stood in the middle of the field, defended it, and struck down the Philistines. The LORD gave a great victory.
During harvest time, three of the thirty leaders went down to David at the cave of Adullam. A group of Philistines was camped in the Valley of Rephaim.
At that time David was in the stronghold, and the Philistine camp was in Bethlehem.
David was thirsty and said, "I wish someone would bring me water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem!"

So the three mighty men broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it to David. But he would not drink it. Instead, he poured it out to the LORD.
He said, "I could never do that, the LORD. This is like the blood of men who risked their lives." So he would not drink it. These were the brave deeds of the three mighty men.
Abishai, Joab's brother and Zeruiah's son, was chief of the Three. He killed three hundred men with his spear and became famous among the Three.
He was honored more than the Three and became their commander, though he was not one of the Three.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was a brave warrior from Kabzeel. He did great deeds. He killed two of Moab's best fighters. On a snowy day he went down into a pit and killed a lion.
He also killed a huge Egyptian. The Egyptian had a spear, but Benaiah went at him with a club. He took the spear from the Egyptian's hand and killed him with it.
These were the brave deeds of Benaiah son of Jehoiada. He became famous with the three mighty men.
He was honored more than the Thirty, but he was not one of the Three. David put him in charge of his bodyguard.
Among the Thirty were Asahel, Joab's brother; Elhanan son of Dodo from Bethlehem;
Shammah the Harodite; Elika the Harodite;
Helez the Paltite; Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa;
Abiezer from Anathoth; Mebunnai the Hushathite;
Zalmon the Ahohite; Maharai the Netophathite;
Heleb son of Baanah the Netophathite; Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah of Benjamin;
Benaiah of Pirathon; Hiddai from the brooks of Gaash;
Abi-albon the Arbathite; Azmaveth the Bahurimite;
Eliahba the Shaalbonite; the sons of Jashen; Jonathan;
Shammah the Hararite; Ahiam son of Sharar the Hararite;
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai the Maacathite; Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite;
Hezro the Carmelite; Paarai the Arbite;
Igal son of Nathan from Zobah; Bani the Gadite;
Zelek the Ammonite; Naharai the Beerothite, Joab son of Zeruiah's armor-bearer;
Ira the Ithrite; Gareb the Ithrite;
and Uriah the Hittite. There were thirty-seven in all.
Again, the LORD was angry with Israel, and He stirred David to act against them. He told David, “Go and count the people of Israel and Judah.”
So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army who was with him, “Go now through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and count the people. Then I will know how many there are.”
Joab replied to the king, “May the LORD your God multiply the people a hundred times, and may my lord the king see it with his own eyes. But why does my lord the king want to do this?”
But the king's word won out over Joab and the army commanders. So Joab and the commanders left the king's presence to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and camped near Aroer, south of the town in the middle of the valley. Then they moved toward Gad and Jazer.
They went to Gilead and the land of Tahtim Hodshi. Then they went to Dan Jaan and around toward Sidon.
They came to the fortress of Tyre and to all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites. Then they went south to the Negev of Judah at Beersheba.
After they had gone through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
Joab reported the number of fighting men to the king: Israel had 800,000 brave men who could draw a sword, and Judah had 500,000.

After David had counted the people, he felt guilty. He said to the LORD, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, the LORD, please take away the guilt of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”
When David got up the next morning, the word of the LORD came to Gad the prophet, David's seer.
“Go and tell David, ‘This is what the LORD says: I am giving you three choices. Choose one of them, and I will carry it out against you.’”

So Gad went to David and told him, “Should seven years of famine come on your land? Or should you run for three months from your enemies while they chase you? Or should there be three days of plague in your land? Now think about it and decide what answer I should give to the One who sent me.”
David said to Gad, “I am in great trouble. Please let us be punished by the LORD, because His mercy is great. But don't let us be punished by people.”
So the LORD sent a plague on Israel from that morning until the set time. Seventy thousand men died, from Dan to Beersheba.

When the angel reached out his hand to destroy Jerusalem, the LORD changed His mind about the disaster and said to the angel who was destroying the people, “Enough! Withdraw your hand.” The angel of the LORD was standing at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.

When David saw the angel striking down the people, he said to the LORD, “I have sinned and done wrong, but these people are like sheep. What have they done? Please let Your hand fall on me and on my father's family.”
That day Gad came to David and said, “Go up and build an altar to the LORD on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
So David went up, as the LORD had commanded through Gad.
When Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants coming toward him, he went out and bowed with his face to the ground before the king.
Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David replied, “To buy the threshing floor from you, to build an altar to the LORD, so that the plague will stop for the people.”
Araunah said to David, “My lord the king may take whatever he wants and offer it up. Here are oxen for the burnt offering, and here are the threshing sledges and the ox yokes for the wood.”
Araunah gave all of this to the king. He also said, “May the LORD your God accept you.”

But the king replied to Araunah, “No, I insist on paying you for it. I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver.
There David built an altar to the LORD and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Then the LORD answered the prayer for the land, and the plague on Israel was stopped.
His servants said to him, "Let us find a young virgin for my lord the king. She will stand before the king and care for him. She will lie in your bosom, my lord the king, and keep you warm."
They searched all over Israel for a beautiful young woman. They found Abishag the Shunammite and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very beautiful. She cared for the king and served him, but the king did not have sexual relations with her.
Adonijah son of Haggith made himself important. He said, "I will be king." He got chariots, horsemen, and fifty men to run before him.
His father had never corrected him or asked, "Why did you do that?" Adonijah was also very handsome. He was born after Absalom.
He spoke with Joab son of Zeruiah and Abiathar the priest. They supported Adonijah.
But Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and David's mighty men did not join Adonijah.
Adonijah sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fattened calves near the stone of Zoheleth by En Rogel. He invited all his brothers, the king's sons, and all the men of Judah who served the king.
But he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or his brother Solomon.
Nathan said to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, "Have you not heard that Adonijah son of Haggith has become king? Our lord David does not know it."
"Now come, let me give you advice. Save your own life and the life of your son Solomon."
"Go to King David and say, 'My lord the king, didn't you swear to your servant that my son Solomon would be king after you and sit on your throne? Why then has Adonijah become king?'"
"While you are still there speaking with the king, I will come in after you and support what you have said."
Bathsheba went to the king in his room. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was serving him.
Bathsheba bowed low before the king. The king said, "What do you want?"
She said to him, "My lord, you swore to your servant by the LORD your God that your son Solomon would be king after me and sit on my throne."
"Now Adonijah has become king, and my lord the king does not know it."
"He has sacrificed many oxen, fattened calves, and sheep. He invited all the king's sons, Abiathar the priest, and Joab the army commander. But he did not invite your servant Solomon."
"My lord the king, all Israel is watching you to see who will sit on your throne after you."
"When my lord the king dies, I and my son Solomon will be punished."
While she was still speaking with the king, Nathan the prophet came in.
They told the king, "Nathan the prophet is here." He came in and bowed with his face to the ground before the king.
Nathan said, "My lord the king, did you say that Adonijah would be king after you and sit on your throne?"

"Today he went down and sacrificed many oxen, fattened calves, and sheep. He invited all the king's sons, the army commanders, and Abiathar the priest. Now they are eating and drinking with him and saying, 'Long live King Adonijah!'"
"But he did not invite me, Zadok the priest, Benaiah your servant, or your son Solomon."
"Did my lord the king do this without telling his servants who should sit on your throne after you?"
King David answered, "Call Bathsheba to me." She came and stood before the king.
The king swore, "As the LORD lives, who has saved me from every trouble,
I will do today what I swore to you by the LORD, the God of Israel: Your son Solomon will be king after me, and he will sit on my throne in my place."
Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground and said, "May my lord King David live forever!"
King David said, "Call Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada to me." They came.
The king said to them, "Take your lord's servants with you. Put my son Solomon on my own mule and take him down to Gihon."
"There Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet will anoint him as king over Israel. Blow the trumpet and say, 'Long live King Solomon!'"
"Then come up after him, and he will come and sit on my throne. He will be king in my place. I have appointed him ruler over Israel and Judah."
Benaiah answered, "Amen! May the LORD God of my lord the king say so too."
"As the LORD has been with my lord the king, so may He be with Solomon. May He make Solomon's throne greater than my lord the king's throne."
So Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and Pelethites went down. They put Solomon on King David's mule and brought him to Gihon.
Zadok the priest took the horn of oil from the tent and anointed Solomon. They blew the trumpet, and all the people said, "Long live King Solomon!"
All the people followed him, playing flutes and rejoicing with great joy. The earth shook with their noise.
Adonijah and all his guests heard it as they finished eating. When Joab heard the trumpet, he asked, "Why is the city so noisy?"
While he was still speaking, Jonathan son of Abiathar the priest arrived. Adonijah said, "Come in, for you are a brave man and bring good news."
Jonathan answered Adonijah, "No! Our lord King David has made Solomon king."
"The king sent Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and the Cherethites and Pelethites. They put Solomon on the king's mule."
"Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anointed him king at Gihon. They went up from there rejoicing, and the city is in an uproar. That is the noise you heard."
"Solomon has also sat on the royal throne."
"The king's servants came to bless our lord King David, saying, 'May God make Solomon's name greater than yours, and his throne greater than your throne.' Then the king bowed on his bed."
The king said, "Blessed be the LORD God of Israel, who has given me someone to sit on my throne today while I can still see it."
All of Adonijah's guests were afraid. They got up and went their own ways.
Adonijah was afraid of Solomon. He got up and went to hold on to the horns of the altar.
Someone told Solomon that Adonijah was afraid of King Solomon and was holding on to the horns of the altar, asking Solomon to swear not to kill him with the sword.
Solomon said, "If he proves to be a worthy man, not a hair of his head will fall to the ground. But if he is found to be wicked, he will die."
King Solomon sent for him. They brought him down from the altar. He came and bowed before King Solomon. Solomon said to him, "Go home."
As David’s time to die drew near, he gave his son Solomon this command:
“I am about to go the way of all the earth. Be strong and act like a man.

Keep the charge of the LORD, your God. Walk in His ways and keep His rules, commands, decisions, and warnings, as written in the Law of Moses. Then you will do well in everything you do, wherever you go.
Then the LORD will keep His promise to me: ‘If your sons live right and walk before Me in truth, with all their heart and all their soul, you will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel.’

And you know what Joab son of Zeruiah did to me. He killed the two commanders of Israel’s armies, Abner son of Ner and Amasa son of Jether. He killed them in peacetime as if in war. He got their blood on the belt around his waist and the sandals on his feet.
So deal with him wisely. Do not let his gray head go down to the grave in peace.
But show kindness to the sons of Barzillai the Gileadite. Let them eat at your table, because they stood by me when I ran from your brother Absalom.

And watch Shimei son of Gera, the Benjaminite from Bahurim, who is with you. He cursed me badly the day I went to Mahanaim. But when he came down to meet me at the Jordan, I swore to him by the LORD, ‘I will not kill you with the sword.’
Now do not let him go unpunished. You are a wise man, and you know what to do to him. Bring his gray head down to the grave in blood.”
Then David died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David.
David had ruled Israel for forty years: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.
So Solomon sat on his father David’s throne, and his kingdom was firmly set.
Adonijah son of Haggith went to Bathsheba, Solomon’s mother. She asked, “Do you come in peace?” “Yes, in peace,” he said.
Then he said, “I have something to say to you.” “Speak,” she said.
“You know,” he said, “that the kingdom was mine, and all Israel expected me to be king. But the kingdom has turned to my brother, because the LORD gave it to him.”
“Now I have just one request of you. Do not turn me down.” “Speak,” she replied.
“Please ask King Solomon—for he will not turn you away—to give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.”
“Very well,” Bathsheba replied. “I will speak to the king for you.”

So Bathsheba went to King Solomon to speak to him about Adonijah. The king rose to greet her, bowed to her, and sat on his throne. Then he had a throne brought for the king’s mother, and she sat at his right hand.
“I have just one small request to make of you,” she said. “Do not turn me down.” “Ask, my mother,” the king replied, “for I will not turn you down.”
So she said, “Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to Adonijah, your brother, as his wife.”

King Solomon answered his mother, “Why do you ask for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Since he is my older brother, you might as well ask for the kingdom for him—and for Abiathar the priest and Joab son of Zeruiah!”
Then King Solomon swore by the LORD: “May God punish me, and even more, if Adonijah does not pay for this request with his life!
And now, as surely as the LORD lives—the One who set me on my father David’s throne and made a house for me as He promised—Adonijah will be put to death today!”
So King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he struck Adonijah down, and Adonijah died.

Then the king said to Abiathar the priest, “Go to your fields in Anathoth. You deserve to die, but I will not kill you now, because you carried the ark of the Lord GOD before my father David, and you suffered everything my father suffered.”
So Solomon removed Abiathar from being priest of the LORD, to fulfill the LORD’s word spoken at Shiloh about the house of Eli.
When Joab heard this—he had sided with Adonijah but not with Absalom—he ran to the tent of the LORD and grabbed the horns of the altar.
King Solomon was told, “Joab has run to the tent of the LORD and is by the altar.” So Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, saying, “Go strike him down!”

Benaiah went into the tent of the LORD and said to Joab, “The king says, ‘Come out!’” But Joab replied, “No, I will die here.” So Benaiah reported to the king, “This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me.”
And the king replied, “Do just as he says. Strike him down and bury him. Remove from me and from my father’s house the innocent blood Joab shed.

The LORD will bring his blood back on his own head, because without my father David knowing it, he killed two men more righteous and better than he: Abner son of Ner, commander of Israel’s army, and Amasa son of Jether, commander of Judah’s army.
Their blood will come back on Joab’s head and on his family forever. But the LORD will give peace to David, his family, his house, and his throne forever.”
So Benaiah son of Jehoiada went up, struck Joab down, and killed him. Joab was buried at his own home in the wilderness.
The king put Benaiah son of Jehoiada in charge of the army in Joab’s place, and he put Zadok the priest in Abiathar’s place.
Then the king sent for Shimei and said to him, “Build a house for yourself in Jerusalem and live there. Do not go anywhere else.”
“On the day you leave and cross the Kidron Valley, know for sure that you will die. Your blood will be on your own head.”
“That is fine,” Shimei replied. “Your servant will do as my lord the king says.” So Shimei lived in Jerusalem for many days.
After three years, two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei was told, “Look, your slaves are in Gath.”
So Shimei saddled his donkey and went to Gath to look for his slaves. He found them and brought them back from Gath.
Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and come back.

The king summoned Shimei and said to him, “Did I not make you swear by the LORD and warn you, ‘On the day you leave and go anywhere, know for sure that you will die’? Yet you have not kept the LORD’s oath or the command I gave you.”
“Why have you not kept the LORD’s oath and the command I gave you?”
The king also said to Shimei, “You know in your heart all the harm you did to my father David. Now the LORD will bring your evil back on your own head.”
“But King Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will stand before the LORD forever.”
Then the king ordered Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and he went out, struck Shimei down, and Shimei died. So the kingdom was firmly established in Solomon’s hands.

Solomon made an alliance with Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He married Pharaoh's daughter and brought her to the City of David. He kept her there until he finished building his palace, the house of the the LORD, and the wall around Jerusalem.
The people were still sacrificing at the high places, because a house for the Name of the the LORD had not yet been built.
Solomon loved the the LORD and walked in the laws of his father David, but he also sacrificed and burned incense at the high places.
The king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there, because it was the most important high place. Solomon offered a thousand burnt offerings on the altar there.
At Gibeon the the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream at night. God said, "Ask what I should give you."

Solomon said, "You have shown great and faithful love to Your servant David, my father. He walked before You in truth, in right living, and with a true heart toward You. You kept that great love for him and gave him a son to sit on his throne, just as it is today."
"And now, O the LORD my God, You have made Your servant king in place of David, my father. But I am only a young boy. I do not know how to lead Your people."
"Your servant is in the middle of Your people, whom You have chosen. They are so many that no one can count them."
"So give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to tell right from wrong. For who can govern this great people?"
The Lord was pleased that Solomon asked for this.
God said to him, "Because you asked for this and did not ask for a long life or riches or the death of your enemies, but asked for understanding to judge fairly,
I will do what you asked. I will give you a wise and understanding heart. No one before you has been like you, and no one after you will be like you."
"I will also give you what you did not ask for: riches and honor, so that no other king will be your equal during your whole life.
And if you walk in My ways and keep My laws and commands, as your father David did, then I will give you a long life."

Then Solomon woke up and realized it had been a dream. He went to Jerusalem and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. He offered burnt offerings and peace offerings, and he held a feast for all his servants.
At that time two prostitutes came to the king and stood before him.
One woman said, "Please, my lord, this woman and I live in the same house. I gave birth to a baby while she was there.
On the third day after I gave birth, she also gave birth. We were alone in the house; no one else was with us. Only the two of us were in the house.
During the night this woman's baby died, because she rolled over on him.
"She got up in the middle of the night and took my son from beside me while I, your servant, slept. She laid him at her breast and laid her dead son at my breast.
When I got up in the morning to nurse my son, he was dead. But when I looked at him closely, I saw he was not the son I had given birth to."

But the other woman said, "No, the living child is mine, and the dead child is yours." But the first woman said, "No, the dead child is yours, and the living child is mine." So they argued before the king.
Then the king said, "One says, 'This is my son who lives, and your son is dead,' while the other says, 'No, your son is dead, and my son is the living one.'"
So the king said, "Bring me a sword." And they brought a sword before the king.
The king said, "Cut the living child in two and give half to one woman and half to the other."

The woman whose son was alive spoke to the king, because she loved her son deeply. She said, "Please, my lord, give her the living child. Do not kill him!" But the other woman said, "He will be neither mine nor yours. Cut him in two!"
Then the king said, "Give the living child to the first woman. Do not kill him; she is his mother."
All Israel heard about the judgment the king had made. They stood in awe of the king, because they saw that God's wisdom was in him to do what was right.
Solomon was king over all Israel.
These were his top officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.
Elihoreph and Ahijah, the sons of Shisha, were secretaries. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was in charge of the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the district governors. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and the king's friend.
Ahishar was in charge of the palace. Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of forced labor.
Solomon had twelve district governors over all Israel. They provided food for the king and his household. Each governor was responsible for one month of the year.
These are their names: Ben-Hur was in the hill country of Ephraim.
Ben-Deker was in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh, and Elon-beth-hanan.
Ben-Hesed was in Arubboth. Sokoh and all the land of Hepher belonged to him.
Ben-Abinadab was in charge of all Naphath-dor. Solomon's daughter Taphath was his wife.
Baana son of Ahilud was in Taanach, Megiddo, and all Beth-shean near Zarethan, below Jezreel. His area ran from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah and beyond Jokneam.
Ben-Geber was in Ramoth-gilead. He also controlled the villages of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan, which had sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars.
Ahinadab son of Iddo was in Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz was in Naphtali. He had married Basemath, another daughter of Solomon.
Baana son of Hushai was in Asher and Bealoth.
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah was in Issachar.
Shimei son of Ela was in Benjamin.
Geber son of Uri was in the land of Gilead, including the lands of Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. There was one governor in that land.
Judah and Israel were as many as the sand on the seashore. They ate, drank, and rejoiced.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the River to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt. Those kingdoms brought tribute and served Solomon all the days of his life.
Solomon's food for one day was thirty cors of fine flour and sixty cors of meal.
He also had ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and one hundred sheep, plus deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fattened poultry.
He ruled over everything west of the River, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and he had peace on all sides.
During Solomon's life, Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan to Beersheba. Each man lived in peace and plenty in his own home.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horses.
Those governors also provided food for King Solomon and everyone who came to his table. They did not fail to bring what was needed.
Each man brought his supplies to the right place at the right time: barley and straw for the chariot horses and other horses.
God gave Solomon great wisdom, very great understanding, and a broad mind like the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the people of the East and all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than all men—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Calcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. His fame spread to all the surrounding nations.
He spoke three thousand proverbs and one thousand and five songs.
He spoke about trees, from the cedar in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He also spoke about animals, birds, creeping things, and fish.
People came from all nations to hear Solomon's wisdom. They were sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard of his wisdom.
When Hiram, king of Tyre, heard that Solomon had been made king in place of his father, he sent his servants to Solomon. Hiram had loved David all his life.
Solomon sent this message to Hiram:
“You know that my father David could not build a temple for the Name of the LORD his God. Wars surrounded him until the LORD gave him victory over his enemies.
But now the LORD my God has given me rest on every side. There is no enemy and no trouble.

So I plan to build a temple for the Name of the LORD my God, just as the LORD promised my father David. He said, ‘Your son, whom I will put on your throne in your place, will build the house for My Name.’

Now please command that cedars be cut for me from Lebanon. My servants will work with your servants. I will pay your servants whatever wages you ask, because you know that no one among us knows how to cut timber like the people of Sidon.”
When Hiram heard Solomon's words, he rejoiced greatly and said, “Blessed be the LORD today! He has given David a wise son to rule over this great people.”
Hiram sent this reply to Solomon: “I have heard your request. I will supply all the cedar and cypress wood you want.

My servants will bring the logs down from Lebanon to the sea. I will make them into rafts and float them to the place you choose. There I will break them apart, and you can carry them away. You will provide food for my royal household.”
So Hiram gave Solomon all the cedar and cypress wood he wanted.
Each year Solomon gave Hiram 20,000 measures of wheat for his household and 20 measures of pure olive oil.
The LORD gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.
King Solomon forced 30,000 men from all Israel to work.
He sent them to Lebanon in shifts of 10,000 a month. They spent one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of the forced labor.
Solomon also had 70,000 men who carried loads and 80,000 men who cut stone in the hills.
Besides these, he had 3,300 supervisors who oversaw the workers.
The king ordered large, costly stones to be cut for the temple foundation. They were hewn stones.
Solomon's builders, Hiram's builders, and the Giblites cut and prepared the wood and stone for building the temple.

In the four hundred eightieth year after the Israelites came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of Solomon's reign over Israel, in the month of Ziv, the second month, he began to build the house of the the LORD.
The house that King Solomon built for the the LORD was sixty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high.
The porch in front of the main hall was twenty cubits long, across the width of the house, and ten cubits deep in front of the house.
He made narrow windows for the house.
Against the walls of the main hall and the inner sanctuary, he built a structure all around the house, and he made side rooms all around.

The lowest floor was five cubits wide, the middle floor six cubits, and the third floor seven cubits. He made offset ledges around the outside of the house so that the beams would not be inserted into the walls of the house.
The house was built with stone finished at the quarry, so no hammer, chisel, or any iron tool was heard in the house while it was being built.
The entrance to the middle floor was on the right side of the house. They went up by winding stairs to the middle floor, and from the middle to the third.
So he built the house and finished it, and he covered the house with beams and boards of cedar.
He built the side rooms against the whole house, each five cubits high, and attached them to the house with cedar beams.
Then the word of the the LORD came to Solomon:

"As for this house you are building, if you walk in My statutes, carry out My ordinances, and keep all My commandments by walking in them, then I will fulfill through you the promise I made to your father David.
And I will dwell among the Israelites and will not abandon My people Israel."
So Solomon built the house and finished it.
He lined the walls of the house with cedar from floor to ceiling, and he overlaid the floor with cypress.
He partitioned off twenty cubits at the rear of the house with cedar boards from floor to ceiling to form an inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place.
The main hall in front of this room was forty cubits long.
The cedar inside the house was carved with gourds and open flowers. Everything was cedar; no stone was visible.
He prepared the inner sanctuary inside the house to set the ark of the covenant of the the LORD there.
The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high. He overlaid it with pure gold, and he also overlaid the cedar altar.
So Solomon overlaid the inside of the house with pure gold, and he stretched gold chains across the front of the inner sanctuary and overlaid it with gold.
He overlaid the whole house with gold, until it was completely finished. He also overlaid the entire altar in the inner sanctuary with gold.
In the inner sanctuary he made two cherubim of olive wood, each ten cubits high.
One wing of the first cherub was five cubits, and the other wing five cubits, so the wingspan was ten cubits from tip to tip.
The second cherub also measured ten cubits; both cherubim had the same size and shape.
The height of one cherub was ten cubits, and so was the other.

He placed the cherubim inside the inner sanctuary. Their wings were spread out so that the wing of one touched one wall, and the wing of the other touched the opposite wall; their other wings touched in the middle of the house.
He also overlaid the cherubim with gold.
He carved all the walls of the house, both inner and outer, with carved figures of cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers.
He overlaid the floors of the house, both inner and outer, with gold.
For the entrance to the inner sanctuary he made doors of olive wood, with five-sided doorposts.
The two doors were made of olive wood, and he carved on them cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, spreading the gold evenly over the carved work.
In the same way he made doorposts of olive wood for the entrance to the main hall, each one-fourth of the wall.
He made two doors of cypress wood, each with two folding panels.
He carved on them cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, fitted evenly over the carved work.
He built the inner courtyard with three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams.
The foundation of the house of the the LORD was laid in the fourth year, in the month of Ziv.
In the eleventh year, in the month of Bul, the eighth month, the house was finished in every detail, according to all its specifications. So he built it in seven years.
It took Solomon thirteen years to finish building his palace.

He built the House of the Forest of Lebanon. It was one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. It stood on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams resting on the pillars.
Cedar panels covered the beams above the pillars. There were forty-five beams, with fifteen in each row.
There were three rows of windows, and each row faced the one across from it.
All the doorways and posts were square, and the windows were set in three matching rows.
He made the Hall of Pillars fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. It had a porch in front, with a roof supported by pillars.
He also built the Hall of the Throne, where he judged cases. Cedar panels covered it from floor to ceiling.
His own house, where he lived, was in another courtyard behind the hall. It was built in the same style. He also built a house for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married. It was like the hall.

All these buildings were made with costly stones. The stones were cut to size and trimmed with saws, both inside and outside. This was done from the foundation to the roofline, and from the outside to the large courtyard.
The foundation was made of large, costly stones. Some were ten cubits long, and some were eight cubits long.
Above them were high-quality stones, cut to size, and cedar beams.
The large courtyard was surrounded by three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams. The inner courtyard of the house of the the LORD and its porch had the same kind of wall.
King Solomon sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre.

Hiram was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali. His father was from Tyre and worked with bronze. Hiram had great wisdom, understanding, and skill for all kinds of bronze work. He came to King Solomon and did all the work Solomon asked for.
He cast two bronze pillars. Each one was eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits around.
He made two bronze capitals to put on top of the pillars. Each capital was five cubits high.
He decorated the capitals with a network of lattice work and chains. There were seven chains for each capital.
He placed two rows of pomegranates around each network to cover the capitals on top. He did the same for the other capital.
The capitals on top of the pillars in the porch were shaped like lilies. They were four cubits high.
On both pillars, just above the rounded part near the network, there were two hundred pomegranates in rows around each capital.
He set up the pillars at the porch of the temple. The pillar on the south he named Jachin, and the pillar on the north he named Boaz.
The tops of the pillars were shaped like lilies. In this way the work on the pillars was finished.
He made the Sea of cast bronze. It was round, ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits high, and thirty cubits around.
Below the rim, gourds went all the way around it. There were ten gourds for every cubit. They were cast in two rows as part of the Sea.
The Sea rested on twelve oxen. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east. All their hind parts pointed toward the center.
The Sea was a handbreadth thick. Its rim was shaped like the rim of a cup, like a lily flower. It held two thousand baths.
He made ten bronze stands. Each stand was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
This was how the stands were made. They had panels, and the panels were set between the frames.
On the panels between the frames were lions, oxen, and cherubim. On the frames above and below the lions and oxen were wreaths of hammered work.
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles. Four legs supported the basin from below. The supports were cast with wreaths on each side.
The opening was inside the crown, which rose one cubit above it. The opening was round, like a bowl, one and a half cubits across. Its sides had engravings, and the panels were square, not round.
The four wheels were under the panels. The axles were attached to the stand. Each wheel was one and a half cubits across.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels. Their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs were all cast metal.
There were four supports at the four corners of each stand. The supports were cast as part of the stand.
On top of each stand was a round band half a cubit high. The supports and panels were cast as part of the stand.
He engraved cherubim, lions, and palm trees on the supports and panels. Wreaths went all around.
He made all ten stands the same size and shape.
He made ten bronze basins. Each one held forty baths. Each basin was four cubits across. One basin sat on each stand.
He put five stands on the south side of the house and five on the north side. He placed the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner.
Hiram also made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. So Hiram finished all the work he had promised to do for King Solomon in the house of the the LORD:
the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals on top of the pillars; the two sets of network that covered the bowl-shaped capitals;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two sets of network, with two rows of pomegranates for each network that covered the two bowl-shaped capitals on the pillars;
the ten stands with the ten basins on them;
the Sea and the twelve oxen under it;
the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls.
All these things Hiram made for King Solomon for the house of the the LORD were made of polished bronze.
Solomon did not weigh these objects, because there were so many. The weight of the bronze could not be measured.
Solomon also made all the furnishings for the house of the the LORD: the gold altar; the gold table that held the Bread of the Presence;
the lampstands of pure gold, five on the right and five on the left in front of the inner sanctuary; the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs;
the cups, snuffers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and censers of pure gold; and the gold hinges for the doors of the inner sanctuary, which is the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the main hall.

So all the work King Solomon had done for the house of the the LORD was finished. Then Solomon brought in the things his father David had set apart as holy: the silver, the gold, and the furnishings. He placed them in the treasuries of the house of the the LORD.

Then Solomon gathered the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the families of Israel, to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the city of David, which is Zion.
All the men of Israel assembled before King Solomon at the feast in the month of Ethanim, the seventh month.
When all the elders of Israel had come, the priests took up the ark.
They brought up the ark of the LORD, the tent of meeting, and all the holy things that were in the tent. The priests and Levites carried them up.
King Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel, who had gathered before the ark, were sacrificing sheep and cattle. There were so many that no one could count them.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner sanctuary of the house, the Most Holy Place, under the wings of the cherubim.
The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark and covered the ark and its poles from above.
The poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the Holy Place in front of the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside. They are still there today.
There was nothing in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had placed there at Horeb, where the LORD made a covenant with the Israelites when they came out of Egypt.
When the priests came out of the Holy Place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD.
The priests could not stand to serve because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD.
Then Solomon said, "The LORD has said that He would dwell in thick darkness.
I have built You a house, a place for You to dwell forever."
Then the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel while they stood there.
He said, "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who spoke with His mouth to my father David and fulfilled it with His hand, saying:
'Since the day I brought My people Israel out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city in any tribe of Israel to build a house for My Name, but I chose David to be over My people Israel.'
My father David had it in his heart to build a house for the Name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD said to my father David, 'Because it was in your heart to build a house for My Name, you did well to have this in your heart.'
'Nevertheless, you will not build the house, but your son who comes from your body will build the house for My Name.'

Now the LORD has fulfilled the word He spoke. I have risen in place of my father David and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised. I have built the house for the Name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
I have provided a place there for the ark, in which is the covenant of the LORD that He made with our fathers when He brought them out of Egypt."
Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven.
He said, "O LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven above or on earth below. You keep Your covenant and faithful love to Your servants who walk before You with all their heart.
You have kept Your promise to Your servant, my father David. You spoke with Your mouth and fulfilled it with Your hand, as it is this day.

Now, O LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant, my father David, what You promised him, saying, 'You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons guard their way to walk before Me as you have walked.'
And now, O God of Israel, please let Your word to Your servant, my father David, be confirmed."
"But will God indeed dwell on the earth? See, the heavens, even the highest heaven, cannot contain You, much less this house that I have built.
Yet turn Your attention to the prayer and plea of Your servant, O LORD my God, to hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You today.
Let Your eyes be open toward this house night and day, toward the place of which You said, 'My Name shall be there,' to hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place.
Hear the plea of Your servant and of Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. Hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and when You hear, forgive."
"If a man sins against his neighbor and is required to take an oath, and he comes to take the oath before Your altar in this house,
then hear from heaven and act. Judge Your servants, condemning the wicked by bringing his guilt on his own head and clearing the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.
When Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they return to You and confess Your Name, praying and pleading before You in this house,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel and bring them back to the land You gave to their fathers.
When the heavens are shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your Name and turn from their sin because You have punished them,

then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants and of Your people Israel. Teach them the good way in which they should walk, and send rain on the land You have given to Your people as an inheritance.
If there is famine in the land, if there is plague, blight, mildew, locust, or caterpillar; if their enemy besieges them in their cities; whatever plague or sickness there is,
whatever prayer or plea is made by any man or by all Your people Israel—each one knowing his own trouble and spreading out his hands toward this house—
then hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and forgive, and act, and give to each man according to all his ways, for You alone know the hearts of all people.
So may they fear You all the days they live in the land You gave to our fathers."
"As for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel but has come from a distant land for Your Name's sake—
for they will hear of Your great Name and Your mighty hand and Your outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this house,

then hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all the foreigner asks of You, so that all the peoples of the earth may know Your Name and fear You, as Your people Israel do, and so that they may know that this house I have built is called by Your Name.
When Your people go out to war against their enemy by the way that You send them, and they pray to the LORD toward the city You have chosen and the house I have built for Your Name,
then hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause."

"If they sin against You—for there is no one who does not sin—and You become angry with them and hand them over to an enemy, so that they are carried away captive to the land of the enemy, far or near,

then if they come to their senses in the land where they were carried captive, and repent and plead with You in the land of their captors, saying, 'We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly,'

and if they return to You with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their enemies who carried them captive, and pray to You toward their land that You gave to their fathers, toward the city You have chosen, and toward the house I have built for Your Name,
then hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause.
Forgive Your people who have sinned against You and all their wrongs against You, and grant them compassion in the sight of their captors, so that they will have compassion on them.
For they are Your people and Your inheritance, whom You brought out of Egypt, out of the iron furnace.
Let Your eyes be open to the plea of Your servant and to the plea of Your people Israel, to hear them whenever they call to You.
For You have set them apart as Your inheritance from among all the peoples of the earth, as You spoke through Your servant Moses when You brought our fathers out of Egypt, O Lord, the LORD."
When Solomon had finished praying all this prayer and plea to the LORD, he rose from before the altar of the LORD, where he had been kneeling with his hands spread out toward heaven.
He stood and blessed the whole assembly of Israel with a loud voice, saying:
"Blessed be the LORD, who has given rest to His people Israel according to all that He promised. Not one word has failed of all His good promise, which He spoke through His servant Moses.
May the LORD our God be with us, as He was with our fathers. May He not leave us or forsake us.
May He turn our hearts to Him, to walk in all His ways and to keep His commandments, statutes, and judgments that He commanded our fathers.

May these words of mine, which I have pleaded before the LORD, be near to the LORD our God day and night, so that He may maintain the cause of His servant and the cause of His people Israel as each day requires,
so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the LORD is God and that there is no other.
Let your hearts therefore be fully committed to the LORD our God, to walk in His statutes and to keep His commandments, as at this day."
Then the king and all Israel with him offered sacrifices before the LORD.
Solomon offered a sacrifice of peace offerings to the LORD: twenty-two thousand cattle and one hundred twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of the LORD.

On that same day the king set apart the middle of the courtyard in front of the house of the LORD, for there he offered the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that was before the LORD was too small to hold the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat of the peace offerings.

So Solomon and all Israel with him held the feast before the LORD our God for seven days, and seven more days—fourteen days in all. A great assembly came from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt.

On the eighth day he sent the people away. They blessed the king and went to their tents, joyful and glad of heart for all the goodness that the LORD had done for His servant David and for His people Israel.
After Solomon finished building the the LORD's temple, the royal palace, and everything else he wanted to build,
the the LORD appeared to Solomon a second time, just as He had appeared to him at Gibeon.

And the the LORD said to him, "I have heard your prayer and your plea, which you have made before Me; I have dedicated this temple you have built to put My name there forever. My eyes and My heart will always be there.
As for you, if you walk before Me as your father David walked, with an honest and upright heart, doing everything I have commanded you, and if you keep My laws and rules,
then I will establish your royal throne over Israel forever, as I promised your father David: 'You will never fail to have a man on the throne of Israel.'
"But if you and your sons turn away from Me and do not keep My commands and laws that I have set before you, and if you go and serve other gods and worship them,
then I will cut Israel off from the land I have given them. I will remove this temple from My sight, and Israel will become a thing of scorn and ridicule among all peoples.
"This temple will become a pile of ruins. Everyone who passes by will be shocked and hiss, saying, 'Why has the the LORD done this to this land and to this temple?'

And people will answer, 'Because they left the the LORD their God, who brought their fathers out of Egypt. They turned to other gods, worshiped them, and served them. That is why the the LORD has brought all this trouble on them.'"
At the end of twenty years, during which Solomon built the two houses—the house of the the LORD and the king's house—
King Hiram of Tyre had supplied Solomon with cedar and cypress timber and gold for all he desired. At that time King Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in the land of Galilee.
So Hiram left Tyre to look at the cities Solomon had given him, but they did not please him.
He said, "What are these cities you have given me, my brother?" So he called them the Land of Cabul, and they are still called that today.
Hiram sent the king 120 talents of gold.
This is the account of the forced labor King Solomon raised to build the house of the the LORD, his own house, the terraces, the wall of Jerusalem, Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer.
Pharaoh king of Egypt had attacked and captured Gezer. He burned it with fire, killed the Canaanites who lived in the city, and gave it as a wedding gift to his daughter, Solomon's wife.
So Solomon rebuilt Gezer, Lower Beth-horon,
Baalath, and Tamar in the wilderness in the land.
He also built all his store cities, the cities for his chariots and horsemen, and everything else he wanted to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout his whole kingdom.
As for all the people left from the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—people who were not Israelites—
Solomon forced their descendants who remained in the land after them, the ones the Israelites could not completely destroy, to do forced labor. They still do this work today.
But Solomon did not force any Israelite to work. They were his soldiers, servants, officials, commanders, and officers over his chariots and cavalry.
These were the chief officers in charge of Solomon's work: 550 officials who supervised the people doing the labor.
Pharaoh's daughter moved from the City of David to the house Solomon had built for her. Then he built the terraces.
Three times a year Solomon offered burnt offerings and peace offerings on the altar he had built for the the LORD, and he burned incense before the the LORD. So he finished the temple.
King Solomon also built a fleet of ships at Ezion-geber, near Eloth in the land of Edom, on the shore of the Red Sea.
Hiram sent his servants, men who knew the sea, to serve in the fleet with Solomon's servants.
They sailed to Ophir and brought back 420 talents of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon.
The queen of Sheba heard about Solomon's fame and about the name of the LORD, so she came to test him with hard questions.
She arrived in Jerusalem with a very large group, with camels carrying spices, a great deal of gold, and precious stones. She came to Solomon and talked with him about everything she had on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. Nothing was hidden from the king that he did not explain to her.
When the queen of Sheba saw all of Solomon's wisdom and the palace he had built,

along with the food on his table, the seating of his servants, the duties of his attendants, their clothing, his cupbearers, and the burnt offering he made at the house of the LORD, she was completely overwhelmed.
She said to the king, "The report I heard in my own country about your words and your wisdom was true.
I did not believe it until I came and saw it with my own eyes. In fact, I had not been told even half of it. Your wisdom and wealth are far greater than the report I heard.
How happy your people must be! How happy your servants are who stand before you all the time and listen to your wisdom!
Praise be to the LORD your God, who delighted in you and put you on the throne of Israel. Because the LORD loved Israel forever, He made you king so you could carry out justice and righteousness."
She gave the king one hundred twenty talents of gold, a very large amount of spices, and precious stones. Never again was so much spice brought in as the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.
Hiram's ships also brought gold from Ophir, along with a very large amount of almug wood and precious stones.

King Solomon used the almug wood to make supports for the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and to make lyres and harps for the singers. No almug wood like that has ever been brought in or seen to this day.
King Solomon gave the queen everything she wanted and asked for, besides what he gave her from his royal generosity. Then she and her servants left and returned to her own country.
The gold that came to Solomon in one year weighed six hundred sixty-six talents.
This was besides what came from the traders, the merchants, and all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land.
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of hammered gold; six hundred shekels of gold went into each shield.
He also made three hundred smaller shields of hammered gold; three minas of gold went into each one. The king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king also made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps, and its back was rounded at the top. There were armrests on both sides of the seat, and two lions stood beside the armrests.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. Nothing like this had ever been made for any kingdom.
All of King Solomon's drinking cups were gold, and all the cups in the House of the Forest of Lebanon were pure gold. In Solomon's days, silver was considered worthless.
The king had a fleet of trading ships at sea with Hiram's fleet. Once every three years the fleet came in bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
So King Solomon became greater than all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom.
The whole world wanted to see Solomon and hear the wisdom God had put in his heart.
Year after year, everyone brought gifts: articles of silver and gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
