Solomon built up his chariots and horsemen. He had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore trees in the foothills.
Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt and from Kue. The king's merchants bought them from Kue at a set price.
A chariot could be imported from Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver, and a horse for one hundred fifty. They also exported them to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.
King Solomon loved many foreign women, along with Pharaoh's daughter—Moabite, Ammonite, Edomite, Sidonian, and Hittite women.

They came from nations about which the LORD had told the Israelites, “You must not marry them, and they must not marry you, because they will surely turn your hearts after their gods.” But Solomon held fast to them in love.
He had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines, and his wives led his heart astray.
When Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods. His heart was not fully devoted to the LORD his God, as the heart of David his father had been.
Solomon followed Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, and Milcom, the detestable god of the Ammonites.
Solomon did evil in the eyes of the LORD. He did not follow the LORD fully, as David his father had done.
Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh, the detestable god of Moab, and for Molech, the detestable god of the Ammonites, on the hill east of Jerusalem.
He did the same for all his foreign wives, who burned incense and sacrificed to their gods.
The LORD became angry with Solomon because his heart had turned away from the LORD, the God of Israel, who had appeared to him twice.
The LORD had commanded him not to follow other gods, but Solomon did not keep what the LORD commanded.

So the LORD said to Solomon, “Because you have done this and have not kept My covenant and My statutes, which I commanded you, I will surely tear the kingdom away from you and give it to your servant.
Yet for the sake of your father David, I will not do it during your lifetime. I will tear it out of your son's hand.
But I will not tear away the whole kingdom. I will give one tribe to your son for the sake of My servant David and for Jerusalem, which I have chosen.”
Then the LORD raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite, from the royal family of Edom.
This happened when David was in Edom. Joab, the commander of the army, had gone up to bury the dead and had struck down every male in Edom.
Joab and all Israel stayed there six months, until he had killed every male in Edom.
But Hadad, who was only a boy at the time, fled to Egypt with some Edomites who had been servants of his father.
They left Midian and went to Paran. They took men from Paran with them and went to Egypt, to Pharaoh king of Egypt. Pharaoh gave Hadad a house, land, and food.
Pharaoh was pleased with Hadad and gave him a wife—the sister of Queen Tahpenes.
The sister of Tahpenes bore him a son named Genubath. Tahpenes weaned him in Pharaoh's palace, and Genubath lived there among Pharaoh's children.
When Hadad heard in Egypt that David had died and that Joab, the commander of the army, was dead, he said to Pharaoh, “Send me away so I can go to my own country.”
Pharaoh said to him, “What do you lack here with me that you want to go to your own country?” “Nothing,” Hadad replied, “but please let me go.”
God also raised up another adversary, Rezon son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer king of Zobah.
Rezon gathered men around him and became the leader of a raiding band when David defeated them. They went to Damascus and settled there, and Rezon ruled in Damascus.
Rezon was Israel's adversary all the days of Solomon, along with the trouble Hadad caused. Rezon ruled over Aram and despised Israel.
Jeroboam son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah, rebelled against King Solomon. His mother was a widow named Zeruah.
This is why he rebelled: Solomon built the Millo and repaired the gap in the wall of the city of David his father.
Jeroboam was a capable man. When Solomon saw that the young man worked hard, he put him in charge of all the forced labor of the house of Joseph.
At that time, when Jeroboam left Jerusalem, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him on the road. Ahijah was wearing a new cloak, and the two of them were alone in the field.
Ahijah took the new cloak he was wearing and tore it into twelve pieces.
He said to Jeroboam, “Take ten pieces, for this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘See, I am going to tear the kingdom out of Solomon's hand and give you ten tribes.
“‘But one tribe will remain his for the sake of My servant David and for Jerusalem, the city I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel.

“‘For they have forsaken Me and worshiped Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians, Chemosh, the god of Moab, and Milcom, the god of the Ammonites. They have not walked in My ways or done what is right in My eyes, or kept My statutes and judgments, as David his father did.
“‘But I will not take the whole kingdom from his hand. I will make him ruler all the days of his life for the sake of David My servant, whom I chose and who kept My commandments and statutes.
“‘Yet I will take the kingdom from his son's hand and give you ten tribes.
“‘I will give one tribe to his son, so that David My servant may always have a lamp before Me in Jerusalem, the city where I have chosen to put My name.
“‘As for you, I will take you, and you will reign over all that your heart desires. You will be king over Israel.

“‘If you obey all I command you and walk in My ways and do what is right in My eyes by keeping My statutes and commandments, as David My servant did, then I will be with you. I will build you a lasting house, as I built for David, and I will give Israel to you.
“‘I will humble David's descendants because of this, but not forever.’”
Solomon tried to kill Jeroboam, but Jeroboam fled to Egypt, to Shishak king of Egypt, and stayed there until Solomon's death.
The rest of the acts of Solomon—all he did and his wisdom—are they not written in the book of the annals of Solomon?
Solomon reigned over all Israel in Jerusalem for forty years.
Solomon died and was buried in the city of David his father. His son Rehoboam became king in his place.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had gathered there to make him king.
Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about this while he was still in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon, and he stayed there.
So they sent for Jeroboam. He and all Israel came and spoke to Rehoboam.
They said, "Your father made our work very hard. Now make the heavy work and the hard burden your father put on us lighter, and we will serve you."
Rehoboam said to them, "Go away for three days, then come back to me." So the people went away.
King Rehoboam asked the elders who had served his father Solomon while he was alive, "How do you advise me to answer these people?"
They answered, "If today you will be a servant to these people and serve them, and if you answer them and speak kind words to them, they will be your servants forever."
But Rehoboam rejected the elders' advice and asked the young men who had grown up with him and were serving him.
He said to them, "What advice do you give? How should we answer these people who said, 'Make the work your father put on us lighter'?"
The young men who grew up with him said, "Tell the people who told you, 'Your father made our load heavy, but make it lighter for us': 'I will be much harder on you than my father was.
My father put a heavy burden on you, but I will make it heavier. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions.'"
On the third day, Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam, just as the king had said, "Come back to me on the third day."
The king answered the people harshly, rejecting the elders' advice.
He spoke to them using the young men's advice and said, "My father made your burden heavy, but I will make it heavier. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with scorpions."
The king did not listen to the people, because this turn of events came from the the LORD, to carry out the word He had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king would not listen to them, they answered the king, "What share do we have in David? We have no part in Jesse's son. Go to your tents, Israel! Look after your own house, David!" Then Israel went home.
But Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites who lived in the cities of Judah.
King Rehoboam sent Adoram, who was in charge of forced labor, but all Israel stoned him to death. King Rehoboam hurried into his chariot and fled to Jerusalem.
So Israel rebelled against David's family, and that is still true today.
When all Israel heard that Jeroboam had returned, they sent for him and made him king over all Israel. Only the tribe of Judah stayed with David's family.
Rehoboam came to Jerusalem and gathered all the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—180,000 chosen warriors—to fight against Israel and win the kingdom back for Rehoboam son of Solomon.
But the word of God came to Shemaiah, the man of God:
"Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people:

This is what the the LORD says: Do not go up and fight against your brothers, the Israelites. Each of you go back home, for this is My doing." Then they obeyed the word of the the LORD and went home, as the the LORD had said.
Jeroboam built Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim and lived there. He also went out from there and built Penuel.
Jeroboam said in his heart, "Now the kingdom may go back to David's family.

If these people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the the LORD in Jerusalem, their hearts will turn back to their master, Rehoboam king of Judah. Then they will kill me and go back to Rehoboam king of Judah."
The king asked for advice and made two golden calves. He said to the people, "It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem. Here are your gods, Israel, who brought you up out of Egypt."
He put one calf in Bethel and the other in Dan.
This became a sin. The people went as far as Dan to worship before one of the calves.
Jeroboam built shrines on high places and made priests from all kinds of people who were not Levites.

Jeroboam set a feast on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, like the feast in Judah. He offered sacrifices on the altar he had built at Bethel to the calves he had made. He also put priests in Bethel for the high places he had made.

On the fifteenth day of the eighth month—the month he had chosen on his own—he offered sacrifices on the altar he had built at Bethel. He set a festival for the Israelites and went up to the altar to burn incense.
Jeroboam was standing by the altar to burn incense. A man of God came from Judah to Bethel by the word of the the LORD.

He cried out against the altar by the word of the the LORD: “Altar, altar! This is what the the LORD says: ‘A son named Josiah will be born to David’s family. He will sacrifice on you the priests of the high places who burn incense on you, and human bones will be burned on you.’”
That day he gave a sign and said, “This is the sign the the LORD has spoken: The altar will split open, and the ashes on it will spill out.”

When the king heard what the man of God cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar and said, “Seize him!” But the hand he stretched out against the man dried up, and he could not pull it back.
The altar split open, and the ashes spilled out from the altar, just as the man of God had said would happen by the word of the the LORD.

The king said to the man of God, “Please ask the the LORD your God to show me favor and pray for me, so my hand will be restored.” The man of God prayed to the the LORD, and the king’s hand was restored and became as it was before.
The king said to the man of God, “Come home with me, eat, and I will give you a gift.”
But the man of God said to the king, “Even if you gave me half your house, I would not go with you. I will not eat bread or drink water in this place.
The LORD commanded me by His word: ‘Do not eat bread, do not drink water, and do not go back the way you came.’”
So he left by another road and did not return by the road he had taken to Bethel.
An old prophet lived in Bethel. His sons came and told him everything the man of God had done that day in Bethel. They also told him the words he had spoken to the king.
Their father asked them, “Which way did he go?” His sons showed him the road the man of God from Judah had taken.
He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” They saddled it, and he rode on it.
He went after the man of God and found him sitting under an oak tree. He asked, “Are you the man of God who came from Judah?” He answered, “I am.”
The old prophet said to him, “Come home with me and eat bread.”
The man of God said, “I cannot go back with you or come with you. I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.
The LORD told me by His word, ‘Do not eat bread, do not drink water, and do not return by the road you took to get here.’”

The old prophet said, “I am also a prophet like you. An angel spoke to me by the word of the the LORD and said, ‘Bring him back with you to your house so he can eat bread and drink water.’” But he was lying to him.
So he went back with the old prophet and ate bread in his house and drank water.
While they were sitting at the table, the word of the the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back.
He cried out to the man of God who had come from Judah, “This is what the the LORD says: ‘Because you disobeyed the the LORD’s word and did not keep the command the the LORD your God gave you,
you came back and ate bread and drank water in the place where He told you, “Do not eat bread and do not drink water,” your body will not be buried in your fathers’ tomb.’”
After he had eaten bread and drunk water, the old prophet saddled the donkey for the prophet he had brought back.
The man left, and a lion met him on the road and killed him. His body was thrown in the road. The donkey stood beside it, and the lion stood beside the body.
Some men passed by and saw the body thrown in the road, with the lion standing beside it. They went and told what they had seen in the city where the old prophet lived.

When the prophet who had brought him back heard this, he said, “He is the man of God who disobeyed the the LORD’s word. That is why the the LORD gave him to the lion, which tore him and killed him, just as the the LORD had said.”
He said to his sons, “Saddle the donkey for me.” They saddled it.
He went and found the body thrown in the road. The donkey and the lion were standing beside the body. The lion had not eaten the body or torn the donkey.
The prophet picked up the body of the man of God, laid it on the donkey, and brought it back. The old prophet came into the city to mourn and bury him.
He laid the body in his own grave and mourned over him, saying, “Oh, my brother!”
After he buried him, he said to his sons, “When I die, bury me in the grave where the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones.
The word he cried out by the the LORD’s word against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines in the cities of Samaria will surely come true.”
Even after this, Jeroboam did not turn from his evil way. He again made priests for the high places from all kinds of people. Anyone who wanted to serve, he made a priest for the high places.
This became the sin of Jeroboam’s family. It led to their ruin and destruction from the face of the earth.
At that time, Abijah, Jeroboam's son, became sick.
Jeroboam said to his wife, "Please get up and disguise yourself so no one knows you're Jeroboam's wife. Go to Shiloh. Ahijah the prophet is there—the one who told me I would be king over this people.
Take ten loaves of bread, some cakes, and a jar of honey with you, and go to him. He will tell you what will happen to the boy."
Jeroboam's wife did as she was told. She got up and went to Shiloh and came to Ahijah's house. Ahijah could not see, because his eyes were dim with age.
Now the LORD had said to Ahijah, "Look, Jeroboam's wife is coming to ask you about her son, for he is sick. Say such and such to her. When she comes, she will be disguised."
When Ahijah heard the sound of her feet as she came in the door, he said, "Come in, wife of Jeroboam. Why do you disguise yourself? I have been sent to you with hard news.
Go tell Jeroboam, 'This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I raised you up from among the people and made you leader over My people Israel.

I tore the kingdom away from David's house and gave it to you. But you have not been like My servant David, who kept My commands and followed Me with all his heart, doing only what was right in My eyes.
You have done more evil than all who were before you. You made other gods and metal images to anger Me, and you turned your back on Me.
Therefore I am bringing disaster on Jeroboam's house. I will cut off from Jeroboam every male in Israel, slave or free. I will burn up Jeroboam's house completely, like dung burned until it is gone.
Anyone belonging to Jeroboam who dies in the city will be eaten by dogs, and anyone who dies in the field will be eaten by birds of the sky, for the LORD has spoken.'
As for you, go home. When your feet enter the city, the child will die.
All Israel will mourn for him and bury him, because he alone of Jeroboam's family will go to the grave, since in him the LORD, the God of Israel, found something good in Jeroboam's house.
The LORD will raise up a king over Israel who will cut off Jeroboam's house this very day—and even now.

The LORD will strike Israel, so it shakes like a reed in water. He will uproot Israel from this good land He gave their fathers, and scatter them beyond the Euphrates River, because they made their Asherah poles, angering the LORD.
He will give Israel up because of Jeroboam's sins, which he committed and which he made Israel commit."
Jeroboam's wife got up and left, and came to Tirzah. As she stepped over the threshold of the house, the child died.
They buried him, and all Israel mourned for him, just as the LORD had said through His servant Ahijah the prophet.
The rest of Jeroboam's acts, how he fought and how he reigned, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years. Then he died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Nadab reigned in his place.

Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned in Judah. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city the LORD chose out of all the tribes of Israel to put His name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.
Judah did evil in the LORD's eyes. They sinned more than their fathers had, and they made Him jealous with their sins.
They also built for themselves high places, sacred stones, and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
There were even male shrine prostitutes in the land. They did all the detestable things the nations had done that the LORD drove out before the Israelites.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt marched against Jerusalem.
He took the treasures of the LORD's house and the treasures of the king's house. He took everything, including all the gold shields Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields in their place and put them in the care of the captains of the guard who watched the entrance to the king's house.
Whenever the king went into the LORD's house, the guards carried them and brought them back to the guardroom.
The rest of Rehoboam's acts and all he did are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all their days.
Rehoboam died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite. His son Abijam reigned in his place.
In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam son of Nebat, Abijam became king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for three years. His mother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
He followed all the sins of his father before him. His heart was not fully devoted to the the LORD his God, unlike the heart of his father David.
Yet, for David's sake, the the LORD his God gave him a lasting family line in Jerusalem. He raised up Abijam's son after him and made Jerusalem strong.
For David had done what was right in the eyes of the the LORD and had not failed to keep any of His commands all his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite.
There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam all through Abijam's life.
The rest of Abijam's deeds, and everything he did, are written in the book of the records of the kings of Judah. There was also war between Abijam and Jeroboam.
Abijam died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Asa became king in his place.
In the twentieth year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Asa became king of Judah.
He ruled in Jerusalem for forty-one years. His mother was Maacah, the daughter of Abishalom.
Asa did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD, as his father David had done.
He removed the male shrine prostitutes from the land and got rid of all the idols his ancestors had made.
He even removed his grandmother Maacah from her place as queen mother, because she had made a detestable image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image and burned it in the Kidron Valley.
The hilltop shrines were not removed, but Asa's heart stayed fully committed to the the LORD all his life.
He brought into the the LORD's temple the silver, gold, and other items that he and his father had set apart as holy.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all through their reigns.
Baasha king of Israel marched against Judah and built up Ramah. He did this to keep anyone from going in or out to Asa king of Judah.

Asa took all the silver and gold left in the treasuries of the the LORD's temple and the royal palace. He put them in the hands of his officials and sent them to Ben-Hadad son of Tabrimmon, the son of Hezion, king of Aram, who ruled in Damascus.

He said, "Let there be a treaty between me and you—just as there was between my father and your father. See, I am sending you a gift of silver and gold. Now break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel so he will leave me alone."
Ben-Hadad listened to King Asa. He sent his army commanders against the towns of Israel. They attacked Ijon, Dan, Abel Beth Maakah, and all Kinnereth, plus all the land of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard about this, he stopped building Ramah and went back to Tirzah.
Then King Asa called all Judah together. No one was excused. They carried away from Ramah the stones and timber Baasha had been using. With them King Asa built up Geba in Benjamin and also Mizpah.
The rest of Asa's deeds, all his strength, everything he did, and the cities he built are written in the book of the records of the kings of Judah. In his old age, though, his feet became diseased.
Asa died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of his father David. His son Jehoshaphat became king in his place.
Nadab son of Jeroboam became king of Israel in the second year of Asa king of Judah. He ruled over Israel for two years.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD. He walked in the ways of his father and committed the same sin his father had caused Israel to commit.
Baasha son of Ahijah, from the tribe of Issachar, plotted against him. He struck Nadab down at Gibbethon, a Philistine town, while Nadab and all Israel were besieging it.
Baasha killed Nadab in the third year of Asa king of Judah and became king in his place.

As soon as Baasha began to reign, he killed Jeroboam's whole family. He did not leave Jeroboam a single person who breathed; he destroyed them all. This happened as the the LORD had said through His servant Ahijah the Shilonite.
This happened because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit. He had made the the LORD, the God of Israel, angry.
The rest of Nadab's deeds, and everything he did, are written in the book of the records of the kings of Israel.
There was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel all through their reigns.
In the third year of Asa king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah became king of all Israel in Tirzah. He ruled for twenty-four years.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD. He walked in the ways of Jeroboam and committed the same sin Jeroboam had caused Israel to commit.
The word of the LORD came to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha, saying,
"Because I raised you from the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel, but you walked in the way of Jeroboam and made My people Israel sin, provoking Me to anger with their sins,
behold, I will sweep away Baasha and his house, and I will make your house like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat.
The one who dies in the city, dogs will eat; and the one who dies in the field, birds of the sky will eat."
The rest of Baasha's acts, what he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel?
Baasha died and was buried with his ancestors in Tirzah. His son Elah became king after him.

The word of the LORD also came through the prophet Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha and his house, because of all the evil he did in the eyes of the LORD, provoking Him to anger by his deeds, and because he became like the house of Jeroboam, and because he struck it down.
In the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah, Elah son of Baasha became king over Israel in Tirzah, and he reigned two years.
While he was in Tirzah, getting drunk in the house of Arza, who was in charge of the palace in Tirzah, his servant Zimri, commander of half his chariots, conspired against him.
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri came in, struck him down, killed him, and reigned in his place.
As soon as Zimri began to reign and sat on the throne, he struck down all the house of Baasha. He did not leave a single male, nor his relatives, nor his friends.
So Zimri destroyed all the house of Baasha, just as the word of the LORD had spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet.
This happened because of all the sins of Baasha and the sins of Elah his son, which they committed and caused Israel to commit, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their worthless idols.
The rest of Elah's acts, and all that he did, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
In the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah, Zimri reigned in Tirzah seven days. The army was camped against Gibbethon, which belonged to the Philistines.
The people in the camp heard, "Zimri has conspired and has also killed the king." So all Israel made Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel that day in the camp.
Omri went up from Gibbethon, and all Israel with him, and they besieged Tirzah.
When Zimri saw that the city was taken, he went into the fortified part of the king's house and burned the king's house down over himself, and he died.
This happened because of the sins he committed, doing evil in the eyes of the LORD, walking in the way of Jeroboam, and because of the sin he caused Israel to commit.
The rest of Zimri's acts and the conspiracy he made are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Then the people of Israel were split in two. Half of the people followed Tibni son of Ginath, wanting to make him king, and half followed Omri.
But the people who followed Omri were stronger than the people who followed Tibni son of Ginath. Tibni died, and Omri became king.
In the thirty-first year of Asa king of Judah, Omri began to reign over Israel, and he reigned twelve years. He reigned in Tirzah for six years.
He bought the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver. He built on the hill and named the city he built Samaria, after Shemer, the owner of the hill.
Omri did evil in the eyes of the LORD, and he did worse than all who were before him.
He walked in all the way of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins, which caused Israel to sin, provoking the LORD God of Israel to anger with their worthless idols.
The rest of Omri's acts that he did, and the might he showed, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Omri died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Ahab became king after him.
In the thirty-eighth year of Asa king of Judah, Ahab son of Omri became king over Israel. Ahab son of Omri reigned over Israel in Samaria twenty-two years.
Ahab son of Omri did evil in the eyes of the LORD, more than all who were before him.
It was not enough for him to walk in the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat. He married Jezebel, the daughter of Ethbaal king of the Sidonians, and he went and served Baal and worshiped him.
He set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he built in Samaria.
Ahab also made an Asherah pole. Ahab did more to provoke the LORD God of Israel to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him.

In his days, Hiel of Bethel rebuilt Jericho. He laid its foundation at the cost of his firstborn son Abiram, and he set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, just as the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun.
Elijah the Tishbite, who lived in Gilead, said to Ahab, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives—the God I serve—there will be no dew or rain in the coming years unless I say so."
Then the word of the LORD came to Elijah:
"Leave here and go east. Hide yourself by the Kerith Brook, east of the Jordan.
You can drink from the brook, and I have told the ravens to feed you there."
So Elijah did what the LORD said. He went and stayed by the Kerith Brook, east of the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening, and he drank from the brook.
After a while, the brook dried up because no rain had fallen in the land.
Then the word of the LORD came to him again:
"Get up and go to Zarephath in Sidon and stay there. I have told a widow there to feed you."
So Elijah got up and went to Zarephath. When he reached the city gate, he saw a widow gathering sticks. He called to her and said, "Please give me a little water in a cup so I can drink."
As she went to get it, he called after her, "Please bring me a piece of bread in your hand."

She said, "As the LORD your God lives, I have no bread. I only have a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug. I am gathering two sticks so I can go home and make a small meal for myself and my son. We will eat it and then die."
Elijah said to her, "Don't be afraid. Go and do as you said. But first make me a small cake from what you have and bring it to me. Then make something for yourself and your son."
"For this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'The jar of flour will not run out, and the jug of oil will not run dry, until the day the LORD sends rain on the land.'"
So the woman went and did what Elijah said. She and her family ate for many days.
The jar of flour did not run out, and the jug of oil did not run dry, just as the LORD had said through Elijah.
After some time, the woman's son became sick. His illness was so bad that he stopped breathing.
The woman said to Elijah, "What do you have against me, man of God? Have you come to remind me of my sin and kill my son?"
Elijah said, "Give me your son." He took the boy from her arms, carried him to the upper room where he was staying, and laid him on his bed.
Then Elijah cried out to the LORD, "the LORD my God, have You also brought tragedy on this widow I am staying with by killing her son?"
Then he stretched himself over the boy three times and cried out to the LORD, "the LORD my God, please let this boy's life return to him."
The LORD heard Elijah's prayer, and the boy's life returned to him, and he lived.
Elijah took the boy and brought him down from the upper room into the house. He gave him to his mother and said, "Look, your son is alive."
The woman said to Elijah, "Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is true."
After many days, in the third year, the word of the LORD came to Elijah: “Go and show yourself to Ahab, and I will send rain on the land.”
So Elijah went to show himself to Ahab. The famine was severe in Samaria.
Ahab called Obadiah, who was in charge of the palace. Obadiah was a man who feared the LORD greatly.
When Jezebel was killing the LORD’s prophets, Obadiah took one hundred prophets and hid them, fifty in one cave and fifty in another. He fed them bread and water.
Ahab said to Obadiah, “Go through the land to all the springs and valleys. Maybe we can find grass to keep the horses and mules alive, so we will not lose all the animals.”
So they divided the land between them to search it. Ahab went one way by himself, and Obadiah went the other way by himself.
As Obadiah was on his way, Elijah met him. Obadiah recognized him, fell on his face, and said, “Is it you, my lord Elijah?”
Elijah answered, “Go tell your lord, ‘Look, Elijah is here.’”
Obadiah said, “What have I done wrong, that you would hand your servant over to Ahab to be killed?

As surely as the LORD your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent someone to look for you. When they said, ‘He is not here,’ he made that kingdom swear it could not find you.
Now you say, ‘Go tell my lord that Elijah is here.’”

As soon as I leave you, the Spirit of the LORD may carry you away to a place I do not know. Then when I tell Ahab and he cannot find you, he will kill me. But I, your servant, have feared the LORD since I was young.
My lord, haven’t you heard what I did when Jezebel was killing the LORD’s prophets? I hid one hundred of the LORD’s prophets, fifty in one cave and fifty in another, and I fed them bread and water.
And now you say, ‘Go tell my lord that Elijah is here,’ and he will kill me!”
Elijah said, “As surely as the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, I will show myself to Ahab today.”
So Obadiah went to meet Ahab and told him. Then Ahab went to meet Elijah.
When Ahab saw Elijah, he said, “Is that you, you troublemaker of Israel?”
Elijah answered, “I have not troubled Israel, but you and your father’s house have, because you have forsaken the LORD’s commands and followed the Baals.
Now summon all Israel to meet me at Mount Carmel. Also bring the four hundred fifty prophets of Baal and the four hundred prophets of Asherah who eat at Jezebel’s table.”
So Ahab sent word through all Israel and gathered the prophets at Mount Carmel.
Elijah went up to all the people and said, “How long will you keep changing your minds? If the LORD is God, follow Him. If Baal is god, follow him.” The people did not answer him.
Then Elijah said, “I am the only prophet of the LORD left, but Baal has four hundred fifty prophets.”

“Let them give us two bulls. Let them choose one bull for themselves, cut it into pieces, and put it on the wood, but not set fire to it. I will prepare the other bull and put it on the wood, but I will not set fire to it.
Then you call on the name of your god, and I will call on the name of the LORD. The God who answers by fire, He is God.” All the people answered, “That is a good plan.”
Elijah said to the prophets of Baal, “Since there are so many of you, choose one bull and prepare it first. Call on the name of your god, but do not light the fire.”

So they took the bull given to them and prepared it. They called on the name of Baal from morning until noon, saying, “Baal, answer us!” But there was no voice and no answer. They danced around the altar they had made.
At noon Elijah made fun of them. He said, “Shout louder! He is a god, isn’t he? Maybe he is deep in thought, or busy, or away on a trip. Maybe he is sleeping and must be awakened.”
So they shouted louder and cut themselves with swords and spears, as they usually did, until their blood flowed.
Midday passed, and they kept prophesying until the time of the evening sacrifice. But there was no voice, no answer, and no one paid attention.
Then Elijah said to all the people, “Come closer to me.” So all the people came closer to him. Then he repaired the altar of the LORD that had been torn down.
Elijah took twelve stones, one for each tribe of the sons of Jacob. The LORD had spoken to Jacob and said, “Your name will be Israel.”
With the stones he built an altar in the name of the LORD. He made a trench around the altar, big enough to hold about two measures of seed.
He arranged the wood, cut the bull into pieces, and laid it on the wood.

Then he said, “Fill four large jars with water and pour it on the burnt offering and on the wood.” They did. Then he said, “Do it a second time,” and they did. Then he said, “Do it a third time,” and they did.
The water ran all around the altar and filled the trench.

At the time of the evening sacrifice, Elijah the prophet came near and said, “O the LORD, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known today that You are God in Israel, and that I am Your servant, and that I have done all these things because You told me to.
Answer me, the LORD! Answer me, so these people will know that You, the LORD, are God, and that You have turned their hearts back to You.”
Then fire from the LORD fell and burned up the burnt offering, the wood, the stones, and the dust. It even licked up the water in the trench.
When all the people saw it, they fell on their faces and said, “The LORD, He is God! The LORD, He is God!”
Elijah said to them, “Seize the prophets of Baal! Don’t let a single one escape!” So they seized them. Elijah brought them down to the Kishon Valley and killed them there.
Then Elijah said to Ahab, “Go up, eat and drink, because I hear the sound of heavy rain.”
So Ahab went up to eat and drink. Elijah went up to the top of Carmel. He bent down to the ground and put his face between his knees.
He said to his servant, “Go up and look toward the sea.” The servant went up, looked, and said, “I see nothing.” Elijah said, “Go again,” seven times.

The seventh time the servant said, “Look, a small cloud, about the size of a man’s hand, is rising from the sea.” Elijah said, “Go tell Ahab, ‘Hitch up your chariot and go down before the rain stops you.’”
In a little while the sky grew dark with clouds and wind, and there was a heavy rain. Ahab rode in his chariot and went to Jezreel.
The LORD’s power came on Elijah. He tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab all the way to Jezreel.
Now Ahab told Jezebel everything Elijah had done, including how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
So Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah with this message: "May the gods punish me severely if by this time tomorrow I have not made your life like the life of one of them."
Elijah was afraid and ran for his life. When he came to Beersheba in Judah, he left his servant there.

He went on alone into the wilderness, traveling about a day. Then he sat down under a broom bush and prayed that he might die. "I have had enough, the LORD," he said. "Take my life, for I am no better than my ancestors."
Then he lay down under the bush and fell asleep. Suddenly an angel touched him and said, "Get up and eat."
He looked around, and there by his head was a loaf of bread baked over hot coals and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and then he lay down again.
The angel of the LORD came back a second time, touched him, and said, "Get up and eat, for the journey is too much for you."
So he got up and ate and drank. Strengthened by that food, he traveled forty days and forty nights until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God.
There he went into a cave and spent the night. And the word of the LORD came to him: "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

He answered, "I have been very zealous for the LORD God Almighty. The Israelites have rejected Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and killed Your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and now they are trying to kill me too."

The LORD said, "Go out and stand on the mountain in the presence of the LORD, for the LORD is about to pass by." Then a great and powerful wind tore the mountains apart and shattered the rocks before the LORD, but the LORD was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake, but the LORD was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake came a fire, but the LORD was not in the fire. And after the fire came a gentle whisper.
When Elijah heard it, he pulled his cloak over his face and went out and stood at the mouth of the cave. Then a voice said to him, "What are you doing here, Elijah?"

He replied, "I have been very zealous for the LORD God Almighty. The Israelites have rejected Your covenant, torn down Your altars, and killed Your prophets with the sword. I am the only one left, and now they are trying to kill me too."
The LORD said to him, "Go back the way you came, and go to the Desert of Damascus. When you get there, anoint Hazael to be king over Aram.
Also, anoint Jehu son of Nimshi to be king over Israel, and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat from Abel Meholah to succeed you as prophet.
Jehu will put to death any who escape the sword of Hazael, and Elisha will put to death any who escape the sword of Jehu.
Yet I reserve seven thousand in Israel—all whose knees have not bowed down to Baal and whose mouths have not kissed him."
So Elijah went from there and found Elisha son of Shaphat. He was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, and he himself was driving the twelfth pair. Elijah went up to him and threw his cloak around him.
Elisha left his oxen and ran after Elijah. "Let me say goodbye to my father and mother," he said, "and then I will follow you." "Go back," Elijah replied. "What have I done to you?"

So Elisha left him and took his yoke of oxen and slaughtered them. He burned the plowing equipment to boil the meat and gave it to the people, and they ate. Then he set out to follow Elijah and became his servant.
Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, gathered all his army. With him were thirty-two kings, along with horses and chariots. He marched up, besieged Samaria, and attacked it.
He sent messengers into the city to Ahab, king of Israel.
Ben-Hadad sent this message: "Your silver and gold belong to me, and your best wives and children belong to me too."
Ahab answered, "As you say, my lord the king, I and everything I have are yours."

The messengers returned with another message from Ben-Hadad: "I sent to take your silver, gold, wives, and children. But tomorrow about this time I will send my servants to search your house and your officials' houses.
They will take everything you value most."
Then Ahab called all the elders of the land and said, "Look and see how this man is looking for trouble. He sent for my wives, children, silver, and gold, and I did not refuse him."
All the elders and the people said, "Do not listen to him or agree."
So Ahab told Ben-Hadad's messengers, "Tell my lord the king, 'I will do everything you first asked, but I cannot do this.'" The messengers carried his answer back.
Ben-Hadad sent back this threat: "May the gods punish me if I don't grind Samaria to dust, leaving not even a handful for each man with me."
Ahab replied, "Don't brag about winning before you have even fought."
When Ben-Hadad heard this message, he and the kings were drinking in the shelters. He ordered his men, "Get ready to attack the city." So they prepared to attack Samaria.
Just then a prophet came to Ahab, king of Israel, and said, "This is what the the LORD says: 'Do you see that huge army? I will hand it over to you today, so you will know that I am the the LORD.'"

Ahab asked, "Who will do this?" The prophet answered, "This is what the the LORD says: 'The young men under the district commanders will do it.'" "Who will start the battle?" Ahab asked. "You will," the prophet said.
Ahab counted the young men under the district commanders: 232. After them he counted all the Israelites: 7,000.
They marched out at noon, while Ben-Hadad and the thirty-two kings helping him were getting drunk in the shelters.
The young men under the district commanders marched out first. Ben-Hadad sent out scouts, who reported, "Men are coming out of Samaria."
Ben-Hadad said, "If they've come in peace, capture them alive. If they've come to fight, capture them alive too."
Those young men and the army behind them left the city.
Each Israelite killed his opponent, and the Arameans ran away. Israel chased them, but Ben-Hadad escaped on horseback with some charioteers.
Ahab went out and struck down the horses and chariots, killing many Arameans.
Then the prophet came to the king of Israel and said, "Go, strengthen yourself and plan carefully, because at this time next year the king of Aram will attack you again."
Meanwhile, the king of Aram's officials said to him, "Their gods are gods of the hills, so they were stronger than us. But if we fight them on the flat land, we will be stronger than them."
"Do this: remove the kings from their commands and put governors in their place.
Raise an army as large as the one you lost, with as many horses and chariots. Then we will fight them on the flat land and surely be stronger." He listened to them and did so.
The next year, at the same time, Ben-Hadad gathered the Arameans and went up to Aphek to fight Israel.

The Israelites were also mustered and given supplies. They went out to meet the Arameans and camped opposite them. The Israelites looked like two small flocks of goats, while the Arameans covered the countryside.

The man of God came to the king of Israel and said, "This is what the the LORD says: 'Because the Arameans said, "The the LORD is a god of the hills, but not a god of the valleys," I will hand this huge army over to you. Then you will know that I am the the LORD.'"
For seven days the two armies camped opposite each other. On the seventh day the battle began, and the Israelites killed 100,000 Aramean foot soldiers in one day.
The rest fled into Aphek, but the city wall fell on 27,000 of them. Ben-Hadad fled into the city and hid in an inner room.

His officials said to him, "We've heard that the kings of Israel are merciful. Let's put sackcloth around our waists and ropes on our heads and go to the king of Israel. Maybe he will spare your life."
So they wore sackcloth and ropes and went to the king of Israel. They said, "Your servant Ben-Hadad says, 'Please let me live.'" Ahab asked, "Is he still alive? He is my brother."
The men took this as a good sign and quickly said, "Yes, your brother Ben-Hadad!" "Go get him," Ahab said. Then Ben-Hadad came out to him, and Ahab had him ride in his chariot.

Ben-Hadad said, "I will return the cities my father took from your father. You may set up trading centers for yourself in Damascus, as my father did in Samaria." Ahab said, "On these terms I will let you go." So he made a treaty with him and sent him away.
At the the LORD's command, one of the sons of the prophets said to his companion, "Strike me." But the man refused.
The prophet said, "Because you did not obey the the LORD's voice, a lion will attack you as soon as you leave." As soon as he left, a lion found him and killed him.
The prophet found another man and said, "Strike me." The man struck him and wounded him.
Then the prophet went and stood by the road, waiting for the king. He disguised himself with a bandage over his eyes.

As the king passed by, the prophet cried out to him, "Your servant went into the middle of the battle. A man turned aside and brought another man to me and said, 'Guard this man. If he gets away, you will pay with your life, or you will pay a talent of silver.'"
"While your servant was busy here and there, the man disappeared." The king of Israel said to him, "That is your own judgment; you have decided it."
The prophet quickly removed the bandage from his eyes, and the king of Israel recognized him as one of the prophets.
The prophet said to him, "This is what the the LORD says: 'Because you let go the man I had set apart for destruction, your life will take his place, and your people will take his people's place.'"
The king of Israel went home to Samaria, angry and upset.
After these things, Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel, next to the palace of Ahab, king of Samaria.

Ahab said to Naboth, "Give me your vineyard so I can make it a vegetable garden. It is close to my house. I will give you a better vineyard than it, or, if you like, I will pay you its price in money."
But Naboth said to Ahab, "May The LORD keep me from giving you the land my fathers left me."
Ahab went home angry and upset because Naboth had said, "I will not give you the land my fathers left me." He lay on his bed, turned his face away, and would not eat.
His wife Jezebel came to him and asked, "Why are you so upset that you will not eat?"

He answered, "I spoke to Naboth the Jezreelite and said, 'Give me your vineyard for money, or, if you prefer, I will give you another vineyard for it.' But he said, 'I will not give you my vineyard.'"
Jezebel his wife said to him, "Are you the king of Israel? Get up, eat, and be happy. I will get Naboth's vineyard for you."
So she wrote letters in Ahab's name, sealed them with his seal, and sent them to the elders and nobles who lived in Naboth's city.
In the letters she wrote, "Call for a day of fasting, and put Naboth in a place of honor among the people.
Seat two scoundrels in front of him and have them say, 'You have cursed God and the king.' Then take him out and stone him to death."
The men of the city—the elders and nobles who lived there—did exactly what Jezebel had written.
They called for a fast and put Naboth in a place of honor.

Then two scoundrels came in and sat across from him. They spoke against Naboth in front of the people and said, "Naboth has cursed God and the king." They took him outside the city, stoned him, and he died.
Then they sent word to Jezebel: "Naboth has been stoned to death."
When Jezebel heard that Naboth had been stoned and was dead, she said to Ahab, "Get up and take possession of Naboth's vineyard in Jezreel. He would not sell it to you for money, but now he is dead."
As soon as Ahab heard that Naboth was dead, he went down to take possession of the vineyard.
Then the word of the the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite:
"Get up and go down to meet Ahab, king of Israel, who is in Samaria. He is in Naboth's vineyard, where he has gone to take possession of it.

Say to him, 'This is what the the LORD says: Have you murdered someone and then taken his property? This is what the the LORD says: In the place where dogs licked up Naboth's blood, dogs will lick up your blood—yes, yours.'"
Ahab said to Elijah, "Have you found me, my enemy?" Elijah answered, "I have found you, because you have given yourself over to doing evil in the sight of the the LORD."
"Look, I am bringing disaster on you. I will wipe you out and kill every male in Israel who belongs to Ahab, whether slave or free.
I will make your family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat, and like the family of Baasha son of Ahijah, because you have made Me angry and led Israel into sin.
The LORD also says this about Jezebel: 'Dogs will eat Jezebel by the wall of Jezreel.'
Anyone from Ahab's family who dies in the city will be eaten by dogs, and anyone who dies in the field will be eaten by birds."
There was no one like Ahab, who gave himself over to doing evil in the sight of the the LORD, because his wife Jezebel pushed him to do it.
He acted in a very disgusting way by following idols, just as the Amorites had done, whom the the LORD drove out before the Israelites.
When Ahab heard these words, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth, fasted, lay in sackcloth, and walked around quietly.
Then the word of the the LORD came to Elijah the Tishbite:

"Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before Me? Because he has humbled himself before Me, I will not bring disaster on him in his own lifetime. I will bring disaster on his family in the days of his son."
For three years there was no war between Aram and Israel.
In the third year, Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, went down to visit the king of Israel.
The king of Israel said to his servants, "Do you know that Ramoth in Gilead belongs to us, but we are doing nothing to take it from the king of Aram?"
He said to Jehoshaphat, "Will you go with me to fight at Ramoth Gilead?" Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, "I am like you, my people are like your people, and my horses are like your horses.
Please ask today for the word of the the LORD."
The king of Israel gathered about four hundred prophets and said to them, "Should I go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should I hold back?" They said, "Go up, and the Lord will give it to the king."
Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there no other prophet of the the LORD here? We could ask him too."

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is still one man we can ask the the LORD through. His name is Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him because he never says anything good about me, only bad." Jehoshaphat said, "The king shouldn't say that."
The king of Israel called one of his officers and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah here quickly."

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, were sitting on their thrones, wearing royal robes, at the threshing floor near the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were prophesying in front of them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns for himself and said, "This is what the the LORD says: With these you will attack the Arameans until they are destroyed."
All the prophets said the same thing: "Go up to Ramoth Gilead and win, because the the LORD will hand it over to the king."
The messenger who had gone to get Micaiah said to him, "Look, all the prophets are saying the same good thing to the king. Please make your answer match theirs and say something good."
Micaiah said, "As surely as the the LORD lives, I will say only what the the LORD tells me."

When he came to the king, the king said to him, "Micaiah, should we go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should we hold back?" Micaiah said, "Go up and win. The the LORD will hand it over to the king."
The king said to him, "How many times must I make you swear to tell me nothing but the truth in the name of the the LORD?"
Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. The the LORD said, 'They have no master. Let each go home in peace.'"
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Didn't I tell you he would not say anything good about me, only bad?"
Micaiah said, "So listen to the word of the the LORD. I saw the the LORD sitting on His throne, and all the armies of heaven standing around Him, on His right and on His left.
The the LORD said, 'Who will trick Ahab into going up to Ramoth Gilead so he will die there?' One said one thing, and another said another.
Then a spirit came forward and stood before the the LORD and said, 'I will trick him.' The the LORD said, 'How?'
He said, 'I will go out and put a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.' The the LORD said, 'You will succeed. Go and do it.'
So now, look, the the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of all your prophets, and the the LORD has spoken disaster against you."
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, "Which way did the Spirit of the the LORD go from me to speak to you?"
Micaiah said, "Look, you will see it on that day when you go into an inner room to hide."
The king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son.
Tell them, 'The king says to put this man in prison and feed him only bread and water until I come home safely.'"
Micaiah said, "If you come back safely, then the the LORD did not speak through me." Then he said, "Listen, all you people!"
The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, went up to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into the battle, but you wear your robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself and went into the battle.
The king of Aram had commanded his thirty-two chariot commanders, "Do not fight with anyone, small or great, except the king of Israel."
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "Surely this is the king of Israel!" So they turned to fight him, and Jehoshaphat cried out.
When the chariot commanders saw that he was not the king of Israel, they turned back from chasing him.

But one soldier shot an arrow at random and hit the king of Israel between the plates of his armor. The king said to his chariot driver, "Turn around and get me out of the battle, because I am wounded."
The battle got worse that day, and the king stayed propped up in his chariot facing the Arameans. The blood from his wound ran down into the bottom of the chariot, and he died that evening.
At sunset, a shout went through the army: "Every man go back to his city, and every man go back to his own land!"
The king died and was brought to Samaria, and they buried him there.
They washed the chariot at the pool of Samaria, and the dogs licked up his blood, just as the the LORD had said.
Everything else Ahab did, including the ivory palace he built and all the cities he built, is written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Ahab died, and his son Ahaziah became king after him.
Jehoshaphat son of Asa became king of Judah in the fourth year of Ahab king of Israel.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-five years. His mother was Azubah daughter of Shilhi.

He followed the good example of his father Asa and did not turn from it. He did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD. But the high places were not removed, and the people still sacrificed and burned incense on them.
Jehoshaphat made peace with the king of Israel.
Everything else Jehoshaphat did, including his brave deeds and the wars he fought, is written in the book of the history of the kings of Judah.
He also removed the rest of the male temple prostitutes who were left from the time of his father Asa.
There was no king in Edom at that time; a governor ruled instead.
Jehoshaphat built trading ships to go to Ophir for gold, but they never sailed because they were wrecked at Ezion Geber.
Ahaziah son of Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Let my servants sail with your servants in the ships," but Jehoshaphat refused.
Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David his father. His son Jehoram became king after him.
Ahaziah son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah. He ruled Israel for two years.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD. He followed the ways of his father and mother, and of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin.
He served Baal and worshiped him, and he made the the LORD, the God of Israel, angry, just as his father had done.
After Ahab died, Moab rebelled against Israel.
Ahaziah fell through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and was injured. He sent messengers with this order: "Go and ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron, if I will recover from this sickness."

But the angel of the the LORD said to Elijah the Tishbite, "Get up and go meet the messengers of the king of Samaria. Say to them, 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you go to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron?'"
So this is what the the LORD says: "You will not get down from the bed you went up to. You will die." Then Elijah left.
The messengers returned to him, and he asked, "Why have you come back?"

They said, "A man came up to meet us and said, 'Go back to the king who sent you and say to him, "This is what the the LORD says: Is it because there is no God in Israel that you send to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron? Therefore you will not get down from the bed you went up to. You will die."'"
The king asked, "What did the man look like who met you and said these things to you?"
They answered, "He wore a garment of hair with a leather belt around his waist." The king said, "That is Elijah the Tishbite."
Then the king sent a captain with his fifty men to Elijah. The captain went up to him while Elijah was sitting on top of the hill. He said, "Man of God, the king says, 'Come down.'"
Elijah answered the captain, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and burn you and your fifty men." Then fire came down from heaven and burned him and his fifty men.
The king sent another captain with his fifty men. This captain said to Elijah, "Man of God, the king says, 'Come down at once.'"
Elijah answered, "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and burn you and your fifty men." Then God's fire came down from heaven and burned him and his fifty men.

The king sent a third captain with his fifty men. The third captain went up, knelt before Elijah, and begged, "Man of God, please let my life and the lives of these fifty servants of yours be important to you.
Fire has already come down from heaven and burned the first two captains and their fifties. So please let my life be important to you too."
The angel of the the LORD said to Elijah, "Go down with him. Do not be afraid of him." So Elijah got up and went down with him to the king.

Elijah said to the king, "This is what the the LORD says: 'Because you sent messengers to ask Baal-Zebub, the god of Ekron, is it because there is no God in Israel to ask for His word? So you will not get down from the bed you went up to. You will die.'"
So Ahaziah died, just as the the LORD had said through Elijah. Because Ahaziah had no son, Jehoram became king after him. This was in the second year of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.
The rest of what Ahaziah did is written in the book of the history of the kings of Israel.
Now when the the LORD was about to take Elijah up to heaven in a whirlwind, Elijah and Elisha were leaving Gilgal.
Elijah said to Elisha, "Please stay here, for the the LORD has sent me to Bethel." But Elisha said, "As the the LORD lives, and as you live, I will not leave you." So they went down to Bethel.
The prophets' followers at Bethel came out to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that the the LORD will take away your master from over you today?" Elisha answered, "Yes, I know. Be quiet."
Then Elijah said to him, "Stay here, please, for the the LORD has sent me to Jericho." But Elisha said, "As the the LORD lives, and as you live, I will not leave you." So they came to Jericho.
The prophets' followers at Jericho came near to Elisha and said to him, "Do you know that the the LORD will take away your master from over you today?" Elisha answered, "Yes, I know. Be quiet."
Then Elijah said to him, "Please stay here, for the the LORD has sent me to the Jordan." But Elisha said, "As the the LORD lives, and as you live, I will not leave you." So the two of them went on.
Fifty men from the prophets' followers went and stood at a distance from them, and the two of them stood by the Jordan.
Elijah took his cloak, rolled it up, and struck the water. It divided to the right and left, and the two of them crossed on dry ground.
When they had crossed, Elijah said to Elisha, "Ask what I can do for you before I am taken from you." Elisha said, "Please let me have twice as much of your spirit."
Elijah said, "You have asked a hard thing. If you see me when I am taken from you, it will be yours; but if not, it will not."
While they were walking and talking, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated the two of them, and Elijah went up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Elisha saw it and cried, "My father, my father! Israel's defender is gone!" He could not see Elijah anymore. Then he grabbed his own clothes and tore them in two.
He picked up Elijah's cloak, which had fallen from him, and went back and stood by the bank of the Jordan.

He took Elijah's cloak that had fallen from him and struck the water. He said, "Where is the the LORD, the God of Elijah?" When he struck the water, it divided to the right and left, and Elisha crossed over.
When the prophets' followers at Jericho saw him from a distance, they said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha." They came to meet him and bowed to the ground before him.

They said to him, "Look, there are fifty strong men among your servants. Please let them go and search for your master. Perhaps the Spirit of the the LORD has carried him away and thrown him on one of the mountains or in one of the valleys." Elisha said, "You must not send them."
But they kept urging him until he gave in, so he said, "Send them." They sent fifty men, who searched for three days but did not find him.
When they came back to Elisha, he was staying in Jericho. He said to them, "Did I not tell you not to go?"
The men of the city said to Elisha, "Look, master, the city is in a good place, as you can see. But the water is bad, and the land is barren."
Elisha said, "Bring me a new bowl, and put salt in it." So they brought it to him.
He went out to the spring of water and threw the salt into it. He said, "Thus says the the LORD, 'I have healed this water; from now on it will not cause death or make the land barren.'"
So the water was healed, just as Elisha had said. It is still good today.
He went up from there to Bethel. As he was walking along the road, some young boys came out of the city and made fun of him. They said to him, "Go up, baldy! Go up, baldy!"
He turned around, looked at them, and cursed them in the name of the the LORD. Then two bears came out of the woods and tore forty-two of the boys to pieces.
From there he went to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.
In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat's rule over Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for twelve years.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD, but not like his father and mother. He removed the sacred stone of Baal that his father had made.
Still, he held on to the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which had led Israel into sin. He did not turn away from them.
Mesha, king of Moab, raised sheep. He used to send the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs and the wool from one hundred thousand rams.
But after Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
So King Jehoram marched out from Samaria and called up all Israel.

He sent a message to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah: "The king of Moab has rebelled against me. Will you go with me to fight against Moab?" Jehoshaphat answered, "I will go. I am like you. My people are like your people, and my horses are like your horses."
Then Jehoram asked, "Which way should we go?" Jehoshaphat replied, "Through the Desert of Edom."
So the king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom set out. After marching around for seven days, there was no water for the army or for the animals with them.
The king of Israel said, "Oh no! Has the the LORD brought these three kings together only to let Moab defeat us?"

But Jehoshaphat asked, "Is there no prophet of the the LORD here? Then we could ask the the LORD through him." One of the servants of the king of Israel answered, "Elisha son of Shaphat is here. He used to serve Elijah."
Jehoshaphat said, "The word of the the LORD is with him." So the king of Israel, Jehoshaphat, and the king of Edom went down to see him.

Elisha said to the king of Israel, "What do you and I have to do with each other? Go to the prophets of your father and your mother!" The king of Israel replied, "No, because the the LORD has brought these three kings together to hand them over to Moab."
Elisha said, "As surely as the the LORD of Hosts lives, before whom I stand, if I did not respect Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or notice you."
Elisha said, "But now bring me someone who plays the harp." While the harpist played, the hand of the the LORD came upon Elisha.
He said, "This is what the the LORD says: 'Make this valley full of ditches.'
The LORD also says, 'You will not see wind or rain, but this valley will be filled with water, and you and your cattle and your animals will drink.'
And this is an easy thing for the the LORD. He will also hand Moab over to you.
You must attack every walled city and every important city. Cut down every good tree, stop up every spring of water, and ruin every good field by covering it with stones."
The next morning, about the time of the morning sacrifice, water came flowing from the direction of Edom, and the land was filled with water.
All the Moabites heard that the kings had come to fight them. So every man who could carry a weapon was called out, and they stood at the border.
When they got up early in the morning, the sun was shining on the water. To the Moabites across the way, the water looked red like blood.
They said, "This is blood! The kings must have fought and killed each other. Now, Moab, take the plunder!"
But when they came to Israel's camp, the Israelites rose up and struck the Moabites, who ran away from them. The Israelites went into the land and attacked Moab.

They destroyed the cities. Each man threw a stone into every good field until it was covered. They stopped up every spring and cut down every good tree. Only Kir Hareseth was left with its stones in place, but the slingers surrounded it and attacked it.
When the king of Moab saw that the battle was too strong for him, he took seven hundred swordsmen to break through to the king of Edom, but they could not.
Then he took his oldest son, who was to rule after him, and offered him as a burnt offering on the wall. Great anger came against Israel, so they withdrew from him and returned to their own land.

One of the wives of the sons of the prophets cried out to Elisha, saying, "Your servant my husband is dead. You know that your servant feared the the LORD. Now the creditor has come to take my two children as slaves."
Elisha said to her, "What shall I do for you? Tell me, what do you have in the house?" She said, "Your servant has nothing in the house except a jar of oil."
He said, "Go, borrow empty jars from all your neighbors. Don't borrow just a few.
Then go in and shut the door behind you and your sons. Pour oil into all these jars, and set aside the full ones."
So she left him and shut the door behind her and her sons. They brought the jars to her, and she poured the oil.
When the jars were full, she said to her son, "Bring me another jar." He said, "There are no more jars." Then the oil stopped.
She went and told the man of God. He said, "Go, sell the oil and pay your debt. You and your sons can live on what is left."
One day Elisha went to Shunem. A wealthy woman lived there, and she urged him to eat. So whenever he passed by, he stopped there to eat.
She said to her husband, "Look, I know that this man who keeps coming by is a holy man of God.
Let's make a small room upstairs and put a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp there for him. Then whenever he comes to us, he can stay there."
One day he came there and went up to the room and lay down.
He said to his servant Gehazi, "Call the Shunammite woman." He called her, and she stood before him.

He said to Gehazi, "Say to her, 'You have gone to all this trouble for us. What can we do for you? Do you want me to speak to the king or to the commander of the army for you?'" She said, "I live among my own people."
Elisha asked, "What then can be done for her?" Gehazi said, "She has no son, and her husband is old."
Elisha said, "Call her." So Gehazi called her, and she stood in the doorway.
Elisha said, "At this time next year, you will hold a son in your arms." She said, "No, my lord, man of God, do not lie to your servant."
The woman became pregnant, and at that time the next year she gave birth to a son, just as Elisha had said.
The boy grew. One day he went out to his father, who was with the reapers.
He said to his father, "My head! My head!" His father said to a servant, "Carry him to his mother."
The servant carried him to his mother. He sat on her lap until noon, and then he died.
She went up and laid him on the bed of the man of God. Then she shut the door and went out.
She called to her husband and said, "Please send me one of the servants and a donkey. I will hurry to the man of God and come back."
He said, "Why go to him today? It is not a new moon or a Sabbath." She said, "All is well."
She saddled the donkey and said to her servant, "Ride fast. Don't slow down unless I tell you."
So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When he saw her coming, he said to his servant Gehazi, "Look, the Shunammite woman is coming."
Elisha said to Gehazi, "Run to meet her and ask, 'Are you well? Is your husband well? Is the boy well?'" She answered, "We are well."

When she reached the man of God at the mountain, she grabbed his feet. Gehazi came to push her away, but the man of God said, "Leave her alone. She is very upset, and the the LORD has hidden it from me and has not told me."
She said, "Did I ask my lord for a son? Didn't I say, 'Don't give me false hope'?"
Elisha said to Gehazi, "Tuck in your belt, take my staff in your hand, and go. If you meet anyone, don't greet him. If anyone greets you, don't answer. Lay my staff on the boy's face."
The boy's mother said, "As surely as the the LORD lives and as you live, I will not leave you." So Elisha got up and followed her.
Gehazi went on ahead and laid the staff on the boy's face, but there was no sound or movement. He came back to meet Elisha and said, "The boy has not woken up."
Elisha came into the house and saw the boy lying dead on his bed.
He went in, shut the door behind the two of them, and prayed to the the LORD.

He went up and lay on the child. He put his mouth on the child's mouth, his eyes on the child's eyes, and his hands on the child's hands. As he stretched himself over the child, the child's body grew warm.
He got up, walked back and forth in the house, and then went up and stretched himself over the boy again. The boy sneezed seven times and opened his eyes.
Elisha called Gehazi and said, "Call the Shunammite woman." He called her, and she came to him. Elisha said, "Pick up your son."
She came in, fell at his feet, and bowed to the ground. Then she picked up her son and went out.

Elisha returned to Gilgal. There was a famine in the land. The sons of the prophets were sitting before him. He said to his servant, "Put on the large pot and cook some stew for the sons of the prophets."

One of them went out into the field to gather herbs. He found a wild vine and gathered from it a lapful of wild gourds. He came back and cut them up into the pot of stew, but no one knew what they were.
They poured out the stew for the men to eat. As they ate it, they cried out, "There is death in the pot, man of God!" And they could not eat it.
Elisha said, "Bring some flour." He threw it into the pot and said, "Pour it out for the people to eat." Then there was nothing harmful in the pot.

A man from Baal-shalishah came bringing the man of God twenty loaves of barley bread from the first ripe grain, along with some heads of new grain in his sack. Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat."
His servant said, "How can I set this before a hundred men?" Elisha said, "Give it to the people to eat. For this is what the the LORD says: 'They will eat and have some left over.'"
So he set it before them. They ate and had some left over, just as the the LORD had said.

Now Naaman was commander of the army of the king of Aram. He was a great man in his master's sight and highly regarded, because through him the the LORD had given victory to Aram. He was a valiant warrior, but he had leprosy.
Now bands of Arameans had gone out and captured a young girl from the land of Israel. She served Naaman's wife.
She said to her mistress, “If only my master would see the prophet in Samaria! Then he would be cured of his leprosy.”
Naaman went to his master and told him what the girl from Israel had said.
So the king of Aram said, “Go, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel.” So Naaman left, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand shekels of gold, and ten sets of clothing.
He took the letter to the king of Israel. It said, “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman to you so you can cure him of his leprosy.”

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, “Am I God, that I can kill and make alive? Why does this man send me a man to be cured of leprosy? Surely you can see he is trying to pick a fight with me.”

When Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had torn his clothes, he sent a message to the king: “Why have you torn your clothes? Let him come to me, and he will know there is a prophet in Israel.”
So Naaman came with his horses and chariots and stood at the door of Elisha's house.
Elisha sent a messenger to him, saying, “Go, wash yourself seven times in the Jordan, and your flesh will be restored and you will be clean.”

But Naaman went away angry and said, “I thought he would surely come out to me, stand, and call on the name of the the LORD his God. I thought he would wave his hand over the place and cure the leprosy.”
“Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean?” So he turned and went away in a rage.
His servants came to him and said, “My father, if the prophet had told you to do something great, wouldn't you have done it? How much more, then, when he says, ‘Wash and be clean’!”
So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, as the man of God had said. His flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
Then Naaman and all his company returned to the man of God. He stood before him and said, “Now I know there is no God in all the earth except in Israel. Please accept a gift from your servant.”
But Elisha said, “As surely as the the LORD lives, whom I serve, I will not accept it.” Naaman urged him to take it, but he refused.

Then Naaman said, “If you won't accept it, please let your servant take two mule-loads of earth. For from now on your servant will no longer offer burnt offerings or sacrifices to any other god but the the LORD.”

“But may the the LORD forgive your servant for this one thing: When my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship there and leans on my arm, I bow down in the temple of Rimmon. When I bow down in the temple of Rimmon, may the the LORD forgive your servant for this.”
Elisha said to him, “Go in peace.” So Naaman left him and traveled a short distance.

But Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said to himself, “My master was too easy on this Aramean Naaman. He did not accept from him what he brought. As surely as the the LORD lives, I will run after him and get something from him.”
So Gehazi hurried after Naaman. When Naaman saw him running after him, he got down from the chariot to meet him. He asked, “Is everything all right?”

Gehazi said, “Everything is all right. My master sent me to say, ‘Two young men from the company of the prophets have just come to me from the hill country of Ephraim. Please give them a talent of silver and two sets of clothing.’”

Naaman said, “Please take two talents.” He urged him, and tied up two talents of silver in two bags, with two sets of clothing. He gave them to two of his servants, and they carried them ahead of Gehazi.
