When Gehazi came to the hill, he took the gifts from their hands and put them in the house. Then he sent the men away, and they left.
Then he went in and stood before his master. Elisha asked him, “Where have you been, Gehazi?” He answered, “Your servant has not gone anywhere.”

Elisha said to him, “Didn't I know what you did when the man turned from his chariot to meet you? Is this the time to take money, clothes, olive groves, vineyards, sheep, cattle, male servants, and female servants?”
“Naaman's leprosy will cling to you and to your descendants forever.” Then Gehazi left Elisha's presence as a leper, as white as snow.
The prophets' disciples said to Elisha, "This place where we live with you is too small for us.
Let us go to the Jordan River. Each of us can get a log there and build a place for us to live." Elisha said, "Go."
One of them said, "Please come with your servants." Elisha said, "I will go."
So he went with them. They came to the Jordan and began cutting down trees.
While one man was cutting a beam, the iron axe head fell into the water. He cried out, "Oh no, my master! It was borrowed!"
The man of God asked, "Where did it fall?" When the man showed him the place, Elisha cut a stick and threw it there, and the iron floated.
Elisha said, "Pick it up." The man reached out his hand and took it.
The king of Aram was at war with Israel. He talked with his officers and said, "I will set up camp at a certain place."
But the man of God sent a message to the king of Israel: "Be careful not to pass through that place, because the Arameans are moving down there."
So the king of Israel sent a warning to the place the man of God had named. This happened more than once or twice.
This made the king of Aram very angry. He called his officers and said, "Which of you is working for the king of Israel?"
One of his officers said, "None of us, my lord the king. Elisha the prophet in Israel tells the king of Israel the words you speak in your bedroom."
The king said, "Go and see where he is, so I can send men to get him." They told him, "He is in Dothan."
So the king sent horses, chariots, and a large army there. They came at night and surrounded the city.
When the servant of the man of God got up early and went out, he saw an army with horses and chariots all around the city. He said, "Oh no, my master! What will we do?"
Elisha said, "Do not be afraid. Those who are with us are more than those who are with them."
Then Elisha prayed, "The LORD, please open his eyes so he can see." The LORD opened the young man's eyes, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
As the Arameans came down to him, Elisha prayed to the LORD, "Please strike this people with blindness." The LORD struck them with blindness, just as Elisha had asked.
Elisha said to them, "This is not the right road, and this is not the right city. Follow me, and I will lead you to the man you are looking for." He led them to Samaria.
When they entered Samaria, Elisha said, "The LORD, open their eyes so they can see." The LORD opened their eyes, and they saw that they were in the middle of Samaria.
When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, "My father, should I kill them? Should I kill them?"
Elisha said, "Do not kill them. Would you kill people you captured with your sword and bow? Put food and water in front of them so they can eat and drink, and then let them go back to their master."
So the king made a great feast for them. They ate and drank, and he sent them away. After that, Aramean raiding parties stopped coming into the land of Israel.
Later, Ben-Hadad king of Aram gathered all his army, went up, and besieged Samaria.
There was a great famine in Samaria while they surrounded it. A donkey's head cost eighty pieces of silver, and a small amount of dove dung cost five pieces of silver.
As the king of Israel was walking on the wall, a woman cried out to him, "Help, my lord the king!"
He said, "If the LORD does not help you, how can I help you? Can I get grain from the threshing floor or wine from the winepress?"

Then the king asked her, "What is wrong?" She answered, "This woman said to me, 'Give me your son so we can eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.' "So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Give me your son so we can eat him,' but she hid her son."
So we cooked my son and ate him. The next day I said to her, 'Give me your son so we can eat him,' but she hid her son."
When the king heard the woman's words, he tore his clothes. As he walked along the wall, the people saw that he was wearing sackcloth under his clothes.
Then he said, "May God punish me, and even more, if Elisha son of Shaphat still has his head by the end of today!"

Elisha was sitting in his house, and the elders were sitting with him. Before the messenger arrived, Elisha said to the elders, "Do you see that this murderer's son has sent someone to cut off my head? When the messenger comes, shut the door and hold him at the door. Don't you hear his master's footsteps behind him?"
While Elisha was still speaking, the messenger came down to him. The king said, "This trouble is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?"

Elisha said, “Hear the word of the the LORD. This is what the the LORD says: ‘About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, a seah of fine flour will sell for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel.’”

The officer who helped the king stand answered the man of God, “Look, even if the the LORD opened windows in heaven, could this happen?” Elisha answered, “You will see it with your eyes, but you will not eat any of it.”
Four men with leprosy were at the city gate. They said to each other, “Why are we sitting here until we die?”

“If we say, ‘Let’s go into the city,’ the famine is there, and we will die. If we stay here, we will die too. So let’s go over to the Aramean camp. If they spare us, we will live; if they kill us, we will only die.”
They got up at twilight and went to the Aramean camp. When they reached the edge of the camp, no one was there.
For the Lord had made the Aramean camp hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a large army. They said to each other, “Look, the king of Israel has hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings to attack us!”
So they ran away in the twilight. They left their tents, horses, and donkeys, and the whole camp just as it was. They ran for their lives.

When these lepers reached the edge of the camp, they went into one tent and ate and drank. They carried off silver, gold, and clothes, hid them, then went to another tent, took things from there, and hid them too.
Then they said to each other, “We are not doing right. Today is a day of good news, and we are keeping quiet. If we wait until morning, we will be punished. Let’s go tell the king’s family.”

So they went and called to the city gatekeepers. They told them, “We went to the Aramean camp, and no one is there—no sound of people. The horses and donkeys are tied up, and the tents are just as they were.”
The gatekeepers shouted the news to the king’s palace.

The king got up at night and said to his servants, “I will tell you what the Arameans have done to us. They know we are hungry, so they left the camp to hide in the fields. They are thinking, ‘When they come out of the city, we will capture them alive and get into the city.’”

One of his servants answered, “Please let some men take five of the horses left in the city. They are like all the Israelites left here—like all the Israelites who are already gone. Let us send them and see.”
So they took two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean camp, saying, “Go and see.”
They followed them to the Jordan. The whole road was full of clothes and supplies the Arameans had thrown away in their hurry. The messengers returned and told the king.
Then the people went out and took things from the Aramean camp. So a seah of fine flour sold for a shekel, and two seahs of barley sold for a shekel, just as the the LORD had said.
Now the king had put the officer who helped him stand in charge of the gate. The people trampled him there, and he died, just as the man of God had said when the king came to him.
It happened just as the man of God had told the king: “At this time tomorrow, in the gate of Samaria, two seahs of barley will sell for a shekel, and a seah of fine flour for a shekel.”

The officer had answered the man of God, “Look, even if the the LORD opened windows in heaven, could this happen?” The man of God had said, “You will see it with your eyes, but you will not eat any of it.”
And so it happened to him: the people trampled him in the gate, and he died.

Elisha had told the woman whose son he brought back to life, "Get up and go with your family. Stay wherever you can, because the LORD has called for a famine. It will come on the land for seven years."
So the woman got up and did what the man of God said. She went with her family and stayed in the land of the Philistines for seven years.
After seven years, the woman came back from the land of the Philistines and went to the king to ask for her house and her field.
The king was talking to Gehazi, the servant of the man of God. He said, "Please tell me all the great things Elisha has done."

While Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha brought a dead man back to life, the woman whose son Elisha brought back to life came to the king and cried out for her house and her field. Gehazi said, "My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha brought back to life."

The king asked the woman, and she told him what had happened. Then the king told one of his officials, "Give back everything that belonged to her, and all the crops from her field from the day she left the land until now."
Elisha came to Damascus while Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, was sick. Someone told him, "The man of God has come here."
The king said to Hazael, "Take a gift with you and go meet the man of God. Ask the LORD through him if I will recover from this illness."

So Hazael went to meet Elisha. He took a gift with him: all the good things of Damascus, carried by forty camels. He came and stood before Elisha and said, "Your son Ben-Hadad, king of Aram, has sent me to ask if he will recover from this illness."
Elisha said to him, "Go and tell him, 'You will surely recover.' But the LORD has shown me that he will surely die."
Elisha stared at him until Hazael felt uncomfortable, and then the man of God wept.

Hazael asked, "Why is my lord weeping?" Elisha answered, "Because I know the harm you will do to the people of Israel. You will set their forts on fire, kill their young men with the sword, smash their little ones, and rip open their pregnant women."
Hazael said, "What is your servant, a dog, that he should do such a big thing?" Elisha answered, "The LORD has shown me that you will be king over Aram."
So Hazael left Elisha and went to his master. Ben-Hadad asked, "What did Elisha say to you?" Hazael answered, "He told me that you would surely recover."
The next day, Hazael took a thick cloth, dipped it in water, and spread it over Ben-Hadad's face, so that he died. Then Hazael became king in his place.
In the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat became king of Judah. Jehoshaphat was king of Judah at that time.
He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled eight years in Jerusalem.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, as Ahab's family had done, because he married Ahab's daughter. He did what was evil in the LORD's sight.
But the LORD did not want to destroy Judah, because of David His servant. He had promised to give David and his descendants a lamp forever.
During his rule, Edom broke free from Judah's control and chose a king for themselves.
Joram went to Zair with all his chariots. He rose up at night and attacked the Edomites who had surrounded him and the chariot commanders. The Edomites fled to their tents.
So Edom has been free from Judah's control to this day. At that same time, Libnah also broke free.
The rest of Joram's acts, and all he did, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
Joram died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Ahaziah became king in his place.
In the twelfth year of Joram son of Ahab, king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram became king of Judah.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled one year in Jerusalem. His mother was Athaliah, the daughter of Omri, king of Israel.
He followed the ways of Ahab's family and did what was evil in the LORD's sight, just as Ahab's family had done, because he was married into Ahab's family.
He went with Joram son of Ahab to fight against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-Gilead. The Arameans wounded Joram.

So King Joram went back to Jezreel to recover from the wounds the Arameans gave him at Ramah while he fought Hazael king of Aram. Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to see Joram son of Ahab, because Joram was sick.
Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets. He said, "Get ready, take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-Gilead.
When you get there, look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi. Go in, make him stand up from among his brothers, and take him into an inner room.
Take the flask of oil, pour it on his head, and say, 'This is what the LORD says: I have anointed you king over Israel.' Then open the door and run. Don't wait.
So the young prophet went to Ramoth-Gilead.
He arrived and found the army commanders sitting together. He said, "I have a message for you, commander." Jehu asked, "For which of us?" The prophet answered, "For you, commander."
Jehu got up and went into the house. The prophet poured the oil on his head and said, "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'I have anointed you king over the the LORD's people Israel.'"
The prophet added, "You must strike down the family of Ahab, your master. I will punish Jezebel for the blood of My servants the prophets and all the the LORD's servants.
I will wipe out every male in Ahab's family, both slave and free, in Israel.
I will make Ahab's family like the family of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the family of Baasha son of Ahijah.
Dogs will eat Jezebel in the plot of ground at Jezreel, and no one will bury her. Then the prophet opened the door and ran.
Jehu went out to his master's servants. They asked him, "Is everything all right? Why did this crazy man come to you?" He answered, "You know the man and what he says."
They said, "That's not true. Tell us now." He told them, "He said this and that to me. He said, 'This is what the LORD says: I have anointed you king over Israel.'"
Then they hurried. Each man took his coat and put it under Jehu on the bare steps. They blew the trumpet and shouted, "Jehu is king!"
So Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, son of Nimshi, made a plan against Joram. (Joram and all Israel had been guarding Ramoth-Gilead against Hazael king of Aram.

But King Joram had gone back to Jezreel to heal from the wounds the Arameans had given him while fighting Hazael king of Aram.) Jehu said, "If you are willing, let no one escape from the city to go and tell the news in Jezreel."
Then Jehu got into his chariot and went to Jezreel, because Joram was lying there. Ahaziah king of Judah had come down to see Joram.

The watchman standing on the tower in Jezreel saw Jehu's troops coming. He said, "I see a group coming." Joram said, "Take a horseman and send him to meet them. Have him ask, 'Is everything all right?'"

So a horseman rode out to meet Jehu and said, "The king says, 'Is everything all right?'" Jehu said, "What do you have to do with peace? Get behind me." The watchman reported, "The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back."
Then Joram sent a second horseman. He came to them and said, "The king says, 'Is everything all right?'" Jehu answered, "What do you have to do with peace? Get behind me."
The watchman reported, "He reached them, but he is not coming back. The driving is like Jehu's driving. He drives like a madman."
Joram said, "Harness the chariot." They harnessed his chariot. Then Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah each went out in his chariot. They met Jehu in the field of Naboth the Jezreelite.
When Joram saw Jehu, he said, "Is it peace, Jehu?" Jehu answered, "How can there be peace while your mother Jezebel is so unfaithful and uses so much witchcraft?"
Joram turned his chariot to run. He said to Ahaziah, "It's a trap, Ahaziah!"
Jehu drew his bow and shot Joram between the shoulders. The arrow went through his heart, and he sank down in his chariot.

Jehu said to Bidkar his officer, "Pick him up and throw him into the field of Naboth the Jezreelite. Remember when you and I rode together behind his father Ahab? The LORD put this heavy burden on him.

I saw the blood of Naboth and the blood of his sons, says the the LORD. I will pay you back in this field, says the the LORD. So now pick him up and throw him into the field, just as the the LORD said."

When Ahaziah king of Judah saw this, he ran toward Beth-haggan. Jehu chased him and said, "Shoot him too!" They shot him in his chariot on the way up to Gur near Ibleam. He escaped to Megiddo and died there.
His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem and buried him with his fathers in his tomb in the City of David.
Ahaziah had become king over Judah in the eleventh year of Joram son of Ahab.
When Jehu came to Jezreel, Jezebel heard about it. She painted her eyes, fixed her hair, and looked out the window.
As Jehu entered the gate, she said, "Is everything all right, Zimri, you murderer of your master?"
He looked up at the window and said, "Who is on my side? Who?" Two or three eunuchs looked down at him.
He said, "Throw her down." They threw her down. Some of her blood splashed on the wall and on the horses, and Jehu trampled her underfoot.
Then he went in and ate and drank. He said, "Take care of this cursed woman and bury her, for she is a king's daughter."
They went to bury her, but they found only her skull, her feet, and the palms of her hands.
They went back and told Jehu. He said, "This is what the the LORD said through His servant Elijah the Tishbite: 'In the plot at Jezreel, dogs will eat Jezebel's flesh.
Her body will be like dung on the ground in the plot at Jezreel, so that no one can say, "This is Jezebel."'"
Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the rulers of Jezreel, the elders, and the guardians of Ahab’s children. The letters said,
“When this letter reaches you, you have your master’s sons with you. You also have chariots, horses, a fortified city, and weapons.
So choose the best and most honest of your master’s sons. Put him on his father’s throne. Then fight to defend your master’s family.”
When the leaders read the letter, they were very afraid. They said, “Two kings could not stand against Jehu. How can we stand?”

So the palace manager, the city governor, the elders, and the guardians sent this message to Jehu: “We are your servants. We will do whatever you tell us. We will not make anyone king. Do what you think is best.”

Jehu wrote a second letter and said, “If you are on my side and will obey me, take the heads of your master’s sons and bring them to me in Jezreel by this time tomorrow.” The king had seventy sons. The leaders of the city were raising them.
When the letter came, they took the king’s sons and killed all seventy. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to Jehu in Jezreel.
A messenger came and told Jehu, “They have brought the heads of the king’s sons.” Jehu said, “Put them in two piles at the city gate until morning.”
In the morning, Jehu went out and stood before all the people. He said, “You are innocent. I am the one who plotted against my master and killed him. But who killed all these?
Know this: Not one word that the LORD spoke against Ahab’s family will fail. The LORD has done what He said through His servant Elijah.”
Then Jehu killed everyone left from Ahab’s family in Jezreel. He killed all the important men, close friends, and priests. He left no survivor.
After that, Jehu set out for Samaria. On the way, he stopped at Beth-eked of the Shepherds.

There he met the relatives of Ahaziah, king of Judah. Jehu asked, “Who are you?” They answered, “We are relatives of Ahaziah. We are going down to greet the sons of the king and the sons of the queen mother.”
Jehu said, “Take them alive!” His men captured them alive and killed them at the pit of Beth-eked. There were forty-two men, and he did not leave one alive.

Jehu left there and found Jehonadab son of Rechab coming to meet him. Jehu blessed him and asked, “Is your heart right with mine, as my heart is with yours?” Jehonadab answered, “It is.” Jehu said, “If it is, give me your hand.” Jehonadab gave him his hand, and Jehu pulled him up into the chariot.
Jehu said, “Come with me and see my strong devotion to the LORD.” So they rode together in his chariot.
When Jehu reached Samaria, he killed everyone left from Ahab’s family there. He destroyed them all, just as the LORD had said through Elijah.
Then Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, “Ahab worshiped Baal a little. Jehu will worship him much more.”

Jehu said, “Now call together all the prophets of Baal, all his worshipers, and all his priests. Do not let anyone miss the meeting, because I have a great sacrifice for Baal. Anyone who does not come will die.” Jehu said this to trick them so he could destroy the worshipers of Baal.
Jehu said, “Set apart a holy meeting for Baal.” So they announced it.
Jehu sent word through all Israel. Every worshiper of Baal came. Not one stayed away. They went into the temple of Baal until it was full from one end to the other.
Jehu told the man in charge of the robes, “Bring out robes for all the worshipers of Baal.” So he brought out the robes.

Then Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab went into the temple of Baal. Jehu said to the worshipers, “Look carefully and make sure no servants of the LORD are here with you. Only worshipers of Baal should be here.”
Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Jehu had placed eighty men outside and said, “If any man I hand over to you gets away, you will pay with your own life.”

As soon as Jehu finished offering the burnt offering, he said to the guards and officers, “Go in and kill them. Do not let anyone escape.” The guards and officers killed them with their swords. They threw the bodies outside. Then they went into the inner room of the temple.
They brought out the sacred stone pillars from the temple of Baal and burned them.
They tore down the pillar of Baal and tore down the temple of Baal. They made it a toilet, and it is still used that way today.
So Jehu wiped out the worship of Baal from Israel.
But Jehu did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led Israel to sin. He kept the golden calves at Bethel and Dan.

The LORD said to Jehu, “You have done well. You did what is right in My eyes, and you did to Ahab’s family everything I wanted. So your sons, down to the fourth generation, will sit on the throne of Israel.”
But Jehu was not careful to follow the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam, who had led Israel to sin.
In those days, the LORD began to reduce Israel’s territory. Hazael defeated Israel throughout its borders.
He took all the land east of the Jordan: the whole land of Gilead, and the regions of Gad, Reuben, and Manasseh. He took it from Aroer by the Arnon Gorge all the way through Gilead and Bashan.
The rest of the acts of Jehu, everything he did, and all his power are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Jehu died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Jehoahaz became king in his place.
Jehu ruled over Israel in Samaria for twenty-eight years.
When Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, saw that her son was dead, she got up and killed all the royal family.

But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash, the son of Ahaziah, and stole him away from among the king's sons who were being killed. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom, so they hid him from Athaliah, and he was not killed.
He stayed hidden with her in the house of the the LORD for six years while Athaliah ruled the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada sent for the captains of the Carites and the guards. He brought them into the house of the the LORD and made a covenant with them. He made them swear an oath, and he showed them the king's son.
He commanded them, "This is what you must do: A third of you who come on duty on the Sabbath will guard the king's house.
A third will be at the gate of Sur, and a third at the gate behind the guards. You will guard the temple.
The other two groups, who are off duty on the Sabbath, will guard the house of the the LORD around the king.
You must surround the king on every side, each man with his weapon in his hand. Anyone who comes inside your lines must be put to death. Stay with the king wherever he goes out or comes in."
The captains did everything Jehoiada the priest commanded. Each man brought his own men, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty, and they came to Jehoiada the priest.
The priest gave the captains the spears and shields that had belonged to King David and were in the house of the the LORD.
The guards stood, each with his weapon in his hand, from the right side of the temple to the left side, around the altar and the temple, to protect the king.
Then Jehoiada brought out the king's son, put the crown on his head, gave him the covenant scroll, and made him king. They anointed him, clapped their hands, and shouted, "Long live the king!"
When Athaliah heard the noise of the guards and the people, she went to the people at the house of the the LORD.

She looked and saw the king standing by the pillar, as was the custom, with the captains and trumpeters beside the king. All the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and shouted, "Treason! Treason!"

Jehoiada the priest ordered the captains in charge of the army, "Take her out between the ranks and kill anyone who follows her with the sword." For the priest had said, "She must not be killed in the house of the the LORD."
So they seized her, and she went by way of the horses' entrance to the king's palace, and there she was put to death.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the the LORD, the king, and the people, that they would be the the LORD's people. He also made a covenant between the king and the people.

Then all the people of the land went to the temple of Baal and tore it down. They smashed its altars and idols completely, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars. Then the priest posted guards over the house of the the LORD.

He took the captains, the Carites, the guards, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of the the LORD. They went through the gate of the guards to the king's palace, and he sat on the throne of the kings.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. They had killed Athaliah with the sword at the king's palace.
Joash was seven years old when he became king.
In the seventh year of Jehu, Joash became king. He ruled forty years in Jerusalem. His mother was Zibiah from Beersheba.
Joash did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD all the days that Jehoiada the priest taught him.
But the high places were not taken away. The people still offered sacrifices and burned incense on them.

Joash said to the priests, “Collect all the money that is brought as sacred gifts into the temple of the the LORD—the census money, money from vows, and any money a person feels moved to bring into the temple of the the LORD.
Let the priests take it from the people they know and use it to fix any damage found in the temple.”
But by the twenty-third year of King Joash, the priests still had not fixed the damage in the temple.

So King Joash called Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, “Why have you not fixed the damage in the temple? Now do not take any more money from your acquaintances. Give it for the repair of the temple.”
The priests agreed not to take money from the people and not to repair the temple themselves.

Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest, cut a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar on the right side as one enters the temple of the the LORD. The priests who guarded the doorway put into the chest all the money brought into the temple of the the LORD.
When they saw that a lot of money was in the chest, the king’s secretary and the high priest went up, counted the money found in the temple of the the LORD, and put it into bags.
They gave the weighed money to the men in charge of the work on the temple of the the LORD. Those men paid it to the carpenters and builders working on the temple of the the LORD.
They also paid masons and stonecutters. They bought wood and cut stone to fix the damage in the temple of the the LORD, and they paid for everything needed to repair it.
But the money brought into the temple of the the LORD was not used to make silver cups, snuffers, bowls, trumpets, or any gold or silver vessels for the temple of the the LORD.
Instead, it was given to the workmen, and they used it to repair the temple of the the LORD.
The men who received the money to pay the workers were not asked to give a detailed report, because they acted faithfully.
Money from guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the temple of the the LORD. It belonged to the priests.
At that time Hazael king of Aram went up and fought against Gath and captured it. Then he turned toward Jerusalem.

King Joash of Judah took all the sacred things his fathers—Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, kings of Judah—had dedicated. He also took his own sacred things and all the gold found in the storerooms of the temple of the the LORD and the king’s palace. He sent them to Hazael king of Aram, and Hazael turned away from Jerusalem.
The rest of the acts of Joash, and all he did, are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
His servants made a plot and struck down Joash at Beth-millo, on the road that goes down to Silla.
His servants Jozabad son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer struck him, and he died. They buried him with his fathers in the City of David, and his son Amaziah became king after him.
In the twenty-third year of Joash son of Ahaziah, king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu began to rule over Israel in Samaria. He ruled seventeen years.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD, and he followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which Jeroboam had made Israel commit. He did not turn away from them.
So the LORD's anger burned against Israel, and He kept handing them over to Hazael king of Aram and to Ben-Hadad son of Hazael all those days.
Jehoahaz begged the LORD, and the LORD listened to him, because He saw how Israel was being crushed. The king of Aram was crushing them.
The LORD gave Israel a rescuer, and they escaped from under Aram's power. The people of Israel lived in their tents again, as they had before.
But they did not leave the sins of the house of Jeroboam, which he had made Israel commit. They kept walking in those sins. The Asherah pole also stayed in Samaria.
Jehoahaz was left with no army except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Aram had destroyed the rest and crushed them like dust.
The rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, and all he did, and his strength, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Jehoahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in Samaria. His son Jehoash became king in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz began to rule over Israel in Samaria. He ruled sixteen years.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD. He did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he had made Israel commit, but he walked in them.
The rest of the acts of Jehoash, and all he did, and his strength in his war with Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
Jehoash died and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. Jeroboam took his place on the throne.

Elisha had become sick with the illness that would kill him. Jehoash king of Israel came down to him and wept over his face. He said, "My father, my father! You were Israel's true defense and strength!"
Elisha said to him, "Take a bow and arrows." So he took a bow and arrows.
Elisha said to the king of Israel, "Put your hand on the bow." He put his hand on it, and Elisha put his hands on the king's hands.

Elisha said, "Open the window eastward." He opened it. Elisha said, "Shoot!" He shot. Then Elisha said, "This is the LORD's arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram. You will strike Aram at Aphek until you destroy them."
Elisha said, "Take the arrows." He took them. Then Elisha said to the king of Israel, "Strike the ground." He struck three times and stopped.
The man of God was angry with him and said, "You should have struck five or six times. Then you would have struck Aram until you destroyed them. But now you will strike Aram only three times."
Elisha died, and they buried him. Bands of Moabites used to raid the land every spring.
As some men were burying a man, they saw a raiding band. They threw the man into Elisha's tomb. When the man touched Elisha's bones, he came back to life and stood up on his feet.
Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel all the days of Jehoahaz.

But the LORD was kind to them and had compassion on them. He turned to them because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He would not destroy them, and He had not yet driven them from His presence.
Hazael king of Aram died, and his son Ben-Hadad became king in his place.
Then Jehoash son of Jehoahaz took back from Ben-Hadad son of Hazael the cities that he had taken from Jehoahaz his father in war. Jehoash defeated him three times and restored the cities of Israel.
In the second year of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash began to reign as king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Jehoaddin, and she was from Jerusalem.
He did what pleased the LORD, but not like his ancestor David. He did everything his father Joash had done.
But he did not remove the high places. The people still sacrificed and burned incense there.
Once he had full control of the kingdom, he killed the servants who had murdered his father the king.

But he did not kill their children, because the Book of the Law of Moses says the LORD commanded, "Parents must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their parents. Each person must die for his own sin."
He also killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and captured Sela in battle. He renamed it Joktheel, and it still has that name today.
Then Amaziah sent messengers to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us meet in battle."

Jehoash king of Israel sent this reply to Amaziah king of Judah: "A thistle in Lebanon sent a message to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son in marriage.' Then a wild animal in Lebanon walked by and trampled the thistle."
"You defeated Edom, and now you are proud. Stay home and enjoy your victory. Why should you stir up trouble and bring disaster on you and Judah?"
But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel attacked, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh in Judah.
Judah was defeated by Israel, and every soldier ran home.

Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash son of Ahaziah, at Beth-shemesh. Then he went to Jerusalem and broke down its wall from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, four hundred cubits.
He took all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the LORD's temple and in the royal treasuries. He also took hostages and returned to Samaria.
The rest of the acts of Jehoash, including his power and his war with Amaziah king of Judah, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jehoash died and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. His son Jeroboam became king in his place.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Amaziah are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Some men in Jerusalem plotted against him, so he fled to Lachish. But they sent men after him to Lachish and killed him there.
They brought his body back on horses and buried him in Jerusalem with his ancestors in the City of David.
Then all the people of Judah chose Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah after Amaziah died.
In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash became king of Israel in Samaria and reigned forty-one years.
He did what the LORD considered evil. He did not turn away from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he had led Israel to commit.
He restored the border of Israel from Lebo-hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, just as the LORD, the God of Israel, had said through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.
The LORD saw how bitterly Israel was suffering. No one was left, slave or free, and there was no one to help Israel.
The LORD had not said He would wipe Israel out completely, so He saved them through Jeroboam son of Joash.
The rest of the acts of Jeroboam, all he did, his power, his wars, and how he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Israel, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam died and was buried with the kings of Israel. His son Zechariah became king in his place.
In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam, king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah became king of Judah.
He was sixteen years old when he became king, and he ruled fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jecoliah, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done.
But the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on them.
The LORD struck the king with leprosy, and he stayed a leper until the day he died. He lived in a separate house, and his son Jotham was in charge of the palace and judged the people of the land.
The rest of the acts of Azariah, and all he did, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
Azariah died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David. His son Jotham became king in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Zachariah son of Jeroboam became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled six months.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD, as his fathers had done. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which led Israel to sin.
Shallum son of Jabesh made a plot against him. He struck him down and killed him in front of the people, and then he became king in his place.
The rest of the acts of Zachariah are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
This happened just as the the LORD had told Jehu: "Your descendants will sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation." And so it was.
Shallum son of Jabesh became king in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah, king of Judah. He ruled one month in Samaria.
Then Menahem son of Gad went up from Tirzah to Samaria. He attacked Shallum son of Jabesh there, killed him, and became king in his place.
The rest of the acts of Shallum, and the plot he made, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Then Menahem attacked Tiphsah and everyone in it and its territory. Because they would not open the gates, he destroyed the city and tore open all the pregnant women.
In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Menahem son of Gad became king of Israel. He ruled ten years in Samaria.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD. All his days, he did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which led Israel to sin.
Pul, king of Assyria, came against the land. Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver so that Pul would support him and help him keep the kingdom.

Menahem collected the money from all the wealthy men of Israel. He took fifty shekels of silver from each man and gave it to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay in the land.
The rest of the acts of Menahem, and all he did, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
Menahem died, and his son Pekahiah became king in his place.
In the fiftieth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled two years.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which led Israel to sin.

Pekah son of Remaliah, his officer, made a plot against him. With Argob and Arieh, and fifty men from Gilead, he struck him down in the king's palace in Samaria and killed him. Then he became king in his place.
The rest of the acts of Pekahiah, and all he did, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
In the fifty-second year of Azariah, king of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled twenty years.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which led Israel to sin.

In the days of Pekah, king of Israel, Tiglath-Pileser, king of Assyria, came and took Ijon, Abel Beth Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and all the land of Naphtali. He carried the people away to Assyria.
Hoshea son of Elah made a plot against Pekah son of Remaliah. He struck him down and killed him, and became king in his place. This was in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah.
The rest of the acts of Pekah, and all he did, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel.
In the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jerusha, the daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done.
But the high places were not taken away. The people still sacrificed and burned incense on them. He built the Upper Gate of the house of the the LORD.
The rest of the acts of Jotham, and all he did, are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
In those days the the LORD began to send Rezin, king of Aram, and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.
Jotham died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David, his father's city. His son Ahaz became king in his place.
In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham became king of Judah.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even sacrificed his son in the fire. He followed the terrible practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.
He offered sacrifices and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.
Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel marched up to fight against Jerusalem. They besieged Ahaz, but they could not overpower him.
At that time Rezin king of Aram recovered Elath for Aram. He drove the people of Judah out of Elath, and the Arameans came and settled there. They are still there today.
Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria with this message: "I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me from the king of Aram and the king of Israel, who are attacking me."
Ahaz took the silver and gold found in the temple of the LORD and in the royal treasuries and sent it as a gift to the king of Assyria.
The king of Assyria listened to him. He marched against Damascus, captured it, and took its people to Kir as captives. He also put Rezin to death.

King Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria. There he saw the altar. King Ahaz sent Uriah the priest a model of the altar and a plan for building it, with every detail of its design.
Uriah the priest built the altar. He followed all the instructions King Ahaz had sent from Damascus. Uriah finished it before King Ahaz returned.
When the king returned from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and offered sacrifices on it.
He burned his burnt offering and grain offering on it. He poured out his drink offering and sprinkled the blood of his peace offerings on the altar.
He also moved the bronze altar that stood before the LORD. It had been in front of the temple, between the new altar and the the LORD's temple. He placed it on the north side of the new altar.

King Ahaz gave orders to Uriah the priest: "On the large altar burn the morning burnt offering and the evening burnt offering, the king's grain offering and his burnt offering, and the grain offering and burnt offering of all the people of the land. Also pour their drink offerings on it. Sprinkle on it all the blood of the burnt offerings and sacrifices. But the bronze altar will be for me to use for seeking guidance."
Uriah the priest did everything King Ahaz commanded.
King Ahaz cut off the panels from the movable stands and removed the basins from them. He also took down the Sea from the bronze oxen that supported it and set it on a stone pavement.
He also removed the covered walkway used on the Sabbath and the king's outer entrance that had been built at the temple of the LORD. He did this because of the king of Assyria.
The rest of the acts of Ahaz, and everything he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah?
Ahaz died and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David. His son Hezekiah became king in his place.
In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah became king of Israel in Samaria. He ruled for nine years.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD, but not like the kings of Israel who had ruled before him.
Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked him. Hoshea became his servant and paid him tribute.

But the king of Assyria found out that Hoshea was plotting against him. Hoshea had sent messengers to So king of Egypt, and he had not sent the yearly tribute to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria arrested Hoshea and put him in prison.
Then the king of Assyria marched through the whole land. He came to Samaria and surrounded it for three years.
In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria captured Samaria. He carried the Israelites away to Assyria and settled them in Halah, Gozan, the Habor River, and the cities of Media.
This happened because the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God. He had brought them up out of Egypt, away from Pharaoh king of Egypt. But they worshiped other gods.
They followed the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out ahead of the Israelites. They also followed customs that the kings of Israel had made.
The Israelites secretly did things that were not right against the LORD their God. They built high places in all their cities, from small guard towers to fortified cities.
They set up sacred stone pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every green tree.
They burned incense on all the high places, just as the nations had done that the LORD drove out ahead of them. They did evil things that made the LORD angry.
They worshiped idols, even though the LORD had told them not to do that.

The LORD warned Israel and Judah through all His prophets and seers. He said, "Turn from your evil ways. Keep My commands and rules. Follow all the Law I gave your ancestors. I sent it to you through My servants the prophets."
But they would not listen. They were stubborn, just like their ancestors, who did not trust the LORD their God.

They rejected His rules and the agreement He made with their ancestors. They rejected the warnings He gave them. They followed worthless idols and became worthless themselves. They copied the nations around them, even though the LORD had told them not to act like those nations.
They ignored all the commands of the LORD their God. They made two metal calves for themselves. They made an Asherah pole. They bowed down to all the stars in the sky. They served Baal.
They sacrificed their sons and daughters in fire. They practiced fortune-telling and sorcery. They gave themselves up to doing evil in the LORD’s eyes, and they made Him angry.
So the LORD was very angry with Israel. He removed them from His presence. Only the tribe of Judah was left.
But even Judah did not keep the the LORD’s commands. They followed the customs that Israel had made.
So the LORD rejected all the people of Israel. He punished them and handed them over to raiders, until He had thrown them out of His presence.
When the LORD tore Israel away from David’s family, the people made Jeroboam son of Nebat king. Jeroboam led Israel away from following the LORD. He caused them to commit a terrible sin.
The Israelites followed all the sins Jeroboam had done. They did not stop.

Finally the LORD removed Israel from His presence, just as He had said through all His servants the prophets. He carried the Israelites away from their own land to Assyria, where they are to this day.

The king of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim. He settled them in the cities of Samaria in place of the Israelites. They took over Samaria and lived in its cities.
At first, when they lived there, they did not worship the LORD. So the LORD sent lions among them, and the lions killed some of them.

They told the king of Assyria, "The nations you moved and settled in the cities of Samaria do not know the law of the God of this land. So He has sent lions among them. The lions are killing them, because they do not know the law of the God of this land."
The king of Assyria ordered, "Send one of the priests you took from there. Let him go live there and teach them the law of the God of this land."
So one of the priests who had been carried away from Samaria came and lived in Bethel. He taught them how to worship the LORD.
But each nation made its own gods. They put them in the high places the people of Samaria had built. Each nation did this in the cities where it lived.
The men of Babylon made Succoth Benoth. The men of Cuth made Nergal. The men of Hamath made Ashima.
The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak. The Sepharvites burned their children in fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.
They worshiped the LORD, but they also chose priests from among themselves for the high places. These priests sacrificed for them in the houses of the high places.
They worshiped the LORD, but they also served their own gods, following the customs of the nations they had come from.
Even today they still follow their old customs. They do not worship the LORD. They do not follow the rules, laws, or commands that the LORD gave the descendants of Jacob. He named them Israel.
The LORD had made an agreement with them. He commanded them, "Do not worship other gods. Do not bow down to them. Do not serve them. Do not sacrifice to them.
The LORD is the One who brought you up from Egypt with great power and a strong arm. Worship Him. Bow down to Him. Sacrifice to Him.
Keep the rules, laws, and commands He wrote for you. You must always do them. Do not worship other gods.
Do not forget the agreement I made with you. Do not worship other gods.
Instead, worship the the LORD your God. He will save you from all your enemies."
But they did not listen. They kept following their old ways.
So these nations worshiped the LORD, but they also served their idols. Their children and grandchildren did the same thing their ancestors did, and they still do it today.
In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz became king of Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as King David had done.

He removed the high places, smashed the stone pillars, and cut down the Asherah poles. He broke the bronze snake Moses had made into pieces, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it. People called it Nehushtan.
Hezekiah trusted in the LORD, the God of Israel. No king of Judah before or after him was like him.
He held tightly to the LORD and did not turn away from Him. He kept the commands the LORD had given through Moses.
The LORD was with him, and he succeeded in everything he did. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him.
He defeated the Philistines all the way to Gaza and the land around it, from watchtower to fortified city.
In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria attacked Samaria and surrounded it.
After three years they captured it. In the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria was taken.
The king of Assyria carried the people of Israel away to Assyria and settled them in Halah, in Gozan on the Habor River, and in the towns of the Medes.
This happened because they did not obey the LORD their God. They broke His covenant and did not do everything Moses, the servant of the LORD, had commanded. They did not listen or obey.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria attacked all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them.

So Hezekiah king of Judah sent a message to the king of Assyria at Lachish. He said, "I have done wrong. Withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand." The king of Assyria demanded three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold from Hezekiah king of Judah.
Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in the temple of the LORD and in the king's storehouses.
At that time Hezekiah king of Judah stripped the gold from the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD, which he had covered with gold, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

The king of Assyria sent his top commander, his chief officer, and his field commander with a large army from Lachish to King Hezekiah in Jerusalem. They marched up to Jerusalem and stopped at the water channel of the Upper Pool, on the road to the Washerman's Field.
They called for the king. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went out to meet them.
The field commander said to them, "Tell Hezekiah: 'This is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What gives you this confidence?
You think you have plans and strength for war, but you are only relying on empty words. Who are you depending on, that you rebel against me?
Look, you are depending on Egypt, that broken reed of a staff. It will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it. That is what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who depend on him.

But if you say to me, 'We are depending on the LORD our God,' isn't this the God whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed? Didn't Hezekiah tell Judah and Jerusalem, 'You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem'?
Come now, make a deal with my master, the king of Assyria. I will give you two thousand horses, if you can put riders on them!
How then can you push back one officer of the least of my master's officials, even though you are depending on Egypt for chariots and horses?
Besides, do you think I came to attack and destroy this place without the LORD's permission? The LORD Himself told me to march against this country and destroy it.'"

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah said to the field commander, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak to us in Hebrew where the people on the wall can hear."

But the commander replied, "Did my master send me to say these things only to your master and you? Didn't he also send me to the people sitting on the wall? They, like you, will have to eat their own waste and drink their own urine."
Then the commander stood and called out in a loud voice in Hebrew, "Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!
The king says: Do not let Hezekiah trick you. He cannot rescue you from my hand.
Do not let Hezekiah talk you into trusting the LORD when he says, 'The LORD will surely save us; this city will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.'
Do not listen to Hezekiah. This is what the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and come out to me. Then each of you will eat from your own vine and fig tree and drink water from your own well.

I will come and take you to a land like your own—a land of grain and new wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land of olive oil and honey. Live, and do not die! Do not listen to Hezekiah, for he is misleading you when he says, 'The LORD will rescue us.'
Did the god of any nation save his land from the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did any of them save Samaria from my hand?
Which of all the gods of these lands has saved his land from me? How then can the LORD save Jerusalem from my hand?"
But the people stayed silent and said nothing, because the king had commanded, "Do not answer him."

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and told him everything the field commander had said.
When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into the house of the LORD.
He sent Eliakim, who was in charge of the palace, Shebna the secretary, and the older priests, all wearing sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz.
They said to him, "This is what Hezekiah says: Today is a day of trouble, rebuke, and disgrace. Children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to deliver them.

Maybe the LORD your God will hear all the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria sent to insult the living God, and will correct him for the words the LORD your God has heard. So pray for the remnant that is left."
So the servants of King Hezekiah went to Isaiah.
Isaiah said to them, "Tell your master, 'This is what the LORD says: Do not be afraid of the words you have heard, the words the servants of the king of Assyria have used to insult Me.'
Look, I will put a spirit in him. He will hear a report and go back to his own country. There I will make him fall by the sword."
When the Rabshakeh heard that the king of Assyria had left Lachish, he went back and found the king fighting against Libnah.
The king of Assyria heard that Tirhakah, king of Cush, had come out to fight against him. So he sent messengers to Hezekiah again and said, "
Say to Hezekiah king of Judah: Do not let your God, whom you trust, fool you by saying, 'Jerusalem will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.'
Look, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the other lands. They destroyed them completely. Do you think you will be rescued? "
Did the gods of the nations my fathers destroyed save them—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar?
Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?"
Hezekiah took the letters from the messengers and read them. Then he went up to the house of the LORD and spread them out before the LORD.
Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: "The LORD, God of Israel, who sits enthroned between the cherubim, You alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth. You made heaven and earth.
The LORD, turn Your ear to me and hear. The LORD, open Your eyes and see. Listen to the words Sennacherib has sent to insult the living God. "
It is true, the LORD, that the kings of Assyria have destroyed the nations and their lands.
They have thrown their gods into the fire and destroyed them, because they were not gods at all. They were only wood and stone, made by human hands.
Now, the LORD our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that You alone, the LORD, are God."
Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent a message to Hezekiah: "This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: I have heard your prayer about Sennacherib king of Assyria. "
This is the word the LORD has spoken against him: 'Virgin Daughter Zion despises you and mocks you; Daughter Jerusalem shakes her head at you.' "
Whom have you insulted and spoken against? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes in pride? Against the Holy One of Israel! "

By your messengers you have insulted the Lord. You said, 'With my many chariots I have climbed to the tops of the mountains, to the farthest parts of Lebanon. I cut down its tallest cedars and its best cypresses. I reached its farthest shelter, its thickest forest.'
'I have dug wells and drunk foreign water. With the soles of my feet I have dried up all the streams of Egypt.' "
Have you not heard? Long ago I planned this; in ancient times I set it in motion. Now I have brought it to pass, so that you could turn fortified cities into piles of rubble.
Their people were weak and afraid. They were like grass in a field, like tender green shoots, like grass on a roof, burned before it grows. "
But I know when you sit and when you go out and come in. I know how you rage against Me.
Because you rage against Me and your pride has reached My ears, I will put My hook in your nose and My bit in your mouth. I will make you go back the way you came. "

This will be a sign for you: This year you will eat what grows by itself. Next year you will eat what grows from that. But in the third year you will plant and harvest, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.
The remnant of Judah that survives will take root below and bear fruit above.
From Jerusalem a remnant will go out, and from Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD will do this. "
So this is what the LORD says about the king of Assyria: He will not enter this city. He will not shoot an arrow here. He will not come against it with a shield or build a siege ramp.
He will go back the way he came. He will not enter this city, declares the LORD.
I will defend this city and save it for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David."
That night the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the Assyrian camp. In the morning, when the people got up, they saw all the dead bodies.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and went home. He returned to Nineveh and stayed there.

One day, while he was worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch, his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer killed him with the sword. Then they escaped to the land of Ararat, and his son Esarhaddon became king after him.

In those days Hezekiah became so sick that he was going to die. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, "This is what the LORD says: Put your house in order, because you are going to die. You will not live."
Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD:
"Please, the LORD, remember how I have walked before you in truth and with a whole heart. I have done what is good in your sight." Then Hezekiah cried and wept bitterly.
Before Isaiah had left the middle courtyard, the word of the LORD came to him.

The LORD said, "Go back and tell Hezekiah, the ruler of My people: This is what the LORD, the God of your father David, says: I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears. Look, I will heal you. On the third day you will go up to the house of the LORD.
I will add fifteen years to your life. I will rescue you and this city from the power of the king of Assyria. I will defend this city for My own sake and for the sake of My servant David."
Then Isaiah said, "Bring a fig cake." They brought it and put it on the sore, and he recovered.
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "What sign will show that the LORD will heal me and that I will go up to the house of the LORD on the third day?"
Isaiah said, "This is the sign to you from the LORD that the LORD will do what He has promised: Will the shadow go forward ten steps, or go back ten steps?"
Hezekiah answered, "It would be easy for the shadow to go forward ten steps. No, let it go back ten steps."
Then Isaiah the prophet cried out to the LORD, and He made the shadow go back the ten steps it had gone down on the stairway of Ahaz.
At that time Merodach-Baladan son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, because he had heard that Hezekiah was sick.

Hezekiah welcomed the messengers and showed them all his treasure house—the silver, the gold, the spices, and the fine oil—his armory, and everything in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his kingdom that Hezekiah did not show them.
Then Isaiah the prophet went to King Hezekiah and asked, "What did these men say, and where did they come from?" Hezekiah replied, "They came from a distant land, from Babylon."
Isaiah asked, "What did they see in your palace?" Hezekiah answered, "They saw everything in my palace. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD:
The time will surely come when everything in your palace, and all that your fathers have stored up until this day, will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left," says the LORD.
"And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."
Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "Will there not be peace and security during my lifetime?"
The rest of Hezekiah's acts, along with all his might and how he made the pool and the tunnel and brought water into the city, are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
Hezekiah died and was buried with his ancestors, and his son Manasseh became king in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Hephzibah.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, like the hateful practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before the people of Israel.

He rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had destroyed. He set up altars for Baal, made an Asherah pole, as Ahab king of Israel had done, and bowed down to worship them. He also worshiped all the stars in the sky.
He built altars in the house of the LORD, the very place where the LORD had said, "I will put My name."
He built altars for all the stars in the sky in the two courtyards of the LORD's house.
He even sacrificed his son in the fire. He practiced sorcery and fortune-telling, and he consulted mediums and spiritists. He did more and more evil in the sight of the LORD, making Him angry.

He carved an Asherah image and put it in the temple. The LORD had told David and his son Solomon, "In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose from all the tribes of Israel, I will put My name forever."

The LORD had also said, "I will not make the feet of Israel wander from the land I gave their fathers, if they are careful to do everything I commanded them and follow all the law My servant Moses gave them."
But they did not listen. Manasseh led them to do more evil than the nations the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke through His servants the prophets. He said,
"Because Manasseh, king of Judah, has done these hateful things—more evil than the Amorites before him—and has made Judah sin with his idols,
I, the LORD, the God of Israel, say this: I am bringing such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that everyone who hears about it will be stunned.
I will stretch over Jerusalem the same measuring line I used on Samaria and the same plumb line I used on Ahab's family. I will wipe Jerusalem clean like a dish—wipe it and turn it upside down.
I will abandon the rest of My people, whom I claimed as My own, and hand them over to their enemies. They will be robbed and plundered by all their enemies.
This is because they have done evil in My eyes and have made Me angry from the day their fathers came out of Egypt until today."
Manasseh also spilled a great deal of innocent blood. He filled Jerusalem from one end to the other with it. This was besides the sin he caused Judah to commit by doing evil in the sight of the LORD.
The rest of Manasseh's acts, everything he did, and the sin he committed are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
Manasseh died and was buried with his fathers in the garden of his house, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned two years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah.
He did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, just as his father Manasseh had done.
He walked in all the ways his father had walked. He served the idols his father had served and worshiped them.
He abandoned the LORD, the God of his fathers, and did not walk in the way of the LORD.
Amon's servants plotted against him and killed the king in his own house.
Then the people of the land struck down everyone who had plotted against King Amon, and they made his son Josiah king in his place.
The rest of Amon's acts are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah.
He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah became king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. His mother was Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah from Bozkath.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD. He followed the way of his father David in everything. He did not turn to the right or to the left.
In the eighteenth year of King Josiah's rule, the king sent Shaphan son of Azaliah son of Meshullam, the secretary, to the the LORD's temple. He said,
"Go to Hilkiah the high priest and have him count the money that has been brought into the the LORD's temple. The doorkeepers collected it from the people.
Give it to the men in charge of the work on the the LORD's temple. They will pay the workers who are repairing the temple.
Give it to the carpenters, builders, and masons. Also use it to buy wood and cut stone to repair the temple.
Do not ask them to report on the money they receive, because they work faithfully."
Hilkiah the high priest said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the the LORD's temple." Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and Shaphan read it.
Then Shaphan the secretary went to the king and reported, "Your servants have emptied out the money found in the temple. They have given it to the men in charge of the work at the the LORD's temple."
Shaphan the secretary also told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." Then Shaphan read it to the king.
When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes.
The king commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant. He said,

"Go and ask the the LORD for me, for the people, and for all Judah. Ask about the words of this book that was found. The the LORD's anger is burning against us because our ancestors did not obey the words of this book. They did not do everything written for us."

So Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to Huldah the prophetess. She was the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, who kept the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem in the second district. They spoke to her.
She said to them, "This is what the the LORD, the God of Israel, says: 'Tell the man who sent you to Me,
the the LORD says He is going to bring disaster on this place and on its people. It will be everything written in the book that the king of Judah has read.
They have left Me and burned incense to other gods. They have made Me angry with everything they have made. So My anger will burn against this place and will not be put out.'
But tell the king of Judah who sent you to ask the the LORD, 'This is what the the LORD, the God of Israel, says: You have heard these words.

Because your heart was soft and you humbled yourself before the the LORD when you heard what I said against this place and its people, that it would become a ruin and a curse, you tore your clothes and wept before Me. I have heard you, says the the LORD.
So I will let you join your ancestors in peace. You will be buried in peace. Your eyes will not see all the trouble I am bringing on this place.'" Then they brought her answer back to the king.
Then the king sent for them, and they gathered all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem to him.

The king went up to the house of the LORD, along with all the men of Judah, all the people of Jerusalem, the priests, and the prophets—everyone, from the least to the greatest. He read to them, in their hearing, all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD.

The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant before the LORD. He promised to follow the LORD and to keep His commandments, rules, and laws with all his heart and all his soul. He also promised to carry out the words of this covenant written in this book. All the people agreed to the covenant.

Then the king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests of the second rank, and the doorkeepers to bring out of the LORD's temple all the items made for Baal, Asherah, and all the stars of heaven. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of Kidron and took their ashes to Bethel.

He also got rid of the pagan priests the kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense on the high places in Judah's cities and around Jerusalem. These priests had burned incense to Baal, the sun, the moon, the constellations, and all the stars of heaven.
He brought the Asherah pole out of the house of the LORD to the Kidron Valley outside Jerusalem. There he burned it, ground it to powder, and threw the dust on the graves of the common people.
He tore down the rooms of the male cult prostitutes that were in the house of the LORD, where women wove hangings for Asherah.

He brought all the priests from the cities of Judah and made the high places unclean, from Geba to Beersheba, where the priests had burned incense. He also tore down the high places by the gates, including the high place at the entrance of the gate of Joshua, the city official, which was on the left side of the city gate.
The priests of the high places did not serve at the LORD's altar in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread with their fellow priests.
He made Topheth, in the Valley of Ben Hinnom, unclean so no one could make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech.

He removed from the entrance to the house of the LORD the horses the kings of Judah had given to the sun. They were in the courtyard near the room of Nathan-melech, an official. Josiah burned the chariots of the sun.

He tore down the altars the kings of Judah had built on the roof of Ahaz's upper room, and the altars Manasseh had built in the two courtyards of the house of the LORD. He took them away, carried their ashes, and threw them into the Kidron Valley.

The king made unclean the high places east of Jerusalem, south of the Mount of Corruption. Solomon, king of Israel, had built them for Ashtoreth, the hated god of the Sidonians; Chemosh, the hated god of Moab; and Milcom, the hated god of the Ammonites.
He smashed the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled their places with human bones.
He even tore down the altar at Bethel, the high place made by Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led Israel into sin. He burned that high place, ground it to powder, and burned the Asherah pole.

As Josiah turned, he saw the tombs on the hillside. He sent for the bones in the tombs and burned them on the altar to make it unclean. This happened as the LORD had said through the man of God who predicted these things.
Then he asked, "What is that monument I see?" The men of the city answered, "It is the tomb of the man of God who came from Judah and announced these things you have done to the altar at Bethel."
"Leave it alone," he said. "Let no one move his bones." So they left his bones alone, along with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria.
Josiah also removed all the shrines of the high places in the cities of Samaria. The kings of Israel had built them to make the LORD angry. He treated them the same way he had treated Bethel.
On the altars he killed all the priests of the high places and burned human bones on them. Then he returned to Jerusalem.
Then the king commanded all the people, "Celebrate the Passover to the LORD your God, as it is written in this Book of the Covenant."
No Passover like this had been celebrated since the days of the judges who led Israel, or during the days of the kings of Israel and Judah.
But in the eighteenth year of King Josiah's reign, this Passover was celebrated to the LORD in Jerusalem.

Josiah also got rid of the mediums, spiritists, household gods, idols, and all the other disgusting things seen in Judah and Jerusalem. He did this to carry out the words of the law written in the book Hilkiah the priest had found in the house of the LORD.
No king before or after Josiah was like him. He turned to the LORD with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength, following all the Law of Moses.
Still, the LORD did not turn from His great anger. His anger burned against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke Him.
The LORD said, "I will remove Judah from My sight, just as I removed Israel. I will reject this city, Jerusalem, which I chose, and the house where I said, 'My name will be there.'"
The rest of Josiah's acts and all he did are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.
In Josiah's days, Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, marched against the king of Assyria at the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to meet him, but Neco killed him at Megiddo as soon as he saw him.

Josiah's servants carried his body in a chariot from Megiddo, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in his father's place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for three months. His mother was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah; she was from Libnah.
He did evil in the eyes of the LORD, just as his fathers had done.
Pharaoh Neco put him in prison at Riblah in the land of Hamath, so he could not rule in Jerusalem. He also forced the land to pay a tax of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.
Pharaoh Neco made Eliakim son of Josiah king in place of his father Josiah. He changed Eliakim's name to Jehoiakim. He took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died.
