Four thousand were gatekeepers, and 4,000 praised the the LORD with the instruments David had made for praising Him.
David divided them into groups for the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
The sons of Gershon were Ladan and Shimei.
The sons of Ladan were Jehiel, the leader, Zetham, and Joel—three in all.
The sons of Shimei were Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran—three in all. These were the leaders of Ladan’s families.
The sons of Shimei were Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These four were Shimei’s sons.
Jahath was the leader, and Zizah was second. Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, so they were counted as one family.
The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel—four in all.
The sons of Amram were Aaron and Moses. Aaron was set apart to care for the most holy things. He and his sons were to burn incense before the the LORD, serve Him, and bless in His name forever.
As for Moses, the man of God, his sons were counted with the tribe of Levi.
Moses’ sons were Gershom and Eliezer.
Gershom’s son was Shebuel, the leader.
Eliezer’s son was Rehabiah, the leader. Eliezer had no other sons, but Rehabiah’s sons were very many.
Izhar’s son was Shelomith, the leader.
Hebron’s sons were Jeriah the leader, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.
Uzziel’s sons were Micah the leader and Isshiah the second.
The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi. Mahli’s sons were Eleazar and Kish.
Eleazar died with no sons, only daughters. Their relatives, the sons of Kish, married them.
Mushi’s sons were Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth—three in all.
These were Levi’s sons by family, the leaders of families. They were counted by name, head by head, twenty years old and older, and they did the work for service in the the LORD’s temple.
David said, “The The LORD, the God of Israel, has given rest to His people and has come to live in Jerusalem forever.”
So the Levites no longer had to carry the tabernacle or any of its equipment for its service.
By David’s last words, the Levites twenty years old and older were counted.
Their place was beside the sons of Aaron to serve in the the LORD’s temple: caring for the courtyards and rooms, keeping all holy things clean, and doing the work of serving God’s house.
They were also in charge of the bread on the table, the fine flour for grain offerings, the unleavened wafers, the baking pan, the mixed flour, and every measure and amount.
They stood every morning to thank and praise the the LORD, and they did the same every evening.
They also offered all the burnt offerings to the the LORD on the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the special feasts, in the right numbers, always before the the LORD.
They guarded the tent of meeting, the holy place, and their relatives, the sons of Aaron, as they served in the the LORD’s temple.
These were the divisions of Aaron's descendants. Aaron's sons were Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.
But Nadab and Abihu died before their father, and they had no sons. So Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests.
David, along with Zadok from Eleazar's descendants and Ahimelech from Ithamar's descendants, divided them by their duties in service.
More family leaders were found among Eleazar's descendants than among Ithamar's. They were divided into sixteen heads of family lines for Eleazar's family and eight for Ithamar's family.
They divided them by drawing lots, mixing both groups together, because both groups had officers of the sanctuary and officers of God.

Shemaiah son of Nethanel, a Levite scribe, wrote them down before the king, the officials, Zadok the priest, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of the family lines of the priests and Levites. One family line was taken for Eleazar, and one for Ithamar.
The first lot fell to Jehoiarib, and the second to Jedaiah.
The third fell to Harim, and the fourth to Seorim.
The fifth fell to Malchijah, and the sixth to Mijamin.
The seventh fell to Hakkoz, and the eighth to Abijah.
The ninth fell to Jeshua, and the tenth to Shecaniah.
The eleventh fell to Eliashib, and the twelfth to Jakim.
The thirteenth fell to Huppah, and the fourteenth to Jeshebeab.
The fifteenth fell to Bilgah, and the sixteenth to Immer.
The seventeenth fell to Hezir, and the eighteenth to Happizzez.
The nineteenth fell to Pethahiah, and the twentieth to Jehezkel.
The twenty-first fell to Jachin, and the twenty-second to Gamul.
The twenty-third fell to Delaiah, and the twenty-fourth to Maaziah.
These were their duties for service: to come into the house of the the LORD according to the rules given by their ancestor Aaron, as the the LORD God of Israel had commanded him.
For the rest of Levi's descendants: from Amram's descendants came Shubael; from Shubael's descendants came Jehdeiah.
For Rehabiah's line, the leader among his sons was Isshiah.
For the Izharites: Shelomoth; for Shelomoth's descendants: Jahath.
For Hebron's descendants: Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.
For Uzziel's descendants: Micah; for Micah's descendants: Shamir.
Micah's brother was Isshiah; for Isshiah's descendants: Zechariah.
For Merari's descendants: Mahli and Mushi. For Jaaziah's descendants: Beno.
For Merari's descendants through Jaaziah: Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri.
Mahli's son was Eleazar, who had no sons.
For Mushi's descendants: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the Levites listed by their family lines.

They also cast lots, just as their relatives, Aaron's descendants, had done. They did this before King David, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the family lines of the priests and Levites. The families of the oldest brother were treated the same as those of the youngest.

David and the army leaders set apart for service the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. These men prophesied with lyres, harps, and cymbals. This was the number of men who did the work for their service.
The sons of Asaph were Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asarelah. They served under Asaph, who prophesied under the king's direction.

The sons of Jeduthun were Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, and Mattithiah—six in all. They served under their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre. He gave thanks and praise to the the LORD.
The sons of Heman were Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamti-Ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth.
All these were the sons of Heman, the king's seer in the words of God. They were to show God's power. God gave Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.

All these served under their fathers in the house of the the LORD. They played cymbals, harps, and lyres for the service of God's house. They served under Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, at the king's direction.
With their brothers, all of them were skilled in singing to the the LORD. There were 288 of them.
They cast lots for their duties. The small and the great were treated the same, and the teacher served along with the student.
The first lot was for Asaph and fell to Joseph.
The second lot was for Gedaliah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The third lot was for Zaccur, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The fourth lot was for Izri, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The fifth lot was for Nethaniah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The sixth lot was for Bukkiah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The seventh lot was for Jesarelah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The eighth lot was for Jeshaiah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The ninth lot was for Mattaniah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The tenth lot was for Shimei, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The eleventh lot was for Azarel, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The twelfth lot was for Hashabiah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The thirteenth lot was for Shubael, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The fourteenth lot was for Mattithiah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The fifteenth lot was for Jeremoth, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The sixteenth lot was for Hananiah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The seventeenth lot was for Joshbekashah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The eighteenth lot was for Hanani, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The nineteenth lot was for Mallothi, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The twentieth lot was for Eliathah, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The twenty-first lot was for Hothir, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The twenty-second lot was for Giddalti, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The twenty-third lot was for Mahazioth, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
The twenty-fourth lot was for Romamti-Ezer, with his sons and brothers—twelve.
These were the groups of gatekeepers. From the Korahites: Meshelemiah son of Kore, one of the sons of Asaph.
Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, and Jathniel the fourth.
Elam was the fifth, Johanan the sixth, and Elioenai the seventh.
The sons of Obed-edom were Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth,
Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, and Peulthai the eighth. For God had blessed Obed-edom.
Shemaiah, Obed-edom’s son, also had sons who led their father’s family, because they were men of great ability.
Shemaiah’s sons were Othni, Rephael, Obed, and Elzabad. His brothers Elihu and Semachiah were also men of great ability.
All these men came from Obed-edom. They, their sons, and their brothers were strong men, able to do the work—62 in all from Obed-edom.
Meshelemiah also had sons and brothers who were capable men—18 in all.
Hosah, a Merarite, also had sons: Shimri the first. Although he was not the firstborn, his father made him the leader.
Hilkiah was the second, Tebaliah the third, and Zechariah the fourth. Hosah had 13 sons and brothers in all.
These groups of gatekeepers, through their chief men, served in the house of the LORD, just as their relatives did.
They cast lots for each gate, by families, for both young and old.
The lot for the east gate fell to Shelemiah. Then they cast lots for his son Zechariah, a wise counselor, and his lot came out for the north gate.
The lot for the south gate fell to Obed-edom, and the lot for the storehouses fell to his sons.
The lot for the west gate and the Shalleketh Gate on the road going up fell to Shuppim and Hosah. Guards were stationed at every watch.
On the east there were six Levites each day, on the north four each day, on the south four each day, and at the storehouses two pairs.
At the Parbar on the west there were four at the road and two at the Parbar.
These were the groups of gatekeepers from the sons of Korah and Merari.
Their fellow Levites were in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries of the dedicated things.
Jehieli came from the family of Ladan, a Gershonite, and was head of that family.
Jehieli’s sons were Zetham and his brother Joel. They were in charge of the treasuries of the house of the LORD.
From the Amramites, Izharites, Hebronites, and Uzzielites:
Shebuel son of Gershom, son of Moses, was the officer in charge of the treasuries.
His relatives through Eliezer were Rehabiah his son, Jeshaiah his son, Joram his son, Zichri his son, and Shelomith his son.

This Shelomith and his brothers were in charge of all the treasuries of the dedicated things that King David, the heads of families, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and the other army commanders had dedicated.
They had dedicated some of the plunder from their battles to repair the house of the LORD.
Everything that Samuel the seer, Saul son of Kish, Abner son of Ner, and Joab son of Zeruiah had dedicated—everything anyone had dedicated—was under the care of Shelomith and his brothers.
From the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were assigned to outside duties as officers and judges over Israel.
From the Hebronites, Hashabiah and his relatives—1,700 capable men—were put in charge of Israel’s affairs west of the Jordan. They handled all the work of the LORD and the service of the king.

As for the Hebronites, Jerijah was the chief according to the family records. In the fortieth year of David’s reign, a search was made, and men of great ability were found among them at Jazer in Gilead.

Jerijah had 2,700 relatives who were capable men and heads of families. King David appointed them to oversee the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh for all the matters of God and of the king.

The Israelites were listed by number: family leaders, commanders of thousands and hundreds, and officers who served the king in every matter of the divisions. These divisions came and went month by month through the year, and each one had 24,000 men.
Jashobeam son of Zabdiel was in charge of the first division for the first month, and his division had 24,000 men.
He was from the family of Perez and was chief of all the army captains for the first month.
Dodai the Ahohite was in charge of the division for the second month, and Mikloth was its leader. That division had 24,000 men.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest was commander for the third month. He was a chief leader, and his division had 24,000 men.
This Benaiah was one of the Thirty mighty men and was their leader. His son Ammizabad was in charge of his division.
Asahel, Joab's brother, was commander for the fourth month, and his son Zebadiah followed him. His division had 24,000 men.
Shamhuth the Izrahite was commander for the fifth month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Ira son of Ikkesh the Tekoite was commander for the sixth month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Helez the Pelonite, from the family of Ephraim, was commander for the seventh month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Sibbecai the Hushathite, a Zerahite, was commander for the eighth month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Abiezer the Anathothite, a Benjamite, was commander for the ninth month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Maharai the Netophathite, a Zerahite, was commander for the tenth month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Benaiah the Pirathonite, from the family of Ephraim, was commander for the eleventh month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Heldai the Netophathite, from Othniel's family, was commander for the twelfth month, and his division had 24,000 men.
Over Israel's tribes: Eliezer son of Zichri was leader of the Reubenites, and Shephatiah son of Maacah was leader of the Simeonites.
Hashabiah son of Kemuel was leader of the Levites, and Zadok was leader of Aaron's line.
Elihu, one of David's brothers, was leader of Judah, and Omri son of Michael was leader of Issachar.
Ishmaiah son of Obadiah was leader of Zebulun, and Jerimoth son of Azriel was leader of Naphtali.
Hoshea son of Azaziah was leader of the sons of Ephraim, and Joel son of Pedaiah was leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh.
Iddo son of Zechariah was leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, and Jaasiel son of Abner was leader of Benjamin.
Azarel son of Jeroham was leader of Dan. These were the leaders of Israel's tribes.
David did not count those younger than twenty years old, because the LORD had promised to make Israel as numerous as the stars in the sky.
Joab son of Zeruiah started the census, but he did not finish, because this brought wrath on Israel. The total was not recorded in the official records of King David.
Azmaveth son of Adiel was in charge of the king's treasuries. Jonathan son of Uzziah was in charge of the storehouses in the fields, cities, villages, and towers.
Ezri son of Chelub was in charge of the field workers who farmed the land.
Shimei the Ramathite was in charge of the vineyards. Zabdi the Shiphmite was in charge of the vineyard produce for the wine cellars.
Baal-hanan the Gederite was in charge of the olive and sycamore trees in the lowlands. Joash was in charge of the oil stores.
Shitrai the Sharonite was in charge of the herds grazing in Sharon. Shaphat son of Adlai was in charge of the herds in the valleys.
Obil the Ishmaelite was in charge of the camels. Jehdeiah the Meronothite was in charge of the donkeys.
Jaziz the Hagrite was in charge of the flocks. All these men were officials over King David's property.
Jonathan, David's uncle, was an advisor, a man of understanding, and a scribe. Jehiel son of Hachmoni was with the king's sons.
Ahithophel was the king's counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king's friend.
After Ahithophel came Jehoiada son of Benaiah, and then Abiathar. Joab was commander of the king's army.

David assembled all the leaders of Israel in Jerusalem: the leaders of the tribes, the leaders of the divisions that served the king, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, the officials in charge of all the king's property and livestock, the palace officials, the warriors, and all the brave fighting men.

David stood up and said, "Listen to me, my brothers and my people. I had it in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of the LORD and for the footstool of our God, and I made plans to build it.
But God told me that I was not to build a house for His name, because I was a man of war who had shed blood.

"The LORD, the God of Israel, chose me from all my father's family to be king over Israel forever. He chose Judah to lead, and from Judah's family He chose my father's family. Among my father's sons, He was pleased to make me king over all Israel.
And from all my sons—for the LORD has given me many sons—He chose my son Solomon to sit on the throne of the kingdom of the LORD over Israel.
"He told me that my son Solomon would build His house and His courts, for He chose him to be His son, and He would be his Father.
He promised to make his kingdom last forever, if he stayed strong to obey His commands and His rules, as he does today.

"So now, in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of the LORD, and while our God listens, keep and seek all the commands of the LORD your God. Then you will possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your children after you forever.

"And you, my son Solomon, know the God of your father. Serve Him with a whole heart and a willing mind. For the LORD searches every heart and understands every thought. If you seek Him, He will be found by you. But if you forsake Him, He will cast you off forever.
Consider now that the LORD has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary. Be strong and do it."
David gave Solomon the plans for the porch and its buildings, storerooms, upper rooms, inner rooms, and the room for the mercy seat.
He gave him the plans for the courts of the LORD's house and all the rooms around it, for the storerooms of God's house and the storerooms for the dedicated things.
He gave plans for the divisions of the priests and Levites and for all the work of service in the LORD's house, and for all the articles used in that service.
He gave the weight of gold for all the gold articles used in every kind of service, and the weight of silver for all the silver articles used in every kind of service.

He gave the weight for the gold lampstands and their lamps, for each lampstand and its lamps, and for the silver lampstands and their lamps, for each lampstand and its lamps, according to the work of each one.
He gave the weight of gold for the tables of the showbread, for each table, and silver for the silver tables.
He gave pure gold for the forks, bowls, and cups, and the weight of gold for each gold basin; and silver for the silver bowls, with the weight for each one.
He gave the weight of refined gold for the altar of incense, and gold for the plan of the chariot—the cherubim that spread their wings and cover the ark of the covenant of the LORD.
David said, "The LORD made all this clear to me in writing by His hand upon me—all the details of the plan."

David said to Solomon, "Be strong and courageous, and do the work. Do not be afraid or discouraged, for the LORD God, my God, is with you. He will not fail you or forsake you until all the work for the service of the LORD's house is finished.

The divisions of the priests and Levites are ready for all the work on God's house. Every willing person skilled in any craft will help you, and the officials and all the people will obey your every command."
Then King David said to the whole assembly, "My son Solomon, whom God has chosen, is young and inexperienced. The task is great, because this temple is not for people but for the the LORD God.

With all my strength I have prepared for the house of my God: gold for gold, silver for silver, bronze for bronze, iron for iron, wood for wood, onyx stones, stones for settings, turquoise, all kinds of precious stones, and marble in abundance.
Besides this, because I delight in the house of my God, I have given from my own treasures of gold and silver for it, over and above all I have prepared for the holy house.
I gave three thousand talents of gold from Ophir and seven thousand talents of refined silver to cover the walls of the buildings.
Gold for the gold articles, silver for the silver, and work for every kind of craft by the hands of the craftsmen. Now who is willing to dedicate himself to the the LORD today?"
Then the leaders of the families, the leaders of the tribes of Israel, the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and the officials in charge of the king's work gave willingly.

They gave for the service of the house of God five thousand talents of gold and ten thousand gold coins, ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand talents of bronze, and one hundred thousand talents of iron.
Those who had precious stones gave them to the treasury of the house of the the LORD, under the care of Jehiel the Gershonite.
The people rejoiced over their willing gifts, because they had given to the the LORD with a whole heart. King David also rejoiced greatly.
David praised the the LORD in the sight of the whole assembly and said, "Blessed are You, the the LORD, God of our father Israel, from everlasting to everlasting.

Yours, the the LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in heaven and on earth is Yours. Yours, the the LORD, is the kingdom, and You are exalted as head over all.
Riches and honor come from You, and You rule over all. In Your hand are power and might, and in Your hand it is to make great and to give strength to all.
Now, our God, we give thanks to You and praise Your glorious name.
But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and we have given You only what comes from Your hand.
For we are foreigners and travelers before You, as were all our fathers. Our days on earth are like a shadow, and there is no lasting hope.
The the LORD our God, all this abundance that we have provided to build You a house for Your holy name comes from Your hand, and all of it is Yours.

I know, my God, that You test the heart and delight in uprightness. In the uprightness of my heart I have willingly given all these things, and now I have seen with joy Your people who are here give willingly to You.
The the LORD, God of our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, keep this desire forever in the hearts of Your people, and direct their hearts toward You.
And give my son Solomon a whole heart to keep Your commandments, Your testimonies, and Your statutes, and to do them all, and to build the temple for which I have made provision."
David said to the whole assembly, "Bless the the LORD your God." Then the whole assembly blessed the the LORD, the God of their fathers, and bowed down and worshiped the the LORD and the king.

The next day they offered sacrifices and burnt offerings to the the LORD: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, with their drink offerings, and many other sacrifices for all Israel.
They ate and drank that day with great joy before the the LORD. Then they made Solomon, son of David, king a second time, anointing him before the the LORD as ruler, and Zadok as priest.
So Solomon sat on the throne of the the LORD as king in place of his father David. He prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.
All the leaders and mighty men, and all of King David's sons, pledged their loyalty to King Solomon.
The LORD greatly exalted Solomon in the sight of all Israel and gave him royal splendor such as no king over Israel ever had before.
David, son of Jesse, reigned over all Israel.
He reigned over Israel forty years: seven years in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.
He died at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor. Then his son Solomon reigned in his place.
The acts of King David, from first to last, are written in the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet, and Gad the seer.
They include all his reign and his power, and the events that happened to him, to Israel, and to all the kingdoms of the lands.
Solomon son of David grew strong in his kingdom, and the LORD his God was with him and lifted him up greatly.
Solomon spoke to all Israel—to the commanders of thousands and hundreds, the judges, and every leader in Israel, the heads of the families.
Solomon and the whole assembly went to the high place at Gibeon, because God’s tent of meeting was there. Moses, the LORD’s servant, had made it in the wilderness.
David had already brought God’s ark from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it, because he had set up a tent for it in Jerusalem.
The bronze altar that Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, had made stood there in front of the LORD’s tabernacle. Solomon and the assembly sought the LORD there.
Solomon went up to the bronze altar before the LORD at the tent of meeting and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
That night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask what I should give you.”
Solomon said to God, “You have shown great faithful love to my father David, and You have made me king in his place.
Now, the LORD God, let Your word to my father David come true, for You have made me king over a people as many as the dust of the earth.
Give me now wisdom and knowledge, so I can lead this people. Who can judge this great people of Yours?”

God said to Solomon, “Because this was in your heart, and you did not ask for riches, wealth, honor, or the lives of those who hate you, and you did not even ask for a long life, but you asked for wisdom and knowledge to judge My people, over whom I have made you king,
wisdom and knowledge are given to you. I will also give you riches, wealth, and honor—more than any king before you had, and more than any king after you will have.”
Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem, and he reigned over Israel.
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen. He stationed them in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.
The king made silver and gold as common as stones in Jerusalem, and cedar as plentiful as sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Solomon’s horses were brought from Egypt and from Kue. The king’s merchants bought them from Kue for a set price.
They brought a chariot out of Egypt for six hundred shekels of silver and a horse for one hundred fifty. They also brought them out for all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.
Solomon decided to build a house for the the LORD's Name and a royal palace for himself.
He put 70,000 men to work carrying loads, 80,000 men to quarry stone in the mountains, and 3,600 men to supervise them.
Solomon sent this message to Hiram, king of Tyre: "Just as you helped my father David by sending him cedar logs to build his palace, please do the same for me.

I am about to build a house for the Name of the the LORD my God. I want to set it apart for Him. I will burn fragrant incense before Him, keep the bread set out all the time, and offer burnt offerings in the morning and evening. We will also bring offerings on the Sabbaths, the New Moons, and the appointed feasts of the the LORD our God. This is a law for Israel to keep forever.
The house I build will be great, because our God is greater than all other gods.
But who can really build a house for Him? Even the highest heavens cannot hold Him. So who am I to build a house for Him, except as a place to burn sacrifices before Him?

Now send me a skilled man who knows how to work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, purple, dark red, and blue cloth. He should know how to carve designs. He will work with the skilled men in Judah and Jerusalem, the men my father David provided.
Also send me cedar, cypress, and algum logs from Lebanon. I know your workers know how to cut trees there. My workers will join your workers.
Send me plenty of wood, because the house I am building will be great and amazing.
I will give your workers 20,000 cors of wheat, 20,000 cors of barley, 20,000 baths of wine, and 20,000 baths of olive oil."
Hiram, king of Tyre, wrote back to Solomon: "Because the the LORD loves His people, He has made you king over them.

Blessed be the the LORD, the God of Israel, who made heaven and earth! He has given King David a wise son. You have good sense and understanding, and you will build a house for the the LORD and a royal palace for yourself.
So now I am sending you Huram-abi, a skilled man who understands his work.

His mother is from the daughters of Dan, and his father was a man from Tyre. He knows how to work with gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, and wood. He also works with purple, blue, fine linen, and dark red cloth. He can carve any design and figure out any plan given to him. He will work with your skilled men and with the skilled men of my lord David your father.
Now let my lord send his servants the wheat, barley, oil, and wine he promised.
We will cut all the wood you need from Lebanon and bring it on rafts by sea to Joppa. Then you can take it up to Jerusalem."
Solomon counted all the foreign men living in Israel, using the census his father David had taken. There were 153,600 of them.
He made 70,000 of them carry loads, 80,000 of them quarry stone in the mountains, and 3,600 of them supervise the people.

Solomon began to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah. That was where the LORD had appeared to his father David. David had prepared the place on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
He began to build on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of his reign.
These are the foundations Solomon laid for building the house of God: The temple was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide.
The porch in front of the temple was twenty cubits long, across the width of the temple. It was one hundred twenty cubits high. Solomon overlaid it inside with pure gold.
He paneled the main hall with cypress wood and overlaid it with fine gold. He decorated it with palm trees and chains.
He adorned the temple with precious stones to make it beautiful. The gold was gold from Parvaim.
He overlaid the temple—its beams, thresholds, walls, and doors—with gold. He carved cherubim on the walls.
He made the Most Holy Place. Its length, across the width of the temple, was twenty cubits, and its width was twenty cubits. He overlaid it with six hundred talents of fine gold.
The nails weighed fifty shekels of gold. He also overlaid the upper rooms with gold.
In the Most Holy Place he made two cherubim of wood and overlaid them with gold.

The wings of the cherubim were twenty cubits long. One wing of the first cherub was five cubits long and touched the wall of the temple. The other wing was five cubits long and touched the wing of the other cherub.
One wing of the second cherub was five cubits long and touched the wall of the temple. The other wing was five cubits long and touched the wing of the first cherub.
The wings of these cherubim spread out twenty cubits. They stood on their feet, and their faces looked toward the temple.
He made the veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen. He wove cherubim into it.
In front of the temple he made two pillars. They were thirty-five cubits high, with a capital five cubits high on top of each.
He made chains for the inner sanctuary and put them on top of the pillars. He made one hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains.
He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right and one on the left. He called the right pillar Jachin and the left pillar Boaz.
He made a bronze altar. It was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and ten cubits high.
He also made the Sea from cast metal. It was round, ten cubits across from rim to rim, and five cubits high. A line of thirty cubits went all the way around it.
Below the rim, figures of bulls circled it. There were ten bulls in each cubit, making ten rows around it. The bulls were cast in two rows as part of the Sea.
The Sea stood on twelve bulls. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east. The Sea rested on them, and their back ends pointed toward the center.
The Sea was a hand's width thick. Its rim was like the rim of a cup and like a lily flower. It could hold three thousand baths.
He made ten basins for washing. He put five on the south side and five on the north. The things used for burnt offerings were rinsed in them, but the Sea was for the priests to wash in.
He made ten gold lampstands, following their design, and put them in the temple. Five were on the south side and five on the north.
He made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the south side and five on the north. He also made one hundred gold sprinkling bowls.
He made the courtyard for the priests, the large courtyard, and doors for the courtyard. He covered the doors with bronze.
He set the Sea on the south side, at the southeast corner.
Huram also made the pots, shovels, and sprinkling bowls. So Huram finished the work he had taken on for King Solomon in the house of God:
the two pillars; the two bowl-shaped capitals on the pillars; the two sets of network that covered the two bowl-shaped capitals on the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, with two rows of pomegranates on each network to cover the two bowl-shaped capitals on the pillars;
the stands and the basins on the stands;
the Sea and the twelve bulls under it;
the pots, shovels, meat forks, and all the other articles. Huram-abi made all these things from polished bronze for King Solomon for the house of the the LORD.
The king had them cast in clay molds in the plain of the Jordan, between Succoth and Zeredah.
Solomon made all these things in such great number that the weight of the bronze could not be measured.
Solomon also made all the articles for the house of God. These included the gold altar and the tables that held the Bread of the Presence.
He made the lampstands of pure gold, with their lamps, to burn in front of the inner sanctuary as required.
He made the flowers, lamps, and tongs of gold—of the purest gold.
He made the wick trimmers, sprinkling bowls, dishes, and censers of pure gold. He also made the gold doors for the innermost room of the temple, the Most Holy Place, and the doors for the main hall.

All the work Solomon did for the house of the LORD was finished. Solomon brought in the things his father David had set apart for God. He put the silver, gold, and all the utensils into the storerooms of God's house.

Then Solomon gathered the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the families, in Jerusalem. They were to bring up the ark of the covenant of the LORD from the City of David, which is Zion.
All the men of Israel came together to the king at the feast in the seventh month.
When all the elders of Israel had come, the Levites lifted up the ark.
They brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy items that were in the tent. The Levite priests brought them up.
King Solomon and all the people of Israel who had gathered before the ark sacrificed sheep and oxen. There were so many that no one could count them.
The priests brought the ark of the covenant of the LORD to its place in the inner room of the temple, the Most Holy Place. They set it under the wings of the cherubim.
The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark. They covered the ark and its poles from above.
The poles were so long that their ends could be seen from the Holy Place in front of the inner room, but they could not be seen from outside. They are still there today.
Nothing was in the ark except the two stone tablets that Moses had put there at Horeb. That was where the LORD made a covenant with the Israelites when they came out of Egypt.
The priests came out of the Holy Place. All the priests who were there had set themselves apart for God's service, so they did not stay in their assigned groups.

The Levite singers—Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and relatives—stood east of the altar. They wore fine linen and played cymbals, harps, and lyres. With them stood 120 priests blowing trumpets.

The trumpeters and singers joined together to praise and thank the LORD with one voice. They raised their voices with trumpets, cymbals, and other instruments as they praised the LORD. They sang, “For He is good, for His faithful love endures forever.” Then the house of the LORD was filled with a cloud.
The priests could not stand to do their work because of the cloud. The glory of the LORD filled the house of God.
Then Solomon said, “The LORD has said that He would dwell in the thick darkness.
But I have built You an exalted house, a place for You to dwell forever.”
Then the king turned around and blessed the whole assembly of Israel while they stood there.
He said, “Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, who has fulfilled with His hands what He spoke with His mouth to my father David, saying, ‘

Since the day I brought My people out of Egypt, I have not chosen a city from any tribe of Israel in which to build a house so that My name would be there, nor have I chosen a man to be ruler over My people Israel.
But now I have chosen Jerusalem for My name to be there, and I have chosen David to rule over My people Israel.’ “
Now it was in the heart of my father David to build a house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the LORD said to my father David, ‘Because it was in your heart to build a house for My name, you did well to have this in your heart.
Nevertheless, you will not build the house, but your son, who will come from your body, will build the house for My name.’ “

Now the LORD has kept the word He spoke. I have taken my father David's place and sit on the throne of Israel, as the LORD promised. I have built this house for the name of the LORD, the God of Israel.
There I have put the ark, which holds the covenant of the LORD that He made with the Israelites.”
Then Solomon stood before the altar of the LORD in front of the whole assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.

Solomon had made a bronze platform five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high. He put it in the middle of the courtyard. He stood on it, knelt before the whole assembly of Israel, and spread out his hands toward heaven. “
O the LORD, God of Israel, there is no God like You in heaven or on earth. You keep the covenant and show faithful love to Your servants who walk before You with all their heart.
You have kept what You promised to Your servant, my father David. You spoke with Your mouth and fulfilled it with Your hand, as it is today.

And now, O the LORD, God of Israel, keep for Your servant, my father David, the promise You made to him when You said, ‘You will never fail to have a man to sit before Me on the throne of Israel, if only your sons are careful to walk in My law as you have walked before Me.’
Now, O the LORD, God of Israel, let Your word be confirmed, which You spoke to Your servant David. “
But will God really dwell with humans on earth? Look, heaven and the highest heaven cannot contain You, much less this house I have built!
Yet please turn Your attention to the prayer and plea of Your servant, O the LORD my God, so that You may hear the cry and the prayer that Your servant is praying before You.
May Your eyes be open toward this house day and night, toward the place You said You would put Your name, so that You may hear the prayer that Your servant prays toward this place.
Hear the prayers of Your servant and Your people Israel when they pray toward this place. Hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and when You hear, forgive. “
If a man sins against his neighbor and is made to take an oath, and he comes to take the oath before Your altar in this house,
then hear from heaven and act. Judge Your servants, repaying the wicked by bringing his own conduct on his head, and vindicating the righteous by rewarding him according to his righteousness.
If Your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against You, and they turn back and confess Your name, praying and pleading before You in this house,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your people Israel. Restore them to the land You gave to them and to their fathers.
When the heavens are shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against You, and they pray toward this place and confess Your name, turning from their sin when You afflict them,

then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants, Your people Israel. Teach them the good way in which they should walk, and send rain on Your land, which You gave to Your people as an inheritance. “
If there is famine in the land, or pestilence, blight, mildew, locusts, or grasshoppers; if their enemies besiege them in any of their cities; whatever plague or sickness there is—
then whatever prayer or plea any person or all Your people Israel may make—each knowing his own affliction and pain, and spreading out his hands toward this house—
then hear from heaven, Your dwelling place. Forgive and repay each man according to all his ways, since You know his heart. For You alone know the hearts of all mankind.
so that they may fear You and walk in Your ways all the days they live in the land You gave to our fathers.

As for the foreigner who is not of Your people Israel, but has come from a distant land because of Your great name, Your mighty hand, and Your outstretched arm—when he comes and prays toward this house,

then hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, and do according to all that the foreigner asks of You. Then all the peoples of the earth will know Your name and fear You, as Your people Israel do, and know that this house I have built is called by Your name.
When Your people go to war against their enemies, wherever You send them, and they pray to You toward this city You have chosen and the house I have built for Your name,
then hear from heaven their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause.
When they sin against You—for there is no one who does not sin—and You become angry with them and deliver them to an enemy who takes them captive to a land far or near,

and if they have a change of heart in the land where they are held captive, and repent and plead with You in the land of their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have done wrong, and we have acted wickedly,’

and if they return to You with all their heart and all their soul in the land of their captivity where they were taken, and pray toward the land You gave to their fathers, the city You have chosen, and the house I have built for Your name,
then hear from heaven, Your dwelling place, their prayer and their plea, and uphold their cause. Forgive Your people who have sinned against You. “
Now, my God, may Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to the prayer offered in this place.

Now arise, O the LORD God, and come to Your resting place, You and the ark of Your might. May Your priests, O the LORD God, be clothed with salvation, and may Your faithful people rejoice in Your goodness.
O the LORD God, do not reject Your anointed. Remember the mercies of Your servant David.”
When Solomon finished praying, fire came down from heaven and burned up the burnt offering and the sacrifices. The glory of the LORD filled the temple.
The priests could not enter the LORD’s house because His glory filled it.

When all the Israelites saw the fire come down and the glory of the LORD on the temple, they knelt with their faces to the ground on the pavement. They worshiped and thanked the LORD, saying, “He is good; His faithful love endures forever.”
Then the king and all the people offered sacrifices before the LORD.
King Solomon sacrificed 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. The king and all the people dedicated God’s house.

The priests stood at their stations, and the Levites played the LORD’s musical instruments that King David had made to praise the LORD—“His faithful love endures forever”—when David led the praise through them. The priests blew trumpets across from them, and all Israel stood.

Solomon set apart the middle of the courtyard in front of the LORD’s house. He offered burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings there, because the bronze altar Solomon had made could not hold the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, and the fat.
At that time Solomon and all Israel with him celebrated the feast for seven days. The crowd was very large, coming from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of Egypt.
On the eighth day they held a solemn assembly. They had dedicated the altar for seven days and celebrated the feast for seven days.

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month, Solomon sent the people to their tents. They were joyful and glad in heart because of the good things the LORD had done for David, Solomon, and His people Israel.
So Solomon finished the LORD’s house and the king’s house. He succeeded in everything he had planned to do in the LORD’s house and in his own house.
The LORD appeared to Solomon at night and said, “I have heard your prayer and chosen this place for Myself as a house of sacrifice.
If I shut the heavens so that no rain falls, or command locusts to devour the land, or send a plague among My people,
and if My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray and seek My face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and forgive their sin and heal their land.
Now My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayer offered in this place.
For I have chosen and set apart this house so that My name may be there forever. My eyes and My heart will be there for all time. “
As for you, if you walk before Me as your father David walked, doing all I command you and keeping My statutes and rules,
then I will establish your royal throne, just as I promised your father David: ‘You will never fail to have a man to rule over Israel.’
But if you turn away and forsake My statutes and commands that I have given you, and go serve and worship other gods,
then I will uproot them from the land I gave them and reject this house I set apart for My name. I will make it a warning story that people mock among all nations.
This temple, now so highly honored, will become a ruin. Everyone who passes by will be appalled and say, ‘Why has the LORD done this to this land and this temple?’

They will answer, ‘Because they forsook the LORD, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of Egypt, and clung to other gods, worshiping and serving them. That is why He brought all this disaster on them.’”
At the end of twenty years, after Solomon had built the temple of the LORD and his own palace,
he rebuilt the towns that Hiram had given him and settled Israelites in them.
Solomon went to Hamath Zobah and captured it.
He also built Tadmor in the desert and all the store cities he had built in Hamath.
He rebuilt Upper Beth Horon and Lower Beth Horon as fortified cities with walls, gates, and bars.
He did the same with Baalath and all his store cities, and with all the cities for his chariots and horses—whatever he wanted to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout his whole kingdom.
There were still people left from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. They were not Israelites.
Solomon made the descendants of these survivors do forced labor, and they still do today.
But Solomon did not make the Israelites slaves for his work. They were his fighting men, commanders of his chariots, and charioteers.
They were also King Solomon’s chief officials—two hundred fifty officials who supervised the men.

Solomon brought Pharaoh’s daughter up from the City of David to the palace he had built for her, because he said, “My wife must not live in the palace of David king of Israel, because the places where the ark of the LORD has entered are holy.”
On the altar of the LORD that he had built in front of the portico, Solomon sacrificed burnt offerings to the LORD,

according to the daily requirement for offerings commanded by Moses—for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the three annual festivals: the Festival of Unleavened Bread, the Festival of Weeks, and the Festival of Tabernacles.

In keeping with the ordinance of his father David, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their duties, and the Levites to lead the praise and assist the priests according to each day’s requirement. He also appointed the gatekeepers by their divisions for each gate, because this was what David the man of God had ordered.
The priests and Levites did not turn from the king’s commands in any matter, including the treasuries.
All Solomon’s work was carried out, from the day the foundation of the temple of the LORD was laid until it was finished. So the temple of the LORD was completed.
Then Solomon went to Ezion Geber and Elath on the coast of Edom.

Hiram sent him ships commanded by his own men, sailors who knew the sea. These joined Solomon’s men and sailed to Ophir and brought back four hundred fifty talents of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon.

The queen of Sheba heard how famous Solomon was. She came to Jerusalem to test him with hard questions. She brought a large group with her. Her camels carried spices, gold, and precious stones. When she met Solomon, she told him everything she had on her mind.
Solomon answered all her questions. He did not leave anything unexplained.
When the queen of Sheba saw Solomon's wisdom and the palace he had built,

and the food on his table, the seats of his officials, the work of his servants and their clothes, his cupbearers and their clothes, and the burnt offerings he made at the house of the LORD, she was amazed.
She said to the king, "The report I heard in my own country about your words and your wisdom is true.
"I did not believe it until I came and saw it with my own eyes. But I now see that I had heard only half of it, and your wisdom is far greater than what people told me.
"How happy your people must be! How happy your servants must be, who stand before you all the time and hear your wisdom!

"Blessed be the LORD your God, who has been pleased with you and placed you on His throne to be king for the LORD your God. Because of His love for Israel, He has made you king forever, so you can do what is right and fair."
She gave the king 120 talents of gold, a large amount of spices, and precious stones. There had never been spices like those the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.
The servants of Hiram and the servants of Solomon also brought gold from Ophir. They brought algum wood too.
King Solomon used the algum wood to make steps for the house of the LORD and for the palace. He also made harps and lyres for the singers. No wood like this had ever been seen in Judah before.
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba everything she wanted and asked for. This was besides what she had brought to the king. Then she and her servants went back to her own country.
The gold that came to Solomon in one year weighed 666 talents.
This was besides what traders and merchants brought. All the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land also brought gold and silver to Solomon.
King Solomon made 200 large shields of hammered gold. Each one used 600 shekels of gold.
He also made 300 smaller shields of hammered gold. Each one used 300 shekels of gold. The king put them in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon.
The king made a large throne of ivory. He covered it with pure gold.
The throne had six steps. A footstool of gold was attached to it. There were armrests on both sides, with a lion standing beside each one.
Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one on each side of every step. No other kingdom had a throne like this.
All King Solomon's drinking cups were gold. All the cups in the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon were gold too. Silver was not worth much in Solomon's time.
The king had ships that sailed with Hiram's men. Once every three years they came back carrying gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.
King Solomon was richer and wiser than any other king on earth.
All the kings of the earth wanted to meet Solomon. They wanted to hear the wisdom God had given him.
Year after year, everyone who came brought gifts. They brought silver and gold items, clothes, weapons, spices, horses, and mules.
Solomon had 4,000 stalls for horses and chariots. He also had 12,000 horsemen. He kept some in the chariot cities and some with him in Jerusalem.
He ruled over all the kings from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt.
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones. He made cedar wood as common as sycamore trees in the lowlands.
Solomon's horses were brought from Egypt and from all other lands.

The rest of Solomon's acts, from beginning to end, are written in the records of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer about Jeroboam son of Nebat.
Solomon ruled in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.
Then Solomon died and was buried in the city of his father David. His son Rehoboam became king after him.
Rehoboam went to Shechem, because all Israel had come there to make him king.
When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard about it, he came back from Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon.
They sent for Jeroboam and brought him back. Then Jeroboam and all Israel went to Rehoboam and said,
“Your father made our load heavy. Now make his hard work lighter and remove the heavy load he put on us, and we will serve you.”
Rehoboam said, “Come back to me in three days.” So the people went away.
King Rehoboam talked with the elders who had served his father Solomon while Solomon was alive. He asked, “What do you advise? How should I answer these people?”
They said, “If you are kind to these people and please them, and speak good words to them, they will be your servants forever.”
But Rehoboam ignored the elders’ advice. Instead, he talked with the young men who had grown up with him and served him.
He asked them, “What do you advise? How should we answer the people who said to me, ‘Lighten the load your father put on us’?”
The young men who had grown up with him said, “Tell the people who said to you, ‘Your father made our load heavy, but you make it lighter for us,’ ‘I am much tougher than my father.’
My father burdened you with a heavy load; I will make it even heavier. My father punished you with whips; I will punish you with sharp, stinging lashes.”
On the third day, Jeroboam and all the people came back to Rehoboam, just as the king had said.
The king answered them harshly. King Rehoboam rejected the elders’ advice.
He spoke to them as the young men had advised: “My father made your load heavy, but I will add to it. My father punished you with whips, but I will punish you with sharp, stinging lashes.”
The king did not listen to the people, because this was from God. He did this to keep the word the LORD had spoken through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam son of Nebat.

When all Israel saw that the king refused to listen to them, they said to the king, “What part do we have in David? We have no share in Jesse’s son. Go to your tents, Israel! Look after your own house, David!” Then all Israel went home.
But Rehoboam still ruled over the Israelites living in the cities of Judah.
King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was in charge of forced labor. But the Israelites stoned him to death. King Rehoboam quickly got into his chariot and escaped to Jerusalem.
So Israel has rebelled against the house of David to this day.
When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he gathered the men of Judah and Benjamin—180,000 chosen fighting men—to fight against Israel and win the kingdom back for Rehoboam.
But the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah the man of God:
“Say to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin,

‘This is what the LORD says: Do not go up to fight against your brothers. Each of you go home, for this is My doing.’” So they obeyed the words of the LORD and turned back from marching against Jeroboam.
Rehoboam lived in Jerusalem and built cities for defense in Judah.
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. These were fortified cities in Judah and Benjamin.
He strengthened their defenses and put commanders in them, with supplies of food, olive oil, and wine.
He put shields and spears in every city and made them very strong. So Judah and Benjamin were his.
The priests and Levites from all over Israel came to him.
The Levites left their pasturelands and property and came to Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them as priests of the LORD.
Jeroboam appointed his own priests for the high places and for the goat and calf idols he had made.
Those from every tribe of Israel who were determined to seek the LORD, the God of Israel, followed the Levites to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
They strengthened the kingdom of Judah and supported Rehoboam son of Solomon for three years, following the ways of David and Solomon.
Rehoboam married Mahalath, who was the daughter of Jerimoth son of David and of Abihail, the daughter of Eliab son of Jesse.
She bore him sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.
He later married Maakah daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.
Rehoboam loved Maakah daughter of Absalom more than all his other wives and concubines. He had eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and he fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters.
Rehoboam appointed Abijah son of Maakah as chief prince among his brothers, to make him king.
He acted wisely by sending some of his sons throughout the districts of Judah and Benjamin, and to all the fortified cities. He gave them abundant provisions and took many wives for them.
When Rehoboam had made his kingdom strong and had become powerful, he and all Israel with him turned away from the law of the LORD.
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because they had sinned against the LORD, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem.
He came with 1,200 chariots and 60,000 horsemen. A huge crowd came with him from Egypt—Libyans, Sukkiites, and Cushites—and no one could count them.
He captured the fortified cities of Judah and reached Jerusalem.

Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah who had gathered in Jerusalem because of Shishak. He said to them, "This is what the LORD says: 'You have forsaken Me, and I also have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.'"
The leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous."

When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, His word came to Shemaiah: "They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them, but I will give them a little deliverance, and My wrath will not be poured out on Jerusalem through Shishak."
Still, they will become his servants, so they can learn the difference between serving Me and serving the kingdoms of other lands.
So Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem and took the treasures of the LORD's temple and the treasures of the king's palace. He took everything, including the gold shields Solomon had made.
King Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace them and put them in the care of the captains of the guard, who watched the door of the king's house.
Whenever the king went into the LORD's temple, the guards carried the shields and then brought them back to the guardroom.
Because Rehoboam humbled himself, the LORD's anger turned away from him, so He did not destroy him completely. Things also went well in Judah.

King Rehoboam grew strong in Jerusalem and ruled there. He was forty-one years old when he became king, and he ruled seventeen years in Jerusalem. That was the city the LORD had chosen from all the tribes of Israel to put His name there. His mother's name was Naamah the Ammonite.
He did evil, because he did not set his heart on seeking the LORD.
The rest of Rehoboam's deeds, from first to last, are written in the records of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer, including family records. Rehoboam and Jeroboam were at war all their days.
Rehoboam died and was buried with his fathers in the City of David. His son Abijah became king after him.
In the eighteenth year of Jeroboam's reign, Abijah became king over Judah.
He reigned in Jerusalem for three years. His mother's name was Micaiah, the daughter of Uriel from Gibeah. There was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.
Abijah went to battle with an army of four hundred thousand chosen men, all strong warriors. Jeroboam lined up against him with eight hundred thousand chosen men, also strong warriors.
Abijah stood on Mount Zemaraim in the hill country of Ephraim and said, "Listen to me, Jeroboam and all Israel.
Don't you know that the the LORD, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom of Israel to David and his sons forever by a lasting agreement?
Yet Jeroboam son of Nebat, Solomon's servant, rebelled against his master.
Some worthless scoundrels gathered around him and opposed Rehoboam son of Solomon when Rehoboam was young and unsure of himself and could not stand against them.

"And now you plan to resist the kingdom of the the LORD, which is in the hands of David's descendants. You are a huge crowd, and you have with you the golden calves that Jeroboam made for you as gods.

Didn't you drive out the the LORD's priests, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and make priests for yourselves like the peoples of other lands? Anyone who brings a young bull and seven rams to be ordained can become a priest for gods that aren't real.
"But as for us, the the LORD is our God, and we have not forsaken Him. The priests who serve the the LORD are Aaron's sons, and the Levites assist in the work.

Every morning and evening they burn burnt offerings and fragrant incense to the the LORD. They set out the bread on the table of pure gold, and they light the lamps on the gold lampstand every evening. We are keeping the the LORD our God's requirements, but you have forsaken Him.

God is with us; He is our leader. His priests blow the trumpets to sound the battle cry against you. People of Israel, don't fight against the the LORD, the God of your ancestors, because you won't win."
Meanwhile, Jeroboam had sent soldiers to circle around behind them. So Judah found the enemy in front and the ambush behind.
When the men of Judah turned around, they saw they were trapped front and back. They cried out to the the LORD, and the priests blew the trumpets.
Then the men of Judah shouted the war cry. As they shouted, God defeated Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
The Israelites fled from Judah, and God handed them over to Judah.
Abijah and his army struck them with a great blow: five hundred thousand of Israel's chosen soldiers fell.
So Israel was humbled at that time, and the people of Judah grew strong because they relied on the the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Abijah chased Jeroboam and captured some of his cities: Bethel with its surrounding villages, Jeshanah with its villages, and Ephron with its villages.
Jeroboam never regained his power during Abijah's reign. The The LORD struck him, and he died.
But Abijah grew stronger. He took fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
The rest of Abijah's deeds, his ways, and his words are written in the records of the prophet Iddo.
Abijah died and was buried in the City of David. His son Asa became king after him. In his days the land had peace for ten years.
Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of the LORD his God.
He took away the foreign altars and high places. He broke the sacred stones and cut down the Asherah poles.
He told the people of Judah to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, and to obey the law and His commands.
He removed the high places and incense altars from all the cities of Judah. The kingdom was at peace under him.
Because the land was at peace, Asa built fortified cities in Judah. There was no war in those years, because the LORD gave him rest.

He said to Judah, “Let us build up these cities and surround them with walls, towers, gates, and bars. The land is still ours, because we have sought the LORD our God. We have sought Him, and He has given us rest on every side.” So they built and did well.
Asa had an army of 300,000 men from Judah. They carried shields and spears. From Benjamin there were 280,000 men who carried shields and bows. All these men were brave soldiers.
Zerah the Cushite marched against them with an army of one million men and three hundred chariots. He came as far as Mareshah.
Asa went out to meet him, and they set up for battle in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah.

Asa cried out to the LORD his God, “the LORD, no one but You can help, whether an army is large or weak. Help us, the LORD our God, because we trust in You. We have come against this huge army in Your name. the LORD, You are our God. Do not let people win against You.”
So the LORD struck down the Cushites before Asa and Judah, and the Cushites ran away.
Asa and his men chased them all the way to Gerar. The Cushites fell until no one was left alive, because they were crushed before the LORD and His army. Asa's men carried off a great deal of plunder.
They attacked all the cities around Gerar, because the fear of the LORD had fallen on them. They plundered all the cities, because there was much wealth in them.
They also attacked the tents where livestock were kept. They took many sheep and camels and went back to Jerusalem.
The Spirit of God came upon Azariah son of Oded.

He went out to meet Asa and said, "Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The LORD is with you when you are with Him. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will forsake you.
For a long time Israel has been without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without law.
But in their trouble they turned to the LORD, the God of Israel, and sought Him, and He was found by them.
In those days there was no peace for the one who went out or the one who came in, because many troubles were on all the people living in the lands.
Nation crushed nation, and city crushed city, because God troubled them with every kind of distress.
But you, be strong, and do not let your hands grow weak, for your work will be rewarded."

When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage and removed the hated idols from all the land of Judah and Benjamin and from the cities he had taken in the hill country of Ephraim. He also renewed the altar of the LORD in front of the porch of the LORD.

He gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the people from Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon who were living among them, because many people from Israel had come over to him when they saw that the LORD his God was with him.
They gathered in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa's reign.
At that time they sacrificed to the LORD seven hundred bulls and seven thousand sheep from the plunder they had brought.
They made an agreement to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and all their soul.
Anyone who would not seek the LORD, the God of Israel, would be put to death, whether small or great, man or woman.
They swore an oath to the LORD with a loud voice, with shouting, and with trumpets and horns.
All Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and sought Him with all their desire, and He was found by them. The LORD also gave them rest on every side.
King Asa also removed Maacah, his grandmother, from being queen mother, because she had made a hateful image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it in the Kidron Valley.
But the high places were not removed from Israel. Yet Asa's heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days.
He brought into the house of God the holy things his father had dedicated and the holy things he had dedicated: silver, gold, and utensils.
There was no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign.
In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha king of Israel attacked Judah and built up Ramah. He did this so no one could leave or enter Asa's land.
Asa took silver and gold from the treasuries of the the LORD's temple and the royal palace. He sent it to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, who ruled in Damascus, and said,
"Make a treaty with me, as our fathers did. I have sent you silver and gold. Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so he will leave me alone."
Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent his army leaders against Israel's cities. They captured Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the storage cities of Naphtali.
When Baasha heard about this, he stopped building up Ramah and left the work unfinished.
Then King Asa brought all Judah together. They carried away the stones and wood Baasha had used in Ramah, and Asa used them to build up Geba and Mizpah.
At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said, "Because you relied on the king of Aram instead of on the the LORD your God, the army of Aram's king has escaped from your hand.
Were not the Cushites and Libyans a huge army with many chariots and horsemen? Yet when you relied on the the LORD, He delivered them into your hand.
The LORD's eyes move back and forth over the whole earth. He wants to give strength to those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him. You have acted foolishly in this. From now on, you will have wars."
Asa was angry with the seer and put him in prison, because he was furious with him over this. At that time Asa also treated some of his people harshly.
The things Asa did, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa got a disease in his feet. It became very bad. Even in his sickness, he did not seek the the LORD, but only the doctors.
Asa died in the forty-first year of his reign.
He was buried in the tomb he had cut for himself in the City of David. He was laid on a funeral bed filled with spices and many mixed perfumes. They also burned a large fire in his honor.
Jehoshaphat, Asa’s son, became king after him. He strengthened Judah against Israel.
He stationed troops in all of Judah’s fortified cities and put garrisons in Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that his father Asa had captured.
The LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he followed the early ways of his father David and did not worship the Baals.
Instead, he sought the God of his father and obeyed His commands. He did not follow Israel’s practices.
So the LORD made his kingdom strong. All Judah brought gifts to Jehoshaphat, and he had great wealth and honor.
His heart was devoted to the ways of the LORD. He also removed the high places and Asherah poles from Judah.
In the third year of his reign, he sent his officials—Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah—to teach in Judah’s cities.
With them were Levites: Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah. Priests Elishama and Jehoram were with them too.
They taught in Judah. They had the Book of the Law of the LORD with them. They traveled through all of Judah’s cities and taught the people.
Fear of the LORD fell on all the kingdoms around Judah. They did not go to war against Jehoshaphat.
Some Philistines brought Jehoshaphat gifts and silver as tribute. The Arabs also brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats.
Jehoshaphat kept growing stronger. He built fortresses and store cities in Judah.
He had much property in Judah’s cities and many warriors in Jerusalem.
This was their registration by families: For Judah, commanders of thousands: Adnah the commander, with 300,000 mighty warriors.
Next to him was Jehohanan the commander, with 280,000.
Next to him was Amasiah son of Zichri, who volunteered for the LORD, with 200,000 mighty men.
From Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man, with 200,000 armed with bows and shields.
Next to him was Jehozabad, with 180,000 ready for war.
These served the king, besides the men he had placed in Judah’s fortified cities.
Jehoshaphat had great wealth and honor. He made a marriage alliance with Ahab.
After some years, he went down to Ahab in Samaria. Ahab killed many sheep and cattle for him and the people with him. Then Ahab urged him to attack Ramoth Gilead.

Ahab, king of Israel, said to Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, "Will you go with me to Ramoth Gilead?" Jehoshaphat answered, "I am like you, and my people are like your people. We will be with you in the war."
Jehoshaphat said, "Please ask today for the word of the LORD."
The king of Israel gathered four hundred prophets. He asked them, "Should we go to war against Ramoth Gilead, or should I hold back?" They said, "Go up. God will give it into the king's hand."
Jehoshaphat asked, "Isn't there another prophet of the LORD here, so we can ask him?"

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "There is still one man we can ask. He is Micaiah son of Imlah. But I hate him, because he never predicts good things for me. He always predicts bad things." Jehoshaphat said, "The king should not say that."
The king of Israel called an officer and said, "Bring Micaiah son of Imlah quickly."

The king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, were sitting on their thrones, wearing royal robes. They were at the threshing floor by the gate of Samaria. All the prophets were speaking in front of them.
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns. He said, "This is what the LORD says: 'With these you will gore Aram until they are destroyed.'"
All the prophets said the same thing: "Go up to Ramoth Gilead and succeed. The LORD will give it into the king's hand."
The messenger who had gone to call Micaiah said to him, "All the prophets are saying good things to the king. Please let your words match theirs, and say something good."
Micaiah said, "As the LORD lives, I will say only what my God tells me."
When Micaiah came to the king, the king asked him, "Micaiah, should we go to Ramoth Gilead to fight, or should I hold back?" Micaiah answered, "Go up and succeed. They will be given into your hand."
The king said, "How many times must I make you swear to tell me only the truth in the name of the LORD?"
Then Micaiah said, "I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd. The LORD said, 'These have no master. Let each one go home in peace.'"
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "Didn't I tell you he would not predict good things for me, but bad things?"
Micaiah said, "So listen to the word of the LORD. I saw the LORD sitting on His throne. All the armies of heaven were standing on His right and on His left.
"The The LORD said, 'Who will trick Ahab, king of Israel, into going up to Ramoth Gilead, so he will fall there?' One said one thing, and another said another.
"Then a spirit came forward and stood before the LORD. He said, 'I will trick him.' The The LORD asked, 'How?'
"The spirit said, 'I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouths of all his prophets.' The The LORD said, 'You will trick him, and you will succeed. Go out and do it.'
"So now the LORD has put a lying spirit in the mouths of these prophets. The The LORD has spoken disaster against you."
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek. He said, "Which way did the Spirit of the LORD go from me to speak to you?"
Micaiah said, "You will see that on the day you go into a back room to hide."
The king of Israel said, "Take Micaiah and send him back to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash the king's son."
The king also said, "Tell them, 'This is what the king says: Put this man in prison. Feed him only bread and water until I return safely.'"
Micaiah said, "If you really come back safely, then the LORD has not spoken through me. Listen, all you people!"
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, went up to Ramoth Gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, "I will disguise myself and go into battle. But you wear your robes." So the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into battle.
The king of Aram had ordered his chariot commanders, "Do not fight anyone, whether important or not. Fight only the king of Israel."
When the chariot commanders saw Jehoshaphat, they said, "That is the king of Israel." They turned to fight him. Jehoshaphat cried out, and the LORD helped him. God turned them away from him.
When the chariot commanders saw he was not the king of Israel, they stopped chasing him.

A man shot an arrow without aiming. It hit the king of Israel between the joints of his armor and his breastplate. The king said to his chariot driver, "Turn around and take me out of the battle, because I am wounded."
The battle grew worse that day. The king of Israel was propped up in his chariot, facing the Arameans, until evening. He died at sunset.
Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, returned safely to his home in Jerusalem.
Jehu son of Hanani, a prophet, went out to meet him. He said to King Jehoshaphat, "Should you help wicked people and love those who hate the the LORD? Because of this, the the LORD is angry with you.
Even so, good things are found in you. You removed the Asherah poles from the land, and you were determined to seek God."
Jehoshaphat lived in Jerusalem. He went out among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and led them back to the the LORD, the God of their fathers.
He appointed judges throughout the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city.
He said to the judges, "Think about what you are doing. You are not judging for people. You are judging for the the LORD. He is with you when you make decisions.
So let the fear of the the LORD be on you. Be careful in what you do, because the the LORD our God does not do wrong. He does not play favorites, and He does not take bribes."
In Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat also appointed some Levites, priests, and family leaders of Israel to handle the the LORD's cases and settle arguments. They returned to Jerusalem.
He told them, "Do this in the fear of the the LORD, faithfully, and with your whole heart.

When a case comes to you from your brothers who live in their cities—whether it is about bloodshed, law, commands, rules, or decisions—warn them so they do not become guilty before the the LORD. If you do not warn them, His anger will come on you and your brothers. Do this, and you will not be guilty.

Amariah the chief priest is in charge of all matters about the the LORD. Zebadiah son of Ishmael, the leader of Judah, is in charge of all the king's matters. The Levites will serve as officials before you. Be brave, and may the the LORD be with those who do good."
After this, the Moabites, Ammonites, and some of the Meunites came to fight against Jehoshaphat.
People came and told Jehoshaphat, “A huge army is coming against you from Aram, from beyond the sea. They are already at Hazazon-tamar,” which is En Gedi.
Jehoshaphat was afraid. He decided to seek the LORD and called for a fast in all Judah.
