The people of Judah came together to ask the LORD for help. They came from every city in Judah to seek the LORD.
Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem in the house of the LORD, in front of the new courtyard.
He said, “The LORD, God of our fathers, are You not God in heaven? You rule all the kingdoms of the nations. Power and might are in Your hand, and no one can stand against You.
“Our God, did You not drive out the people who lived in this land before Your people Israel? Did You not give it forever to the descendants of Abraham, Your friend?
They have lived in it and built a sanctuary there for Your name.

If disaster comes on us—sword, judgment, plague, or famine—we will stand before this house and before You, because Your name is in this house. We will cry to You in our trouble, and You will hear and save us.
“Now look! The Ammonites, Moabites, and people of Mount Seir are coming. You did not let Israel invade them when Israel came from Egypt, so Israel turned away from them and did not destroy them.
Now they are paying us back by coming to drive us out of the land You gave us as our possession.
Our God, will You not judge them? We have no strength against this large army that is coming against us. We do not know what to do, but our eyes are on You.”
All the people of Judah stood before the LORD with their wives and children, even their little ones.
The Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel son of Zechariah, son of Benaiah, son of Jeiel, son of Mattaniah, a Levite from the descendants of Asaph, in the middle of the assembly.

He said, “Listen, all you people of Judah and Jerusalem, and King Jehoshaphat. This is what the LORD says to you: Do not be afraid or discouraged because of this huge army. The battle is not yours but God's.
Tomorrow go down against them. They will come up by the Ascent of Ziz, and you will find them at the end of the valley before the wilderness of Jeruel.

“You will not need to fight this battle. Take your positions, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD for you. O Judah and Jerusalem, do not be afraid or discouraged. Go out against them tomorrow, and the LORD will be with you.”
Jehoshaphat bowed with his face to the ground. All the people of Judah and Jerusalem fell down before the LORD to worship Him.
The Levites from the Kohathites and Korahites stood up to praise the LORD, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.

Early in the morning they got up and went out to the wilderness of Tekoa. As they were leaving, Jehoshaphat stood and said, “Listen to me, people of Judah and Jerusalem! Believe in the LORD your God, and you will be made strong. Believe His prophets, and you will succeed.”

After talking with the people, he chose singers for the LORD. They praised the LORD in holy splendor as they marched in front of the army. They sang, “Give thanks to the LORD, for His mercy endures forever.”
As they began to sing and praise, the LORD set ambushes against the Ammonites, Moabites, and people of Mount Seir who had come against Judah, and they were defeated.
The Ammonites and Moabites turned against the people of Mount Seir to destroy and wipe them out. After they finished with the people of Seir, they helped destroy one another.
When Judah came to the watchtower in the wilderness, they looked at the crowd. There were dead bodies lying on the ground, and no one had escaped.

Jehoshaphat and his people came to take the plunder. They found a lot of goods, clothing, and valuable items. They took more than they could carry. It took them three days to collect the plunder because there was so much.
On the fourth day they gathered in the Valley of Berachah, because there they blessed the LORD. That is why the place is called the Valley of Berachah to this day.
Then all the men of Judah and Jerusalem returned, with Jehoshaphat leading them. They went back to Jerusalem with joy, because the LORD had given them joy over their enemies.
They came to Jerusalem and went to the house of the LORD with harps, lyres, and trumpets.
The fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the lands when they heard that the LORD had fought against the enemies of Israel.
So Jehoshaphat's kingdom was at peace, and his God gave him rest on every side.
Jehoshaphat was thirty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Azubah, the daughter of Shilhi.
He walked in the way of his father Asa and did not turn away from it. He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD.
But the high places were not removed. The people still had not set their hearts on the God of their fathers.
The rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, from first to last, are written in the records of Jehu son of Hanani, which are included in the book of the kings of Israel.
After this, Jehoshaphat king of Judah made an alliance with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did evil.
He joined with him to build ships to go to Tarshish. They built the ships at Ezion-geber.

Eliezer son of Dodavahu from Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat: “Because you have joined with Ahaziah, the LORD will destroy what you have made.” The ships were wrecked and could not sail to Tarshish.
Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Jehoram became king after him.
Jehoshaphat had other sons: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, another Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. These were all the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Israel.
Their father gave them many gifts of silver, gold, and valuable things, along with fortified cities in Judah. But he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because Jehoram was the oldest son.
After Jehoram took control of his father's kingdom, he made himself strong. Then he killed all his brothers with a sword, along with some of the leaders of Israel.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king. He ruled eight years in Jerusalem.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel, just as Ahab's family did, because Ahab's daughter was his wife. He did what was evil in the eyes of the the LORD.
But the the LORD did not want to destroy David's family. He had made an agreement with David and promised that David's family line would continue forever.
During his rule, Edom broke free from Judah's control and chose its own king.
Jehoram went out with his commanders and all his chariots. The Edomites surrounded him, but he and his chariot commanders attacked at night.
Edom has stayed free from Judah to this day. At that same time, Libnah also broke free, because Jehoram had left the the LORD, the God of his fathers.
He also built high places in the hills of Judah. He led the people of Jerusalem into unfaithfulness and led Judah away from the the LORD.

A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet. It said, "This is what the the LORD, the God of your father David, says: You have not followed the ways of your father Jehoshaphat or the ways of Asa, king of Judah.

Instead, you have followed the ways of the kings of Israel. You have led Judah and the people of Jerusalem into unfaithfulness, just as Ahab's family did. You have also killed your brothers, who were better men than you.
So the the LORD will strike your people, your children, your wives, and everything you own with a terrible disease.
You will become very sick. Your intestines will come out because of the sickness, and this will go on day after day."
Then the the LORD turned the Philistines and the Arabs who lived near the Cushites against Jehoram.
They came up into Judah and broke into it. They carried off everything found in the king's house, along with his sons and wives. Only his youngest son, Jehoahaz, was left.
After all this, the the LORD struck Jehoram with a disease in his intestines that could not be healed.
After two years, his intestines came out because of the disease, and he died in great pain. His people did not make a fire for him, as they had for his fathers.

Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled eight years in Jerusalem. He died without anyone mourning him. He was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.

The people living in Jerusalem made Ahaziah, his youngest son, king in his place. The raiders who came with the Arabs to the camp had killed all his older brothers. So Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, began to rule.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled one year in Jerusalem. His mother's name was Athaliah, the daughter of Omri.
He also followed the ways of Ahab's family, because his mother advised him to do wrong.
He did what was evil in the eyes of the LORD, just as Ahab's family had done. After his father died, they became his advisers and led him to ruin.
He also followed their advice and went with Jehoram son of Ahab, king of Israel, to fight Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth Gilead. The Arameans wounded Joram.

Joram returned to Jezreel to recover from the wounds he got at Ramah while fighting Hazael king of Aram. Ahaziah son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to see Joram son of Ahab, because Joram was sick.
But God used his trip to bring him to Joram. When he got there, he went out with Joram to meet Jehu son of Nimshi, whom the LORD had anointed to destroy Ahab's family.
While Jehu was carrying out judgment on Ahab's family, he found the leaders of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers, who served Ahaziah, and he killed them.

He looked for Ahaziah and caught him while he was hiding in Samaria. They brought him to Jehu and killed him. They buried him, because they said, “He is the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought the LORD with all his heart.” After that, Ahaziah's family had no one left to rule the kingdom.
When Athaliah, Ahaziah's mother, saw that her son was dead, she rose up and destroyed all the royal family of Judah.

But Jehoshabeath, the king's daughter, took Joash son of Ahaziah and hid him among the king's sons who were being killed. She put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Jehoshabeath was the daughter of King Jehoram and the wife of Jehoiada the priest. She was also Ahaziah's sister. She hid Joash from Athaliah, so she did not kill him.
He stayed with them six years, hidden in the temple of God, while Athaliah ruled the land.

In the seventh year, Jehoiada grew strong and made a covenant with the commanders of hundreds: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri.
They traveled through Judah and gathered the Levites from all its cities, along with the heads of Israel's families, and they came to Jerusalem.
The whole group made a covenant with the king in the house of God. Jehoiada said to them, "Look, the king's son will rule, just as the LORD promised about David's sons.
This is what you must do: One third of you priests and Levites who come on duty on the Sabbath are to guard the gates.
One third are to guard the royal palace, and one third are to guard the Foundation Gate. All the people are to stay in the courtyards of the house of the the LORD.
No one may enter the house of the the LORD except the priests and Levites on duty. They may enter because they are holy, but all the people must keep the the LORD's rules.
The Levites must surround the king with weapons in their hands. Anyone who enters the temple must be put to death. Stay close to the king wherever he goes."

The Levites and all Judah did everything Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each man brought his own group, both those coming on duty on the Sabbath and those going off duty, because Jehoiada had not dismissed any of the divisions.
Then Jehoiada the priest gave the commanders of hundreds the spears and the large and small shields that had belonged to King David and were kept in the house of God.
He placed all the people, each with a weapon in hand, from the south side of the temple to the north side, around the altar and the temple.
Then they brought out the king's son. They put the crown on him and gave him the Testimony. They proclaimed him king, and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him and said, "Long live the king!"
When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and cheering the king, she went to the people in the house of the the LORD.

She saw the king standing by his pillar at the entrance. The captains and trumpeters stood beside the king. All the people of the land were rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers were leading the praise with instruments. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, "Treason! Treason!"

Then Jehoiada the priest brought out the commanders who were in charge of the army. He said to them, "Bring her out between the ranks, and put to death with the sword anyone who follows her." The priest had said, "Do not put her to death in the house of the the LORD."
So they seized her. When she reached the entrance of the Horse Gate of the king's house, they put her to death there.
Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king, that they would be the the LORD's people.
All the people went to the house of Baal and tore it down. They smashed its altars and images, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, in front of the altars.

Jehoiada put the Levitical priests in charge of the house of the the LORD, as David had assigned them, to offer burnt offerings to the the LORD, as it is written in the Law of Moses, with joy and song, as David had ordered.
He also stationed gatekeepers at the gates of the house of the the LORD, so that no one who was unclean in any way could enter.

He took the commanders, the nobles, the rulers of the people, and all the people of the land, and brought the king down from the house of the the LORD. They entered the king's house through the Upper Gate and seated the king on the royal throne.
All the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet, because Athaliah had been killed with the sword.
Joash was seven years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah, and she was from Beersheba.
Joash did what was right in the eyes of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada chose two wives for him, and he had sons and daughters.
After this, Joash decided to repair the house of the LORD.

He gathered the priests and Levites and said, “Go out to the cities of Judah and collect money from all Israel year by year to repair the house of your God. Hurry with this.” But the Levites did not hurry.

So the king called Jehoiada the chief priest and said, “Why haven’t you required the Levites to bring in from Judah and Jerusalem the tax that Moses, the servant of the LORD, set for Israel for the tent of meeting?”
For the sons of that wicked woman Athaliah had broken into the house of God and had used all the dedicated things of the house of the LORD for the Baals.
At the king’s command, they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of the LORD.
Then they made a proclamation in Judah and Jerusalem that the people should bring to the LORD the tax Moses, God’s servant, had set for Israel in the wilderness.
All the leaders and all the people rejoiced. They brought their gifts and dropped them into the chest until it was full.

Whenever the chest was brought by the Levites to the king’s officials, and they saw that there was much money, the king’s secretary and the chief priest’s officer would empty the chest and carry it back to its place. They did this day by day and collected a large amount of money.

The king and Jehoiada gave it to those who did the work on the house of the LORD. They hired stonecutters and carpenters to repair the house of the LORD, and also workers in iron and bronze to strengthen it.
The workers labored, and the repair work went forward. They rebuilt the house of God according to its plan and strengthened it.

When they finished, they brought the rest of the money to the king and Jehoiada. They made articles for the house of the LORD—articles for service, for burnt offerings, and bowls, and gold and silver vessels. Burnt offerings were offered regularly in the house of the LORD all the days of Jehoiada.
Jehoiada grew old and full of days and died. He was 130 years old when he died.
They buried him with the kings in the City of David, because he had done good in Israel, for God, and for His house.
After Jehoiada died, the leaders of Judah came and bowed down to the king, and the king listened to them.
They left the house of the LORD, the God of their fathers, and worshiped the Asherah poles and idols. Because of this guilt, God’s anger came on Judah and Jerusalem.
He sent prophets to bring them back to the LORD, and they warned them, but they would not listen.

Then the Spirit of God came on Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest. He stood above the people and said, “This is what God says: Why do you break the the LORD’s commands? You will not succeed. Because you have left the LORD, He has left you.”
They plotted against him at the king’s command and stoned him to death in the courtyard of the house of the LORD.

King Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada, Zechariah’s father, had shown him. Instead, he killed Jehoiada’s son. As Zechariah was dying, he said, “May the LORD see this and hold you accountable.”
At the end of the year, the army of Aram came against Joash. They invaded Judah and Jerusalem and killed all the leaders of the people. They sent all the plunder to the king of Damascus.
The army of Aram came with a small force, but the LORD handed over a very large army to them, because Judah had left the LORD, the God of their fathers. So they carried out judgment on Joash.

When the Arameans left, they left Joash badly wounded. His own servants plotted against him because he had shed the blood of the son of Jehoiada the priest. They killed him on his bed, and he died. He was buried in the City of David, but not in the tombs of the kings.
Those who plotted against him were Zabad son of Shimeath, an Ammonite woman, and Jehozabad son of Shimrith, a Moabite woman.
The accounts of his sons, the many prophecies against him, and the rebuilding of the house of God are written in the commentary on the Book of the Kings. His son Amaziah became king after him.
Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jehoaddan, from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, but not with a whole heart.
When his kingdom was strong, Amaziah killed the servants who had murdered his father the king.

But he did not kill their sons, because it is written in the Law, in the Book of Moses, where the LORD commanded: "Fathers must not be put to death for their children, and children must not be put to death for their fathers; each person must die for his own sin."

Amaziah gathered the people of Judah and organized them by family groups under commanders of thousands and hundreds. He counted everyone twenty years old and older in Judah and Benjamin and found 300,000 choice men who could serve in the army. They carried spears and shields.
He also hired 100,000 strong soldiers from Israel for 100 talents of silver.
But a man of God came to him and said, "O king, do not let Israel's army go with you, because the LORD is not with Israel—not with any of the Ephraimites.
But if you do go, be strong for battle; yet God will make you stumble before the enemy, because God has power to help and to make stumble."
Amaziah asked the man of God, "But what about the hundred talents I gave to the Israelite troops?" The man of God answered, "The LORD is able to give you much more than this."
So Amaziah dismissed the troops that had come from Ephraim. They were to go home. But they were furious with Judah and returned home in a rage.
Amaziah strengthened himself and led his people out. He went to the Valley of Salt and struck down 10,000 men of Seir.
The men of Judah captured another 10,000 alive and took them to the top of a cliff. They threw them down, and all were dashed to pieces.
But the troops Amaziah had sent back, not letting them go with him to battle, raided towns of Judah from Samaria to Beth-horon. They killed 3,000 people and carried off much plunder.
After Amaziah returned from defeating the Edomites, he brought back the gods of the people of Seir and set them up as his gods. He bowed down to them and burned incense to them.
Therefore the LORD was angry with Amaziah, and He sent a prophet to him, who said, "Why have you sought the gods of a people who could not save their own people from your hand?"

While the prophet was still speaking, Amaziah said to him, "Have we made you an advisor to the king? Stop! Why should you be struck down?" So the prophet stopped, but not before saying, "I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel."
After some time, Amaziah king of Judah made plans and sent to Joash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, "Come, let us meet face to face."

Joash king of Israel replied to Amaziah king of Judah: "A thornbush in Lebanon sent to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son in marriage.' Then a wild beast in Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush.
You say, 'Look, I have struck down Edom,' and your heart has lifted you up to boast. Now stay at home. Why should you stir up trouble so that you fall and Judah with you?"
But Amaziah would not listen, for it was from God, so that He might deliver them into the hand of Joash, because they had sought the gods of Edom.
So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh in Judah.
Judah was defeated by Israel, and every man fled to his tent.

Joash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Joash son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh. He brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate, a distance of four hundred cubits.
He took all the gold and silver and all the articles found in the house of God with Obed-edom, and the treasures of the king's house, and the hostages, and returned to Samaria.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Amaziah, from beginning to end, are they not written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel?
From the time Amaziah turned away from following the LORD, a conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent men after him to Lachish and killed him there.
They carried him back on horses and buried him with his fathers in the City of Judah.
All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt the town of Eloth and brought it back under Judah's control after Amaziah died.
Uzziah was sixteen when he became king, and he ruled for fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jecoliah, and she was from Jerusalem.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done.
He sought the LORD during the days of Zechariah, who taught him to honor God. As long as he sought the LORD, God gave him success.
He went to war against the Philistines. He broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod. Then he built cities near Ashdod and in Philistia.
God helped him defeat the Philistines, the Arabs who lived in Gur-baal, and the Meunites.
The Ammonites paid tribute to Uzziah. His fame spread all the way to the border of Egypt, because he had become very strong.
Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and the Angle. He made them stronger.

He also built towers in the desert and dug many wells, because he had large herds in the western hills and on the plains. He had farmers and grape growers in the hills and in Carmel, because he loved the land.
Uzziah had an army ready for battle. It was organized into groups based on the records kept by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer. They worked under Hananiah, one of the king's officials.
The total number of family leaders among the fighting men was 2,600.
Under them served an army of 307,500 trained soldiers. This powerful force helped the king fight his enemies.
Uzziah gave all the soldiers shields, spears, helmets, armor, bows, and stones for slings.

In Jerusalem he had skilled workers build machines for the towers and corners. These machines could shoot arrows and throw large stones. His fame spread far and wide, because God helped him in amazing ways until he became strong.
But when he became strong, he grew proud, and this led to his ruin. He sinned against the LORD his God and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense on the incense altar.
Azariah the priest followed him in, along with eighty brave priests of the LORD.

They stood against King Uzziah and said to him, "It is not for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD. That duty belongs to the priests, the sons of Aaron, who have been set apart to burn incense. Get out of the holy place, because you have sinned against God, and you will not be honored by the LORD God."
Uzziah became angry. While he was angry with the priests, a skin disease broke out on his forehead right there in the temple of the LORD, near the incense altar.

Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked at him and saw that he had a skin disease on his forehead. They hurried him out of the temple. He also hurried to leave, because the LORD had struck him.

King Uzziah had the skin disease until the day he died. He lived in a separate house because of it, and he was kept away from the temple of the LORD. His son Jotham was in charge of the palace and ruled the people of the land.
The other things Uzziah did, from beginning to end, are written in the visions of Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz.
Uzziah died and was buried with his ancestors in the royal burial field, because people said, "He has leprosy." Then his son Jotham became king in his place.
Jotham was twenty-five years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother was Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Uzziah had done. But he did not enter the LORD's temple. The people still acted corruptly.
He built the Upper Gate of the LORD's temple. He also did a lot of work on the wall of Ophel.
He built cities in the hill country of Judah. He also built forts and towers.

He fought the king of the Ammonites and defeated them. That year the Ammonites gave him one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand cors of wheat, and ten thousand cors of barley. They gave him the same amounts in the second and third years.
Jotham grew strong because he followed the ways of the LORD his God.
The rest of Jotham's story, including all his wars and his ways, is written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for sixteen years.
Jotham died and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David. His son Ahaz became king after him.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. He did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD, like his father David.
He followed the ways of the kings of Israel. He also made metal images for the Baals.
He burned incense in the Valley of Ben Hinnom and burned his sons in the fire. He followed the terrible practices of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.
He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.
So the LORD his God handed him over to the king of Aram. They defeated him and took many captives to Damascus. God also gave him into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with a great blow.
In one day, Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 strong men of Judah, because they had left the LORD, the God of their fathers.
Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the king's son, Azrikam the palace official, and Elkanah, who was second to the king.
The Israelites took 200,000 of their relatives captive—women, sons, and daughters. They also took much plunder and brought it to Samaria.

But a prophet of the LORD named Oded was there. He went out to meet the army as it returned to Samaria and said to them, "Because the LORD, the God of your fathers, was angry with Judah, He gave them into your hand. But you have killed them with such fury that it reaches heaven.
Now you plan to make the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem your slaves. But are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?
Now listen to me and send back the captives you took from your brothers, for the LORD's fierce anger is on you."
Then some leaders of Ephraim—Azariah son of Jehohanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai—stood up against those coming from the war.
They said to them, "Do not bring the captives here, or we will be guilty before the LORD. Are you trying to add to our sins and guilt? Our guilt is already great, and fierce anger is on Israel."
So the armed men left the captives and the plunder before the leaders and the whole assembly.

The men who were named took charge of the captives. They clothed those who had no clothes from the plunder. They gave them clothes and sandals, food and drink, and oil. They put the weak ones on donkeys and brought them to their brothers at Jericho, the city of palms. Then they returned to Samaria.
At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria for help.
The Edomites had come again and struck Judah and carried away captives.

The Philistines also raided the cities of the lowlands and the Negev of Judah. They captured Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soco and its villages, Timnah and its villages, and Gimzo and its villages, and settled there.
For the LORD humbled Judah because of Ahaz king of Israel, for he had led Judah to live without restraint and had been very unfaithful to the LORD.
Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came against him and attacked him instead of strengthening him.
Although Ahaz took a portion from the LORD's temple and from the king's palace and the officials and gave it to the king of Assyria, it did not help him.
In the time of his distress King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD.

He sacrificed to the gods of Damascus that had defeated him, for he said, "Because the gods of the kings of Aram help them, I will sacrifice to them so that they will help me." But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.
Ahaz gathered the vessels of the house of God and cut them in pieces. He shut the doors of the LORD's temple and made altars for himself in every corner of Jerusalem.
In every city of Judah he made high places to burn incense to other gods, and he angered the LORD, the God of his fathers.
The rest of his acts and all his ways, from first to last, are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in the city, in Jerusalem, but they did not bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel. His son Hezekiah reigned in his place.
Hezekiah was twenty-five years old when he became king. He ruled in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years. His mother's name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done.
In the first month of the first year of his rule, Hezekiah opened the doors of the LORD's house and repaired them.
He brought in the priests and Levites and gathered them in the square on the east side.
He said to them, "Listen to me, Levites. Set yourselves apart now, and set apart the house of the LORD, the God of your fathers. Take all the unclean things out of the holy place.
Our fathers were unfaithful. They did evil in the eyes of the LORD our God. They left Him and turned their faces away from the LORD's dwelling place. They turned away from Him.
They also shut the doors of the porch and put out the lamps. They did not burn incense or offer burnt sacrifices in the holy place to the God of Israel.
So the LORD's anger has fallen on Judah and Jerusalem. He has made them an object of terror, ruin, and scorn, as you can see with your own eyes.
That is why our fathers fell by the sword, and our sons, daughters, and wives are in captivity.
Now it is in my heart to make a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel, so that His fierce anger will turn away from us.
Now, my sons, do not be careless, for the LORD has chosen you to stand before Him, to serve Him, to assist Him, and to burn incense."

The Levites who went to work were Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah from the Kohathites; Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel from the Merarites; Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah from the Gershonites;
from the descendants of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeiel; from the descendants of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah;
from the descendants of Heman, Jehiel and Shimei; and from the descendants of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel.
They gathered their fellow Levites, set themselves apart, and went in to clean the house of the LORD, as the king had commanded and as the LORD had said.

The priests went into the inner part of the LORD's house to clean it. They carried all the unclean things they found in the temple of the LORD out to the courtyard of the LORD's house. The Levites took them and carried them out to the Kidron Valley.

They began to set the temple apart on the first day of the first month. By the eighth day they had reached the porch of the LORD. They spent eight more days setting apart the LORD's house, finishing on the sixteenth day of the first month.
Then they went in to King Hezekiah and reported, "We have cleaned the whole house of the LORD, the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, and the table of the showbread with all its utensils.
We have also prepared and set apart all the articles that King Ahaz removed when he was unfaithful. They are now in front of the altar of the LORD."
Early the next morning King Hezekiah gathered the city leaders and went up to the house of the LORD.

They brought seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats as a sin offering for the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah. The king told the priests, the descendants of Aaron, to offer them on the altar of the LORD.

So the priests slaughtered the bulls and sprinkled their blood on the altar. They slaughtered the rams and sprinkled their blood on the altar. They also slaughtered the lambs and sprinkled their blood on the altar.
Then they brought the goats for the sin offering before the king and the people, and they laid their hands on them.

The priests slaughtered them and sprinkled their blood on the altar as a sin offering to make atonement for all Israel, because the king had said, "The burnt offering and the sin offering are for all Israel."

Hezekiah placed the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, harps, and lyres, as David, Gad the king's seer, and Nathan the prophet had commanded. The command came from the LORD through His prophets.
The Levites stood with David's instruments, and the priests stood with the trumpets.
Hezekiah gave the order to offer the burnt offering on the altar. When the burnt offering began, the song to the LORD began too, along with the trumpets and the instruments of David, king of Israel.
The whole crowd bowed in worship, while the singers sang and the trumpeters played. All this continued until the burnt offering was finished.
When the offerings were finished, the king and everyone with him knelt and worshiped.
King Hezekiah and his officials told the Levites to praise the LORD with the words of David and Asaph the seer. So they praised Him with joy, bowed their heads, and worshiped.

Then Hezekiah said, "Now that you have set yourselves apart to the LORD, come near and bring sacrifices and thank offerings to the house of the LORD." So the people brought sacrifices and thank offerings, and everyone whose heart was willing brought burnt offerings.
The burnt offerings the people brought were seventy bulls, one hundred rams, and two hundred lambs. All of these were for a burnt offering to the LORD.
The dedicated animals were six hundred bulls and three thousand sheep.

But there were not enough priests to skin all the burnt offerings, so their fellow Levites helped them until the work was done and until more priests had been set apart. The Levites had been more eager to set themselves apart than the priests.
There were also many burnt offerings, along with the fat of the fellowship offerings and the drink offerings for the burnt offerings. So the service of the house of the LORD was restored.
Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced at what God had done for the people, because it had happened so suddenly.
Hezekiah sent word to all Israel and Judah. He also wrote letters to Ephraim and Manasseh, asking them to come to the LORD's house in Jerusalem and celebrate Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel.
The king, his officials, and the whole group in Jerusalem decided to celebrate the Passover in the second month.
They could not celebrate it at the usual time because the priests had not made themselves holy yet, and the people had not gathered in Jerusalem.
This plan pleased the king and all the group.

They decided to send a message through all Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, telling people to come to Jerusalem to celebrate Passover to the LORD, the God of Israel. Most of the people had not kept it the way the law said.

Following the king's command, runners went through all Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his leaders. The letters said, "People of Israel, come back to the LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. Then He will come back to the few of you who escaped from the kings of Assyria.
"Do not be like your fathers and brothers. They were unfaithful to the LORD, the God of their fathers, and He let them be ruined, as you can see.
"Now do not be stubborn like your fathers. Give yourselves to the LORD and come to His holy place, which He set apart forever. Serve the LORD your God, so His anger will turn away from you.

"If you come back to the LORD, your brothers and children will be treated with kindness by the people who took them away. They will come back to this land, because the LORD your God is kind and merciful. He will not turn away from you if you come back to Him."
The runners went from town to town in Ephraim and Manasseh, all the way to Zebulun. The people laughed at them and made fun of them.
But some men from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.
God's hand was also on Judah. He gave them one heart to obey the king and his leaders, as the LORD had said.
A very large crowd came to Jerusalem in the second month to celebrate the Feast of Unleavened Bread. It was a huge group.
They stood up and removed the altars in Jerusalem. They also took away all the incense altars and threw them into the Kidron Valley.
On the fourteenth day of the second month, they killed the Passover lambs. The priests and Levites felt ashamed, so they made themselves holy. Then they brought burnt offerings to the LORD's house.
They stood where they were supposed to stand, following the Law of Moses, the man of God. The priests sprinkled the blood that the Levites handed to them.
Many in the crowd had not made themselves holy, so the Levites killed the Passover lambs for everyone who was not clean. This made the lambs holy for the LORD.

Many people had come from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun. They had not cleaned themselves, but they ate the Passover in a way not allowed by the law. So Hezekiah prayed for them: "May the LORD, who is good, forgive
everyone who has set his heart on seeking God, the LORD, the God of his fathers, even if he is not clean in the way the holy place requires."
The LORD heard Hezekiah and healed the people.
The Israelites in Jerusalem celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy. The Levites and priests praised the LORD every day with loud music, using the LORD's instruments.
Hezekiah spoke kindly to all the Levites who served the LORD with skill. They ate the festival food for seven days, offering peace offerings and thanking the LORD, the God of their fathers.
The whole group decided to celebrate for seven more days, so they celebrated seven more days with joy.
King Hezekiah of Judah gave the group 1,000 bulls and 7,000 sheep. The leaders gave 1,000 bulls and 10,000 sheep. The priests made themselves holy in large numbers.
All the people of Judah rejoiced, along with the priests, the Levites, all the people who came from Israel, the foreigners who came from Israel, and the people living in Judah.
There was great joy in Jerusalem. Nothing like it had happened in Jerusalem since the days of Solomon son of David, king of Israel.
Then the priests and Levites stood up and blessed the people. Their voice was heard, and their prayer reached God's holy home in heaven.

When all this had ended, the Israelites who were there went out to the towns of Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. They smashed the stone pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and tore down the high places and altars throughout Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, and Manasseh. After they had destroyed all of them, the Israelites went back to their own towns and their own property.

Hezekiah appointed the priests and Levites to their divisions. Each group had its own duties. The priests and Levites were to offer burnt offerings and fellowship offerings, to serve, to give thanks, and to praise the LORD at the gates of His temple.
The king gave part of his own wealth for the morning and evening burnt offerings and for the burnt offerings on the Sabbaths, New Moons, and appointed feasts, as the Law of the LORD required.
He also told the people living in Jerusalem to give the priests and Levites their share, so they could give all their time to the Law of the LORD.

As soon as the order spread, the Israelites gave large amounts of the first crops of grain, new wine, olive oil, and honey, and all the produce of the fields. They brought a large tithe of everything.
The men of Israel and Judah who lived in the towns of Judah also brought a tithe of their herds and flocks and a tithe of the holy things dedicated to the LORD their God. They piled them in heaps.
They began piling them up in the third month and finished in the seventh month.
When Hezekiah and his officials came and saw the heaps, they praised the LORD and blessed His people Israel.
Hezekiah asked the priests and Levites about the heaps.

Azariah the chief priest, from the family of Zadok, answered, "Since the people began to bring their contributions into the temple of the LORD, we have had plenty to eat, with much left over, because the LORD has blessed His people. This large amount is what is left."
Then Hezekiah ordered them to prepare storerooms in the temple of the LORD, and they did.
They faithfully brought in the contributions, tithes, and dedicated gifts. Conaniah the Levite was in charge of them, and his brother Shimei was second.

Jehiel, Azaziah, Nahath, Asahel, Jerimoth, Jozabad, Eliel, Ismachiah, Mahath, and Benaiah were supervisors under Conaniah and Shimei. King Hezekiah and Azariah, the official in charge of the temple of God, had appointed them.
Kore son of Imnah the Levite, the gatekeeper at the East Gate, was in charge of the freewill offerings given to God. He distributed the contributions made to the LORD and the most holy gifts.
Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah, Amariah, and Shecaniah served under him. They faithfully gave out the supplies to their fellow Levites in the priestly towns, by divisions, to great and small alike.
Besides the males three years old and older who were listed by family records, everyone who came to the temple of the LORD each day for service received a share, according to their divisions.
The priests were enrolled by their ancestral families, and the Levites twenty years old and older were enrolled according to their duties and divisions.
The enrollment included all the little children, wives, sons, and daughters of the whole assembly, because they had faithfully set themselves apart as holy.

For the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who lived in the pasturelands around their towns, men were named in each town to distribute portions to every male among the priests and to every Levite who was enrolled.
This is what Hezekiah did throughout Judah. He did what was good, right, and faithful before the LORD his God.
In everything he did for the service of God's temple, for the law and commands, and in seeking his God, he worked with all his heart, and he prospered.
After these things and these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah. He besieged the fortified cities, intending to capture them for himself.
When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come and that he intended to wage war against Jerusalem,
he consulted with his officials and military leaders about blocking the water from the springs outside the city, and they helped him.
A large group of people gathered and stopped up all the springs and the stream that flowed through the land. They said, "Why should the kings of Assyria come and find plenty of water?"

Hezekiah took courage and rebuilt all the broken sections of the wall. He raised towers on it and built another wall outside. He repaired the Millo in the City of David and made large numbers of weapons and shields.
He appointed military officers over the people and gathered them to him in the square at the city gate. He spoke encouragingly to them, saying,
"Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or discouraged because of the king of Assyria and the huge army with him, for there is a greater power with us than with him.
He has only human strength, but we have the LORD our God to help us and to fight our battles." The people gained confidence from the words of Hezekiah king of Judah.
After this, Sennacherib king of Assyria, while besieging Lachish with all his forces, sent his servants to Jerusalem to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all Judah who were in Jerusalem, saying,
"Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria: On what are you trusting, that you stay in Jerusalem under siege?
Isn't Hezekiah misleading you, handing you over to die by famine and thirst, while he says, 'The LORD our God will rescue us from the hand of the king of Assyria'?
Hasn't Hezekiah removed his high places and altars and told Judah and Jerusalem, 'You must worship before one altar and burn incense on it'?
Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the peoples of the lands? Were the gods of the nations of those lands ever able to rescue their lands from my hand?
Who among all the gods of these nations that my fathers destroyed was able to rescue his people from my hand? How then can your God rescue you from my hand?

Now do not let Hezekiah deceive you or mislead you like this. Do not believe him, for no god of any nation or kingdom has been able to rescue his people from my hand or from the hand of my fathers. How much less will your God rescue you from my hand!"
His servants spoke even more against the LORD, the God of Israel, and against His servant Hezekiah.

He also wrote letters insulting the LORD, the God of Israel, and speaking against Him, saying, "Like the gods of the nations of the lands who did not rescue their people from my hand, so the God of Hezekiah will not rescue His people from my hand."
They shouted in Hebrew to the people of Jerusalem on the wall to frighten them and terrify them, so they could take the city.
They spoke about the God of Jerusalem as they did about the gods of the peoples of the earth, things made by human hands.
King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz cried out in prayer to heaven about this.

The LORD sent an angel, who destroyed all the fighting men, commanders, and officers in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he returned to his own land in disgrace. And when he went into the temple of his god, some of his own sons killed him with the sword.
So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem from the hand of Sennacherib king of Assyria and from the hand of all others, and He gave them peace on every side.
Many brought offerings to Jerusalem for the LORD and valuable gifts for Hezekiah king of Judah, so that he was highly respected by all nations after that.
In those days Hezekiah became ill and was at the point of death. He prayed to the LORD, who answered him and gave him a miraculous sign.
But Hezekiah did not respond to the kindness shown to him; instead his heart became proud. So the LORD's anger came upon him and upon Judah and Jerusalem.
Then Hezekiah humbled himself for the pride of his heart, he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so the LORD's wrath did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.
Hezekiah had very great riches and honor. He made treasuries for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields, and all kinds of valuable articles.
He made storehouses for grain, new wine, and olive oil, and stalls for all kinds of livestock and pens for flocks.
He built cities and acquired great numbers of flocks and herds, for God had given him very great wealth.
It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and channeled the water down to the west side of the City of David. Hezekiah prospered in all his work.
So when envoys of the rulers of Babylon were sent to him to ask about the miraculous sign that had happened in the land, God left him to test him and to know everything in his heart.
The rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his kind acts are written in the vision of the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.
Hezekiah died and was buried on the upper part of the tombs of David's descendants. All Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem honored him at his death. And his son Manasseh reigned in his place.
Manasseh was twelve years old when he became king, and he ruled fifty-five years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the sight of the LORD, following the disgusting practices of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.
He rebuilt the high places his father Hezekiah had torn down. He set up altars for the Baals, made Asherah poles, and bowed down to worship and serve all the stars in the sky.
He built altars in the the LORD's house, even though the LORD had said, "My name will be in Jerusalem forever."
He built altars for all the stars in the sky in the two courtyards of the the LORD's house.

He sacrificed his sons by fire in the Valley of Ben Hinnom. He practiced fortune-telling, magic, and sorcery, and he talked with mediums and spirits. He did many evil things that made the the LORD angry.

He even put a carved idol, which he had made, in God's house. God had said to David and his son Solomon, "In this house and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen from all the tribes of Israel, I will put My name forever.
I will not again remove Israel from the land I gave your ancestors, if only they are careful to obey all I commanded them through Moses—all the law, the rules, and the commands."
Manasseh led Judah and the people of Jerusalem to do more evil than the nations the the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.
The LORD spoke to Manasseh and his people, but they would not listen.
So the the LORD brought the army commanders of the king of Assyria against them. They captured Manasseh with hooks, tied him with bronze chains, and took him to Babylon.
While he was suffering, he begged the the LORD his God and humbled himself greatly before the God of his ancestors.
He prayed to the the LORD, and the the LORD answered him. He heard Manasseh's prayer and brought him back to Jerusalem and put him back on his throne. Then Manasseh knew that the the LORD is God.

After that, he built an outer wall for the City of David west of Gihon in the valley, reaching to the Fish Gate. He made the wall around Ophel much higher. He also placed army commanders in all the fortified cities of Judah.
He removed the foreign gods and the idol from the the LORD's house. He also removed all the altars he had built on the temple hill and in Jerusalem, and he threw them outside the city.
He repaired the the LORD's altar and offered peace offerings and thank offerings on it. He told Judah to serve the the LORD, the God of Israel.
But the people still sacrificed on the high places, though only to the the LORD their God.
The rest of Manasseh's deeds, his prayer to God, and the words of the prophets who spoke to him in the name of the the LORD, the God of Israel, are written in the records of the kings of Israel.

His prayer and how God was moved by his request, all his sin and wrongdoing, and the places where he built high places and set up wooden poles and carved idols before he humbled himself, are written in the records of the prophets.
Manasseh died and was buried in his own house. Then his son Amon became king in his place.
Amon was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he ruled two years in Jerusalem.
But he did evil in the the LORD's sight, as his father Manasseh had done. Amon sacrificed to all the carved idols his father Manasseh had made, and he served them.
He did not humble himself before the the LORD as his father Manasseh had. Instead, Amon sinned more and more.
Then his servants plotted against him and killed him in his own house.
But the people of the land killed all those who had plotted against King Amon. Then they made his son Josiah king in his place.
Josiah was eight years old when he became king, and he ruled in Jerusalem for thirty-one years.
He did what was right in the eyes of the the LORD, and he walked in the ways of his father David. He did not turn to the right or to the left.

In the eighth year of his rule, while he was still young, he began to seek the God of his father David. In the twelfth year, he began to clean Judah and Jerusalem of the high places, the Asherah poles, the carved images, and the metal images.

He had the altars of the Baals torn down. He broke the incense altars that stood above them. He smashed the Asherah poles, the carved images, and the metal images. He ground them to dust and scattered the dust over the graves of the people who had sacrificed to them.
He burned the bones of the priests on their altars, and he made Judah and Jerusalem clean.
He did the same in the towns of Manasseh, Ephraim, and Simeon, and as far as Naphtali, and in the ruined places around them.
He tore down the altars and the Asherah poles. He crushed the carved images to powder and cut down all the incense altars in the land of Israel. Then he went back to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his rule, after he had made the land and the temple clean, he sent Shaphan son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the city official, and Joah son of Joahaz the recorder to repair the temple of the the LORD His God.

They went to Hilkiah the high priest. They gave him the money that had been brought into God's house. The Levites who guarded the door had collected it from Manasseh, Ephraim, and all the rest of Israel, and from all Judah and Benjamin and the people of Jerusalem.
They put it into the hands of the men in charge of the work on the the LORD's house. Those men gave it to the workers who were repairing the house of the the LORD.
They gave it to the carpenters and builders to buy cut stone and wood for the beams and to repair the buildings that the kings of Judah had let fall into ruin.
The men worked faithfully. The Levites in charge were Jahath and Obadiah from the family of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam from the family of Kohath. All of those Levites were skilled musicians.
They were in charge of the laborers and directed all the workers from job to job. Some of the Levites were secretaries, officials, and gatekeepers.
While they were bringing out the money that had been brought into the the LORD's house, Hilkiah the priest found the Book of the Law of the the LORD given through Moses.
Hilkiah said to Shaphan the secretary, "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the the LORD." He gave the book to Shaphan.
Shaphan brought the book to the king and reported, "Your servants are doing everything they were given to do.
They have paid out the money found in the the LORD's house and given it to the supervisors and workers."
Then Shaphan the secretary told the king, "Hilkiah the priest has given me a book." Shaphan read from it in front of the king.
When the king heard the words of the Law, he tore his robes.
The king gave orders to Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Abdon son of Micah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king's servant. He said,

"Go and ask the the LORD for me and for those left in Israel and Judah. Ask about the words of this book that was found. The the LORD's anger is great because our ancestors did not keep the the LORD's word. They did not do everything written in this book."

Hilkiah and the king's men went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum son of Tokhath son of Hasrah, who kept the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem, in the Second District. They spoke to her as the king had told them.
She said to them, "This is what the the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Tell the man who sent you to me,
'This is what the the LORD says: I am going to bring disaster on this place and on its people. All the curses written in the book that was read in front of the king of Judah will come true.

Because they have left Me and burned incense to other gods, and because they have made Me angry with everything their hands have made, My wrath will be poured out on this place and will not be put out.'
Tell the king of Judah, who sent you to ask the the LORD,

'This is what the the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the words you heard: Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before God when you heard what He said against this place and its people, and because you humbled yourself before Me, tore your robes, and wept before Me, I have heard you, says the the LORD.

I will gather you to your ancestors, and you will be buried in peace. Your eyes will not see all the disaster I am bringing on this place and on its people.'" Then they took her answer back to the king.
The king sent for all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.

He went up to the house of the the LORD with all the people of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, the priests, and the Levites. Everyone from the least to the greatest was there. He read to them all the words of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in the house of the the LORD.

The king stood in his place and made a covenant before the the LORD. He promised to follow the the LORD and to keep His commands, His rules, and His laws with all his heart and all his soul. He promised to do the words of the covenant written in this book.
He had everyone in Jerusalem and Benjamin stand and agree to it. The people of Jerusalem did what the covenant with God, the God of their ancestors, required.

Josiah removed all the detestable idols from all the land that belonged to the Israelites. He made everyone in Israel serve the the LORD their God. As long as he lived, they did not stop following the the LORD, the God of their ancestors.
Josiah kept a Passover to the the LORD in Jerusalem, and the Passover lamb was slaughtered on the fourteenth day of the first month.
He appointed the priests to their duties and encouraged them in the work of the house of the the LORD.

He said to the Levites who taught all Israel and who were holy to the the LORD, "Put the holy ark in the house that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built. It is not to be carried on your shoulders. Now serve the the LORD your God and His people Israel.
Prepare yourselves by families in your divisions, according to the instructions written by David king of Israel and by his son Solomon.
Stand in the holy place according to the groups of the families of your fellow countrymen, the lay people, and according to the divisions of the Levite families.
Slaughter the Passover lambs, make yourselves holy, and prepare the lambs for your fellow countrymen, so they may observe the Passover according to the word of the the LORD given through Moses."
From his own possessions Josiah contributed to the lay people, to all who were present, 30,000 lambs and goats for the Passover offerings, and 3,000 bulls.

His officials also contributed willingly to the people, priests, and Levites. Hilkiah, Zechariah, and Jehiel, the chief officials of the house of God, gave the priests 2,600 Passover offerings and 300 bulls.
Additionally, Conaniah and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethanel, along with Hashabiah, Jeiel, and Jozabad, the leaders of the Levites, contributed 5,000 Passover offerings and 500 bulls to the Levites.
So the service was ready; the priests stood in their places and the Levites in their divisions according to the king's command.
They slaughtered the Passover lambs, and the priests splashed the blood, while the Levites skinned the animals.
They set aside the burnt offerings to give them to the divisions of the families of the people to offer to the the LORD, as it is written in the Book of Moses; and they did the same with the bulls.
They roasted the Passover animals over the fire according to the rule, and boiled the holy offerings in pots, cauldrons, and pans, and brought them quickly to all the lay people.

Afterward, they made preparations for themselves and for the priests, because the priests, the descendants of Aaron, were busy from morning till night offering the burnt offerings and the fat portions. So the Levites made preparations for themselves and for the priests, the descendants of Aaron.

The singers, the descendants of Asaph, were at their stations according to the command of David, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun the king's seer. The gatekeepers at each gate did not need to leave their posts, because their fellow Levites made preparations for them.
So all the service of the the LORD was carried out that day to celebrate the Passover and to offer burnt offerings on the altar of the the LORD, according to the command of King Josiah.
The Israelites who were present also celebrated the Passover at that time, as well as the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days.

No such Passover had been observed in Israel since the days of Samuel the prophet; none of the kings of Israel had ever celebrated such a Passover as did Josiah, together with the priests, Levites, all Judah and Israel who were present, and the people living in Jerusalem.
This Passover was observed in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign.
After all this, when Josiah had set the temple in order, Neco king of Egypt marched up to fight at Carchemish on the Euphrates, and Josiah went out to meet him.

But Neco sent messengers to him, saying, "What is the issue between you and me, O king of Judah? I have not come against you today, but I am fighting another kingdom. God has told me to hurry. Stop opposing God, who is with me, or He will destroy you."
But Josiah did not turn away from him; instead, he disguised himself to fight. He did not listen to Neco's words from the mouth of God, but went to fight in the Valley of Megiddo.
There the archers shot King Josiah, who said to his servants, "Take me away, for I am badly wounded!"

So his servants took him out of his chariot, put him in his second chariot, and brought him to Jerusalem, where he died. He was buried in the tombs of his fathers, and all Judah and Jerusalem mourned for Josiah.
Then Jeremiah mourned for Josiah, and to this day all the singing men and women speak of Josiah in their sad songs. They made this a custom in Israel, and indeed they are written in the Laments.
As for the rest of the acts of Josiah, along with his deeds of faithful love, they are written in the Law of the the LORD.
And his first and last acts are written in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah.
The people of the land took Jehoahaz son of Josiah and made him king in Jerusalem in place of his father.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three years old when he became king, and he reigned three months in Jerusalem.
The king of Egypt removed him from office in Jerusalem and made the land pay a fine of one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold.
Then the king of Egypt made Eliakim, Jehoahaz's brother, king over Judah and Jerusalem. He changed Eliakim's name to Jehoiakim. He also took Jehoahaz to Egypt.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem. He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD his God.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up against him. He bound Jehoiakim with bronze chains and took him to Babylon.
Nebuchadnezzar also carried some of the articles from the house of the the LORD to Babylon and put them in his temple there.
The rest of the acts of Jehoiakim, the wicked things he did, and what happened to him are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah. His son Jehoiachin became king in his place.
Jehoiachin was eight years old when he became king, and he reigned three months and ten days in Jerusalem. He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD.

At the turn of the year, King Nebuchadnezzar sent for him and brought him to Babylon, along with the valuable articles from the house of the the LORD. He made Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's brother, king over Judah and Jerusalem.
Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.
He did evil in the eyes of the the LORD his God and did not humble himself before Jeremiah the prophet, who spoke for the the LORD.
He also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear an oath before God. Zedekiah stiffened his neck and hardened his heart instead of turning to the the LORD, the God of Israel.

All the leaders of the priests and the people became more and more unfaithful, following all the disgusting practices of the other nations. They defiled the house of the the LORD, which He had set apart as holy in Jerusalem.
The The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent warnings to them through His messengers again and again, because He had pity on His people and on His dwelling place.
But they mocked God's messengers, ignored His words, and laughed at His prophets. This went on until the wrath of the the LORD against His people grew so great that there was no healing.

So He brought up against them the king of the Chaldeans, who killed their young men with the sword even in the sanctuary. He showed no pity for young men or young women, for the old or the weak. The the LORD gave everything into his hand.

He carried to Babylon all the articles from God's house, both large and small, and the treasures of the the LORD's? Wait no. Need fix: treasures of the the LORD's? The span must wrap "the LORD" only, not possessive? Instruction: tetragrammaton rendered as span. If possessive, maybe the LORD's. We can avoid possessive by "the treasures of the house of the LORD". Let's adjust.
He carried to Babylon all the articles from God's house, both large and small, and the treasures of the house of the the LORD, the king, and his officials.
They burned God's house, tore down Jerusalem's wall, burned all its palaces, and destroyed all its valuable objects.
He took into exile in Babylon those who survived the sword. They became servants to him and his sons until the kingdom of Persia took over.
This happened so that the word of the the LORD spoken through Jeremiah would be fulfilled. The land finally enjoyed its Sabbath rests. It lay empty and kept its Sabbaths for seventy years.

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, to fulfill the word of the the LORD spoken by Jeremiah, the the LORD stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia. Cyrus made a proclamation throughout his whole kingdom and also put it in writing. He said:

"Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has appointed me to build a house for Him in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who among you of all His people? May the the LORD his God be with him, and let him go up."

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, the LORD carried out the word He had spoken through Jeremiah. The LORD stirred the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, and Cyrus sent a message through all his kingdom. Cyrus also put it in writing:
“This is what Cyrus king of Persia says: ‘The LORD, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth and has appointed me to build a house for Him in Jerusalem in Judah.
Whoever among you belongs to His people, may his God be with him, and may he go up to Jerusalem in Judah and build the house of the LORD, the God of Israel. He is the God who is in Jerusalem.
And let every survivor, wherever he lives, be helped by the men of his area with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, along with a freewill offering for the house of God in Jerusalem.’”
Then the family leaders of Judah and Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites rose up. God had stirred the spirit of each of them, and they went up to build the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.
All their neighbors supported them with silver and gold items, goods, livestock, and costly gifts, in addition to all the freewill offerings.
King Cyrus brought out the articles from the house of the LORD that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from Jerusalem and placed in the house of his god.
Cyrus king of Persia had Mithredath the treasurer bring them out and count them to Sheshbazzar, the leader of Judah.
There were 30 gold basins, 1,000 silver basins, and 29 silver utensils.
There were also 30 gold bowls, 410 silver bowls of a second kind, and 1,000 other articles.
In all, there were 5,400 gold and silver articles. Sheshbazzar brought all of them when the exiles went up from Babylon to Jerusalem.
These are the people of the province who came up from captivity after King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon carried them away to Babylon. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispar, Bigvai, Rehum, and Baanah. This is the number of the Israelite men:
The descendants of Pahath-moab, through the lines of Jeshua and Joab, 2,812.
The descendants of Ater, through Hezekiah, 98.
The people of Kiriath-arim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743.
The people of Ramah and Geba, 621.
The people of Bethel and Ai, 223.
The people of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 725.
The priests: the descendants of Jedaiah, through the family of Jeshua, 973.
The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua and Kadmiel, through Hodaviah, 74.
The singers: the descendants of Asaph, 128.
The gatekeepers: the descendants of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai, 139.
The temple servants: the descendants of Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth,
The descendants of Solomon's servants: Sotai, Hassophereth, Peruda,
All the temple servants and the descendants of Solomon's servants totaled 392.
These are the people who came up from Tel Melah, Tel Harsha, Cherub, Addan, and Immer, but they could not prove their fathers' houses or their descent to show they were Israelites:
the descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, 652.
From the priests: the descendants of Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, who married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and took their name.
They searched for their family records but could not find them, so they were removed from the priesthood.
The governor told them not to eat the most holy food until a priest could decide the matter with the Urim and Thummim.
Besides these were 7,337 male and female servants, and 200 male and female singers.
When they arrived at the house of the LORD in Jerusalem, some family leaders gave freewill offerings to rebuild God's house on its site.
They gave as much as they could: 61,000 gold darics, 5,000 silver minas, and 100 priestly garments for the treasury.
The priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and some of the people settled in their own towns, and all Israel settled in their towns.
In the seventh month, the Israelites had settled in their towns, and the people gathered in Jerusalem as one man.

Then Jeshua son of Jozadak, his fellow priests, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and his brothers began to build the altar of the God of Israel so they could offer burnt offerings on it, just as it is written in the Law of Moses, the man of God.
Even though they were afraid of the peoples around them, they set the altar on its foundations and offered burnt offerings on it to the LORD, morning and evening.
They celebrated the Festival of Booths just as it is written, offering the daily burnt offerings in the right number for each day.
After that, they offered the regular burnt offering, the new moon offerings, and all the appointed feasts of the LORD. They also offered every freewill offering brought to the LORD.
They began to offer burnt offerings to the LORD on the first day of the seventh month, even though the foundation of the LORD's temple had not yet been laid.

They gave money to the stonecutters and carpenters, and food, drink, and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre, so the cedar logs from Lebanon could be brought by sea to Joppa, as King Cyrus of Persia had allowed.

In the second month of the second year after they came to the house of God in Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Jeshua son of Jozadak, and the rest of their brothers, the priests and Levites, and all who had returned from captivity to Jerusalem began the work. They appointed Levites twenty years old and older to oversee the work on the house of the LORD.
Jeshua, his sons and brothers, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, and the sons of Henadad with their sons and brothers, the Levites, stood together to supervise the workers on the house of God.

When the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the LORD, the priests in their robes stood with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, stood with cymbals to praise the LORD, as David, king of Israel, had directed.

They sang, praising and thanking the LORD: “He is good; His faithful love to Israel lasts forever.” Then all the people shouted a loud shout of praise to the LORD because the foundation of the house of the LORD had been laid.
But many of the older priests, Levites, and family leaders who had seen the first temple wept loudly when they saw the foundation of this temple laid. Many others shouted with joy.
The people could not tell the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people were shouting so loudly. The sound was heard far away.
When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the people who had been taken into exile were building a temple for the LORD, the God of Israel,

they came to Zerubbabel and the family leaders and said, "Let us build with you, for we seek your God just as you do, and we have sacrificed to Him since the days of Esarhaddon, king of Assyria, who brought us here."

But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other family leaders told them, "You have no share with us in building a house for our God. We will build it ourselves for the LORD, the God of Israel, just as King Cyrus of Persia commanded us."
Then the people of the land discouraged the people of Judah and made them afraid to build.
They also hired counselors to work against them and frustrate their plans all the days of King Cyrus of Persia, and until the reign of King Darius of Persia.
At the beginning of the reign of King Ahasuerus, they wrote an accusation against the people living in Judah and Jerusalem.
In the days of King Artaxerxes of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their associates wrote to King Artaxerxes. The letter was written in Aramaic and translated.
Rehum the commander and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to King Artaxerxes in this way:
Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates—the Dinaites, Apharsathchites, Tarpelites, Apharsites, Arkvites, Babylonians, Susanchites, Dehavites, Elamites,
and the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Osnappar brought over and settled in the cities of Samaria and in the rest of the region beyond the River—wrote this letter.
This is a copy of the letter they sent to him:

"Let it be known to the king that the Jews who came up from you to us have gone to Jerusalem. They are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are finishing its walls and repairing its foundations.
Let it now be known to the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are completed, they will not pay tribute, taxes, or tolls, and the royal revenue will suffer.
Now, because we serve the king and do not want to see him dishonored, we are sending this to inform the king.

Let a search be made in the records of your ancestors. In those records you will find that this city has long been rebellious and harmful to kings and provinces. Uprisings have been stirred up in it since ancient times. That is why this city was destroyed.
We are informing the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls are completed, you will have no share in the region beyond the River."
King Artaxerxes sent this reply to Rehum the commander, Shimshai the scribe, and their associates in Samaria and the rest of the region beyond the River:
"Greetings. Peace be with you. The letter you sent has been read clearly in my presence.
I ordered a search, and it was found that this city has risen up against kings for a long time. Rebellion and revolt have been made in it.
Powerful kings have ruled over Jerusalem and governed the whole region beyond the River, and tribute, taxes, and tolls were paid to them.
Now issue an order to stop these men. This city must not be rebuilt until I give further orders.
Be careful not to neglect this matter. Why should the damage increase and harm the kings?"
When the copy of the letter was read before Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates, they hurried to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop by force.
Then the work on the house of God in Jerusalem stopped until the second year of the reign of King Darius of Persia.
The prophets Haggai and Zechariah son of Iddo prophesied to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem. They spoke in the name of the God of Israel.
Then Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak began to rebuild the house of God in Jerusalem. The prophets of God were with them and helped them.
At that time Tattenai, the governor of the province Beyond the River, Shethar-boznai, and their associates came to the builders and said, “Who gave you permission to build this house and finish it?”
Then we asked them, “What are the names of the men who are building this building?”
But God was watching over the Jewish leaders, so no one stopped them until the report reached King Darius and an answer came back.
This is a copy of the letter that Tattenai, governor of Beyond the River, Shethar-boznai, and their associates, the officials in the province Beyond the River, sent to King Darius.
They sent this report to him, and it said, “To King Darius: Peace and prosperity.

Let it be known to the king that we went to the province of Judah, to the house of the great God. It is being built with large stones, and timber is being placed in the walls. The work is moving forward quickly and is going well for them.
Then we asked those leaders, ‘Who gave you permission to build this house and finish it?’
We also asked for their names, so we could report to you the names of the men in charge. “‘
We are servants of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the house that was built many years ago. A great king of Israel built and finished it.
