But because our ancestors angered the God of heaven, He handed them over to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean. He destroyed this house and carried the people away to Babylon.
In the first year of King Cyrus of Babylon, King Cyrus issued a decree to rebuild this house of God.

He also brought out from the temple in Babylon the gold and silver objects that belonged to the house of God. Nebuchadnezzar had taken them from the temple in Jerusalem and brought them to Babylon. King Cyrus gave them to a man named Sheshbazzar, whom he had appointed governor. “‘
He told him, “Take these objects and go put them in the temple in Jerusalem. Let the house of God be rebuilt on its original site.” “‘
Then Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem. From that time until now it has been under construction, but it is not yet finished.’ “

Now if it pleases the king, let a search be made in the royal archives in Babylon to see whether King Cyrus really did issue a decree to rebuild this house of God in Jerusalem. Then let the king send us his decision about this.”
Then King Darius gave an order, and they searched in the archives in Babylon, where the records were kept.
A scroll was found in the fortress at Ecbatana in the province of Media. This is what was written in it:

“In the first year of King Cyrus, King Cyrus gave an order about God's house in Jerusalem: Let the house be rebuilt as a place where sacrifices are offered. Let its foundations be firmly laid. It is to be sixty cubits high and sixty cubits wide.
It is to have three layers of large stones and one layer of new timber. The cost is to be paid from the king's treasury.

Also, the gold and silver items from God's house that Nebuchadnezzar took from the temple in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon must be returned. They are to be taken back to the temple in Jerusalem and put in their place in God's house.”
“Now, Tattenai, governor of the province beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and your associates, the officials in that province: Stay away from there.
Leave the work on this house of God alone. Let the governor of the Jews and the Jewish elders rebuild this house of God on its site.

“I also give this order about what you are to do for those Jewish elders as they rebuild this house of God: Pay them in full from the king's treasury, from the taxes of the province beyond the River, so the work does not stop.

Give them whatever they need—bulls, rams, and lambs for burnt offerings to the God of heaven, plus wheat, salt, wine, and oil—just as the priests in Jerusalem ask. Give it to them every day without fail.
Then they can offer pleasing sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons.
“I also decree that if anyone changes this order, a beam will be pulled from his house and he will be impaled on it. His house will be made a pile of rubble.

May the God who has caused His name to dwell there overthrow any king or people who lifts a hand to change this or to destroy this house of God in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have issued this decree. Let it be carried out with diligence.”
Then Tattenai, governor of the province beyond the River, Shethar-bozenai, and their associates carried out the decree diligently, just as King Darius had ordered.

The Jewish elders built and were successful, encouraged by the preaching of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah son of Iddo. They finished building by the command of the God of Israel and by the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, king of Persia.
This temple was completed on the third day of the month Adar, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius.
Then the people of Israel—the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the exiles—celebrated the dedication of this house of God with joy.
For the dedication of this house of God, they offered one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering for all Israel, one for each tribe.
They also appointed the priests to their divisions and the Levites to their groups to serve God in Jerusalem, as written in the Book of Moses.
On the fourteenth day of the first month, the exiles celebrated the Passover.
The priests and Levites had purified themselves, and all of them were clean. They slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their fellow priests, and for themselves.
The Israelites who had returned from exile ate it, along with everyone who had separated himself from the unclean practices of the peoples of the land to seek the LORD, the God of Israel.

They observed the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because the LORD had made them joyful and had turned the heart of the king of Assyria toward them, strengthening their hands for the work on the house of God, the God of Israel.
After these things, during the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra son of Seraiah, son of Azariah, son of Hilkiah,
son of Shallum, son of Zadok, son of Ahitub,
son of Amariah, son of Azariah, son of Meraioth,
son of Zerahiah, son of Uzzi, son of Bukki,
son of Abishua, son of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the chief priest.

This Ezra came up from Babylon. He was a skilled scribe in the Law of Moses, which the LORD, the God of Israel, had given. The king gave him everything he asked for, because the hand of the LORD his God was on him.
In the seventh year of King Artaxerxes, Ezra went up to Jerusalem with some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants.
He arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of the seventh year of the king.
He had started the trip from Babylon on the first day of the first month, and he reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month, because the good hand of his God was on him.
For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the LORD, to obey it, and to teach its rules and decisions in Israel.
This is a copy of the letter that King Artaxerxes gave to Ezra the priest, the scribe, who understood the words of the LORD's commands and rules for Israel:
“Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven: Greetings.
“I make a decree that any of the people of Israel in my kingdom, including their priests and Levites, who wants to go to Jerusalem with you, may go.
You are sent by the king and his seven counselors to check on Judah and Jerusalem, using the Law of your God that is in your hand.
You are to take the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely given to the God of Israel, whose home is in Jerusalem.
Take also all the silver and gold you find in the whole province of Babylon, along with the freewill offerings of the people and priests for the house of their God in Jerusalem.
“With this money, buy bulls, rams, and lambs, along with their grain offerings and drink offerings, and offer them on the altar of the house of your God in Jerusalem.
You and your brothers may do whatever seems best to you with the rest of the silver and gold, according to the will of your God.
“Deliver to the God of Jerusalem the articles given to you for worship in the house of your God.
You may take any other needs for the house of your God from the royal treasury.
I, King Artaxerxes, give this order to all the treasurers in the province west of the Euphrates: Give Ezra the priest, the scribe of the Law of the God of heaven, everything he asks for,
up to one hundred talents of silver, one hundred cors of wheat, one hundred baths of wine, one hundred baths of olive oil, and salt without limit.
Whatever the God of heaven commands must be done fully for the house of the God of heaven, so that wrath will not come on the kingdom of the king and his sons.
We also tell you that no tax, tribute, or toll may be collected from any of the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, or other workers of this house of God.

And you, Ezra, using the wisdom of your God that is in your hand, appoint judges and officials to govern all the people in the province west of the Euphrates—all who know the laws of your God. Teach those who do not know them.
Anyone who does not obey the Law of your God and the law of the king must be punished quickly—by death, banishment, loss of property, or prison.”
Blessed be the LORD, the God of our fathers, who put this in the king's heart to honor the house of the LORD in Jerusalem.

He also showed me kindness before the king, his counselors, and all the king's powerful officials. Because the hand of the LORD my God was on me, I gained courage and gathered leaders from Israel to go up with me.
These are the family leaders and their family records of the people who came back with me from Babylon while King Artaxerxes ruled.
From the sons of Phinehas, Gershom; from the sons of Ithamar, Daniel; from the sons of David, Hattush.
From the sons of Shecaniah, from the sons of Parosh, Zechariah, and with him were listed 150 men.
From the sons of Pahath-Moab, Eliehoenai son of Zerahiah, and with him 200 men.
From the sons of Shecaniah, the son of Jahaziel, and with him 300 men.
From the sons of Adin, Ebed son of Jonathan, and with him 50 men.
From the sons of Elam, Isaiah son of Athaliah, and with him 70 men.
From the sons of Shephatiah, Zebadiah son of Michael, and with him 80 men.
From the sons of Joab, Obadiah son of Jehiel, and with him 218 men.
From the sons of Shelomith, the son of Josiphiah, and with him 160 men.
From the sons of Bebai, Zechariah son of Bebai, and with him 28 men.
From the sons of Azgad, Johanan son of Hakkatan, and with him 110 men.
From the last of the sons of Adonikam, these were their names: Eliphelet, Jeiel, and Shemaiah, and with them 60 men.
From the sons of Bigvai, Uthai and Zabbud, and with them 70 men.
I gathered them at the river that flows to Ahava, and we camped there three days. I looked over the people and the priests, but I found no Levites there.
So I sent for these leaders: Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and Meshullam. I also sent for Joiarib and Elnathan, who were teachers.
I sent them to Iddo, the leader at Casiphia. I told them exactly what to say to Iddo and his relatives, the temple servants at Casiphia, so they would bring us workers for the house of our God.
Because the gracious hand of our God was on us, they brought us Sherebiah, a wise and thoughtful man, from the sons of Mahli son of Levi son of Israel, along with his sons and brothers, 18 men.
They also brought Hashabiah and with him Jeshaiah from the sons of Merari, along with his brothers and their sons, 20 men.
They also brought 220 temple servants, whom David and the leaders had assigned to help the Levites. All of them were listed by name.
There by the Ahava River I called for a fast, so we could humble ourselves before our God and ask Him for a safe journey for us, our children, and all our possessions.

I was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road, because we had told the king, "The hand of our God is good to all who seek Him, but His power and anger are against all who forsake Him."
So we fasted and prayed to our God about this, and He answered us.
Then I set apart twelve of the leading priests, along with Sherebiah, Hashabiah, and ten of their brothers.
I weighed out to them the silver, gold, and articles that the king, his advisers, his officials, and all the Israelites present had given for the house of our God.
I weighed out 650 talents of silver, 100 talents of silver articles, and 100 talents of gold.
I also weighed out 20 gold bowls worth 1,000 darics, and two fine bronze articles as valuable as gold.
I said to them, "You are holy to the the LORD, and these articles are holy. The silver and gold are a freewill offering to the the LORD, the God of your fathers."
Guard them carefully until you weigh them in the rooms of the house of the the LORD in Jerusalem before the leading priests, Levites, and family leaders of Israel.
So the priests and Levites took charge of the silver, gold, and articles to carry them to Jerusalem, to the house of our God.
On the twelfth day of the first month we left the Ahava River to go to Jerusalem. The hand of our God was on us, and He protected us from enemies and ambushes along the way.
We arrived in Jerusalem and rested there three days.

On the fourth day, in the house of our God, we weighed the silver, gold, and articles into the hands of Meremoth son of Uriah the priest, along with Eleazar son of Phinehas, and the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui.
Everything was counted and weighed, and the total weight was recorded at that time.

The exiles who had returned from captivity offered burnt offerings to the God of Israel: twelve bulls for all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-seven lambs, and twelve male goats as a sin offering. All of this was a burnt offering to the the LORD.
They also gave the king's orders to the royal officials and governors west of the Euphrates, and these officials supported the people and the house of God.

After these things, when the leaders had finished their work, they came to me and said, "The people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, have not kept themselves separate from the peoples of the lands. They have followed the disgusting practices of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites.

They have taken some of their daughters as wives for themselves and their sons. So the holy seed has mixed with the peoples of the lands. Even worse, the officials and leaders were the first to do this."
When I heard this, I tore my clothes and my robe. I pulled hair from my head and beard, and I sat there shocked.
Everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel gathered around me because of the sin of the exiles. I sat there shocked until the evening sacrifice.
At the evening sacrifice, I rose from my fasting with my clothes and robe torn. I fell to my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God.
I said, "O my God, I am too ashamed and disgraced to lift up my face to You, my God, because our sins are piled higher than our heads and our guilt has reached the heavens.

Since the days of our ancestors, we have been deeply guilty. Because of our sins, we, our kings, and our priests have been handed over to the kings of other lands. We have faced the sword, captivity, robbery, and public shame, just as we do today.

But now, for a short time, the LORD our God has shown us grace. He has left us a remnant and given us a secure place in His holy place. Our God has given us new hope and a little strength in our slavery.

We are slaves, but our God has not abandoned us in our slavery. He has shown us kindness before the kings of Persia. He gave us new life to rebuild the house of our God, repair its ruins, and give us a protective wall in Judah and Jerusalem.
And now, our God, what can we say after all this? We have disobeyed Your commands.

"You commanded us through Your servants the prophets, 'The land you are entering to take is unclean. The people of those lands have filled it with their unclean practices and disgusting actions from one end to the other.'

'So do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take their daughters for your sons. Do not seek their peace or prosperity forever. Then you will be strong, enjoy the good things of the land, and leave it to your children forever.'
After all that has happened to us because of our evil deeds and great guilt, You, our God, have punished us less than we deserved. You have left us this remnant.
Should we break Your commands again and marry into these peoples who do such disgusting things? Would You not be angry enough to destroy us completely, leaving no remnant or escape?
O the LORD, God of Israel, You are righteous. That is why we are left as a remnant today. Here we are before You in our guilt. No one can stand before You because of this."

While Ezra was praying and confessing, weeping and throwing himself down before the house of God, a very large crowd of Israelites—men, women, and children—gathered around him. The people wept bitterly.

Then Shecaniah son of Jehiel, one of the descendants of Elam, spoke up to Ezra: "We have been unfaithful to our God. We have married foreign women from the peoples of the land. But even now there is hope for Israel in this.

So now let us make a covenant with our God to send away all these women and their children, following the advice of my lord and of those who fear the command of our God. Let it be done according to the Law.
Get up, because this matter is your responsibility. We are with you. Be strong and do it."
Then Ezra rose and made the leading priests, the Levites, and all Israel swear an oath to do this. They swore.

Then Ezra got up from in front of the house of God and went to the room of Jehohanan son of Eliashib. He did not eat bread or drink water there, because he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles.
A proclamation was sent throughout Judah and Jerusalem to all the exiles to gather in Jerusalem.
Anyone who did not come within three days would have all his property taken away and would be removed from the assembly of the exiles.

So within three days all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered in Jerusalem. It was the twentieth day of the ninth month. All the people sat in the square in front of the house of God, shaking with fear because of this matter and because of the heavy rain.
Then Ezra the priest stood up and said to them, "You have been unfaithful. You have married foreign women and added to Israel's guilt.
Now confess to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the peoples of the land and from your foreign wives."
The whole assembly answered in a loud voice, "We will do exactly as you say."
But the people said, "It is the rainy season. We cannot stand outside, and this is not a one- or two-day job, because many of us have sinned in this matter.

Let our leaders stand for the whole assembly. Let everyone in our towns who has married a foreign woman come at the set times, along with the elders and judges of each town, until the fierce anger of our God over this matter is turned away."
Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah opposed this plan. Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite supported them.
So the exiles did this. Ezra the priest chose men who were heads of families, all listed by name. They sat down on the tenth day of the tenth month to look into the matter.
They finished dealing with all the men who had married foreign women by the first day of the first month.
Among the priests, men were found who had married foreign women: from the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah.
They promised to send their wives away, and each man brought a ram from the flock as a guilt offering for his sin.
From the descendants of Immer: Hanani and Zebadiah.
From the descendants of Harim: Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel, and Uzziah.
From the descendants of Pashhur: Elioenai, Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethanel, Jozabad, and Elasah.
From the Levites: Jozabad, Shimei, Kelaiah (that is, Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah, and Eliezer.
From the singers: Eliashib. From the gatekeepers: Shallum, Telem, and Uri.
From the people of Israel: from the descendants of Parosh: Ramiah, Izziah, Malchijah, Mijamin, Eleazar, Malchijah, and Benaiah.
From the descendants of Elam: Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi, Jeremoth, and Elijah.
From the descendants of Zattu: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad, and Aziza.
From the descendants of Bebai: Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai, and Athlai.
From the descendants of Bani: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal, and Jeremoth.
From the descendants of Pahath-moab: Adna, Chelal, Benaiah, Maaseiah, Mattaniah, Bezalel, Binnui, and Manasseh.
From the descendants of Harim: Eliezer, Isshijah, Malchijah, Shemaiah, and Shimeon.
From the descendants of Benjamin: Malluch and Shemariah.
From the descendants of Hashum: Mattenai, Mattattah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh, and Shimei.
From the descendants of Bani: Maadai, Amram, and Uel.
From the descendants of Nebo: Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jaddai, Joel, and Benaiah.
All these had married foreign women, and some of them had children by these wives.
These are the words of Nehemiah son of Hacaliah. In the month of Kislev, in the twentieth year, I was in the fortress at Susa.
Hanani, one of my brothers, came with some men from Judah. I asked them about the Jews who had survived the exile and about Jerusalem.
They said to me, “Those who survived the exile and are back in the province are in great trouble and disgrace. Jerusalem's wall is broken down, and its gates have been burned with fire.”
When I heard these things, I sat down and wept. For some days I mourned and fasted and prayed before the God of heaven.
I said, “O LORD, God of heaven, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of love with those who love Him and keep His commands.

Let Your eyes be open and Your ears attentive to hear the prayer Your servant is praying before You day and night for Your servants, the people of Israel. I confess the sins we Israelites, including myself and my father's family, have committed against You.
We have acted very wickedly toward You. We have not obeyed the commands, rules, and laws You gave Your servant Moses. “
Remember what You told Your servant Moses: ‘If you are unfaithful, I will scatter you among the nations.’

But if you return to Me and obey My commands, then even if your people are scattered to the ends of the earth, I will gather them from there and bring them to the place I chose for My name to dwell. “
They are Your servants and Your people, whom You redeemed by Your great power and Your mighty hand.

Lord, please let Your ear be attentive to the prayer of Your servant and to the prayer of Your servants who delight in honoring Your name. Give Your servant success today, and grant him mercy in the presence of this man.” Now I was the king's cupbearer.
In the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, wine was set before him. I took the wine and gave it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence before.
The king said to me, "Why is your face sad? You aren't sick. This can only be sadness of heart." I was very afraid.
I said to the king, "May the king live forever! Why shouldn't my face be sad when the city where my fathers are buried lies in ruins and its gates have been burned?"
The king said to me, "What are you seeking?" Then I prayed to the God of heaven.
I said to the king, "If it pleases the king, and if your servant has found favor with you, send me to Judah, to the city where my fathers are buried, so I can rebuild it."
The king, with the queen sitting beside him, asked me, "How long will your trip take, and when will you return?" It pleased the king to send me, and I set a time for him.
I also said to the king, "If it pleases the king, let letters be given to me for the governors beyond the River, so they will let me pass through until I reach Judah."

And give me a letter to Asaph, keeper of the king's forest, so he will give me timber to make beams for the gates of the fort by the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I will live in. The king granted these things because the good hand of my God was on me.
Then I came to the governors beyond the River and gave them the king's letters. The king had also sent army officers and horsemen with me.
When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite official heard about this, they were very upset that someone had come to seek the good of the people of Israel.
I came to Jerusalem and stayed there three days.
Then I got up during the night with a few men. I had not told anyone what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem. The only animal with me was the one I rode.
I went out at night through the Valley Gate toward the Dragon Spring and the Dung Gate, looking over the walls of Jerusalem. They were broken down, and the gates had been burned.
Then I went on to the Fountain Gate and the King's Pool, but there was no room for the animal under me to get through.
So I went up the valley at night and inspected the wall. Then I turned back and entered through the Valley Gate.
The officials did not know where I had gone or what I was doing. I had not yet told the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the officials, or anyone else who would do the work.
Then I said to them, "You see the trouble we are in. Jerusalem is in ruins, and its gates have been burned. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem so we will no longer be a disgrace."
I told them how the hand of my God had been good to me and what the king had said to me. They said, "Let us rise up and build." So they strengthened their hands to do the good work.
But when Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite, and Geshem the Arab heard about it, they mocked us and despised us. They said, "What is this you are doing? Are you rebelling against the king?"
I answered them, "The God of heaven will give us success. We, His servants, will rise up and build. But you have no part, right, or claim in Jerusalem."

Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate. They dedicated it and set its doors in place. They worked as far as the Tower of the Hundred and the Tower of Hananel, and they dedicated that part too.
The men of Jericho rebuilt the next section. Zakkur son of Imri rebuilt next to them.
The sons of Hassenaah rebuilt the Fish Gate. They put its beams, doors, bolts, and bars in place.
Next to them, Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired the wall. Meshullam son of Berechiah, son of Meshezabel, repaired next to him. Zadok son of Baana also repaired next to him.
The men of Tekoa repaired the next section. But their leaders did not help with the work their supervisors gave them.
Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired the Old Gate. They put its beams, doors, bolts, and bars in place.
Men from Gibeon and Mizpah repaired next to them. These included Melatiah of Gibeon and Jadon of Meronoth. Those towns were under the governor of the province west of the Euphrates River.
Uzziel son of Harhaiah, a goldsmith, repaired next to them. Hananiah, a perfume maker, repaired next to him. They rebuilt Jerusalem’s wall as far as the Broad Wall.
Rephaiah son of Hur, ruler of half of Jerusalem’s district, repaired next to them.
Jedaiah son of Harumaph repaired next to them, across from his house. Hattush son of Hashabneiah repaired next to him.
Malkijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-Moab repaired another section and the Tower of the Ovens.
Shallum son of Hallohesh, ruler of the other half of Jerusalem’s district, repaired next to them. He worked with his daughters.
Hanun and the people of Zanoah rebuilt the Valley Gate. They put its doors, bolts, and bars in place. They also repaired a thousand cubits of wall as far as the Dung Gate.
Malkijah son of Recab, ruler of the district of Beth Hakkerem, repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and put its doors, bolts, and bars in place.

Shallun son of Kol-Hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it, put a roof over it, and set its doors, bolts, and bars in place. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Siloam by the King’s Garden, as far as the steps going down from the City of David.
Nehemiah son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth Zur, repaired next to him. He worked up to the place across from David’s tombs, the artificial pool, and the House of the Heroes.
The Levites repaired next to him under Rehum son of Bani. Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, repaired next to him for his district.
Their fellow Levites repaired next to him under Binnui son of Henadad, ruler of the other half of the district of Keilah.
Ezer son of Jeshua, ruler of Mizpah, repaired another section next to him. He worked from the place across from the steps to the armory to the corner.
Baruch son of Zabbai eagerly repaired another section next to him. He worked from the corner to the entrance to the house of Eliashib the high priest.
Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired another section next to him. He worked from the entrance to Eliashib’s house to the end of it.
The priests from the surrounding region repaired next to him.
Benjamin and Hasshub repaired in front of their own house. Next to them, Azariah son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah, repaired beside his house.
Binnui son of Henadad repaired another section next to him. He worked from Azariah’s house to the corner.
Palal son of Uzai worked across from the corner and the tower that sticks out from the upper palace near the courtyard of the guard. Pedaiah son of Parosh worked next to him.
The temple servants who lived on the hill of Ophel made repairs next to them. They worked up to the place across from the Water Gate on the east and the tower that sticks out.
The men of Tekoa repaired another section next to them. They worked from the large tower that sticks out to the wall of Ophel.
Above the Horse Gate, the priests repaired, each in front of his own house.
Zadok son of Immer repaired next to them in front of his house. Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, the guard at the East Gate, repaired next to him.
Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, repaired another section next to him. Meshullam son of Berechiah repaired next to them in front of his living quarters.
Malkijah, one of the goldsmiths, repaired next to him as far as the house of the temple servants and the merchants. This was across from the Inspection Gate and as far as the room above the corner.
Between the room above the corner and the Sheep Gate, the goldsmiths and merchants repaired.
When Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he got angry and very upset. He mocked the Jews.

In front of his brothers and the army of Samaria, he said, "What are these weak Jews doing? Do they think they can rebuild it? Will they offer sacrifices? Can they finish in one day? Can they bring stones back to life from piles of burned rubble?"
Tobiah the Ammonite was standing beside him, and he said, "Even if a fox climbed on it, their stone wall would fall apart!"
Hear us, our God, because we are looked down on. Turn their insults back on them, and let them be plundered in a land where they are captives.
Do not cover up their guilt, and do not wipe away their sin from Your sight, because they have made You angry in front of the builders.
So we built the wall until all of it was joined together up to half its height, because the people were eager to work.
But when Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the people of Ashdod heard that the walls of Jerusalem were being repaired and that the gaps were being closed, they became very angry.
They all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and cause trouble there.
We prayed to our God and posted guards day and night to protect ourselves from them.
In Judah people were saying, "The workers are worn out, and there is too much rubble. We can't rebuild the wall by ourselves."
Our enemies said, "They won't know or see anything until we are right among them. Then we'll kill them and stop the work."
The Jews who lived near them came and told us ten times over, "Wherever you turn, they will attack us."
So I stationed people behind the lowest parts of the wall, at the open spots. I placed them by families, with their swords, spears, and bows.

After I looked things over, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, "Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome. Fight for your brothers, your sons, your daughters, your wives, and your homes."
When our enemies heard that we knew about their plan and that God had ruined it, we all went back to the wall, each to his own work.
From that day on, half of my men worked on the building, and half held the spears, shields, bows, and armor. The leaders stood behind all the people of Judah.
The builders and the carriers worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.
Each builder had his sword strapped at his side while he worked. The man who blew the trumpet stayed beside me.
I said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, "The work is big and spread out, and we are far apart on the wall.
Wherever you hear the trumpet sound, gather to us there. Our God will fight for us."
So we worked from dawn until the stars came out, while half of them held spears.
I also told the people at that time, "Let every man and his servant stay inside Jerusalem at night. Then they can guard us at night and work during the day."
Neither I, nor my brothers, nor my servants, nor the guards with me took off our clothes. Each man kept his weapon with him, even when he went for water.
About that time, the people and their wives raised a loud complaint against their fellow Jews.
Some said, "We have many sons and daughters. We need grain so we can eat and stay alive."
Others said, "We are pledging our fields, vineyards, and homes to get grain during the famine."
Still others said, "We have borrowed money to pay the king's tax on our fields and vineyards."

Then some said, "We are from the same family as our fellow Jews, and our children are just as good as theirs. Yet we are forcing our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters are already slaves, but we can do nothing because our fields and vineyards belong to others."
When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I became very angry.
After thinking it over, I rebuked the nobles and officials. I said to them, "You are charging interest to your own brothers!" Then I called a large meeting against them.

I said, "We have done our best to buy back our Jewish brothers who were sold to other nations. Now you are selling your own brothers, and they would have to be bought back by us." They were silent because they had nothing to say.
So I said, "What you are doing is wrong. Shouldn't you live in fear of our God so our enemies from other nations won't mock us?
I and my brothers and my servants are also lending them money and grain. Please, let's stop charging this interest.
Please restore to them this very day their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses, along with the interest on the money, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been taking from them."
"We will restore it," they replied, "and we won't take anything more from them. We will do as you say." Then I summoned the priests and made them swear to do as they had promised.

I also shook out the folds of my robe and said, "May God shake out of his house and property every man who doesn't keep this promise. May he be shaken out and left with nothing!" Then the whole assembly said, "Amen," and praised the the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.

Also, from the day King Artaxerxes appointed me governor of Judah, from his twentieth year to his thirty-second year—twelve years in all—neither I nor my brothers ate the food allowed for the governor.

The earlier governors before me had made life hard for the people. They took bread and wine from them, plus forty shekels of silver. Their servants also ruled over the people. But I didn't do that, because I feared God.
Instead, I devoted myself to the work on this wall, and my servants were gathered there to work. We didn't buy any land.
There were 150 Jews and officials at my table, along with visitors from the surrounding nations.

Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and some birds were prepared for me. Every ten days there was plenty of wine of all kinds. Yet I didn't ask for the food allowed for the governor, because the people were already carrying a heavy load.
Remember me kindly, my God, for all I have done for this people.
When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies heard that I had rebuilt the wall and that no gap was left in it—though I had not yet put doors in the gates—
Sanballat and Geshem sent me this message: "Come, let us meet together in one of the villages in the plain of Ono." But they were planning to harm me.
I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?"
Four times they sent me the same message, and I answered them the same way.
The fifth time, Sanballat sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand.

It said, "It is reported among the nations—and Gashmu says it—that you and the Jews are planning to rebel. That is why you are building the wall. You are also to be their king, according to these reports.
You have also set up prophets in Jerusalem to proclaim about you, 'A king is in Judah.' Now these things will be reported to the king. So come now, and let us talk together."
I sent back this reply: "No such things as you say have been done. You are inventing them in your own mind."
For they were all trying to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done." But now, strengthen my hands.

I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was confined. He said, "Let us meet in the house of God, inside the temple, and let us close the temple doors, for they are coming to kill you—by night they are coming to kill you."
I answered, "Should a man like me run away? What man like me could go into the temple and live? I will not go in."
Then I realized that God had not sent him. He had spoken this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him.
He was hired to frighten me into sinning, so they could give me a bad name and discredit me.
"My God, remember Tobiah and Sanballat for what they have done, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who were trying to frighten me."
So the wall was completed on the twenty-fifth day of Elul, in fifty-two days.
When all our enemies heard about this, all the nations around us were afraid and lost their confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God.
Also in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and letters from Tobiah came to them.
For many in Judah were bound to him by oath, because he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.
They also kept telling me about his good deeds and reporting my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to frighten me.
When the wall was finished and the doors were set in place, Nehemiah appointed the gatekeepers, singers, and Levites.
He put his brother Hanani and Hananiah, the commander of the citadel, in charge of Jerusalem, because Hananiah was a faithful man who feared God more than most people.

He told them, "Do not open the gates of Jerusalem until noon. While the gatekeepers are still on duty, have them shut and bar the doors. Also appoint guards from the people of Jerusalem, each at his post and each near his own house."
The city was large and spacious, but few people lived in it, and the houses had not yet been rebuilt.

My God put it into my heart to gather the nobles, the officials, and the people so they could be listed by family. I found the family records of those who had first returned, and this is what was written in them.
These are the people of the province who returned from exile. Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, had carried them away, but they came back to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah. Here is the number of the men of Israel:
The sons of Pahath-moab, through the line of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818.
The sons of Ater, through Hezekiah, 98.
The men of Bethlehem and Netophah, 188.
The men of Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, 743.
The men of Ramah and Geba, 621.
The men of Bethel and Ai, 123.
The men of the other Nebo, 52.
The sons of the other Elam, 1,254.
The sons of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, 721.
The priests: the sons of Jedaiah, from the family of Jeshua, 973;
The Levites: the sons of Jeshua, through Kadmiel, from the line of Hodevah, 74.
The singers: the sons of Asaph, 148.
The gatekeepers: the sons of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita, and Shobai, 138.
The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth,
The sons of Solomon's servants: Sotai, Sophereth, Perida,
All the temple servants and the sons of Solomon's servants totaled 392.
Some people came up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they could not prove their family lines or show that they were Israelites.
They were the sons of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, 642 in all.
Some priests also could not prove their family line: the sons of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, who had married a daughter of Barzillai the Gileadite and took that family's name.
They searched the family records, but their names were not found, so they were not allowed to serve as priests.
The governor told them, "Do not eat any of the most holy things until a priest can use the Urim and Thummim to decide the matter."
Besides them, there were 7,337 male and female servants, and 245 singers, men and women.
Some of the family leaders gave money for the work. The governor gave 1,000 darics of gold, 50 bowls, and 530 priestly garments to the treasury.
Other family leaders gave 20,000 darics of gold and 2,200 minas of silver to the treasury.
The rest of the people gave 20,000 darics of gold, 2,000 minas of silver, and 67 priestly garments.

The priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and some of the people, along with all Israel, settled in their towns. When the seventh month came, the people of Israel were living in their towns.
All the people gathered as one man in the square in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, which the LORD had commanded for Israel.
So on the first day of the seventh month, Ezra the priest brought the Law before the men and women and everyone else who could understand.
He read from it from early morning until noon in the square in front of the Water Gate, to the men, women, and those who could understand. All the people listened closely to the Book of the Law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform made for this. Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah stood on his right. Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam stood on his left.
Ezra opened the book where all the people could see it, because he was above them. When he opened it, all the people stood up.
Ezra praised the LORD, the great God, and all the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” as they raised their hands. Then they bowed down and worshiped the LORD with their faces to the ground.

The Levites—Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the other Levites—helped the people understand the Law while the people stayed in their places.
They read from the Book of the Law of God clearly. They explained it so the people could understand what was read.

Nehemiah the governor, Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were teaching the people said to all the people, “This day is holy to the LORD your God. Do not mourn or weep.” All the people were weeping because they heard the words of the Law.

Then he said to them, “Go, eat rich food, drink something sweet, and send portions to those who have nothing ready. This day is holy to our Lord. Do not be sad, for the joy of the LORD is your strength.”
So the Levites calmed all the people. They said, “Be still, for the day is holy. Do not be sad.”
Then all the people went to eat and drink, to send portions, and to celebrate with great joy, because they understood the words that had been explained to them.
On the second day, the heads of all the families, along with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law.
They found written in the Law that the LORD had commanded through Moses that the Israelites should live in booths during the feast in the seventh month.

They also found that they should make this known and spread it through all their cities and in Jerusalem: “Go out to the hills and bring branches of olive, wild olive, myrtle, palm, and other leafy trees to make booths, as it is written.”

So the people went out and brought them. They made booths for themselves, each on his own roof, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, and in the squares by the Water Gate and the Gate of Ephraim.

The whole group of those who had returned from exile made booths and lived in them. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not celebrated like this. There was very great rejoicing.

Day by day, from the first day to the last, Ezra read from the Book of the Law of God. They celebrated the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, as required by the Law.
On the twenty-fourth day of this month, the Israelites gathered together. They fasted, wore sackcloth, and put dust on their heads.
The people of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners. They stood and confessed their sins and the sins of their ancestors.
They stood where they were and read from the Book of the Law of the LORD their God for a quarter of the day. For another quarter, they confessed their sins and worshiped the LORD their God.
The Levites—Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani—stood on the stairs. They cried out to the LORD their God with a loud voice.

Then the Levites—Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah—said: “Stand up and bless the LORD your God forever and ever. ‘Blessed be Your glorious name. May it be lifted above every blessing and praise.’

You alone are the LORD. You made the heavens, the highest heavens and all their armies. You made the earth and everything on it, the seas and everything in them. You give life to all things, and the armies of heaven worship You.
You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram. You brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham.

You found his heart faithful to You. You made a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Girgashites to his children. You kept Your promise because You are righteous. “
You saw the suffering of our fathers in Egypt. You heard their cry at the Red Sea.
You did signs and wonders against Pharaoh, his servants, and all the people of his land, because You knew they had treated our fathers with pride. You made a name for Yourself that lasts to this day.
You split the sea before them, and they crossed on dry ground. You threw their enemies into the deep like a stone into wild water.
You led them with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night to light the road they should take. “
You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke to them from heaven. You gave them fair rules, true laws, and good commands.
You showed them Your holy Sabbath. You gave them commands, rules, and laws through Your servant Moses.
You gave them bread from heaven for their hunger and water from the rock for their thirst. You told them to go in and take the land You had promised to give them. “
But they and our fathers became proud and stubborn. They did not obey Your commands.

They refused to listen. They forgot the wonders You had done for them. They became stubborn and chose a leader to take them back to slavery in Egypt. But You are a forgiving God. You are kind and full of mercy. You are slow to anger and rich in faithful love, and You did not leave them.
Even when they made a metal calf and said, ‘This is your god who brought you up out of Egypt,’ they did terrible things that insulted You.
You, in Your great mercy, did not leave them in the desert. By day the pillar of cloud did not stop guiding them on their way. By night the pillar of fire lit the road they should follow.
You gave Your good Spirit to teach them. You did not keep Your manna from their mouths, and You gave them water for their thirst.
For forty years You took care of them in the desert. They had everything they needed. Their clothes did not wear out, and their feet did not swell.
You gave them kingdoms and peoples. You gave them land on every side. They took the land of Sihon, king of Heshbon, and the land of Og, king of Bashan.
You made their children as many as the stars in the sky. You brought them into the land You had told their fathers to enter and own.

So their children went in and took the land. You brought the Canaanites who lived there under their control. You gave their kings and the people of the land into their hands to do with them as they wanted.

They captured strong cities and rich land. They took houses full of good things, wells already dug, vineyards, olive groves, and many fruit trees. They ate, were full, grew fat, and enjoyed Your great goodness. “
But they turned against You and rebelled. They threw Your law aside. They killed Your prophets, who had warned them to come back to You. They did terrible things that insulted You.

So You let their enemies rule over them. When they were in trouble, they cried out to You, and You heard them from heaven. In Your great mercy, You gave them leaders who saved them from their enemies.

But as soon as they were safe, they did evil again in Your sight. So You handed them over to their enemies, who ruled them. Yet when they cried out to You again, You heard from heaven and saved them many times because of Your mercy.
You warned them to return to Your law. But they were proud and did not listen to Your commands. A person can live by obeying them. But they were stubborn and refused to listen.
You were patient with them for many years. By Your Spirit, You warned them through Your prophets. Yet they would not listen, so You gave them to the peoples of other lands.
Yet in Your great mercy, You did not destroy them or leave them, because You are a gracious and merciful God. “

So now, our God, the great, mighty, and awesome God who keeps His covenant of faithful love, do not let all this hardship seem small in Your eyes. This hardship has come on us, our kings, our leaders, our priests, our prophets, our fathers, and all Your people, from the days of the kings of Assyria until today.
You are right in everything that has happened to us, because You have been faithful, while we have done wrong.
Our kings, leaders, priests, and fathers did not obey Your law. They did not listen to Your commands and teachings that You gave them.
Even in their own kingdom, while enjoying Your great goodness that You had given them, in the wide and rich land You set before them, they did not serve You or turn from their evil ways.
So here we are today, slaves in the land You gave our fathers to eat its fruit and enjoy its goodness. Here we are, slaves in it!
Its rich harvest goes to the kings You have placed over us because of our sins. They rule over our bodies and our animals as they please, and we are in great trouble.
Because of all this, we are making a binding agreement. We are putting it in writing, and our leaders, Levites, and priests are signing it.”
Those who put their seal on the covenant were Nehemiah the governor, son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah;
Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah. These were the priests.
The Levites were Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, and Kadmiel.
Their relatives were Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, Hanan,
The leaders of the people were Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, Bani,

The rest of the people—the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and everyone who had separated themselves from the peoples of the lands to follow the Law of God, along with their wives, sons, and daughters, all who could understand—

joined their fellow Israelites and leaders. They took on a curse and an oath to walk in God's Law, which was given through Moses, God's servant, and to carefully obey all the commandments of the the LORD our Lord, along with His rules and laws.
“We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land, and we will not take their daughters for our sons.

If the peoples of the land bring goods or grain to sell on the Sabbath, we will not buy from them on the Sabbath or on any holy day. We will also let the land rest in the seventh year and cancel every debt.
“We take on the duty of giving one third of a shekel each year for the service of the house of our God:

for the bread set out before God, the regular grain offering, the regular burnt offering on Sabbaths, new moon festivals, and appointed feasts, and for holy things and sin offerings to pay for Israel's sins, and for all the work in the house of our God.

“We, the priests, Levites, and people, have cast lots for the wood offering. We will bring it to the house of our God by family groups at set times each year, to burn on the altar of the the LORD our God, as it is written in the Law.
We also promise to bring the first crops from our land and the first fruit from every tree each year to the house of the the LORD.
“We will bring to the house of our God, to the priests who serve there, the firstborn of our sons and of our cattle, as the Law says, along with the firstborn of our herds and flocks.

We will bring the first portion of our dough, our gifts, the fruit of every tree, wine, and oil to the priests in the rooms of the house of our God. We will also bring the Levites a tenth of our crops, because the Levites collect the tithes in all the towns where we work.
“A priest, a descendant of Aaron, will be with the Levites when they receive the tithe. The Levites will bring a tenth of the tithes to the house of our God, to the rooms of the storehouse.

The people of Israel and the Levites will bring the gifts of grain, wine, and oil to those rooms, where the holy vessels are kept, along with the priests who serve, the gatekeepers, and the singers. We will not neglect the house of our God.”

Now the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem. The rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of every ten to live in Jerusalem, the holy city, while the remaining nine-tenths stayed in their own towns.
The people blessed all the men who volunteered to live in Jerusalem.

These are the leaders of the province who settled in Jerusalem. In the villages of Judah, however, each person lived on his own property in his own town—the Israelites, priests, Levites, temple servants, and descendants of Solomon’s servants.

At Jerusalem, some of the descendants of Judah and Benjamin settled. From the descendants of Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, from the descendants of Perez.
Also Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, a descendant of Shelah.
The descendants of Perez who settled in Jerusalem totaled 468 brave men.
From the descendants of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah.
After him came Gabbai and Sallai, 928 men.
Joel son of Zichri was the officer in charge of them, and Judah son of Hassenuah was over the second district of the city.
From the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib; Jachin.
Seraiah son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the chief official of the house of God.
Their relatives who did the work of the temple numbered 822 men. Also Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah.
His relatives, the heads of families, numbered 242 men. Also Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer.
Their relatives numbered 128 mighty men of valor. Zabdiel son of Haggedolim was their overseer.
From the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni.
Shabbethai and Jozabad, two of the leaders of the Levites, supervised the outside work of the house of God.
Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, led in thanksgiving and prayer. Bakbukiah was second among his relatives, and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.
The Levites in the holy city totaled 284.
The gatekeepers were Akkub, Talmon, and their relatives, who kept watch at the gates—172 men.
The rest of the Israelites, along with the priests and Levites, were in all the cities of Judah, each on his own family land.
The temple servants lived on the hill of Ophel, with Ziha and Gishpa over them.

The overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, from the descendants of Asaph, who were the singers in charge of the service of the house of God.
For the king had given a command about them, and there was a set provision for the singers each day.
Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, a descendant of Zerah son of Judah, was the king’s agent in all matters concerning the people.
As for the villages with their fields, some of the people of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba and its villages, in Dibon and its villages, in Jekabzeel and its villages,
in Hazar-shual, in Beersheba and its villages,
in Ziklag, in Meconah and its villages,
in En-rimmon, in Zorah, in Jarmuth,
in Zanoah, Adullam, and their villages, in Lachish and its fields, and in Azekah and its villages. So they settled from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom.
The descendants of Benjamin from Geba lived in Michmash, Aija, Bethel and its villages,
in Lod, Ono, and the Valley of Craftsmen.
Some of the Levites of Judah also settled in Benjamin’s territory.
These are the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra,
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the heads of the priests and their relatives in the days of Jeshua.
The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah, who led the thanksgiving songs, he and his relatives.
Bakbukiah and Unni, their relatives, stood across from them during their shifts.
Jeshua was the father of Joiakim, Joiakim was the father of Eliashib, and Eliashib was the father of Joiada.
Joiada was the father of Jonathan, and Jonathan was the father of Jaddua.
In the days of Joiakim, these were the family heads of the priests: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah;
of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan;
of Melicu, Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;
of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai;
of Iddo, Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam;
of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin, Piltai;
of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jonathan;
of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi;
of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber;
of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; and of Jedaiah, Nethaneel.
In the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, the Levites and priests were recorded as family heads until the reign of Darius the Persian.
The sons of Levi, the family heads, were written in the Book of the Chronicles up to the days of Johanan son of Eliashib.

The leaders of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, Jeshua son of Kadmiel, and their relatives. They stood opposite each other to praise and give thanks, one group facing another, as David, the man of God, had commanded.
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers who guarded the storerooms at the gates.
These served in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe.

At the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, they sought the Levites from all their places to bring them to Jerusalem. They were to celebrate the dedication with joy, thanksgiving, singing, and with cymbals, harps, and lyres.
The singers gathered from the area around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites.
They also came from Beth-gilgal and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, because the singers had built villages for themselves around Jerusalem.
The priests and Levites purified themselves, and then they purified the people, the gates, and the wall.
Then I brought the leaders of Judah up onto the wall and set up two large thanksgiving choirs. One went to the right on top of the wall toward the Dung Gate.
Hoshaiah and half the leaders of Judah followed them:
Some of the priests' sons played trumpets: Zechariah son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph.
His relatives were Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah, and Hanani. They played the musical instruments of David, the man of God. Ezra the scribe went before them.
At the Fountain Gate they went straight up the steps of the City of David, along the ascent of the wall, above David's house, to the Water Gate on the east.
The second thanksgiving choir went the other way. I followed it with the other half of the people on top of the wall. We passed the Tower of the Furnaces to the Broad Wall.
We passed above the Gate of Ephraim, the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel, the Tower of the Hundred, and stopped at the Sheep Gate. We stood at the Gate of the Guard.
So the two thanksgiving choirs stood in God's house. I stood there too, along with half the officials.
The priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah played trumpets.
Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Johanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer also played. The singers sang loudly, led by Jezrahiah.
That day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, because God had given them great joy. The women and children rejoiced too, and the joy of Jerusalem was heard far away.

On that day men were appointed over the storerooms for the contributions, firstfruits, and tithes. They were to gather into them, from the fields of the cities, the portions required by the Law for the priests and Levites. Judah rejoiced over the priests and Levites who served.
They performed the service of their God and the service of purification, as did the singers and gatekeepers. They followed the commands of David and his son Solomon.
For in the days of David and Asaph, long ago, there were leaders of the singers and songs of praise and thanksgiving to God.

In the days of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel gave daily portions to the singers and gatekeepers. They set apart what was holy for the Levites, and the Levites set apart what was holy for the sons of Aaron.
On that day, the people listened as the Book of Moses was read. They found a written rule that no Ammonite or Moabite should ever be allowed into the assembly of God.
This was because those nations had not met the Israelites with bread and water. They had also hired Balaam to curse Israel, but our God turned the curse into a blessing.
When the people heard the law, they separated everyone of mixed background from Israel.
Before this happened, Eliashib the priest, who was close to Tobiah, had been put in charge of a room in the house of our God.

He had made a large room for Tobiah. Earlier, that room had held the grain offering, the incense, the temple vessels, the tithes of grain, wine, and olive oil, and the supplies for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers. It had also held the gifts for the priests.
While all this was happening, I was not in Jerusalem. I had gone to King Artaxerxes of Babylon in the thirty-second year of his reign. After some time, I asked the king for permission to return.
When I came back to Jerusalem, I learned about the evil thing Eliashib had done for Tobiah by giving him a room in the courtyards of God's house.
I was very angry, so I threw all of Tobiah's belongings out of the room.
I ordered the rooms to be cleaned, and then I brought back the vessels of God's house, along with the grain offering and the incense.
I also learned that the Levites had not been given their shares. Because of that, the Levites and singers who were supposed to do the work had gone back to their own fields.
So I rebuked the officials and said, "Why has the house of God been neglected?" Then I gathered the Levites and singers and put them back in their places.
After that, all Judah brought the tithes of grain, new wine, and olive oil into the storehouses.

I put Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, Pedaiah the Levite, and Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, in charge of the storehouses. They were trusted men, and their job was to hand out supplies to their brothers.
I prayed, "Remember me for this, my God. Do not wipe out the good things I have done for Your house and for its services."

In those days, I saw people in Judah treading winepresses on the Sabbath. They were bringing in grain, loading it on donkeys, and carrying wine, grapes, figs, and all kinds of loads into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. I warned them not to sell food on that day.
People from Tyre who lived there brought in fish and all kinds of goods, and they sold them on the Sabbath to the people of Judah in Jerusalem.
I argued with the nobles of Judah and said, "What evil thing are you doing? You are ruining the Sabbath by working on it."
I also said, "Didn't your fathers do the same thing? That is why our God brought all this trouble on us and on this city. Now you are bringing even more anger on Israel by ruining the Sabbath."

As evening came before the Sabbath, I ordered the doors of Jerusalem's gates to be shut, and I said they should not be opened until after the Sabbath. I also stationed some of my servants at the gates so that no load could be brought in on the Sabbath day.
Once or twice, merchants and sellers of all kinds of goods spent the night outside Jerusalem.
I warned them, "Why do you camp outside the wall? If you do this again, I will use force against you." After that, they did not come on the Sabbath.

Then I told the Levites, "Purify yourselves and come guard the gates, so that the Sabbath day will be kept holy." I also prayed, "Remember me for this too, my God, and be kind to me because of Your great faithful love."
In those days, I also saw Jews who had married women from Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.
Half of their children spoke the language of Ashdod or the language of another people. They did not know how to speak the language of Judah.

I argued with them, cursed them, struck some of them, and pulled out their hair. Then I made them promise before God, "You will not give your daughters to their sons, and you will not take their daughters for your sons or for yourselves."

I said, "Didn't King Solomon of Israel sin because of women like these? Among many nations there was no king like him. He was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Even so, foreign women led him into sin.
Shall we then listen to you and do all this great evil, trespassing against our God by marrying foreign women?"
One of the sons of Joiada, son of Eliashib the high priest, was married to a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite. I drove him away from me.
I prayed, "Remember them, my God, because they made the priesthood and its covenant unclean, along with the Levites."
So I cleansed them from everything foreign. I also set up duties for the priests and Levites, giving each man his own work.
I made sure wood was brought for the offerings at the right times, and I made sure the first crops were brought in. I prayed, "Remember me, my God, and treat me well."
In the days of King Ahasuerus, who ruled over 127 provinces from India to Ethiopia,
this happened. In those days King Ahasuerus was sitting on his royal throne in the fortress at Susa.
In the third year of his reign, he gave a feast for all his officials and servants. The army of Persia and Media was there, along with the nobles and governors of the provinces.
For 180 days he showed them the wealth and glory of his kingdom and the splendor of his greatness.
When those days were over, the king gave a seven-day feast in the palace garden for all the people in Susa, from the greatest to the least.

The garden was decorated with white and violet hangings, held by cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings on marble pillars. Gold and silver couches rested on a mosaic floor of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and other costly stones.
Drinks were served in gold cups, and the cups were all different. Royal wine was plentiful, because the king was generous.
The drinking followed the king's rule: no one was forced, because the king had told his officials to serve each man as he wished.
Queen Vashti also gave a feast for the women in the royal palace of King Ahasuerus.
On the seventh day, when the king was happy from wine, he commanded the seven eunuchs who served him: Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carkas.
He told them to bring Queen Vashti before him, wearing the royal crown, so he could show her beauty to the people and officials, because she was lovely to look at.
But Queen Vashti refused to come when the king sent for her through the eunuchs. The king became very angry, and his wrath burned within him.
Then the king spoke to the wise men who understood the times, for this was the king's usual way with everyone who knew law and justice.
The men closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, seven princes of Persia and Media. They saw the king's face and sat first in the kingdom.
He asked, "What does the law say should be done to Queen Vashti, because she did not obey the command of King Ahasuerus given through the eunuchs?"
Memucan answered in front of the king and the princes, "Queen Vashti has done wrong not only against the king, but against all the princes and all the peoples in every province of King Ahasuerus.
When the queen's action becomes known to all women, they will look down on their husbands. They will say, 'King Ahasuerus commanded Queen Vashti to come before him, but she did not come.'
This very day the noble ladies of Persia and Media who have heard about the queen's behavior will say the same thing to all the king's officials. Then there will be much contempt and anger."

"If it pleases the king, let a royal decree go out from him and be written among the laws of the Persians and Medes, so it cannot be changed. Let it say that Vashti may never again come before King Ahasuerus, and let the king give her royal position to another woman who is better than she is.
When the king's decree is announced throughout his whole kingdom, every woman, great and small, will honor her husband."
The king and the princes liked this advice, and the king did what Memucan said.

He sent letters to all the provinces of his kingdom, to each province in its own writing and to each people in its own language. The letters said that every man should be master in his own house and speak in the language of his own people.
After these things, King Ahasuerus's anger cooled down. He remembered Vashti, what she had done, and what had been decided about her.
Then the king's servants who served him said, "Let beautiful young women be found for the king.

Let the king choose officials in every part of his kingdom. They can gather all the beautiful young women to the women's house in the fortress of Susa. Put them under Hegai, the king's eunuch who guards the women, and give them beauty treatments.
The young woman who pleases the king will become queen instead of Vashti." This idea pleased the king, so he did it.
In the fortress of Susa there was a Jewish man named Mordecai. He was the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin.
He had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives taken with Jeconiah, king of Judah, when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried them away.

Mordecai had raised Hadassah, also called Esther. She was his uncle's daughter, and she had no father or mother. She was beautiful in face and form. When her parents died, Mordecai took her in as his own daughter.
When the king's order and law were heard, many young women were gathered to the fortress of Susa under Hegai. Esther was also taken to the king's house and placed under Hegai, who guarded the women.

She pleased him and won his favor. He quickly gave her beauty treatments, special food, and seven chosen young women from the king's house. He also moved her and her young women to the best place in the women's house.
Esther did not tell anyone her people or family, because Mordecai had told her not to.
Every day Mordecai walked in front of the courtyard of the women's house to learn how Esther was doing and what would happen to her.

Each young woman had twelve months of beauty treatments before she could go to King Ahasuerus. This followed the women's rules: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and other beauty treatments.
When a young woman went to the king, she could take from the women's house to the king anything she asked for.

She would go in the evening and return in the morning to the second women's house, under Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch who guarded the concubines. She would not go to the king again unless he was pleased with her and called her by name.

When it was Esther's turn to go to the king, she asked for nothing except what Hegai, the king's eunuch in charge of the women, suggested. Esther was the daughter of Abihail, Mordecai's uncle, and Mordecai had adopted her. Esther won favor with everyone who saw her.
Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus in the royal house in the tenth month, the month of Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign.

The king loved Esther more than all the other women. She won more favor and kindness from him than all the other young women. He placed the royal crown on her head and made her queen instead of Vashti.
The king gave a great feast for all his officials and servants. It was Esther's feast. He also gave tax relief to the provinces and gave gifts with royal generosity.
When the young women were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.
Esther still did not tell anyone her family or people, just as Mordecai had commanded her. She continued to follow Mordecai's instructions, as she had done when he raised her.
In those days, while Mordecai sat at the king's gate, two of the king's eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the doorway, became angry. They planned to harm King Ahasuerus.
Mordecai learned about it and told Queen Esther. Esther told the king, using Mordecai's name.
After the matter was looked into and found true, the two men were hanged on a gallows. The event was written down in the book of the king's daily records.
After these events, King Xerxes honored Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, by giving him a position higher than all the other officials.
All the king's officials at the royal gate bowed down to Haman because the king had commanded it, but Mordecai refused to bow or show respect.
The officials asked Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the king's command?"
They spoke to him day after day, but he would not listen, so they reported the matter to Haman to see whether Mordecai would keep refusing, since he had told them he was a Jew.
When Haman saw that Mordecai would not bow or show respect, he became furious.
Haman also learned who Mordecai's people were, and he scorned the idea of punishing Mordecai alone. Instead, he planned to destroy all the Jews throughout King Xerxes' kingdom.

In the twelfth year of King Xerxes, during the first month, called Nisan, Haman had the lot cast before him to choose a day and month. The lot is called Pur, and it selected the twelfth month, called Adar.

Then Haman said to King Xerxes, "There is a certain people scattered among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws differ from those of every other people, and they do not obey the king's laws, so it is not in the king's best interest to tolerate them.
If it pleases the king, let an order be written to destroy them, and I will pay ten thousand talents of silver into the royal treasury for the men who carry out this business."
So the king removed his signet ring from his finger and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.
The king said to Haman, "Keep the money and do with the people as you please."

On the thirteenth day of the first month, the royal scribes were summoned. They wrote out every command Haman had dictated to the king's governors and officials in each province, using the script and language of that province. They wrote it in the name of King Xerxes and sealed it with the king's signet ring.

The letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces with orders to destroy, kill, and wipe out all the Jews—young and old, women and children—and to seize their possessions on a single day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar.
A copy of the text was to be issued in every province and published to all the peoples so they would be ready for that day.
The couriers went out, spurred on by the king's command, and the edict was issued in the citadel of Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.
When Mordecai learned all that had been done, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth and ashes. He went out into the city and cried out with a loud, bitter cry.
He went as far as the king's gate, because no one dressed in sackcloth was allowed to enter it.
In every province, wherever the king's command and order reached, there was great mourning among the Jews. They fasted, wept, and cried out in sorrow, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
When Esther's young women and her eunuchs came and told her, the queen was very upset. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear so he could take off his sackcloth, but he would not accept them.
Then Esther called for Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs who had been appointed to serve her. She ordered him to go to Mordecai and find out what was happening and why.
Hathach went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the king's gate.
Mordecai told him everything that had happened to him, including the exact amount of money Haman had promised to pay into the king's treasury to destroy the Jews.

Mordecai also gave him a copy of the written order that had been issued in Susa to destroy them. He told Hathach to show it to Esther, explain it to her, and order her to go to the king to beg for mercy and plead for her people.
Hathach went back and told Esther what Mordecai had said.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and told him to go to Mordecai and say:

“All the king's servants and the people in the king's provinces know that anyone, man or woman, who goes to the king in the inner court without being called must be put to death. The only exception is if the king holds out his golden scepter, and then that person lives. But I have not been called to go to the king for thirty days.”
They told Mordecai what Esther had said.
Then Mordecai told them to reply to Esther: “Do not think to yourself that you will be safe in the king's palace while the rest of the Jews are not.
“If you stay silent now, help and rescue will come to the Jews from somewhere else, but you and your family will be destroyed. Who knows? Maybe you were made queen for a time like this.”
Then Esther told them to reply to Mordecai:

“Go and gather all the Jews in Susa. Fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. My young women and I will fast too, as you do. Then I will go to the king, even though it is against the law. If I die, I die.”
Mordecai went away and did everything Esther had commanded.
