"We found the jail locked tight and the guards standing at the doors. But when we opened it, no one was inside."
The temple guard captain and the chief priests heard this and wondered what had happened.
Then someone came and told them, "Look! The men you put in jail are standing in the temple and teaching the people."
The captain went with the officers and brought them back. They did not use force because they were afraid the people might stone them.
They brought the apostles and made them stand before the council. The high priest questioned them.
He said, "We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name. But look, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching. You want to bring this man's blood on us."
Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than people.
The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging Him on a tree.
God raised Him to His right hand as Prince and Savior, to give Israel a chance to turn from sin and receive forgiveness of sins.
We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God gave to those who obey Him."
When they heard this, they were furious and wanted to kill them.
But a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law who was respected by all the people, stood up in the council. He ordered the men to be put outside for a short time.

Then he said to them, "Men of Israel, be careful what you plan to do to these men. "Some time ago Theudas appeared. He claimed to be someone important, and about four hundred men joined him. He was killed, and all his followers were scattered. They came to nothing.

After him, Judas the Galilean appeared during the census. He drew people after him, but he died too, and all his followers were scattered. "So now I tell you, stay away from these men and leave them alone. If this plan or work comes from people, it will fail.
But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You might even find yourselves fighting against God."
They agreed with him. They called the apostles in, beat them, ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
The apostles left the council rejoicing because they had been counted worthy to suffer shame for the Name.
Every day, in the temple and from house to house, they never stopped teaching and telling the good news that Jesus is the Christ.
In those days, as the number of believers grew, the Greek-speaking believers complained to the Hebrew-speaking believers that their widows were being left out of the daily food distribution.
So the Twelve called all the believers together and said, “It wouldn’t be right for us to stop preaching God’s word to serve food.
Brothers, choose seven men from among you who are known for their good reputation and are full of the Spirit and wisdom. We will put them in charge of this work.
Then we can give our full attention to prayer and to preaching God’s word.”

This plan pleased everyone. They chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolaus, who was from Antioch and had become a Jewish convert.
They brought these men to the apostles, who prayed and laid their hands on them.
So God’s word spread, and the number of believers in Jerusalem grew quickly. A large number of priests also came to believe.
Stephen was full of grace and power. He did great miracles and signs among the people.
But some men from the synagogue of the Freedmen, and from the synagogues of Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and Asia, began to argue with Stephen.
But they could not stand against his wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke.
So they secretly got some men to say, “We heard him speak against Moses and against God.”
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the teachers of the law. They seized Stephen and brought him before the council.
They also set up false witnesses, who said, “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and the law.
We have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs Moses gave us.”
Everyone in the council looked at him closely and saw that his face looked like an angel’s face.
The high priest asked, "Are these things so?"
Stephen said, "Brothers and fathers, listen. The God of glory appeared to our father Abraham while he was in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.
He said to him, 'Leave your land and your relatives, and go to the land I will show you.'
So Abraham left the land of the Chaldeans and lived in Haran. After his father died, God moved him to this land where you now live.
God gave him no inheritance in it, not even a small piece of land. But He promised to give it to him as a possession, and to his descendants after him, even though he had no child yet.
God said that his descendants would be strangers in a foreign land, and that they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years.
'But I will judge the nation they serve,' God said, 'and after that they will come out and worship Me in this place.'

He gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision. So Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day. Isaac became the father of Jacob, and Jacob became the father of the twelve patriarchs." "
The patriarchs were jealous of Joseph and sold him into Egypt. But God was with him.
He rescued him from all his troubles and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Pharaoh made him ruler over Egypt and over his whole household." "
Then a famine and great suffering came over all Egypt and Canaan, and our fathers could not find food.
When Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there the first time.
On their second visit, Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Pharaoh learned about Joseph's family.
Then Joseph sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives—seventy-five people in all." "
So Jacob went down to Egypt. He and our fathers died there.
Their bodies were moved to Shechem and buried in the tomb Abraham had bought from the sons of Hamor in Shechem for a sum of silver." "
As the time drew near for the promise God had made to Abraham, our people grew and multiplied in Egypt.
Then a new king came to power in Egypt who did not know Joseph.
He tricked our people and oppressed our fathers by forcing them to leave their babies outside so they would not survive." "
At that time Moses was born. He was beautiful to God, and he was cared for in his father's house for three months.
When he was put outside, Pharaoh's daughter took him in and raised him as her own son.
Moses was taught all the wisdom of the Egyptians, and he was powerful in both speech and action." "
When Moses was forty years old, he decided to visit his brothers, the Israelites.
He saw one of them being treated unfairly, so he defended him and avenged him by killing the Egyptian.
Moses thought his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation through him, but they did not understand.
The next day he appeared to them while they were fighting. He tried to make peace between them and said, 'Men, you are brothers. Why are you hurting each other?'
But the man who was wronging his neighbor pushed Moses away and said, 'Who made you a ruler and judge over us?
Do you want to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian yesterday?'
When Moses heard this, he fled to the land of Midian. There he became a foreigner and had two sons." "
After forty years had passed, an angel appeared to Moses in a flame of fire in a bush in the wilderness near Mount Sinai.
Moses saw it and was amazed. As he went closer to look, the voice of the Lord came to him:
'I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.' Moses trembled with fear and did not dare to look.
The Lord said to him, 'Take the sandals off your feet, because the place where you are standing is holy ground.
I have clearly seen the suffering of My people in Egypt. I have heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. Now come, I will send you to Egypt.'" "

This Moses, whom the people had rejected when they said, 'Who made you a ruler and judge?'—this is the one God sent to be their ruler and redeemer, with the help of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
He led them out of Egypt, performing wonders and signs in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
This is the Moses who said to the Israelites, 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your own brothers.'" "
This is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai. He received living words from God to pass on to us.
But our fathers refused to obey him. They pushed him away and turned back to Egypt in their hearts.
They said to Aaron, 'Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.'
In those days they made an idol shaped like a calf, offered a sacrifice to it, and celebrated what they had made with their own hands." "

But God turned away from them and let them worship the stars in the sky. This is what the prophets wrote: 'Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
No, you carried the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Rephan, the idols you made to worship. So I will send you beyond Babylon.'" "
Our fathers had the tabernacle of the testimony in the wilderness. It was made just as God commanded Moses, following the pattern he had seen.
Our fathers who came after Joshua brought it with them when they took the land from the nations God drove out before them. It stayed there until the time of David,
who found favor with God and asked to build a house for the God of Jacob.
But Solomon built the house for Him." "
Yet the Most High does not live in houses made by human hands. As the prophet says,
'Heaven is My throne, and the earth is My footstool. What kind of house will you build for Me?' says the Lord. 'Or what is the place where I can rest?
Did not My hand make all these things?'" "
You stubborn people with closed hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did.
Which prophet did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who predicted the coming of the Righteous One. And now you have become His betrayers and murderers—
you who received the law given through angels but did not obey it."
When they heard this, they were furious and clenched their teeth at him.
But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
"Look," he said, "I see heaven opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God."
They shouted loudly, covered their ears, and rushed at him together.
They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.
While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit."
Then he knelt down and cried out in a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." After saying this, he died.
Saul approved of Stephen’s death. That same day, a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem. Everyone except the apostles was scattered throughout Judea and Samaria.
Some devout men buried Stephen and mourned deeply over him.
Saul was ruining the church. He went into homes, dragged out men and women, and put them in prison.
The believers who were scattered traveled around and told people the good news.
Philip went down to a city in Samaria and preached about Christ to the people there.
The crowds listened closely to what Philip said. They heard his words and saw the signs he did.
Evil spirits cried out with loud voices and came out of many people. Many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
So the city was filled with great joy.
A man named Simon had been practicing magic in that city. He amazed the people of Samaria and claimed to be someone great.
Everyone, from the least to the greatest, paid attention to him. They said, “This man is the power of God called Great.”
They followed him because he had amazed them with his magic for a long time.
But when they believed Philip as he preached the good news about God’s kingdom and the name of Jesus Christ, men and women were baptized.
Simon himself believed and was baptized. Then he stayed close to Philip and was amazed at the great signs and miracles he saw.
The apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted God’s word, so they sent Peter and John to them.
When Peter and John arrived, they prayed for the new believers to receive the Holy Spirit.
The Spirit had not yet come on any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Then Peter and John laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the apostles’ hands, he offered them money.
He said, “Give me this power too, so that anyone I lay my hands on will receive the Holy Spirit.”
Peter said to him, “May your money be destroyed along with you, because you thought you could buy God’s gift with money!
You have no part or share in this, because your heart is not right with God.
So repent of this wickedness and pray to the Lord. Maybe He will forgive the evil thought in your heart.
I can see that you are full of bitterness and bound by sin.”
Simon answered, “Pray to the Lord for me, so that none of what you said will happen to me.”
After Peter and John had warned them and preached the Lord’s word, they returned to Jerusalem. On the way, they preached the good news in many Samaritan villages.
An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip. He said, “Get up and go south to the road that leads down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” That road runs through the desert.
So Philip got up and went. He met an Ethiopian man, a eunuch who was an important official in charge of all the treasure of Candace, queen of Ethiopia. He had come to Jerusalem to worship.
Now he was on his way home. He was sitting in his chariot and reading the prophet Isaiah.
The Holy Spirit said to Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay close to it.”
Philip ran up and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. Philip asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
The man said, “How can I understand unless someone explains it to me?” Then he invited Philip to climb up and sit with him.
The passage he was reading said, “He was led like a sheep to be killed. Like a lamb before the one who shears it, He did not open His mouth.
In His humiliation, justice was taken from Him. Who can describe His family? His life was taken from the earth.”
The eunuch asked Philip, “Who is the prophet talking about—himself or someone else?”
Then Philip began with that passage and told him the good news about Jesus.
As they traveled along the road, they came to some water. The eunuch said, “Look, there’s water! What’s stopping me from being baptized?”
He ordered the chariot to stop. Both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and Philip baptized him.
When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away. The eunuch did not see him anymore, but he went on his way rejoicing.
Philip was found at Azotus. He traveled through the towns and preached the good news in every city until he reached Caesarea.
Saul was still threatening to kill the Lord's disciples. He went to the high priest
and asked for letters to the synagogues in Damascus. That way, if he found any men or women who belonged to the Way, he could bring them tied up to Jerusalem.
As he neared Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him.
He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?"
"Who are You, Lord?" Saul asked. "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting," He replied.
"Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do."
The men traveling with Saul stood speechless. They heard the voice but did not see anyone.
Saul got up from the ground. His eyes were open, but he could not see. So they led him by the hand into Damascus.
For three days he was blind. He did not eat or drink anything.
In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." "Here I am, Lord," he answered.
The Lord told him, "Get up and go to the house of Judas on Straight Street. Ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, because he is praying.
In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come in and place his hands on him so he can see again."
"Lord," Ananias answered, "I have heard from many people about this man and all the harm he did to Your saints in Jerusalem.
And he has authority from the chief priests to arrest everyone who calls on Your name."
But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is My chosen instrument to carry My name to the Gentiles, to kings, and to the people of Israel.
I will show him how much he must suffer for My name."

So Ananias went to the house and entered it. He placed his hands on Saul and said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit."
At once something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized.
After he had eaten, he regained his strength. Saul stayed with the disciples in Damascus for several days.
Right away he began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

Everyone who heard him was amazed. They asked, "Isn't this the man who caused trouble in Jerusalem for those who call on this name? And hasn't he come here to take them as prisoners to the chief priests?"
Yet Saul grew more and more powerful. He confused the Jews living in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Messiah.
After many days, the Jews made plans to kill him.
But Saul learned about their plot. They watched the city gates day and night so they could kill him.
But at night his disciples took him and lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall.
When Saul came to Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples. But they were all afraid of him. They did not believe he was a disciple.

Then Barnabas took him to the apostles. He told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and that the Lord had spoken to him. He also told how Saul had preached boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus.
So Saul stayed with them and moved about freely in Jerusalem. He spoke boldly in the name of the Lord.
He talked and argued with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they tried to kill him.
When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee, and Samaria enjoyed peace. It was strengthened and grew in numbers as it lived in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit.
As Peter traveled about the country, he went to visit the Lord's people who lived in Lydda.
There he found a man named Aeneas, who was paralyzed and had been in bed for eight years.
"Aeneas," Peter said to him, "Jesus Christ heals you. Get up and roll up your mat." At once Aeneas got up.
All those who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.
In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha, which means Dorcas. She was always doing good and helping the poor.
About that time she became sick and died. Her body was washed and placed in an upstairs room.
Lydda was near Joppa, so when the disciples heard that Peter was there, they sent two men to him. They urged him, "Please come to us without delay."

Peter went with them. When he arrived, they took him to the upstairs room. All the widows stood around him, crying and showing him the robes and other clothing that Dorcas had made while she was still with them.
Peter sent them all out of the room. Then he knelt down and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, "Tabitha, get up." She opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up.
He gave her his hand and helped her up. Then he called the believers and the widows and presented her to them alive.
This became known all over Joppa, and many people believed in the Lord.
Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.
In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius. He was a centurion, an officer in the Roman army, from the Italian Cohort.
He and his whole household were devout and feared God. He gave many gifts to the poor and prayed to God always.
About three in the afternoon, he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come to him and say, "Cornelius!"
He stared at the angel in fear and said, "What is it, Lord?" The angel said, "Your prayers and your gifts to the poor have gone up as a memorial before God.
Now send men to Joppa and bring back Simon, who is called Peter.
He is staying with Simon the tanner, whose house is by the sea."
When the angel who spoke to him had left, Cornelius called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who served him.
He told them everything and sent them to Joppa.
The next day, as they were on their way and getting close to the city, Peter went up on the roof to pray. It was about noon.
He became hungry and wanted to eat. While they were preparing food, he fell into a trance.
He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet coming down. It was lowered to the earth by its four corners.
In it were all kinds of four-footed animals, along with reptiles of the earth and birds of the sky.
A voice said to him, "Get up, Peter. Kill and eat."
But Peter said, "No, Lord! I have never eaten anything impure or unclean."
The voice spoke to him again a second time: "What God has made clean, you must not call impure."
This happened three times, and then the sheet was taken back up into heaven.
While Peter was wondering what the vision meant, the men sent by Cornelius arrived. They had asked for Simon's house, and they stood at the gate.
They called out and asked if Simon, who was called Peter, was staying there.
While Peter was thinking about the vision, the Spirit said to him, "Look, three men are looking for you.
Get up and go downstairs. Go with them and do not doubt anything, because I have sent them."
Peter went down to the men and said, "I am the one you are looking for. Why have you come?"
They said, "Cornelius, a centurion, is a righteous and God-fearing man. He is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation. A holy angel told him to send for you and to hear what you have to say."
So Peter invited them in and gave them a place to stay. The next day he got up and went with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa went with him.
The next day they arrived in Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
When Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and worshiped him.
But Peter lifted him up and said, "Stand up. I am only a man myself."
Talking with him, Peter went inside and found many people gathered.
He said to them, "You know it is against our law for a Jew to associate with or visit someone from another nation. But God has shown me that I should not call any person unclean.
That is why I came without arguing when I was sent for. So I ask, why did you send for me?"
Cornelius said, "Four days ago I was in my house praying at this hour, three in the afternoon. Suddenly a man in shining clothes stood before me.
He said, 'Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your gifts to the poor have been remembered before God.
So send to Joppa and bring back Simon, who is called Peter. He is staying in the house of Simon the tanner by the sea.'
So I sent for you right away, and you have done well to come. Now we are all here in the presence of God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you to tell us."
Then Peter opened his mouth and said, "I now understand that God does not show favoritism.
In every nation, anyone who fears Him and does what is right is acceptable to Him.
"He sent His message to the people of Israel, announcing the good news of peace through Jesus Christ, who is Lord of all.
You know what happened throughout Judea, starting in Galilee after the baptism that John preached.
"God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and power, and He went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him.
We are witnesses of everything He did in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They killed Him by hanging Him on a tree.
"But God raised Him up on the third day and made Him appear,
not to all the people, but to witnesses God had chosen beforehand—us, who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead.
"He commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that He is the One God appointed as Judge of the living and the dead.
All the prophets testify about Him that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name."
While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit came on all who heard the message.
The Jewish believers who had come with Peter were amazed that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even on the Gentiles.
For they heard them speaking in tongues and praising God. Then Peter said,
"Can anyone keep these people from being baptized with water? They have received the Holy Spirit just as we have."
So he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for a few days.
The apostles and the brothers throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles had also received the word of God.
When Peter went up to Jerusalem, the Jewish believers argued with him.
They said, "You went into the home of men who were not circumcised and ate with them."
But Peter explained everything to them in order:
"I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision. A large sheet was coming down from heaven, lowered by its four corners, and it came right to me.
When I looked closely at it, I saw four-footed animals of the earth, wild beasts, reptiles, and birds of the sky.
Then I heard a voice say to me, 'Get up, Peter; kill and eat.'
I said, 'No, Lord! Nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.'
But the voice answered from heaven a second time, 'What God has made clean, you must not call common.'
This happened three times, and then everything was pulled back up into heaven.
Right then, three men sent to me from Caesarea stopped at the house where we were staying.
The Spirit told me to go with them and not to hesitate. These six brothers went with me too, and we entered the man's house.
"He told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house. The angel said, 'Send to Joppa and bring Simon, who is called Peter.
He will speak words to you by which you and your whole household will be saved.'
As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell on them, just as He had fallen on us at the beginning.
Then I remembered the word of the Lord. He had said, 'John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit.'
So if God gave them the same gift He gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I to stop God?"
When they heard this, they quieted down and praised God. They said, "Then God has given even the Gentiles the chance to turn from sin and live."
Now the believers who had been scattered by the persecution that began after Stephen was killed traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch. They spoke the word only to Jews.
But some of them were men from Cyprus and Cyrene. When they came to Antioch, they spoke to the Greek-speaking people and preached the Lord Jesus.
The hand of the Lord was with them, and a large number believed and turned to the Lord.
The news about them reached the church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to Antioch.
When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he was glad. He encouraged everyone to stay true to the Lord with all their heart.
He was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith, and many people were added to the Lord.
Then Barnabas went to Tarsus to look for Saul.
When he found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they met with the church and taught many people. The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
One of them, named Agabus, stood up and predicted through the Spirit that a great famine would spread over the whole world. This happened during the reign of Claudius.
So the disciples decided that each one would give what he could to help the brothers living in Judea.
They did this, sending their gift to the elders through Barnabas and Saul.
About that time, King Herod began to harm some people in the church.
He had James, the brother of John, killed with a sword.
When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he went on to arrest Peter too. This was during the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
After arresting him, he put him in prison and handed him over to four groups of four soldiers to guard him. Herod planned to bring him out for a public trial after Passover.
So Peter was kept in prison, but the church prayed earnestly to God for him.
The night before Herod was going to bring him to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers. He was bound with two chains, and guards stood at the door.
Suddenly an angel of the Lord appeared, and a light shone in the cell. He struck Peter on the side and woke him up. "Quick, get up!" he said, and the chains fell off Peter's wrists.
Then the angel said to him, "Put on your clothes and sandals." Peter did so. Then the angel said, "Wrap your cloak around you and follow me."
Peter followed him out of the prison, but he did not know that what the angel was doing was really happening. He thought he was seeing a vision.
They passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate that led to the city. It opened by itself, and they went out. They walked down one street, and then the angel left him.
Then Peter came to himself and said, "Now I know for sure that the Lord sent His angel and rescued me from Herod's power and from all that the Jewish people were expecting."
When he realized this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John, who was also called Mark. Many people were gathered there and were praying.
He knocked at the outer door, and a servant girl named Rhoda came to answer it.
When she recognized Peter's voice, she was so happy that she did not open the gate. Instead, she ran in and told them that Peter was standing at the door.
"You are out of your mind!" they told her. But she kept insisting it was true. Then they said, "It must be his angel."
But Peter kept on knocking. When they opened the door and saw him, they were amazed.

Peter motioned with his hand for them to be quiet. Then he told them how the Lord had brought him out of prison. He said, "Tell James and the other believers about this." Then he left for another place.
When morning came, there was a big uproar among the soldiers about what had happened to Peter.
After Herod searched for him and could not find him, he questioned the guards and ordered them to be put to death. Then Herod left Judea and went down to Caesarea, where he stayed.

Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him together and, after winning over Blastus, the king's trusted servant, they asked for peace. They depended on the king's country for food.
On the set day, Herod put on his royal robes, sat on his throne, and gave a speech to them.
The people shouted, "This is the voice of a god, not of a man!"
Right away, because Herod did not give glory to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down. He was eaten by worms and died.
But the word of God kept spreading and growing.
When Barnabas and Saul finished their work, they returned from Jerusalem, bringing with them John, who was also called Mark.
Now in the church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon (called Niger), Lucius from Cyrene, Manaen (who grew up with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul.
While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work I have called them to do."
So after they fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
Sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and sailed from there to Cyprus.
When they arrived at Salamis, they preached the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. John was with them as their helper.
They traveled through the whole island until they came to Paphos. There they found a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet named Bar-Jesus.
He was an attendant of the proconsul, Sergius Paulus. The proconsul was an intelligent man, and he sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.
But Elymas the sorcerer (that is what his name means) opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
Then Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked straight at Elymas
and said, "You are a child of the devil and an enemy of everything that is right! You are full of all kinds of deceit and trickery. Will you never stop perverting the straight ways of the Lord?

Now the hand of the Lord is against you. You will be blind for a time and will not see the sun." Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped around, looking for someone to lead him by the hand.
When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.
From Paphos, Paul and his companions sailed to Perga in Pamphylia. John left them there and returned to Jerusalem.
From Perga they went on to Pisidian Antioch. On the Sabbath they entered the synagogue and sat down.
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the leaders of the synagogue sent word to them: "Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak."
Paul stood up, motioned with his hand, and said, "Fellow Israelites and you Gentiles who worship God, listen to me!
The God of the people of Israel chose our ancestors. He made the people great while they lived in Egypt, and with mighty power He led them out of that country.
For about forty years He put up with them in the wilderness. "
He destroyed seven nations in Canaan and gave their land to His people as an inheritance.
All this took about four hundred fifty years. After that, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet.
Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin. He ruled for forty years.
After removing Saul, God made David their king. He testified about David: 'I have found David, son of Jesse, a man after My own heart. He will do everything I want him to do.' "
From this man's descendants God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, just as He promised.
Before Jesus came, John preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
As John was finishing his work, he said, 'Who do you think I am? I am not the one you are looking for. After me comes Someone whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.' "
Fellow children of Abraham and you God-fearing Gentiles, this message of salvation has been sent to us.
The people of Jerusalem and their rulers did not recognize Jesus. Yet by condemning Him, they fulfilled the words of the prophets that are read every Sabbath.
Though they found no reason to put Him to death, they asked Pilate to have Him executed.
When they had done everything that was written about Him, they took Him down from the cross and laid Him in a tomb. "
But God raised Him from the dead.
For many days He appeared to those who had traveled with Him from Galilee to Jerusalem. They are now His witnesses to our people.
We bring you the good news: What God promised our ancestors,
He has fulfilled for us, their children, by raising up Jesus. As it is written in the second Psalm: 'You are My Son; today I have become Your Father.'
God raised Him from the dead so He will never decay, as He has said: 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings promised to David.'
It is also stated elsewhere: 'You will not let Your Holy One see decay.' "
Now David served God's purpose in his own generation. Then he died and was buried with his ancestors, and his body decayed.
But the one whom God raised from the dead did not see decay.
Therefore, my friends, I want you to know that through Jesus the forgiveness of sins is announced to you.
Through Him everyone who believes is set free from every sin—a freedom you could not get under the law of Moses.
Be careful that what the prophets said does not happen to you:
'Look, you scoffers, wonder and perish, for I am going to do something in your days that you would never believe, even if someone told you.'"
As Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people invited them to speak further about these things on the next Sabbath.
When the synagogue was dismissed, many of the Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas. They talked with them and urged them to continue in the grace of God.
On the next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy. They began to contradict what Paul was saying and insulted him.
Then Paul and Barnabas answered them boldly: "We had to speak the word of God to you first. Since you reject it and do not consider yourselves worthy of eternal life, we now turn to the Gentiles.
For this is what the Lord has commanded us: 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
When the Gentiles heard this, they were glad and honored the word of the Lord. And all who were appointed for eternal life believed.
The word of the Lord spread through the whole region.
But the Jews stirred up the God-fearing women of high standing and the leading men of the city. They started a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their region.
So they shook the dust off their feet in warning to them and went to Iconium.
And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went into the Jewish synagogue together and spoke so effectively that a large number of Jews and Greeks believed.
But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
So they stayed there a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who confirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders.
The people of the city were divided. Some sided with the Jews, and others with the apostles.
When the Gentiles and Jews, along with their leaders, planned to mistreat them and stone them,
they learned of it and fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region.
And there they kept preaching the good news.
In Lystra a man sat who was lame in his feet. He had been crippled from birth and had never walked.
He listened to Paul speaking. Paul looked straight at him and saw that he had faith to be healed.
He said in a loud voice, "Stand up straight on your feet!" And he jumped up and began to walk.
When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they shouted in the Lycaonian language, "The gods have come down to us in human form!"
They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because Paul was the main speaker.
The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the gates. He wanted to offer sacrifices with the crowds.
But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting,

"Men, why are you doing these things? We too are only human beings like you. We are bringing you good news, so that you may turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them.
"In past generations He let all the nations go their own way.
"Yet He has not left Himself without witness, doing good and giving you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness."
Even with these words, they barely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
Then some Jews came from Antioch and Iconium. They won the crowds over, stoned Paul, and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead.
But when the disciples gathered around him, he got up and went back into the city. The next day he and Barnabas left for Derbe.
They preached the gospel in that city and made many disciples. Then they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
strengthening the disciples and encouraging them to remain true to the faith. "We must go through many hardships to enter the kingdom of God," they said.
Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for them in each church. With prayer and fasting, they committed them to the Lord, in whom they had put their trust.
After going through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia.
They preached the word in Perga, then went down to Attalia.
From Attalia they sailed to Antioch, where they had been committed to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
When they arrived, they gathered the church together and reported all that God had done through them, and how He had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
And they stayed there a long time with the disciples.
Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised the way Moses taught, you cannot be saved."

This led to a serious argument between Paul and Barnabas and those men. So the church decided to send Paul, Barnabas, and a few others to Jerusalem. They would ask the apostles and elders about this question.
The church sent them on their way. They traveled through Phoenicia and Samaria, telling how the Gentiles had turned to God. This brought great joy to all the brothers.
When they reached Jerusalem, the church, the apostles, and the elders welcomed them. Then they reported everything God had done through them.
But some of the believers who belonged to the Pharisees stood up and said, "The Gentiles must be circumcised and told to obey the law of Moses."
The apostles and elders met to consider this issue.
After much discussion, Peter stood up and said, "Brothers, you know that long ago God chose me from among you to tell the Gentiles the good news so they could believe.
God knows everyone's heart. He showed that He accepted them by giving them the Holy Spirit, just as He did to us.
He made no difference between us and them, because He made their hearts clean by faith.
So why are you testing God by putting a heavy load on the disciples? Neither we nor our fathers could carry that load.
Instead, we believe we are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, just like they are."
The whole crowd became quiet. They listened to Barnabas and Paul tell about the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
When they finished, James spoke up: "Brothers, listen to me.
Simeon has told us how God first cared for the Gentiles by choosing some of them to belong to Him.
The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written:
'After this I will return and rebuild David's fallen tent. I will repair its ruins and set it up again.
Then the rest of humanity may seek the Lord. That includes all the Gentiles who are called by My name,' says the Lord, who does these things.
These things have been known for ages.
So my decision is not to make things hard for the Gentiles who are turning to God.
Instead, we should write to them and tell them to stay away from food offered to idols, from sexual sin, from meat of strangled animals, and from blood.
For Moses has been preached in every city for many generations, and his words are read in the synagogues every Sabbath."

Then the apostles and elders, along with the whole church, decided to choose some men from their group and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They chose Judas, called Barsabbas, and Silas. These were leaders among the brothers.
They sent this letter with them: "The apostles and elders, your brothers, send greetings to the Gentile brothers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia.
We have heard that some men from our group went out without our permission. They upset you and troubled your minds with their words.
So we all agreed to choose some men and send them to you with our dear friends Barnabas and Paul.
"These men have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So we are sending Judas and Silas. They will tell you the same things in person.
It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to place any heavier burden on you than these necessary things:
Stay away from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from strangled meat, and from sexual sin. If you keep away from these things, you will do well. Goodbye."
So the men were sent off. They went down to Antioch, gathered the church together, and gave them the letter.
When the people read it, they were glad because of its encouraging message.
Judas and Silas were prophets. They said many words to encourage and strengthen the brothers.
After staying there for a while, they were sent back in peace to the men who had sent them.
But Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch. They and many others taught and preached the word of the Lord.
After some days, Paul said to Barnabas, "Let's go back and visit the brothers in every city where we preached the word of the Lord. We can see how they are doing."
Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark.
But Paul did not think it was right to take him, because he had left them in Pamphylia and had not continued with them in the work.
They disagreed so sharply that they separated. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus.
Paul chose Silas and left. The brothers sent him off, trusting him to the Lord's grace.
He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
Paul went to Derbe and then to Lystra. There he found a disciple named Timothy. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer, but his father was Greek.
The believers in Lystra and Iconium said good things about Timothy.
Paul wanted Timothy to travel with him. So he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who lived there, since everyone knew Timothy’s father was Greek.
As they traveled from city to city, they gave the people the rules that the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had decided they should follow.
So the churches grew strong in faith and increased in number every day.
They traveled through Phrygia and Galatia, because the Holy Spirit kept them from speaking the word in Asia.
When they came to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus would not let them.
So they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas.
During the night Paul had a vision. A man from Macedonia stood there and begged him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.”
After Paul saw the vision, we quickly decided to leave for Macedonia. We believed God had called us to tell them the good news.
We sailed from Troas straight to Samothrace, and the next day we went to Neapolis.
From there we went to Philippi, a Roman colony and the leading city of that part of Macedonia. We stayed there for several days.
On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river. We thought there was a place of prayer there. We sat down and talked with the women who had gathered.
One of them was a woman named Lydia. She sold purple cloth and was from the city of Thyatira. She worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart so she would pay attention to what Paul said.
After she and her household were baptized, she invited us, “If you think I am faithful to the Lord, come and stay at my house.” She kept urging us.
One day, as we were going to the place of prayer, a female slave met us. She had a spirit that could tell the future. She made a lot of money for her owners by telling fortunes.
She followed Paul and us and shouted, “These men are servants of the Most High God. They are telling you the way to be saved.”
She kept doing this for many days. Paul became annoyed. He turned and said to the spirit, “In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to come out of her.” And the spirit left her at that very hour.
When her owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to the authorities.
They brought them to the magistrates and said, “These men are Jews, and they are troubling our city.
They are teaching customs that we Romans are not allowed to accept or practice.”
The crowd joined in attacking them. The magistrates ordered that they be stripped and beaten with rods.
After giving them many blows, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to guard them carefully.
The jailer put them in the inner prison and locked their feet in stocks.
About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them.
Suddenly a great earthquake shook the prison so hard that its foundations moved. At once all the doors opened, and everyone’s chains came loose.
The jailer woke up and saw the prison doors open. He thought the prisoners had escaped. He drew his sword and was about to kill himself.
But Paul shouted in a loud voice, “Don’t do anything to hurt yourself! We are all here!”
The jailer called for lights, rushed in, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas.
He brought them out and asked, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
They answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved—you and your household.”
Then they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to everyone in his house.
At that hour of the night, he took them and washed their wounds. Then he and all his family were baptized right away.
He brought them into his house and set food before them. He was full of joy because he had come to believe in God, along with his whole household.
When day came, the magistrates sent the officers with the order, “Release those men.”
The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent orders to release you. So now come out and go in peace.”

Paul said to them, “They beat us in public without a trial, even though we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. Now are they going to throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and lead us out.”
The officers reported these words to the magistrates. When they heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they were afraid.
They came and apologized to them. Then they led them out and asked them to leave the city.
After leaving the prison, they went to Lydia’s house. They saw the brothers, encouraged them, and then left.
After traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, Paul and Silas came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
As was his custom, Paul went into the synagogue and, for three Sabbaths, reasoned with them from the Scriptures.
He explained and proved that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead. He also said, "This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ."
Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas. A large number of God-fearing Greeks and quite a few leading women did too.

But the Jews became jealous. They gathered some wicked men from the marketplace, formed a mob, and threw the city into an uproar. They rushed to Jason's house, looking for Paul and Silas so they could bring them out to the crowd.
When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, shouting, "These men have caused trouble all over the world, and now they have come here too.
Jason has welcomed them, and they all act against Caesar's decrees, saying there is another king, Jesus."
The crowd and the city officials were disturbed when they heard this.
They took money as security from Jason and the others, then let them go.
As soon as it was night, the believers sent Paul and Silas to Berea. When they arrived, they went to the Jewish synagogue.
The Bereans were more open-minded than the Thessalonians. They received the message with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures every day to see if these things were true.
Many of them believed, including quite a few Greek women of high standing and several men.
But when the Jews in Thessalonica learned that Paul was preaching God's word in Berea, they came there too and stirred up the crowds.
The believers immediately sent Paul to the coast, but Silas and Timothy stayed there.
The men who escorted Paul took him as far as Athens. They returned with instructions for Silas and Timothy to join him as soon as possible.
While Paul was waiting for them in Athens, he was deeply troubled to see that the city was full of idols.
So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the God-fearing people, and in the marketplace every day with anyone who happened to be there.

Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers began to argue with him. Some asked, "What is this babbler trying to say?" Others said, "He seems to be preaching about foreign gods," because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection.
They took him and brought him to the Areopagus, asking, "May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?
You are bringing some strange ideas to our ears, and we want to know what they mean."
All the Athenians and the foreigners living there spent their time doing nothing but talking about and listening to the latest ideas.
"Men of Athens, I see that you are very religious in every way.
"As I was walking around and looking at your objects of worship, I found an altar with this inscription: 'To an unknown god.' What you worship without knowing, I now proclaim to you.
"The God who made the world and everything in it is the Lord of heaven and earth. He does not live in temples built by human hands.
He is not served by human hands, as if He needed anything. Instead, He gives everyone life and breath and all things.
"From one man He made every nation of people to live on the whole earth. He set the times and places where they should live.
God did this so that people would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from any one of us.
"For in Him we live and move and have our being. As some of your own poets have said, 'We are His offspring.'
Since we are God's offspring, we should not think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image made by human skill and imagination.
"In the past God overlooked such ignorance, but now He commands all people everywhere to repent.
For He has set a day when He will judge the world with justice by the man He has chosen. He has given proof of this to everyone by raising Him from the dead."
When they heard about the resurrection of the dead, some mocked, but others said, "We will hear you again about this."
But some men joined him and believed. Among them were Dionysius, a member of the Areopagus, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.
After this, Paul left Athens and went to Corinth.

There he found a Jew named Aquila, who was from Pontus. Aquila had recently come from Italy with his wife, Priscilla. They had left Rome because Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave the city. Paul went to them.
Because Paul and Aquila were both tentmakers, Paul stayed with them and worked.
Every Sabbath, he talked in the synagogue. He tried to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul gave all his time to teaching the message. He told the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
But the Jews opposed him and insulted him. So Paul shook out his clothes and said to them, “You are responsible for your own fate. I am innocent. From now on, I will go to the Gentiles.”
Paul left the synagogue and went into the home of Titius Justus, a man who worshiped God. His house was next door to the synagogue.
Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, along with his whole family. Many people in Corinth also heard Paul, believed, and were baptized.
One night the Lord spoke to Paul in a vision. He said, “Do not be afraid. Keep speaking. Do not stay silent.
For I am with you, and no one will attack you to hurt you. I have many people in this city.”
So Paul stayed there for a year and six months. He taught God's word to the people.
While Gallio was governor of Achaia, the Jews joined together against Paul. They brought him to the judge's seat.
They said, “This man is talking people into worshiping God in a way that breaks our law.”
Paul was about to speak, but Gallio said to the Jews, “If this were a crime or a serious wrong, I would listen to you.
But this is about words, names, and your own law. You will have to settle it yourselves. I do not want to be the judge of these things.”
Then he sent them away from the judge's seat.
The crowd grabbed Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judge's seat. Gallio did not care about any of this.

Paul stayed in Corinth for many more days. Then he said goodbye to the brothers and sisters. He had his hair cut in Cenchreae because he had made a vow. Then he sailed for Syria, taking Priscilla and Aquila with him.
They came to Ephesus. Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there. He went into the synagogue and talked with the Jews.
They asked him to stay longer, but he would not.
He said goodbye and told them, “I will come back to you again, if God is willing.” Then he sailed away from Ephesus.
He landed at Caesarea. He went up and greeted the church. Then he went down to Antioch.
After spending some time there, he left. He traveled through the areas of Galatia and Phrygia. He strengthened all the believers.
A Jew named Apollos came to Ephesus. He was born in Alexandria. He was a skilled speaker and knew the Scriptures well.
He had been taught about the Lord's way. He was very eager in spirit. He spoke and taught the truth about Jesus. But he knew only John's baptism.
He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. Priscilla and Aquila heard him. They took him aside and explained God's way to him more clearly.

Apollos wanted to go to Achaia. The believers encouraged him. They wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. When he arrived, he helped the believers very much. They had believed because of God's grace.
In public, he strongly showed the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. He used the Scriptures to prove it.
While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul traveled through the upper regions and came to Ephesus. He found some disciples there.
He asked them, "Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?" They answered, "No, we haven't even heard that there is a Holy Spirit."
Paul asked, "Then what baptism did you have?" They said, "John's baptism."
Paul said, "John baptized with a baptism of repentance. He told the people to believe in the One coming after him. That One is Jesus."
When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.
Paul laid his hands on them, and the Holy Spirit came on them. They spoke in tongues and prophesied.
There were about twelve men in all.
Paul went into the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months. He argued and persuaded people about the kingdom of God.

But some became stubborn and refused to believe. In front of the crowd, they spoke against the Way. So Paul left them and took the disciples with him. He talked every day in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
This went on for two years, so all the Jews and Greeks who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord.
God did extraordinary miracles through Paul's hands.
People even carried handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched his skin to the sick. Their diseases left them, and evil spirits went out of them.
Some Jewish exorcists who traveled around tried to use the name of the Lord Jesus over people who had evil spirits. They said, "I command you by Jesus, whom Paul preaches."
Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest named Sceva were doing this.
But the evil spirit answered them, "I know Jesus, and I know about Paul. But who are you?"
Then the man with the evil spirit jumped on them and overpowered them both. He beat them so badly that they ran out of the house naked and wounded.
Everyone in Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks, heard about this. Fear came over all of them, and the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor.
Many believers came and confessed their sins. They also told about the things they had done.
Many who had practiced magic brought their books and burned them in front of everyone. They added up the value of the books and found it was fifty thousand silver coins.
In this way the word of the Lord spread and grew strong.
After these things were finished, Paul decided in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem. He planned to travel through Macedonia and Achaia. He said, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome."
He sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia. Paul stayed in Asia for a while.
About that time there was a serious disturbance about the Way.
A silversmith named Demetrius made silver shrines of Artemis. This gave the craftsmen a lot of work.
He called them together, along with the workers in related trades. He said, "Men, you know that we make our living from this business.
You can see and hear that this Paul has persuaded many people, not only in Ephesus but almost all of Asia. He says that gods made by human hands are not really gods.

This is dangerous for us. Our trade could be ruined. Also, the temple of the great goddess Artemis could be thought worthless, and her greatness could be destroyed. All of Asia and the whole world worship her."
When they heard this, they were furious. They shouted, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
The whole city was filled with confusion. The crowd rushed together into the theater. They dragged along Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's travel companions from Macedonia.
Paul wanted to go in among the crowd, but the disciples would not let him.
Even some of the Asiarchs, who were his friends, sent a message urging him not to risk going into the theater.
The assembly was in confusion. Some people shouted one thing, and others shouted another. Most of them did not know why they had come together.
The Jews pushed Alexander forward. He motioned with his hand and wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
But when they found out he was a Jew, they all shouted the same thing for about two hours: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
The city clerk quieted the crowd. He said, "Men of Ephesus, who doesn't know that the city of the Ephesians is the temple keeper of the great Artemis and of the image that fell from heaven?
Since these things can't be denied, you should be calm and not do anything rash.
You have brought these men here, but they are not temple robbers, and they have not spoken against our goddess.
So if Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against each other.
If you want anything more, it must be settled in the lawful assembly.
We are in danger of being charged with rioting today. There is no reason for this commotion, and we won't be able to explain it."
After he said this, he dismissed the assembly.
After the uproar ended, Paul sent for the disciples, encouraged them, said goodbye, and left for Macedonia.
He traveled through those regions and, after giving them much encouragement, came to Greece.
He stayed there three months. When the Jews plotted against him as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to go back through Macedonia instead.
He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica; Gaius from Derbe; and Timothy, Tychicus, and Trophimus from Asia.
These men went on ahead and waited for us in Troas.
After the Festival of Unleavened Bread, we sailed from Philippi. Five days later we reached them in Troas, where we stayed seven days.
On the first day of the week, we gathered to break bread. Paul planned to leave the next day, so he spoke to them and kept talking until midnight.
There were many lamps in the upstairs room where we were gathered.
A young man named Eutychus was sitting in the window. As Paul kept on speaking, Eutychus became very sleepy, fell into a deep sleep, and fell from the third floor. He was picked up dead.
Paul went down, threw himself on the young man, and took him in his arms. "Don't be alarmed," he said. "He is still alive."
Then Paul went back upstairs, broke bread, and ate. He talked with them for a long time, until daylight, and then left.
The people took the young man home alive and were greatly comforted.
We went on ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, where we planned to take Paul on board. He had arranged this because he wanted to go there on foot.
When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and went to Mitylene.
We sailed from there and arrived the next day off Chios. The day after that we reached Samos, and the next day we arrived at Miletus.
Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so he wouldn't have to spend time in Asia. He was in a hurry to get to Jerusalem, if possible, by the day of Pentecost.
From Miletus he sent to Ephesus for the elders of the church.
When they arrived, he said to them, "You know how I lived among you the whole time I was in Asia, from the first day I arrived.
I served the Lord with all humility, with tears, and with the trials that came to me because of the plots of the Jews.
I didn't hold back anything that would help you. I taught you in public and from house to house.
I told Jews and Greeks alike that they must turn to God in repentance and have faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. "
And now, compelled by the Spirit, I am going to Jerusalem. I don't know what will happen to me there.
Except that in every city the Holy Spirit warns me that prison and suffering are waiting for me.
But I don't count my life as valuable to myself, if only I can finish my race and complete the work the Lord Jesus gave me: to tell the good news of God's grace. "
Now I know that none of you, among whom I went about preaching the kingdom, will ever see me again.
So I tell you today that I am innocent of the blood of all people.
For I didn't shrink from telling you God's whole plan.
Watch yourselves and all the flock. The Holy Spirit has made you overseers to shepherd the church of God, which He bought with His own blood. "
I know that after I leave, fierce wolves will come in among you and won't spare the flock.
Even from your own group, men will rise up and twist the truth to pull the disciples away after themselves.
So stay alert. Remember that for three years I never stopped warning each of you night and day with tears.
Now I commit you to God and to the word of His grace, which can build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who have been made holy. "
I didn't want anyone's silver, gold, or clothing.
You know that these hands of mine worked to meet my own needs and the needs of those who were with me.
In everything I did, I showed you that by working hard you must help the weak. Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, who said, 'It is more blessed to give than to receive.'"
After saying this, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.
They all wept loudly. They fell on Paul's neck and kissed him.
They were especially sad because he had said they would never see his face again. Then they walked with him to the ship.
After we were separated from them, we sailed straight to Cos. The next day we sailed to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
There we found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, boarded it, and set sail.
After we saw Cyprus and left it on our left, we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, because the ship was unloading its cargo there.
In Tyre we found some disciples and stayed with them for seven days. Through the Spirit, they told Paul not to go to Jerusalem.
When our time there was over, we left. Everyone, including the women and children, walked with us out of the city. We knelt on the beach and prayed.
Then we said goodbye to each other, got on the ship, and they went back home.
We finished the trip from Tyre and arrived at Ptolemais. We greeted the brothers and stayed with them one day.
The next day we left and came to Caesarea. We stayed in the home of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven.
He had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.
While we stayed there for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.

He came to us, took Paul's belt, tied his own feet and hands, and said, "This is what the Holy Spirit says: 'The Jews in Jerusalem will tie up the man who owns this belt and hand him over to the Gentiles.'"
When we heard this, we and the local believers begged Paul not to go up to Jerusalem.
Paul answered, "Why are you crying and making me so sad? I am ready not only to be tied up but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus."
When he would not be persuaded, we stopped and said, "The Lord's will be done."
After those days, we got ready and went up to Jerusalem.
Some disciples from Caesarea went with us. They brought us to the home of Mnason, an old disciple from Cyprus, where we were to stay.
When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us warmly.
The next day Paul went with us to see James, and all the elders were there.
After greeting them, he told them one by one what God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
When they heard this, they praised God. Then they said to Paul, "Brother, you can see how many thousands of Jews have believed. They are all eager to keep the law.
They have heard that you teach all the Jews who live among the Gentiles to turn away from Moses. You tell them not to circumcise their children or follow our customs.
What should we do? They will certainly hear that you have come." "So do this: Four men among us have made a vow.

Take them with you, join them in the purification ceremony, and pay their expenses so they can shave their heads. Then everyone will know that the rumors about you are false and that you yourself keep the law.
As for the Gentile believers, we have already written to them. We decided they should stay away from food offered to idols, from blood, from meat of strangled animals, and from sexual sin."
The next day Paul took the men, joined them in the purification ceremony, and went into the temple. He announced the end of the days of purification, when an offering would be made for each of them.
When the seven days were almost over, some Jews from Asia saw Paul in the temple. They stirred up the whole crowd and grabbed him.
They shouted, "Men of Israel, help! This man teaches everyone everywhere against our people, the law, and this place. He has even brought Greeks into the temple and made this holy place unclean."
They had seen Trophimus, who was from Ephesus, with him in the city, so they thought Paul had brought him into the temple.
The whole city was stirred up. The people ran together, seized Paul, dragged him out of the temple, and the doors were shut.
While they were trying to kill him, word reached the commander of the Roman soldiers that all Jerusalem was in an uproar.
He quickly took soldiers and officers and ran down to the crowd. When they saw the commander and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
The commander came close, arrested him, and ordered him to be bound with two chains. Then he asked who he was and what he had done.
Some in the crowd shouted one thing, and others shouted something else. Because he could not learn the truth in all the noise, he ordered Paul to be taken to the barracks.
When Paul reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because of the violence of the crowd.
The crowd followed and shouted, "Get rid of him!"
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the commander, "May I say something to you?" The commander asked, "Do you know Greek?
Aren't you the Egyptian who started a revolt a while ago and led four thousand armed rebels into the desert?"
Paul said, "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia. I am a citizen of an important city. Please let me speak to the people."
The commander gave permission. Paul stood on the steps, motioned to the crowd with his hand, and when there was a great silence, he spoke to them in Hebrew.
“Brothers and fathers, listen to my defense before you now.”
When they heard him speaking in Hebrew, they became even quieter. Then he said:
“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but raised in this city. I studied under Gamaliel and was taught to follow our fathers’ law exactly. I was just as eager to serve God as all of you are today.
I persecuted this Way even to death. I arrested men and women and put them in prison.

The high priest and the whole council can testify to this. I received letters from them to our brothers in Damascus. I went there to bring back those believers as prisoners to Jerusalem to be punished.
“About noon, as I was on my way and getting close to Damascus, a bright light from heaven suddenly flashed around me. I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me,”
“Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
“Who are You, Lord?” I asked. “I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting,” He replied.
“My companions saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the One speaking to me.
“What should I do, Lord?” I asked. “Get up and go into Damascus. There you will be told everything you are appointed to do.”
“Because I could not see from the brightness of that light, my companions led me by the hand into Damascus.
A man named Ananias lived there. He was devout according to the law and respected by all the Jews there. He came and stood beside me and said,”
“Brother Saul, receive your sight.” “At that very moment I could see him.
Then he said,” “The God of our fathers has chosen you to know His will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear His voice.
You will be His witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
And now, why are you waiting? Get up and be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling on His name.”
“When I returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance.
I saw the Lord saying to me,” “Hurry and leave Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about Me.”
“Lord, they know that in every synagogue I imprisoned and beat those who believe in You.
And when the blood of Your witness Stephen was being shed, I stood there approving and guarding the clothes of those who were killing him.”
“Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.”
They listened to him until he said this. Then they shouted, “Take him away from the earth! He doesn't deserve to live!”
As they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and tossing dust into the air,
the commander ordered Paul to be brought into the barracks. He said Paul should be examined by flogging so he could find out why the people were shouting against him like this.
As they tied him up with straps, Paul said to the centurion standing there, “Is it legal for you to flog a Roman citizen who hasn't been condemned?”
When the centurion heard this, he went to the commander and reported it. “What are you about to do?” he asked. “This man is a Roman citizen.”
The commander came and asked Paul, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” Paul said.
The commander replied, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum of money.” “But I was born a citizen,” Paul said.
At once those who were about to examine him stepped back. The commander was afraid too, because he had learned that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had put him in chains.

The next day, wanting to know exactly what the Jews were accusing him of, the commander released Paul and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to meet. Then he brought Paul down and placed him before them.
Paul looked straight at the Sanhedrin and said, “Brothers, I have lived before God with a clear conscience in every way up to this day.”
The high priest Ananias ordered those standing near him to strike Paul on the mouth.
Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you hypocrite! You sit to judge me by the law, yet you order me to be beaten against the law?”
Those standing by said, “Do you dare insult God’s high priest?”
Paul replied, “Brothers, I did not know that he was high priest. For it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”

Paul knew that one group was Sadducees and the other Pharisees, so he cried out in the Sanhedrin, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. I am on trial because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead.”
When he said this, a dispute broke out between the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the crowd was split in two.
The Sadducees say there is no resurrection, and no angel or spirit, but the Pharisees believe in both.
A loud uproar started. Some of the teachers of the law who were Pharisees stood up and argued, saying, “We find nothing wrong with this man. What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?”
The argument grew so fierce that the commander feared Paul would be torn to pieces by them. He ordered the soldiers to go down, take Paul away from them by force, and bring him into the barracks.
The next night the Lord stood by Paul and said, “Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so you must also testify in Rome.”
When daylight came, the Jews formed a plot and bound themselves under a curse, saying they would not eat or drink until they had killed Paul.
More than forty men took part in this plan.
They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have bound ourselves under a solemn curse to taste nothing until we have killed Paul.
Now then, you and the Sanhedrin must tell the commander to bring Paul down to you, as if you were going to look into his case more carefully. We are ready to kill him before he gets close.”
But when Paul’s sister’s son heard about the ambush, he went to the barracks and told Paul.
Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the commander, because he has something to report to him.”
So the centurion took him to the commander and said, “Paul, the prisoner, called for me and asked me to bring this young man to you, because he has something to say to you.”
The commander took the young man by the hand, stepped aside with him, and asked, “What is it you have to report to me?”
He said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the Sanhedrin tomorrow, as if they were going to question him more closely.

Do not give in to them, because more than forty of their men are waiting to ambush him. They have bound themselves under a curse not to eat or drink until they have killed him, and now they are ready, waiting for your permission.”
The commander sent the young man away and ordered him, “Do not tell anyone that you have reported these things to me.”
Then he called two centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen to travel to Caesarea at the third hour of the night.
Provide horses for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Governor Felix.”
He wrote a letter that said:
“Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent Governor Felix: Greetings.
This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them, but I came with the soldiers and rescued him after learning that he is a Roman citizen.
Wanting to know the charge they had against him, I brought him down to their Sanhedrin.
I found that he was being accused over questions about their law, but there was no charge against him that deserved death or chains.
When I was told that a plot was being made against the man, I sent him to you at once. I also ordered his accusers to state their case against him before you.”
So the soldiers followed their orders and took Paul by night to Antipatris.
The next day they returned to the barracks, leaving the horsemen to go on with him.
When they reached Caesarea, they delivered the letter to the governor and brought Paul before him.
After reading it, he asked what province Paul was from. Learning that he was from Cilicia,
he said, “I will hear your case when your accusers arrive.” Then he ordered that Paul be kept under guard in Herod’s Praetorium.
